entries.body:
## 慈 (Cí) — Tenderness

*Say "tsuh," rising. Seven lines across three chapters, and it is the first of the book's three treasures.*

**Locked: 慈 → "tenderness."** *(Not "compassion," not "mercy," not "maternal love," not "filial piety." 孝 (xiào) → "devotion.")*

慈 is the **first of the three treasures** — 一曰慈 — and the book stakes something large on it: 慈故能勇, *"tenderness, and so you can be brave."* A word that cannot produce courage is the wrong word for it.

**Compassion**, the usual English, cannot. Compassion is *suffering-with*: it sits down beside. It is also a Buddhist word in English by now, carrying karuṇā into a text written before Buddhism reached China. Ch 67 needs something that gets up and fights — 夫慈，以戰則勝，以守則固, *"with 慈, fight and you win; defend and you hold firm."*

### The graph, and it is a pair with 孝

**慈 is 心 (*xīn* — heart) under 兹 (*zī*)**, which in its older form doubles 幺 (*yāo* — a skein of silk) and carries the sense *to grow, to multiply*. The heart that increases toward something. *Shuowen*: 慈，愛也 — *"慈 is 愛 (ài — love)."*

It never appears alone in this book outside ch 67. Twice it appears welded to **孝** (*xiào*), and the two graphs are a matched pair pointing opposite ways:

> 孝，善事父母者。从老省，从子，子承老也
> *Shuowen — "孝 is one who serves their father and mother well. From an abbreviated 老 (lǎo — old) and from 子 (zǐ — child): **the child bears up the old**."*

**孝 is a child holding up an elder. 慈 is a heart growing toward a child.** One goes up the generations, one comes down. 孝慈 is not two virtues in a list; it is a circuit, and 河上公 says so — 乃有孝慈**相牧養**也, *"then there is 孝慈, tending each other."*

That reciprocity is what *filial piety and love* destroys. **Devotion and tenderness** keeps it: two words, two directions, one relation.

### Why tenderness, and why it has to be able to fight

Ch 67 is the test, because it uses 慈 five times and asks it to do incompatible work — to be the softest of the three treasures and the one that wins wars.

> 慈故能勇
> *"tenderness, and so you can be brave"*

> 今捨慈且勇 … 死矣
> *"now, to abandon tenderness and grab at courage … that is death"*

> 天將救之，以慈衛之
> *"when nature would rescue someone, it guards them with tenderness"*

The claim is not that gentleness is secretly strong. It is that **courage without something to be tender toward is not courage, it is appetite** — which is precisely the distinction the third treasure draws with 敢 (*gǎn* — the forward press to take). *Tenderness* can be fierce in English; a parent's is the ordinary example, and that is the register the graph is already in.

**Compassion cannot be fierce**, and *mercy* is worse: mercy is what the strong extend to the defeated, which reverses the chapter.

### Where the book puts it

慈 belongs to the same argument as 仁 (*rén* — humaneness) and sits on the other side of it. 仁 is the **named** virtue, the one you can be praised for, and the book treats its visibility as a symptom: 大道廢，有仁義. 慈 is never treated that way. It is a treasure, and at ch 19 it is what the people **return to** once the named virtues are cut off:

> 絕仁棄義，民復孝慈
> *"sever humaneness, abandon duty, and the people return to devotion and tenderness"*

**The unnamed thing survives the removal of the named one.** That is the chapter's whole mechanism, and it only reads if 仁 and 慈 take clearly different English.

### What is set aside

**compassion.** Suffering-with, and Buddhist in English. 慈 is 愛 — the heart growing toward — and it has to produce 勇 (*yǒng* — courage) at ch 67.

**mercy.** Runs downhill from the strong to the beaten.

**maternal love.** The direction is right and the narrowing is not: 慈 is the parent's side of a circuit, not a gendered sentiment, and the book's feminine is a principle rather than a role.

**filial piety** for 孝. A Victorian sinology compound that names an institution and a duty; the graph shows a child taking an elder's weight. And in both places 孝 occurs it is bonded to 慈, so it never has to carry the direction alone.

### Left open

**Whether tenderness can survive being the first treasure.** English treats tenderness as a mood — something felt, and usually briefly. 慈 at ch 67 is closer to a **stance you fight from**, and the entry's own argument leans on a parent's ferocity to make that plausible. It is plausible. It is not obvious, and a reader who has not been handed the graph may hear only softness.

The alternative would be a harder word that then fails at ch 18 and ch 19, where 慈 is what a household quietly has. **No single English does both jobs comfortably.** Tenderness does the ch 67 job at a cost, and the cost is paid at 18 and 19 rather than the other way round — which is the right way to pay it, because ch 67 is where the book is making a claim and ch 18 is where it is describing a symptom.

## 雌 (Cí) — The Hen

*Say "tsuh," rising. Two appearances in two chapters, and both are addressed to you. The book's word for the female as a place a person can stand.*

**Locked: 雌 (*cí*) → "the hen," and its partner 雄 (*xióng*) → "the rooster."** *(Not "the female," which is 牝 (pìn)'s English. Not "the feminine" or "yielding energy," which turn a bird into an abstraction. Not "the receptive" or "the passive," which add a quality no line names. Not "the Hen," since a capital makes her a doctrine.)* *(The English was settled in the verse before this entry, at chapters 10 and 28. The entry argues for it and holds it. That 雌 and 牝 (pìn — the female) get two entries, not one, is Shalom's call, 2026-10-26.)*

### The graph: the mother among birds

> 雌，鳥母也。从隹此聲。
> *"雌: the mother among birds. From 隹 (zhuī — a short-tailed bird), with 此 (cǐ) as its sound."* — the *Shuowen Jiezi* (the Han dictionary)

**The class is 隹 (*zhuī*), the short-tailed bird, and 此 (*cǐ* — this) gives only the sound.** The Shuowen defines its partner in matching words: 雄，鳥父也 — *"雄: the father among birds."* It defines the other pair the same way among animals that walk: 牝 (*pìn*) is 畜母 (*chù mǔ* — "the mother among livestock") and 牡 (*mǔ*) is 畜父 (*chù fù* — "the father among livestock"). Two pairs of words for mother and father, one for beasts and one for birds, and the Tao Te Ching uses both (`glossary/pin-牝.md`).

**So the hen's English has to be a bird's.** The book's English gives 牝 and 牡 *the female* and *the male* at chapters 6, 55 and 61. 雌 and 雄 need words of their own, and the graph says which. English ornithology has the exact pair, *cock* and *hen*, for the male and female of any bird (a *cock pheasant*, a *hen harrier*). *Cock* is unusable in modern English, so 雄 is *the rooster*.

### Two lines, and both are asked of you

> *Know the rooster, hold to the hen,*
> *serve as the world's ravine.*
>
> 知其雄，守其雌，
> 為天下谿。
>
> — chapter 28

> *When the gate of the sky opens and closes, can you be the hen?*
>
> 天門開闔，能為雌乎？
>
> — chapter 10

**Neither line describes the hen.** The first tells you to hold to her, and the second asks whether you can be her. 守 (*shǒu* — to hold to) is a post you are answerable for (`glossary/shou-守.md`), and 為 (*wéi* — to be, to serve as) is a part you play.

**The female is the opposite.** 牝 (*pìn*) stands in five lines, and in every one she is spoken about: she has a gate, she mates, she lies beneath. No line asks the reader to be her. So the book keeps one word for the female as a body and another for the female as a stance, and that is why the two characters have separate entries. The pattern is a reason to look, not a proof (`process/principles/distribution-locates.md`). Looking, it holds in every line.

### Chapter 28: know the one, hold to the other

**The hen is the first of three pairs, and each pair is built the same way.** 知其雄，守其雌 (*"know the rooster, hold to the hen"*), 知其白，守其黑 (*zhī qí bái, shǒu qí hēi* — "know the white, hold to the black"), 知其白，守其辱 (*zhī qí bái, shǒu qí rǔ* — "know the white, hold to the soiled"). You know one side and hold to the other. The rooster is not refused. It is known, and the hen is chosen with that knowledge.

**Both commentators read the pair as a position.** Wang Bi: 雄先之屬，雌後之屬也。知為天下之先也，必後也 — *"the rooster belongs to the class of going first, the hen to the class of coming after. To know how to be first in the world, one must be behind."* Heshang Gong: 雄以喻尊，雌以喻卑 — *"the rooster figures the honored, the hen the lowly,"* and 去之強梁，就雌之柔和，如是則天下歸之，如水流入深谿也 — *"set aside the swagger and come to the hen's soft harmony; then the world returns to you, as water flows into a deep ravine."*

**The line goes straight on to the ravine.** Holding to the hen, you serve as the world's 谿 (*xī* — ravine), the low place water runs to (`glossary/gu-谷.md`). The hen is where the chapter's lowness begins, and the ravine is what it makes of you.

### Chapter 10: the gate opens, and the hen answers

**Wang Bi reads the hen as the one who answers.** 雌應而不倡，因而不為 — *"the hen responds and does not lead the call; she goes along and does not act."* 倡 (*chàng*) is to lead the singing, the first voice that others follow. The rooster crows, and the hen answers. Of the gate of the sky he says 天門謂天下之所由從也，開闔，治亂之際也 — *"the gate of the sky is where the world passes through; its opening and closing are the turns between order and disorder."* At those turns, be the hen, 則物自賓而處自安矣 — *"and things come as guests of themselves and settle in their places."*

**Heshang Gong reads the gate as the breath.** 治身天門謂鼻孔，開謂喘息，闔謂呼吸也 — *"in caring for the body, the gate of the sky is the nostrils; opening is breathing out, closing is breathing in."* And on the hen: 治身當如雌牝安靜柔弱，治國應變和而不唱 — *"in caring for the body, be like the hen and the female: calm, still, soft and yielding; in governing the state, respond to change in harmony and do not lead the call."* He and Wang Bi agree on the hen. She answers, and she does not lead.

**The line's own graph is contested.** Our base text reads 能為雌乎 (*néng wéi cí hū* — "can you be the hen?"). The Siku edition of Wang Bi prints 能無雌乎 (*néng wú cí hū* — "can you be without the hen?") in its lemma, and its editors note that the commentary's sense reads 為 (*wéi* — to be). Heshang Gong's text also reads 無 (*wú* — without). But his own comment, quoted above, tells the reader to be like the hen, which is what 為 asks. The verse follows 為. `notes/manuscript.md`, `sources/variants.yaml`.

### What the commentators did with her

**Both merge her with the female.** Wang Bi, glossing chapter 61, writes 牝，雌也 — *"the female is the hen,"* and retells that chapter's 牝 and 牡 as hen and rooster. Heshang Gong, above, joins them in one phrase: 雌牝 (*cí pìn* — "the hen and the female"). The text keeps them apart, and so do the two entries. What the commentators hear in both is right: stillness, softness, answering rather than leading. But the hen is the stance and the female is the body, and the book never confuses them.

### 雄 (xióng — the rooster)

**The rooster stands once, and only to be known.** 知其雄 (*zhī qí xióng* — "know the rooster," 28). He has no other line. *Rooster* is narrower than 雄, which is the male of any bird; the pairing with *the hen* carries the sense. 雞 (*jī* — the fowl) at chapter 80 reads *chickens*, which keeps *rooster* free for 雄 (`chapters/080.md`).

### What is set aside

**"the female."** It is 牝 (*pìn*)'s English, in chapters 6, 55 and 61. A rendering already spoken for by another character is not available (`process/principles/already-spoken-for.md`). Giving the hen *the female* would erase the book's line between the body and the stance.

**"the feminine," "yielding energy."** They turn a bird into a quality. A hen can be held to, and a person can try to be one. *The feminine* is a category, and the pointing test fails. *Energy* is the mechanistic overlay this edition watches for.

**"the receptive," "the passive."** No line says she receives, and Wang Bi's hen is not passive: she answers. 應 (*yìng* — to respond) is an act. *Passive* hands her the verdict the rooster's admirers would give her, and the line passes none (`process/principles/no-verdict-the-chinese-lacks.md`).

**"the Hen."** A capital makes her a principle. Only the Tao keeps one.

### Working register

| Where 雌 (*cí*) stands | English | Chapters |
|---|---|---|
| the object of 守 (*shǒu* — hold to) | *hold to the hen* | 28 (守其雌 *shǒu qí cí*) |
| the complement of 為 (*wéi* — to be) | *can you be the hen?* | 10 (能為雌乎 *néng wéi cí hū*) |

**Her pronoun is *she*.** 雌 says she is the hen, and the line is about her. Standing rule 1 forbids *he* for the sage: the Chinese never says whether the sage is a woman or a man, and *he* would make the male the default.

### What no rule can enforce

***Soft* and *yielding* cannot be ruled out here, though the hen is not their word.** Chapter 10 holds 柔 (*róu* — soft), which its verse renders *"Gathering the breath to softness,"* so forbidding *soft* for the hen would flag a correct line. *Yielding* is 弱 (*ruò*)'s English across the book. Both commentators call the hen soft, and that is their reading, not her name.

***Yin* is ruled out and cannot go on the list.** The checker matches strings, not words, and *yin* sits inside words the verse prints. 陰 (*yīn*) stands once in the book, in chapter 42, and never names the hen.

**The lock holds in this book only.** Forbidding *female* for the hen depends on this book's split, which gives *female* to 牝 (*pìn*). The I Ching vendors these locks as its own and draws its own lines between its animals, so this entry carries `binds: [taoteching]`, as `glossary/pin-牝.md` does.

### Left open

**What *rooster* costs.** 雄 is the male of any bird, and *rooster* is the farmyard's. *Hen* is wide in English, the female of any bird, and *rooster* is not. The pair stands, and the asymmetry is the price of losing *cock*.

**Whether the hen is a bird or a place in a line.** Both commentators read her as a position: after, low, answering. The text names a bird. The English keeps the bird, so a reader can see what the commentators saw in her without being told it.

**What chapter 10 asks, if the other reading is right.** The verse follows 為 (*wéi* — to be) on the strength of Wang Bi's own commentary. If 無 (*wú* — without) was the reading, chapter 10 asks whether you can do without the hen when the gate opens, which is a different question, and a stranger one. Neither commentator answers it.
entries.shuowen: The mother among birds. From 隹 (zhuī — a short-tailed bird), with 此 (cǐ) as its sound.

entries.body:
## 大 (Dà) — Great

*Say "dah," falling hard. Fifty-one appearances across twenty-four chapters, which makes it one of the most common characters in the book and the one the Tao is finally named with.*

**Locked: 大 → "great."** *(Lowercase. Licensed flexions: **large** where the scale is physical or political, **greater** in comparatives, **master** of a craftsman.)*

### The graph: a person standing with their arms out

說文解字 (*Shuōwén Jiězì*, c. 100 CE) defines it in eleven characters, and the last four are the whole entry:

> 天大，地大，人亦大。故**大象人形**。
> *"Sky is big, earth is big, humans are also big. Therefore **大 depicts a human form**."*

The graph is a figure seen head-on — arms spread, legs apart — and the oracle-bone form is the same figure with thicker strokes. Not a mountain, not an ocean, not a firmament. **A person taking up as much room as a person can take up.** It is bigness measured on a body, which is why it can mean a large state, a severe illness, and a senior craftsman without straining.

**And the dictionary defines the character by quoting this book.** 天大，地大，人亦大 is Chapter 25's own line. That it is cited with 人 (*rén* — human) rather than 王 (*wáng* — king), six centuries before our earliest surviving witness for 人, bears on a fork this edition has left open — `notes/manuscript.md` · Ch 25, and `WORKLIST.md` T4-8.

### 大 is a radical, and its family is made by marking the same body

凡大之屬皆从大 — *"all of the 大 class follow 大."* 說文 groups a set of characters that are **one standing figure with one mark added**, and where the mark goes is the whole meaning:

| | the mark | 說文 | what it becomes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **天** (*tiān*) | a line **above the head** | 顛也。至高無上。**从一大** | *the crown of the head* → **sky** |
| **立** (*lì*) | a line **beneath the feet** | 住也。**从大立一之上** | *standing on the ground* → **to stand** |
| **夫** (*fū*) | a line **through the topknot** | 丈夫也。从大，**一以象簪也** | *a hairpin* → a capped adult man |
| **亦** (*yì*) | marks at **both sides** | **人之臂亦也**。象兩亦之形 | *the armpits* → borrowed for **also** |

**Above the head is the sky; below the feet is standing; through the hair is adulthood; at the sides are the armpits.** The book's whole vocabulary of scale and position is built by putting marks on a person.

**What this is not.** 大 is **not** 人 (*rén*) with a stroke added, though it looks like it. 說文 makes both **independent pictographs of the same subject**: 人 is 象**臂脛**之形, *"the form of arms and shins,"* seen in profile; 大 is 象**人形**, the human form seen head-on with the arms out. Siblings, not parent and child. **天 from 大 is a real derivation and 說文 states it; 大 from 人 is a resemblance.**

**And it bears directly on two locks.** 天 is locked to **sky** (`tian-天.md`) precisely because 顛 is a body part — *"a word for the crown of your head is not a word for an afterlife."* The graph family says the same thing about 大: **scale in this book is measured outward from a body, not downward from a heaven.** That is the strongest single argument for keeping 大 ordinary, and it is why *vast* — a word with no body in it — was refused.

**The honest limit.** 說文 is c. 100 CE, centuries after the oracle-bone forms, and it rationalises elsewhere in ways this glossary flags — 士's 一 + 十 and the Han cosmology on 王. But 天 as 大 with a head-mark, 亦 as armpits and 夫 as a hairpin are standard paleography rather than 說文's speculation. Whether Laozi or his readers saw any of it is unknowable; that the characters are built this way is not.

### Four jobs, one word

| what 大 is doing | where | English |
|---|---|---|
| **physical or political size** | 大國 (*dà guó* — a large state), 60, 61 ×5 · 大軍 (*dà jūn* — a large army), 30 | large |
| **the superlative frame 大▢若▢** | 大方 (square), 大器 (vessel), 大音 (sound), 大象 (image), 41 · 大成, 大盈, 大直, 大巧, 大辯, 45 | great |
| **severity** | 大患 (*dà huàn* — great trouble), 13 ×3 · 大偽 (hypocrisy), 18 · 大迷 (confusion), 27 · 禍莫**大**於… (no disaster greater than), 46 ×2, 69 | great / greater |
| **seniority and mastery** | 大匠 (*dà jiàng* — the master carpenter), 74 ×2 · 大丈夫 (*dà zhàng fū* — the great person), 38 | master / great |

English *great* reaches all four — great size, the great square, great trouble, a great carpenter — because it is, like 大, the general-purpose word rather than a specialist one. That coverage is the whole case for it, and it is why the flexions above are narrow: they mark the two places where ordinary English will not say *great* at all (a *large* state; *no greater* disaster).

### The counter-term is 小, and Chapter 34 puts both on the Tao

小 (*xiǎo* — small) shadows 大 through the book: 大小多少 (*dà xiǎo duō shǎo* — "great or small, many or few," 63), 治大國若烹小鮮 ("governing a large state is like cooking a small fish," 60), the large and small states of 61, and 小國寡民 ("a small state, few people," 80).

**Chapter 34 gives the Tao both names in three lines** — 常無欲，可名於**小** (*"ever desireless, it can be named small"*) and 萬物歸焉而不為主，可名為**大** (*"the countless things return to it, and without acting as their master, it can be called great"*). Both fit. Neither holds. That is the same joke Chapter 25 tells at length, and it is why 大 is a *name* in this book rather than a description.

### Chapter 25 — the word is chosen because it fails

強為之名曰大 (*qiǎng wèi zhī míng yuē dà* — "forcing a name on it, I call it great") is the only place the book names the Tao outright, and 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*, d. 249 CE) explains that the naming is a defeat:

> 吾所以**字**之曰道者，取其可言之稱**最大**也。責其字定之所由，則**繫於大**。**大有繫則必有分，有分則失其極矣。**
> *"The reason I 字 it 'Tao' is that I take the greatest of speakable designations. But press for what fixes that designation and it ties to 大 — and 大, once tied, must have divisions; having divisions, it loses its utmost."*

**Naming it 大 costs it its utmost.** The chapter has just spent three lines saying no name can hold a thing without form, and then reaches for the most ordinary word available: *big*. The inadequacy is the argument.

### What is set aside

**"Vast."** The strongest rival, and the one that reaches furthest into the chapter where 大 matters most — it has more force in English than *great*, which has been worn smooth by use, and it suits the Tao-naming and the cosmic members of the 41 and 45 frames. **It fails on about two-thirds of the fifty-one lines, and it fails at the argument.**

- *No disaster **vaster** than discontent* is unusable, and the comparative 禍莫大於 appears three times (46 ×2, 69).
- *Vast trouble*, *vast hypocrisy*, *vast confusion* — 大 in those lines means **severe**, not spatially immense (13, 18, 27).
- *The vast carpenter* (74), *the vast person* (38) — 大 there is **seniority**.
- *Vast skill*, *vast argument* — 大巧若拙 and 大辯若訥 need a superlative, not a size (45).
- 下士聞道，**大**笑之 — laughing **aloud** (41) is not a magnitude at all.

**And the deeper objection: 大 is not an elevated word in Chinese.** It is a person with their arms out. Rendering it with an English word that carries *more* charge than the original would make Chapter 25's forced name sound like it succeeded — which reverses the passage. A worn word is the faithful one here, and the wear is doing work. *Vast* is also, separately, spoken for: it currently renders 廣 (*guǎng* — broad) at ch 41 and 恢 (*huī* — vast) at ch 73, both of which sit alongside 大 or would want the word back.

**"The Great," capitalized.** A capital turns a forced, admittedly failing name into a title, which is the one thing the passage denies it. Standing rule 3.

**"Mighty," "grand," "supreme," "cosmic."** Each imports a register 大 does not have — power, ceremony, rank, or the firmament — where the character offers only a body's worth of room.

### Left open

**Whether *large* at 60–61 is a flexion or a fault.** Six lines of 大國 read *the large state*, and the political sense genuinely resists *great state*, which in English means *admirable*. But the same six lines are the ones where 大 and 小 are a matched pair, and the pair reads better when both sit in one register.

**Whether 大匠 is 大 at all.** *"Master carpenter"* treats 大 as seniority, but 大匠 was also a Han office — Master of Works — and if the phrase is a fixed title then the character is not flexing, it is simply part of a name. The commentaries do not settle it.

**Whether the 大▢若▢ frame wants *the greatest*.** 大方無隅 reads *"the great square has no corners"*; 王弼 glosses the series as absolutes, not comparatives. *The greatest square* would say what he says, and would lose the frame's flatness. The frame is shared across chapters 41 and 45 and has to be decided as one thing, not line by line.
entries.render: great — large where the scale is physical or political, greater in comparatives, master of a craftsman

entries.body:
## 道 (Dào) — The Tao

*Say "dow," rhyming with "now," falling, like a word set down. Seventy-five appearances across thirty-seven chapters: the book's first word, and half of its name.*

**Locked: 道 → "the Tao"** (the name, left untranslated) **/ "way"** (a common noun with an owner: *the way of nature*, *the way of people*; and the verb in the book's first line, *made a way*). *(Never "the Way," never "the Path.")*

道 is a road. Before it was anything else it was the ordinary word for a way through the country that people walk, and the word never lost that meaning: Laozi himself uses it for a road you could stand on (53). From the road grew the walking of it, the leading of others along it, the telling of it, and the right way to do a thing. Laozi takes this common word and points it at what everything goes by, then tells us in his first line that no way you could lay out is that.

### The graph: a head on the road

**Our vendored 說文解字 (*Shuōwén Jiězì*, c. 100 CE): 所行道也。从辵从𩠐。一達謂之道** — *"the road that is walked. From 辵 (chuò) and 𩠐 (shǒu). A road that runs straight through is called 道."*

That last clause is a surveyor's definition. The 爾雅 (*Ěryǎ*), the oldest Chinese word-list, grades roads by how many ways they branch: 一達謂之道路, *"one that goes straight through is called a 道 road,"* while a road that forks has another name, and a crossroads another. So 道 is not any road. It is the road that does not branch.

**辵 (*chuò*) — walking along a road.** Usually written 辶 at the left and bottom of a character. It is two pictures stacked:

- **彳 (*chì*)** — the left half of **行 (*xíng*)**, whose oldest graph is **a crossroads**, two streets meeting, seen from above. 說文 on 行: 人之步趨也。从彳从亍 — *"a person's stepping and hurrying."* 彳 alone is a step, a stretch of street.
- **止 (*zhǐ*)** — **a foot**, drawn with its toes. In early graphs a foot means going.

So 辵 is a foot on a street. 說文 glosses it 乍行乍止, *"now going, now stopping"*: the stop-and-start of someone actually walking. *(辵's own 說文 entry comes from outside this repository's selection, which holds only the characters the Laozi uses.)*

**𩠐 (*shǒu*) — a head, drawn with its hair.** This is the old form of **首 (*shǒu* — head)**. 說文 says of it: 古文𦣻也。巛象髮 — *"the ancient form of the head-graph; the 巛 on top is the hair."* Below the hair is a face, and in the oldest forms the eye is the clearest thing in it.

**Two jobs at once.** Xu Shen counts the head as part of the meaning. Modern reconstruction hears it as the sound as well: Old Chinese 道 is roughly *\*l'uːʔ* and 首 roughly *\*hljuʔ*, close enough that 首 almost certainly helped to spell 道. Both can be true. Many characters chose a sound-part that also suited the sense.

**What the head is doing there.** Three readings, from safest to boldest:

1. **The head goes first.** 首 means not only *head* but *first, foremost, the leading end*. A head on the road is the part of a walker that leads, the face set toward where you are going. The verb that grows from 道 says exactly this: **導 (*dǎo*)**, 道 with 寸 (*cùn* — a hand) added, is *to lead, to guide*. 說文: 導，導引也, *"to lead along."*
2. **The head stands for the person**, a part for the whole, as English counts "heads." On this reading 道 is simply someone on a road.
3. **A carried head.** Shirakawa Shizuka read the graph as a head carried to clear and purify a road into foreign country. It is a striking proposal and a disputed one. We record it and do not build on it.

**The bronzes draw the whole scene.** In the Zhou bronze inscriptions 道 is usually written as 行, the crossroads, with the head standing inside it, often with a foot beneath. Some forms add a hand, the shape that later became 導, *to lead*. The seal script squeezed the crossroads down to 辵, and that is the form we print.

**And the oldest copy of this book draws a person.** In the Guodian bamboo slips (c. 300 BCE), most of the copyists write 道 as **人 (*rén* — a person) standing inside 行 (a crossroads)**. Only one hand writes the head-and-walking form we know. The earliest surviving Laozi writes its central word as a person standing in the road.

### What the word already meant

By Laozi's century 道 was a common word with four live senses, and a reader of the book hears all of them:

- **A road.** 大道甚夷，而人好徑 (53) — *"the great Tao is very level, yet people love to take shortcuts."* 徑 (*jìng*) is a footpath, a cut across the fields. Laozi is talking about roads.
- **To lead.** The sense that became 導.
- **To tell.** The 詩經 (*Shījīng* — the Book of Songs): 中冓之言，不可道也 — *"the words of the inner chamber cannot be told."* Chinese still uses 道 for *to say*.
- **The right way to do things.** By Confucius's time the word was already moral, and already reached toward the cosmic: 朝聞道，夕死可矣 — *"hear the way in the morning, and you may die content in the evening"* (論語 4.8). His students said he rarely spoke of 天道, *the way of the sky* (論語 5.13).

So 道 was not a plain word that Laozi made philosophical. It was a plain word that everyone was already using for *the right way*: the way of the former kings, the way of the gentleman. Laozi's move is to take it **under** all of those. His 道 is not a way to behave. It is what every way, and every thing, goes by.

### What the book does with it

Watch what he says of it, and the verbs give it away:

- **It comes before.** 有物混成，先天地生 (25) — *"something mixed and complete, born before sky and earth."* 象帝之先 (4) — *"it seems older than any god,"* where 帝 (*dì*) is the high ancestor-deity.
- **Its name is forced.** 吾不知其名，強字之曰道 (25) — *"I do not know its name. Forcing a label on it, I call it the Tao."* 字 (*zì*) is a courtesy name, the name a person is called by rather than the name they are given.
- **It moves and is used.** 反者道之動；弱者道之用 (40) — *"returning is the Tao's movement; yielding is the Tao's use."* Movement and use, not substance.
- **It gives birth.** 道生一 (42), 道生之 (51) — *"the Tao births the one,"* *"the Tao gives birth to the countless things."*
- **It follows only what it is.** 道法自然 (25) — *"the Tao models itself on being what it is."* Nothing stands above it.
- **It shelters.** 道者萬物之奧 (62) — *"the Tao is the sanctuary of the countless things."* 奧 (*ào*) is the innermost corner of a house.

**The oldest readers name it from motion.** 韓非 (*Hán Fēi*), on ch 1: 聖人觀其玄虛，用其周行，強字之曰道 — *"the sage watches its dark emptiness, makes use of its going-round, and forces the style 道 on it."* The name comes from 周行 (*zhōu xíng*), *going all the way round*, the phrase of chapter 25. **王弼 (*Wáng Bì*)** defines it in four characters: 道者，物之所由也 — *"the Tao is what things go by"* (51). 由 (*yóu*) is *by way of, through*. And on chapter 25: 道取於無物而不由也 — *"it is called 道 because there is nothing that does not go by it."* **河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*)** gives the reason from the other end: 見萬物皆從道所生，故字之曰道 — *"seeing that the countless things all come from it, I style it 道."*

All three explain the name through the road. The Tao is not named for what it *is*. It is named for the fact that everything travels it.

### What is set aside

- ***the Way*** — the honest literal, and the reason it is forbidden is the capital. Capitalized and alone, *the Way* becomes a creed. It belongs to the early Christian name for itself (*the Way*, Acts 9:2), to every "way of life" sold since, and to a one-word answer to a question the book keeps open. Forbidden as the name; *way*, lowercase and with an owner, is kept.
- ***the Path*** — true to the road, but too small and too private. A path is one person's track through the woods, and 說文 says 道 is the road that runs straight through. Forbidden capitalized; *path* stays available as an ordinary word.
- ***God*, *the Absolute*, *the One*** — each imports what the text refuses: a person who creates and judges, or a metaphysical substance. 象帝之先 sets the Tao before the high deity, and 天地不仁 (5) says *"sky and earth are not concerned with humaneness."* And *the One* is 一's word: 道生一, *the Tao births the one* (42), so the two cannot be the same.
- ***Nature*** — already spoken for. *Nature* is 天 (*tiān*)'s English where 天 takes a verb (*the way of nature*), and *of itself* is 自然's (25). The ladder 人法地，地法天，天法道，道法自然 needs four different words.
- ***the operating system, the source code*** — a modern metaphor, and it does catch three true things: the Tao is impersonal, it works without issuing commands (無為, 自然), and it runs beneath what is visible. It fails the pointing test. Laozi points at water, valleys and uncarved wood, and the graph is a person on a road under open sky. A machine metaphor brings in mechanism and design, which the book never names, and it will date faster than the text it explains. It can serve in commentary as a lens. It is never the word.

### Why the name stays untranslated

Chapter 25 says the name is forced, so we leave it visibly as a name. **"The Tao"** keeps the gesture: a word that does not pretend to define. It is also already an English word, and it carries less freight than *the Way* or *God*. We spell it *Tao* rather than the pinyin *Dao* only because that is the form English readers know. Either way it is pronounced *dào*.

**What stays untranslated is the name, not the word.** The first line teaches this: 道可道 → *"The Tao that can be made a way."* *Tao* and *way* stand in the same sentence, so the reader learns what the name means before learning anything else.

### Working register

| Use | English | Chapters | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| the name | **the Tao** | throughout | 道生一 → *"the Tao births the one"* |
| the name, qualified | **the great Tao, the clear Tao…** | 18, 34, 41, 53 | 大道汎兮 → *"the great Tao overflows"* |
| a common noun with an owner | **way** | 9, 47, 73, 77 ×3, 79, 81 ×2 | 天之道 → *"the way of nature"*; 人之道 → *"the way of people"* (77); 聖人之道 → *"the way of the sage"* (81) |
| the verb in 道可道 | **made a way** | 1 | *"The Tao that can be made a way"* |
| 不道, the negation | **not-Tao** | 30, 55 | 是謂不道，不道早已 → *"this is called not-Tao. Not-Tao comes to an early end"* |

*Made a way* is a construction, not 道's English. The supplied *made* belongs to the line (`process/principles/supplied-verb-is-scaffolding.md`), so `render:` carries *way* alone.

### 道 and 德

The book is the 道**德**經, named for both. If 道 is what everything goes by, **德 (*dé* — integrity)** is that way received into one thing and kept whole there. 道生之，德畜之 (51) — *"the Tao gives birth to the countless things, integrity rears them."* Source and its presence in things, the grain of everything and the same grain running true through one life. See `de-德.md`.

### What no rule can enforce

**Lowercase *way* cannot be forbidden, and the boundary it marks can only be held by a reader.** The lock bans *the Way* and *the Path* with their capitals, which the checker reads as part of the violation. But whether a given 道 is the name or an owned way is a judgment about the line, and no check can make it. *Way* is also an ordinary English word that many lines use with no 道 in sight (13, 39). The ruling is: **the name is *the Tao*; a way that belongs to someone or something is *way*.**

### Left open

**Three owned ways still read *Tao*.** 長生久視之道 (59) is grammatically *the way of long life and lasting sight*, but reads *"the Tao of deep roots, firm base, long life, and enduring vision."* 我道大 (67), *"my Tao is great,"* has an owner in 我 (*wǒ* — I). 古之道 (14), *"the ancient Tao,"* has antiquity as its owner. Each can be argued: the speaker of 67 means the Tao they teach, and 14's ancient way is plainly the Tao. But the line in the register above does not yet decide them, and it should.

**The speech sense surfaces once, and the English drops it.** 道之出口 (35) is *"the Tao, when it leaves the mouth"*, that is, when it is spoken. It is the one line after chapter 1 that sets the name beside the act of telling, and *"the Tao is bland in the mouth"* turns the mouth that speaks into a mouth that tastes.

**And the first line still breaks a pun.** 道可道 holds the road and the telling in one verb. *Made a way* keeps the road and loses the telling (`chapters/001.md` → Notes). No English word holds both, and every map of this word is, by the book's own first line, not the thing. We draw it anyway, because a map can still say *this way*, and we hold it loosely.
entries.shuowen: The road that is walked. From 辵 (chuò — walking along a road) and 𩠐 (shǒu — a head). A road that runs straight through is called 道.

entries.body:
## 得 & 失 (Dé, Shī) — Getting & Losing

*Say "duh," rising, and "shr," level. 得 stands thirty-three times in thirty lines across nineteen chapters; 失 seventeen times across eight. The commonest verbs of having in the language, and the book weighs them against each other in chapter after chapter.*

**Recommended: 得 → "get" · 失 → "lose."** *(Not "attain" or "obtain," which make getting an achievement, and *attain* the Buddhist one. Not "find," which at chapter 62 turns a saying into the Sermon on the Mount. Not "gain," a ledger word that makes 得 profit.)* **Four flexions:** *received* at chapters 39 and 22 (where the getting is the one), *unavoidable* for the idiom 不得已 (bù dé yǐ — it cannot be helped) at chapters 30 and 31, *touch* at chapter 14, and *find* at chapter 62, the last two kept by Shalom's call (2026-11-19).

### The graph: a step, and a hand letting go

> 得，行有所得也。从彳，㝵聲。
> *"得: to go and get something. From 彳 (chì — a step), with 㝵 (dé) for the sound."* — Shuowen (說文, *Shuōwén* — Xu Shen's dictionary, c. 100 CE)

> 失，縱也。从手，乙聲。
> *"失: to let go. From 手 (shǒu — a hand), with 乙 (yǐ) for the sound."* — Shuowen

**得 is getting by going: a step toward a thing, and the thing in hand.** Its sound part 㝵 is the older graph of the word itself, 貝 (*bèi* — a cowry) and 又 (*yòu* — a hand): picking up a shell, the money of the day. The step was added later, *picked up on the road*. **失 is a hand opening.** The Shuowen's 縱 is *to release*, the hand that lets something slip out. One character closes the hand, the other opens it, and the book never lets you have the first without the second.

**And 得 is 德 (dé — integrity)'s twin in sound**, which the old dictionaries pun on: 德者，得也, *"integrity is what you got"* (`glossary/de-德.md`). The book's integrity is the getting that is not a grabbing.

### Thirty lines, and what the book does with having

> *Getting it is a shock.*
> *Losing it is a shock.*
>
> 得之若驚，
> 失之若驚，
>
> — chapter 13

**Chapter 13 sets the pair side by side, and gives them one reaction.** Getting favor and losing it are the same shock (Heshang Gong: 得寵榮驚者，處高位如臨深危也, *"one shocked by getting favor stands in a high place as if over a deep drop"*). Chapter 44 asks which is the sickness, 得與亡孰病 (*dé yǔ wáng shú bìng* — "getting or losing, which is the sickness?"), and Wang Bi answers for the reader: 得多利而亡其身，何者為病也, *"getting much profit and losing your body: which is the sickness?"* Chapter 23 makes the pair a law of company, the Tao gladly *gets* those who are the same as the Tao, and loss gladly gets those who are the same as loss.

> *Sky received the one, and so became clear.*
>
> 天得一以清；
>
> — chapter 39

**Chapter 39 is the hardest line, and Wang Bi reads both halves of the pair into it.** 物皆各得此一以成，既成而舍以居成，居成則失其母，故皆裂發歇竭滅蹶也, *"each thing gets this one and is completed; once completed, it lets the one go to settle in its completion, and settled there it loses its mother, and so all split, burst, cease, run dry, die out and topple."* The one is gotten, then let go, then lost. That is why the English takes *received* there: the line is the first step of Wang Bi's three, and *got* in a list of sky, earth and spirit sounds like grabbing, which is what the one is not. The flexion is scoped to chapter 39, and it was the chapter's English from its rebuilding (`WORKLIST-CLOSED.md` D39).

### Chapter 62: seek, and you find, kept with its echo

> *Did they not say: seek, and you find;*
> *commit a crime, and you are spared?*
>
> 不曰：求以得，
> 有罪以免邪？
>
> — chapter 62

***Seek, and you find* is Matthew 7:7**, *"seek, and ye shall find,"* word for word. It fails the hymn test on the strongest possible ground, and it changes the saying: Matthew's seeker finds God's answer; the ancients' seeker simply gets what they seek. Wang Bi: 以求則得求，以免則得免, *"seek, and you get what you seek; seek to be spared, and you are spared."* *Seek, and you get* was proposed for this reason. **The line keeps *find*** (Shalom's call, 2026-11-19), and the echo of Matthew is recorded here as a known cost, so that no later pass takes it for an oversight. Wang Bi's plainer getting stays in this entry for a reader who wants it.

### Getting as a modal, and the idiom

**Before a verb, 得 is *can*, *get to*.** 搏之不得 (*bó zhī bù dé* — "reach for it, and you cannot get it," 14) reads *touch*, and keeps it: Heshang Gong frames chapter 14's triad as colour, sound and form, 無色 · 無聲 · 無形, so the three lines are sight, hearing and touch. Chinese has 見 (*jiàn* — to see) and 聞 (*wén* — to hear) for the first two and uses the generic 得 for the third; English has *touch*. *Grasp* was the line until 2026-09-08 and is ruled out: it is 執 (*zhí*)'s locked English, and 執古之道 (*"Grasp the ancient Tao"*) stands thirteen lines below, so the English would tell the reader they cannot grasp it and then to grasp it. The Chinese uses two characters for two acts (`chapters/014.md`). Then 不可得而親 and its five siblings at chapter 56, where 可 (*kě* — can)'s *cannot* carries the line; 吾得執而殺之 (*wú dé zhí ér shā zhī* — "I could seize them and kill them," 74). The English modal absorbs it, as English does.

**不得其死 (*bù dé qí sǐ* — "not get their death") at chapter 42 is an idiom**, dying before one's span. Heshang Gong: 不得以壽命死也, *"they do not get to die of their allotted years."* *Do not die a natural death* renders it.

**不得已 has two parses, and the English must keep them apart.** At chapters 30 and 31 it is the idiom *it cannot be helped*: force used only when there is no other way. At chapter 29, 吾見其不得已 (*wú jiàn qí bù dé yǐ*), Heshang Gong reads 不得 plus a closing 已: 我見其不得天道人心已明矣, *"I see they do not get the Tao of nature or the people's hearts; that is clear."* So chapter 29 is a getting, *"I see they will not get it"* (Shalom's call, 2026-11-19), and the flexion *unavoidable* is scoped to 30 and 31 only.

**難得之貨 is 貨 (huò — goods)'s fixed phrase**, *rare goods* (3, 12, 64), and 得 is absorbed in it (`glossary/huo-貨.md`).

### 失: one hand, and it opens

失 is *lose* in every line but one: 23's *loss* (a noun of it), 26's *lightness loses the root*, 29 and 64's *those who grasp it lose it*, 33's *does not lose their place*, 38's four losses down the ladder. Wang Bi on chapter 23 says what losing is: 失，累多也, *"to lose is to carry too much."* The hand that grasps too much is the hand that lets go.

**The exception is chapter 73's 疏而不失** (*shū ér bù shī* — "wide-meshed, yet it loses nothing"), which reads *nothing slips through*. The idiom is good English and it performs the opening hand. It also drops the verb the book uses for the grasper's loss at 29 and 64, and so hides that nature's net, unlike the grasper, loses nothing. Heshang Gong: 無有所失, *"nothing is lost."*

### What is set aside

**"Attain," "attainment."** The achievement word, and in Buddhist English the word for realization; 無所得 (*wú suǒ dé* — "nothing to attain") is the Heart Sutra's. It makes 得 a spiritual summit, and the book's getting is plain.

**"Obtain."** Latin, and the register of a requisition form.

**"Gain."** A ledger word: profit, the increase on an investment. At chapter 44 it makes the question one of accounts, which is Wang Bi's *getting much profit* but not the line's bare *getting*. It cannot be forbidden yet, since chapters 22 and 44 print it.

**"Acquire."** Acquisition is buying and collecting; chapter 46's 欲得 (*yù dé* — wanting to get) is plainer. With `glossary/yu-欲.md`, the line becomes *wanting to get* (`WORKLIST.md` T2-86).

**"Find," elsewhere.** Kept at chapter 62 by Shalom's call, with its Matthew echo. At chapter 52, 既得其母 (*jì dé qí mǔ* — "once you get the mother"), it is natural English and harmless, and it is held open below.

**"Forfeit."** For 失: a penalty, which the book's losing never is. Losing is what a grasping hand does to itself.

### Working register

| line | grammar | English |
|---|---|---|
| 得之 · 失之 (13) · 得之 ×3 (23) · 得志 (31) · 得所欲 (61) | a verb, with an object | *get* · *lose* |
| 少則得 (22) | a verb, the one | *receive* — flexion, Shalom's call |
| 得與亡 (44) | a verb, or its noun | *getting* (recommended) |
| 求以得 (62) | a verb | *find* — flexion, Shalom's call |
| 天得一 ×7 (39) | a verb, the one | *received* — flexion |
| 不得已 (30, 31) | an idiom | *unavoidable* — flexion |
| 吾見其不得已 (29) | 不得 + a closing 已 | *will not get it* |
| 搏之不得 (14) | a modal, the third sense | *cannot touch* — flexion, Shalom's call |
| 吾得執 (74) | a modal | *could* |
| 不可得而 (56) ×6 | a modal, inside 可's *cannot* | *you cannot* |
| 不得其死 (42) | an idiom | *do not die a natural death* |
| 既得其母 (52) | a verb | *find* (held open) |
| 難得之貨 (3, 12, 64) | 貨's phrase | *rare goods* |
| 失 (13, 23, 26, 29, 33, 38, 64) | a verb, or its noun | *lose* · *loss* |
| 疏而不失 (73) | a verb | *loses nothing* (recommended) |

### What no rule can enforce

***Gain* and *acquire* are ruled out for 得, and cannot be forbidden yet**, because chapters 44 and 46 print them now. *Find* is a flexion at 62 and held open at 52, so it can never go on the list.

***Loss* at chapter 44 renders 亡 (*wáng* — to be gone), not 失.** Chapter 44 holds no 失, so no rule sees two characters sharing one English. 亡 is gone, perished, as at chapter 33's 死而不亡 (*"dies but does not vanish"*), and it wants its own word when chapter 44 is next open.

### Left open

**Three lines would change, and each is Shalom's call.** 44 (*Gain or loss* → *Getting or losing*, with 亡 as above), 46 (with T2-86, *wanting to get*), 73 (*nothing slips through* → *it loses nothing*). Chapter 62 keeps *find*.

**Chapter 52's *find*.** *Find our mother, and you know her children* is good English, and Wang Bi's 得本以知末 (*"get the root to know the branches"*) is a getting. *Find* suggests she was lost, which chapter 52 does not say; *get* sounds like taking possession of a mother. Left as it stands until the line is read again.

**Chapter 39 waits on 靈.** Its seven 得 keep *received*, and the chapter is to be rewritten once, with `glossary/shen-ling-神靈.md`'s *potent* and `glossary/gui-jian-貴賤.md`'s pricing together.

## 德 (Dé) — Integrity

*Pronounced "duh," on a gently rising tone, as if asking a small question.*

Half of the book's own name. It is the 道德經 — the *Dao De Jing* — the Classic of the Way **and its 德**. Whatever this word means, Laozi set it on the cover beside 道, its equal. We cannot afford to get it wrong — and for a century, in English, we did.

### The trouble with "virtue"

The standard rendering has long been *virtue*, and the choice was not foolish. Latin *virtus* once meant **inherent power, efficacy, the potency proper to a thing** — we still say "the healing virtue of a herb," or that something happens "by virtue of" another. In that older sense the word was almost exactly right. But English narrowed it to Sunday-school morality — piety, propriety, good citizenship — and that is the very meaning Laozi writes *against*. In Chapter 38 he ranks 德 *above* benevolence, righteousness, and ritual (仁義禮), and insists the highest 德 does not even know itself as 德. To translate it "virtue" is to hand the reader the one connotation the text spends its whole energy dismantling.

So we set *virtue* aside — not because it was always wrong, but because it stopped being right.

### The graph

德 assembles from three parts, and it rewards watching them lock together:

- **彳 (chì)** — a footstep; going; conduct. It is the left half of 行, "road / to walk." 德 is never still. It *moves*.
- **直 (zhí)** — straight, upright. And 直 is itself a tiny picture: an **eye (目) above a single vertical stroke** — *to look straight ahead*. Directness of the gaze became directness of the character.
- **心 (xīn)** — the heart-mind.

Read together: **a straight-seeing heart, in motion** — trueness traveling straight out of an undivided center into the way one moves through the world.

Here is the detail that changes everything. In the oldest **Shang oracle-bone** forms, 德 has *no heart*. It is only 彳 + 直 — to go straight, to survey a road directly, to hold a true course. The **heart arrives later**, in the bronze inscriptions of the Zhou. You can watch, inside the life of a single character, a civilization growing an *interior*: what began as straightness of *path* became straightness of *soul*.

And one more thread, easy to miss and impossible to unsee. 德 is a near-twin of **得 (dé), "to get, to obtain"** — reconstructed almost identically in Old Chinese, and the old dictionaries pun on the pair openly: *德者，得也* — "De is what you have got." So 德 is not only how you *go*; it is **what you were given**. In the early Zhou it named the charismatic potency a ruler *received* — from Heaven, from the ancestors — the standing that made his rule legitimate. Laozi inherits that ancient sense of *received power* and does something quietly radical: he strips off the politics and the Heaven-favor and keeps only the pure kernel — **a potency received from the source and held intact within a thing.**

### What 德 becomes in Laozi's hands

Set the pieces together and one coherent thing appears. If **道 is the whole, undivided Way of all things, then 德 is that Way received into a single thing and kept intact there** — the Tao made local. The Tao, un-fragmented, *in you*.

See how steadily he uses it:

- *道生之，德畜之* (Ch 51) — the Tao gives them life; their **德** rears them. De is the Tao's care operating from *inside* each creature.
- *孔德之容，惟道是從* (Ch 21) — the form of great **德** follows the Tao alone. De is what the Tao looks like once it takes a body.
- *含德之厚，比於赤子* (Ch 55) — a person with abundant **德** is like a newborn. Not a saint — an *infant*: maximally whole, nothing yet spent, nothing yet divided.
- *玄德* (Ch 10, 51, 65) — "dark," hidden **德**: the power to give birth, nourish, and lead *without possessing or controlling*. Potency with the ego removed.

And notice, just as carefully, what 德 is **not**. It is not social morality — Laozi keeps it a rung above the moral virtues and unconscious of itself. It is not 氣 (qì), the breath — that is fuel, the thermodynamics of a living body; 德 is the *intactness and rightness of the whole*, not its energy. And it is not generic "power" — it never slides into force or strength (力, 強), which Laozi distrusts. 德 is quieter than any of these: **the uncontrived, un-fragmented capacity to be exactly and fully what you are.**

### Why we land on *integrity*

Say the English word slowly and its own root opens: *integer* — **whole, untouched, undivided, intact.** It holds two meanings at once, and they are precisely the two halves of 德:

- **Structural integrity** — soundness, wholeness, a thing fully and intactly itself. This is the 德 of the newborn in Chapter 55, of the uncarved block, of everything Laozi loves that has not yet been split.
- **Moral integrity** — straightness, trueness of conduct. This is 彳 + 直 + 心 almost letter for letter: *to walk straight from the heart.* And "integrity" carries that ethical weight **without piety, without stuffiness**, free of the social-morality freight that drowns "virtue."

There is a deeper reason the word belongs to *this* translation in particular. Our whole reading of Laozi turns on **un-fragmentation** — 抱一, embrace the One; 復歸於樸, return to the uncarved block; the infant; the undivided center. *Integrity* is simply the English name for **un-fragmented wholeness.** It is not an import into our system; it is the keystone the other stones were already leaning toward. With it, 德 clicks home: the intact wholeness you received from the Tao, kept undivided, carried straight into the world.

### Working register

**德 = "integrity," everywhere.** One word, no exceptions, even in the rare line where 德 is a thing's own nature acting upon it (*"integrity rears them"*, 51). Retire *virtue*, *power*, and *lifeforce*. For 玄德, use **"profound integrity,"** as the 玄 lock rules (`glossary/xuan-miao-玄妙.md`).

Hear it in the hard places:

- Ch 38 — *上德不德，是以有德* → **"The highest integrity does not do integrity, and so it has integrity."**
- Ch 41 — *上德若谷* → **"The highest integrity seems a valley."**
- Ch 51 — *道生之，德畜之* → **"The Tao gives birth to the countless things, integrity rears them."**
- Ch 55 — *含德之厚* → **"A person with abundant integrity is like a newborn."**

### Left open

*Integrity* is not flawless. It has picked up a faint modern corporate echo — "business integrity," the poster on the break-room wall. We are betting that the older, structural sense — *intactness* — is strong enough to carry the weight, and that set against the deadening piety of "virtue" it will strike a modern ear as both truer and more alive. But this is finally the ear's decision, not the dictionary's. A living translation keeps testing its own keywords; if some later chapter makes *integrity* buckle, we will hear it, and we will come back to this page. For now it stands — **the Way, made whole, in a single thing.**

---

*Entry standard, going forward: begin with the live problem, not a definition; read the character as a picture and watch it change over time; let the cross-textual evidence argue the case; name what we set aside and why; and leave any real tension open rather than pretending it closed.*

## 帝 (Dì) — A God, and the One That Was Deposed

*Say "dee," falling. **One appearance in the whole book**, as the last word of Chapter 4 — and the most contested character in the history of translating Chinese into English.*

**Locked: 帝 → "god." 象帝之先 → "older than any god."** *(Settled 2026-08-31.)*

***Any*, not *the*, and the choice is load-bearing twice over.**

**It refuses to assert what the field has not settled.** Whether the Shang had a single high god is an open question in the scholarship, so *the high god* would smuggle a whole theological architecture in through the definite article — where nobody would notice it, because articles are not words readers weigh. **The definite article confers status exactly as a capital does** (standing rule 3): *the* high god reads as a title, *any* god reads as a category. It is the fault of *the Source* and *the One*, wearing a different part of speech.

**And it is the stronger claim, which the argument below needs.** If the Tao precedes only *the* high god, a claimant may answer *"my line descends from a different power."* If it precedes **any** god, the chain of descent has no floor anywhere. **The universal quantifier closes the escape the definite article leaves open.**

---

### The line is about where 帝 stands, not what 帝 is

Chapter 4 ends 象帝之先 — *"…before 帝."* The word names a god, and English has only ever done two things with it: **inflate it** into *God*, *the Lord*, *the Creator* — or **erase it** into an ancestor, a beginning, nothing at all.

Both destroy the line, and for the same reason. **They treat the sentence as a claim about what 帝 *is*, when it is a claim about where 帝 *stands*.** Inflate the word and the line becomes incoherent, because a God with something before him is not the Christian God. Erase it and the line becomes empty, because the whole point is *which* thing the Tao is said to precede.

**And the thing it precedes is not what it looks like.** 帝 is chosen for a reason that is neither purely theological nor purely political — because by the time this chapter was written, **those two things had become the same word.**

---

### The graph: a calyx, a fire, or a pivot — but not a person

**說文解字 (c. 100 CE) is wrong here, and the reason it is wrong is the whole story in miniature.** Xu Shen gives 諦也，王天下之號也。从丄，朿聲 — *"帝 means 諦 (*dì* — to scrutinize); the title of one who rules the world. From 丄 (the archaic 上, 'above'), with 朿 (*cì* — a thorn) as sound."* Modern palaeography rejects that analysis. **By Xu Shen's day 帝 had meant *emperor* for three centuries, and he read the graph backwards from the word he knew.** The dictionary that preserves the oldest Chinese lexicography had already lost this one to the political meaning.

The oracle-bone graph is genuinely disputed. The three live readings:

- **A flower calyx** — the ring of sepals where blossom joins stem; the original form of 蒂 (*dì* — calyx, peduncle). **The part that holds the fruit and is not the fruit.**
- **A bundle of sacrificial firewood, or an altar** — linking the graph to 禘 (*dì*), the name of a great ancestral sacrifice.
- **A circumpolar asterism** at the north celestial pole *(Pankenier)* — the still point the sky turns around.

**None of the three is a person.** A calyx, a fire, a pivot: a joint, a rite, a centre of rotation. Whatever 帝 was, the graph is not a man on a throne and not a maker of worlds.

**And whether the Shang had a single high god is contested in the field**, not settled — *"Was There a High God Ti in Shang Religion?"* is a live question. 帝 in the oracle bones may name a supreme power over rain, harvest, war and the king's illnesses; it may be a collective term for the pantheon; it may be an honorific for the royal father. **The English must not settle what the scholarship has not.**

---

### 帝 was already a deposed god, and that is why it is the right word

This is the part the standard renderings lose, and it is chronology, not interpretation.

**Shang (to c. 1046 BCE):** 帝 / 上帝 is the high power. The living king does not sacrifice to 帝 directly — his **ancestors** do the petitioning, from the 宗 (*zōng*), the ancestral temple. Authority runs *king → ancestors → 帝*.

**Zhou conquest (c. 1046 BCE):** the Zhou **displace 帝 with 天 (*tiān*)** and invent 天命 (*tiān mìng* — the Mandate of Heaven) to justify having overthrown the Shang. This is documented as a legitimation device, effectively state propaganda: one legitimate ruler at a time, holding a mandate a god can withdraw. The Zhou king styles himself **天子 (*tiān zǐ*) — the child of 天.**

**So 帝 does not come to Laozi as the reigning god. It comes as the god a dynasty took down and replaced — the *previous* administration's highest power.**

**Warring States, 288 BCE:** King Min of Qi takes the title 東帝 (*dōng dì* — Di of the East) and King Zhao of Qin takes 西帝 (*xī dì* — Di of the West). **The first living human beings to claim the word.** It lasts months; both drop it on Su Dai's advice that two 帝 would only compete.

**221 BCE:** 秦始皇帝 (*Qín Shǐ Huáng Dì*) welds it permanently to the throne, and 帝 means *emperor* from then on.

**Chapter 4 is not attested at Guodian (~300 BCE); its earliest witness is Mawangdui, c. 200 BCE.** So the earliest readers we can actually document read 帝 **after** kings had grabbed it and after Qin had made it imperial. **They heard the god and the emperor in one word, and they heard a word that had already been deposed once.**

**"Empty theology" and "a critique of the emperor" are therefore not alternatives to choose between. In this character they are the same object**, and that is the answer to why Laozi reached for 帝 rather than for 天.

---

### What the line actually does: it takes the floor out of legitimation

Read the chapter's last two lines together, because they are one move:

> 吾不知**誰之子**，象**帝**之先。
> *I do not know **whose child** it is… before **帝**.*

**誰之子 — "whose child" — is not idle. 子 (*zǐ* — child) is the load-bearing word of Chinese political legitimacy, and this book uses it that way elsewhere.** Chapter 62 has **天子** (*tiān zǐ*) — the ruler, *the child of the sky*. Chapter 54 has 子孫以祭祀不輟 — *"descendants never break off the sacrifices,"* the ancestral cult running down the generations. Authority in both the Shang and the Zhou settlement is **inherited downward from a highest power**: the Shang king through his ancestors to 帝, the Zhou king directly as 天's child.

**Chapter 4 names both ends of that apparatus and pulls them apart.**

- Line 2 puts the Tao at the ancestral temple: 似萬物之**宗** — 說文 on 宗: **尊祖廟也。从宀从示**, *"the temple where ancestors are honoured; from 宀 (a roof) and 示 (the altar."* But it is hedged — 似, **it only *seems* to be the ancestor.**
- Line 6 denies it a parent: **吾不知誰之子**, *I do not know whose child it is.* **A thing with no parent cannot be inherited from, and cannot be claimed by descent.**
- Line 7 places it before 帝 itself: **帝之先.**

**Put those together and the genealogy of rule runs out of floor.** If something with **no parentage** stands **before any god**, then there is no ultimate ancestor at the bottom of the chain, and every claim of the form *"I rule because I descend from the highest"* is standing on nothing. **The Son of Heaven is a child; this has no parent and got there first.**

That is not a lament about a particular ruler. **It is a critique of legitimation by descent — which is the mechanism of dynasty itself.** And it is made without naming a single king, which is why it survived.

**It also explains the choice of 帝 over 天.** 天 is the *Zhou's* word, with the Mandate welded to it. To argue against the Zhou settlement in the Zhou's own vocabulary is to argue inside their frame. **Naming 帝 reaches behind that settlement to the god the Zhou themselves deposed, and says: even that one was not first.** The book does the same move to the Zhou's word in its own place — Chapter 25's ladder runs 人法地，地法天，天法道，道法自然, sky modelling the Tao and the Tao modelling only being-so-of-itself. **Two chapters, two of the age's highest powers, each demoted using its own name.**

---

### The hardest question in the chapter: is 象 "seems," or is it *image*?

**Chapter 4 hedges five times in seven lines** — 似 twice, 或 twice, 吾不知 once. It is the most epistemically cautious chapter in the book. So a great deal turns on whether the final word 象 (*xiàng*) is a **sixth hedge** or the one thing the chapter is willing to assert.

**似 is this book's word for *seems*, and Chapter 4 uses it twice.** Its five occurrences are all comparative hedges: 似萬物之宗 and 似或存 here, 似鄙 at Chapter 20, 似不肖 twice at Chapter 67.

**象 is this book's word for *image*, and four of its five occurrences are unambiguously the noun** — and all four are central:

> 無物之**象** (14) — *the image of no-thing*
> 其中有**象** (21) — *within it there is an image*
> 執大**象**，天下往 (35) — *hold the great image, and the world comes*
> 大**象**無形 (41) — *the great image has no form*

**The fifth is this line.** If Laozi wanted a third *seems*, 似 was in his hand — he had just used it twice in the same seven lines. Switching to 象 for a third hedge is unmotivated; switching to 象 to name what the thing **is** is not.

**Both commentators read it as a hedge.** 王弼 paraphrases: 不亦**似**帝之先乎 — *"is it not as if before 帝?"* 河上公 simply asserts 道自在天帝之前. Their reading is old and it is defensible: 象 as "to resemble" is ordinary classical usage.

**But 王弼's own system argues against his paraphrase.** He built a hermeneutic on 言 / 象 / 意 (*words / image / meaning*), and in it 大象 — the great image — is **the essence itself**, the image that has no form. He treats 象 as a technical term everywhere else and flattens it here.

**And Laozi's chapters end on their strongest word, not their weakest.** 以此 (21) · 玄之又玄，眾妙之門 (1) · 道法自然 (25). A chapter that has hedged five times and then closes *"it also seems to…"* would be uniquely limp.

**So the reading this entry recommends: 象 is the noun.** The chapter refuses every assertion it might make about the Tao — and then, in its last three characters, names the one thing it will say: **an image, and older than the god.** Not a greater god behind the god. **A god-shaped place with an image of no-thing in it.** That is the empty theology, stated positively, and it is why 無物之象 at Chapter 14 reads as the same thought.

*The traditional reading is not refuted, only outweighed. Anyone rendering* seems *here is in the company of both commentaries, and the line still works. What it loses is the landing.*

---

### Why this word above all others: the Term Question

**帝 is the word the missionaries fought over for two generations, and the man who won that fight built the English Tao Te Ching.**

The **Term Question** was the long dispute over which Chinese word would be conscripted to mean the Christian *God*: 神 (*shén*), 上帝 (*shàng dì* — "the 帝 above"), or 天主 (*tiān zhǔ*). It was never resolved by agreement. **The Chinese Union Bible was printed in two editions**, one using 上帝 and one using 神, because the parties could not be reconciled.

**James Legge (1815–1897) led the 上帝 party, and his side won** — by 1910 it had prevailed. Legge came to China with the London Missionary Society; his 1891 Tao Te Ching still underlies countless later versions. **The man who rendered 象帝之先 for the English-speaking world had spent decades arguing, in print and as doctrine, that 帝 means God.**

*(Traffic ran both ways, which is what makes the overlay so hard to see from inside English. The Chinese Union Bible renders John 1:1 as 太初有道，道與神同在，道就是神 — "In the beginning was the **Tao**; the Tao was with 神; the Tao **was** 神." Two of Laozi's central words were drafted to carry Logos and God before most English readers ever met either. See `process/overlay-audit.md`.)*

**The irony is exact.** Legge's God is an eternal creator with no antecedent. **Chapter 4's whole point is that 帝 has one.**

---

### What is set aside, and why

**"God"** — imports monotheism, creation from nothing, and a personal will, none of which 帝 carries in the oracle bones. Worse here than elsewhere: a God with something before him is not the Christian God, so the word makes the line unreadable in its own terms. It also takes Legge's side in a missionary controversy the Chinese text is not a party to.

**"the Lord"** — the same import in older clothes, plus a feudal relation (lordship, service, obedience) 帝 does not name.

**"the Creator"** — the worst, because the chapter argues the opposite. The Tao only 似 *seems* to be the ancestor of the countless things, and its own parentage is unknown. A chapter this careful about not asserting an origin cannot be handed a Creator in its final line.

**"Heaven"** — a double error: it imports the Christian afterlife **and** takes 天's English, already ruled on here (天 → *sky* / *nature*, never a realm). **And it destroys the argument**, because the whole force of 帝 is that it is *not* 天 — it is the god 天 replaced.

**"the Emperor"** — right for 221 BCE onward, and it collapses the line into politics alone. The reason to keep *god* is that the word carries both, and the reader should feel the second meaning arriving under the first.

**"the ancestor"** — what we had, borrowed from 宗 three lines up. It flattens a **god** into a **forebear** and makes the chapter say one thing twice, destroying the 宗 / 帝 bracket that holds it together.

**"the high god"** — this entry's own earlier recommendation, refused. It asserts a **singular supreme deity at the top of a hierarchy**, which is precisely what the scholarship on Shang religion has not settled, and it smuggles that assertion in through the definite article rather than through a word anyone would notice. *The* confers status the way a capital does.

**"the gods," "the pantheon"** — the opposite over-reach: they assert a plural set and a structure. 帝 is one word and the line makes one claim.

**Lowercase, always.** *any god*, never *any God* and never *the High God*. Capitals confer status (standing rule 3), and capitalizing here would re-import through typography exactly what the wording refuses.

---

### Working register

**帝 → "god," and at its one occurrence, *any god*.** No flexion, no sweep. The whole weight falls on three characters:

> 吾不知誰之子，象帝之先。
> *I do not know whose child it is. An image, older than any god.*

**Lowercase, always, and without the definite article.** The small *g* says: this **was** a god to the people who used the word — not a metaphor, not a personified force we are being polite about — and it was **not *the* God.** The bare *any* says the text is not describing the architecture of the divine. Between them they restore the god the English had deleted without installing a theology the Chinese does not hold.

---

### Left open

**Whether to name him at all.** *"before Dì"* would treat 帝 as we treat 道 — an untranslated proper name, glossed once. It is honest about how much is contested, and it refuses to decide for the reader. It is also opaque, and it asks someone who has met one Chinese word to meet a second by Chapter 4. **Recommended against, without confidence.**

**Whether 象 is image or *seems*.** Argued above; the recommendation departs from both commentaries, which is not a thing to do lightly. **If Shalom keeps the traditional reading, the political argument above survives intact** — it rests on 誰之子, 宗 and 帝, not on 象.

**And a genuine strain, left standing: 帝 is a *name*, and *any god* is a *category*.** Laozi wrote one specific word — a power with a cult, a history, a deposition and a theft — and the rendering answers with a class. That loss is real, and it is accepted on the division of labour this repository runs on: **the line has to be true and to land; the entry carries the deep meaning.** A reader who wants the bronze-age god the Zhou deposed and the Qin stole has to come here, which is what entries are for.

**Locked 2026-08-31.** The `forbidden:` list is safe to enforce because **帝 occurs in one chapter and nothing else in Chapter 4 can legitimately claim any of those words** — there is no 天 (*tiān*) in this chapter, no ruler, and no maker. *God*, *the Lord* and *Creator* are capitalised in the list, so the capital is the violation and the lowercase *god* we use stays legal; *heaven*, *emperor* and *the high god* are lowercase and catch any casing.

**What is still open is 象 (*xiàng*), and it is settled against this entry's first instinct.** An earlier draft argued 象 here is the noun *image* — the book's term at 無物之象 (14), 其中有象 (21), 執大象 (35), 大象無形 (41) — on the grounds that 似 is the dedicated hedge and is already used twice in this chapter. **The grammar defeats it.** In all four places where 象 is unambiguously a noun it is *marked* as one, by 之, by 有, or by 大. **At 象帝之先 it stands bare before a noun phrase, which is the shape of verb plus object** — and both commentaries read it as a comparison. Chapter 4 is also 象's first appearance in the book, so an English *image* would land where no reader can yet hear the thread. The line reads *"It seems older than any god."*
entries.render: god — *any god* at its one occurrence

entries.body:
## 父 · 甫 (Fù · Fǔ) — The Father

*Say "foo," falling, for 父; "foo," dipping and then lifting, for 甫. One word in two spellings, three appearances across two chapters. The book's father: named far less often than its mother, and named all the same.*

**Locked: 父 (*fù*) and 甫 (*fǔ*) → "father," in every line.** *(Not "origin," a word with no body, the father's version of *the Source*. Not "root," which is 根's (gēn — root). Shalom's call, 2026-10-26: ch 42 first, then ch 21, the same day.)*

### The graph: a hand that holds a tool, and a seedling in a field

**父 is a hand holding something up.** The oracle-bone graph is 又 (*yòu* — a right hand) gripping a short stick or a stone axe. Many paleographers read the object as the axe, and 斧 (*fǔ* — axe) still carries 父 inside it. The Shuowen reads it as a staff, and defines the word by what the one holding it does:

> 父，矩也。家長率教者。从又舉杖。
> *"父: the carpenter's square. The head of the family, who leads and teaches. From 又 (yòu — a hand) raising 杖 (zhàng — a staff)."*

矩 (*jǔ* — the carpenter's square) is the measure a thing is made true by. The Shuowen's father is the one who sets the measure and **teaches**, which is worth holding beside ch 42, where the father is the father of learning. The picture stops at the household: the Shuowen is a Han dictionary, about 100 CE, and its family head with a staff is a Han reading. Neither chapter puts the father in a house.

**甫 began as a seedling in a field.** The oracle-bone graph is a sprout, 屮 (*chè* — a sprout), over 田 (*tián* — a field): the first form of 圃 (*pǔ* — a garden). In the bronzes the sprout was rewritten as 父 to give the sound, and the field wore down into 用 (*yòng* — to use). The Shuowen, which saw only that later shape, took it apart accordingly:

> 甫，男子美稱也。从用、父，父亦聲。
> *"甫: a fine name for a man. From 用 (yòng — use) and 父 (fù — father), and 父 also gives the sound."*

A few scholars doubt that the seedling graph and 甫 are one character, but most read it so. **Where this picture stops matters more than the picture.** The seedling is the history of a spelling. By the time the book was written, 甫 was the respectful word for a man, the one in names like Zhong Shanfu of the *Odes*. The seedling is lovely, and it is not what the word in ch 21 says.

### Three lines, and in each a father is where something starts

> *From ancient times until today, the Tao's name has never been erased.*
> *In this name, I observe the father of the many.*
> *How do I know the father of the many is so? By this.*
>
> 自古及今，其名不去，
> 以閱眾甫。
> 吾何以知眾甫之狀哉？以此。
>
> — chapter 21

> *What others teach, I also teach:*
> *The strong and rigid do not die a natural death.*
> *I take this as the father of learning.*
>
> 人之所教，我亦教之。
> 強梁者不得其死，
> 吾將以為教父。
>
> — chapter 42

**In both chapters the father is the one a thing starts from, and in neither is he a man in a house.** In ch 21 he is the father of the many, 眾 (*zhòng* — the many) used of things, not people, and you observe him through the Tao's name. In ch 42 he is the father of learning: the first lesson, the one the rest of learning comes from. The line's Chinese above reads 教父 (*jiào fù* — "the father of teaching"), and the English follows the Mawangdui silk's 學父 (*xué fù* — "the father of learning"), the older reading (`notes/manuscript.md` → Ch 42). Ch 21's 狀 (*zhuàng* — shape) is likewise rendered by the witnesses' 然 (*rán* — so).

### One word, written two ways

**The oldest witnesses write 父 in ch 21.** Where our base text, Wang Bi's, writes 眾甫 (*zhòng fǔ*), both Mawangdui silks write 眾父 (*zhòng fù* — "the father of the many"). Guodian, the oldest witness of all, holds neither chapter. So the word in every early copy that has these lines is 父, and 甫 is the received spelling (`sources/variants.yaml`).

**The two sounded almost alike, and the scribes traded them.** The Shuowen itself says 父 gives 甫 its sound. The honorific is one word in two spellings even for a single man. The *Zuo Commentary* mourns Confucius as 尼父 (*Ní fù* — "Father Ni"). Zheng Xuan, the Han commentator, writes the same title with the other character in his note on the capping rite of the *Yili*: 甫，是丈夫之美稱。孔子為尼甫 — *"甫 is a fine name for a grown man. Confucius was Ni-fu,"* written 尼甫. A reader of the time heard one word, whichever character the scribe chose.

**And the commentators read them as one.** Heshang Gong glosses the two chapters in the same three words, below. Nothing in any witness or any commentary treats 甫 and 父 as two words with two senses.

### What the commentators did with it

Both commentators turn the father into a *beginning*. That is evidence for what the word means, and it is where *origin* and *root* came from.

**Heshang Gong, ch 21:** 閱，禀也。甫，始也。言道禀與萬物始生，從道受氣 — *"閱 (yuè) means to bestow. 甫 (fǔ) means beginning. It says the Tao bestows on the countless things their first life, and they receive 氣 (qì — breath) from the Tao."*

**Heshang Gong, ch 42:** 父，始也。老子以強梁之人為教戒之始也 — *"父 (fù) means beginning. Laozi takes the strong and rigid person as the beginning of teaching and warning."*

**Wang Bi, ch 21:** 衆甫，物之始也。以無名說萬物始也 — *"眾甫 (zhòng fǔ) is the beginning of things. It is by the nameless that the beginning of the countless things is explained."*

**Wang Bi, ch 42:** 故得其違教之徒，適可以為教父也 — *"so a follower who goes against the teaching can serve exactly as the father of teaching."* The one who refuses the lesson becomes the lesson.

**Every one of these glosses 父 with 始 (*shǐ* — beginning), and a gloss says what a word means; it is not the word.** English *the father of*, as in *the father of medicine* or *the father of history*, already names the one a thing began from. Heshang Gong's sense stays inside the English, and the word stays the word Laozi wrote (`process/principles/commentary-is-not-a-rendering.md`).

### The first draft said *origin* and *root*, and the father was restored

The first version of this translation rendered 甫 as *"the origin of the many"* in ch 21 and 父 as *"the root of learning"* in ch 42; both were formerly the English, taken from the commentators' 始. On 2026-10-26 Shalom restored the father, for two reasons.

**The first is Laozi's own wording.** The word is *father* in every witness that holds these lines. *Origin* and *root* were a commentator's sense put in place of the author's word, and the English *the father of* keeps the sense without losing the word.

**The second is that a rule written to protect the feminine must not be used to erase the masculine.** This edition's first standing rule holds that no one is subordinated: the female is never put under, and the male is never the default. It refuses the male where the text merely *assumes* him, as when the sage becomes *he*, or a rank word presumes a man. It does not reach a father the text names on purpose, and since this restoration the rule says so in its own words: its aim is the end of all subordination, not the masculine put under the feminine. Cooling 父 into *origin* would have let that rule lie over the text like an overlay, removing a masculine presence that is authentically there. That is the same flinch the mother's entry refuses when it keeps 母 (*mǔ* — mother) from becoming *the Source*. An edition that kept the mother a mother and turned the father into a root would build its feminine center by subtraction. **The feminine center holds because the mother is named, not because the father is unnamed.**

The book itself keeps both. Ch 42, the chapter that names the father of learning, opens with the countless things that 負陰而抱陽 (*fù yīn ér bào yáng* — "carry yin on their backs and embrace yang"). Ch 28 says 知其雄，守其雌 (*zhī qí xióng, shǒu qí cí* — "know the rooster, hold to the hen"): the masculine is to be known, not erased. The male among animals, 牡 (*mǔ* — the male), whom the Shuowen defines as 畜父 (*chù fù* — "the father among livestock"), stands beside the female in chapters 55 and 61 (`glossary/pin-牝.md`).

### The mother and the father, both reached through a name

> *The nameless is the beginning of sky and earth.*
> *The named is the mother of the countless things.*
>
> 無名，天地之始；
> 有名，萬物之母。
>
> — chapter 1

**Ch 1 reaches the mother through naming, and ch 21 reaches the father through a name.** *The named is the mother of the countless things* in ch 1; in ch 21, *in this name, I observe the father of the many*. And ch 52 calls the beginning a mother outright: 天下有始，以為天下母 (*tiān xià yǒu shǐ, yǐ wéi tiān xià mǔ* — "the world has an origin, which serves as the mother of the world"). Heshang Gong calls the father 始 (*shǐ* — beginning) as well. In the book's own terms, the beginning of things is both: the mother, often and warmly, and the father, twice.

The book does not say whether these are one beginning seen from two sides or two. It names the mother far more often: `python3 tools/concordance.py 母` prints every line.

### What is set aside

- **"origin"**, the English of ch 21 until 2026-10-26. It was then 始 (*shǐ* — beginning)'s English at ch 52, so a reader comparing the chapters would have taken 甫 for 始, which is Heshang Gong's gloss and not the text. Ch 52 reads *beginning* since 2026-11-19 (`glossary/mu-母.md`). What still rules it out: it is a word with no body, the father's version of *the Source* (`process/principles/already-spoken-for.md`).
- **"root"**, the English of ch 42 until 2026-10-26. It is spoken for by 根 (*gēn* — root), the book's root of the plant, in chapters 6, 16, 26 and 59, and by 本 (*běn* — root, trunk) in ch 39. It turns a person into a plant, and it was a gloss.
- **"the Source," "the progenitor," "the first cause."** Each cools the father into an abstraction, the same flinch the mother's entry refuses. *First cause* is also Aristotle's and the schoolmen's, a theology the book never touches.
