- **"patriarch."** It adds rule: a father who governs a household. The Shuowen's family head leads and teaches, but neither chapter gives the father any power over anyone (`process/principles/no-verdict-the-chinese-lacks.md`).
- **"forefather," "ancestor."** They put him in the past and at the ancestral altar. That is 祖 (*zǔ* — ancestor), a different word. The father of ch 21 is observed *today*, through a name that has never been erased.
- **"the Father."** A capital would make him the God of the creeds, and fail the hymn test outright. He is lowercase, like the mother (`CLAUDE.md` standing rule 3).
- **"teacher"** for ch 42's 學父. It drops the father, and it hands the line to Wang Bi's reading, in which the stubborn are the model, over the plain one, in which the lesson is the first one.

### Working register

| Line | Our English | Why |
|---|---|---|
| ch 21 · 以閱眾甫 | *I observe the father of the many* | 眾 (*zhòng*) of things, so *the many* (`glossary/zhong-眾.md`) |
| ch 21 · 吾何以知眾甫之狀哉 | *How do I know the father of the many is so?* | the repetition kept: one father, said twice |
| ch 42 · 吾將以為教父 | *I take this as the father of learning* | the silk's 學父 (*xué fù*); no possessive, since 吾 (*wú* — I) only adopts it |

**The phrase is always *the father of*.** The book never sets 父 alone as a subject; it is always someone's or something's father. Keep the genitive in the English, as the mother keeps hers.

**Outside the verse, 父母 (*fù mǔ*) is "father and mother,"** never *parents*, wherever a commentary or the Shuowen pairs them (`CHANGELOG.md`, 2026-10-26).

### Left open

**Does *father* bring a God the Father into ch 21?** It is the hazard of the word. Ch 21 is the book's haziest chapter, only vague, only elusive, deep and dim, and an English reader may hear *the father of the many* as the creeds' Father of all. What resists that hearing is in the line: the father is never addressed, never praised, never a subject. He is *observed*, through a name, and the chapter answers how it knows him with two words, *by this*. Whether lowercase and the mother beside him are enough is a question for readers, and the reading notes owe it a thread (`notes/reading.md`).

**Why the received text wrote 甫.** The base text keeps 甫, so its Source table, and the Character Atlas built from it, show the honorific rather than the father. A reader of the Chinese meets the father only through this entry and the chapter note. Whether the received editors chose 甫 on purpose, as the more respectful and less domestic spelling, or simply out of habit, no witness says.

**The Beida bamboo text has not been checked at either line.** If it differs, the fork belongs in `sources/variants.yaml`.

## 復命 (Fù Mìng) — Returning What You Were Sent With

*Say "foo ming," both syllables falling. Two lines, both in Chapter 16, and it names the third rung of the chain that ends in clear-seeing.*

**Locked: 復命 → "returning to what is given."** *(Never "returning to destiny," never "restoring destiny," never anything built on "the mandate" — and not the past tense, "what **was** given.")*

**The present tense carries the decision.** *Was given* puts the giving behind us, in a naming chain whose other members — 靜 (*jìng* — stillness) and 常 (*cháng* — the ever-present) — are timeless. *Is given* is ongoing: what any thing is given, always. And the passive keeps the giver **present but unnamed**, which is what the Chinese does: 命's graph has a mouth in it and never says whose.

### It is a name, not a new thing

This is the single most useful fact about the term, and it is easy to miss. Chapter 16 describes **one event** and then names it four times over, each name becoming the subject of the next line:

| Chinese | What it does |
|---|---|
| 各復歸其根 | the event: **each returns to its root** |
| 歸根**曰**靜 | that return **is called** 靜 (*jìng* — stillness) |
| 是謂**復命** | it **is called** 復命 |
| 復命**曰**常 | 復命 **is called** 常 (*cháng* — the ever-present) |
| 知常**曰**明 | knowing 常 **is called** 明 (*míng* — clear-seeing) |

曰 (*yuē*) is *"is called"*; 是謂 (*shì wèi*) is *"this is called."* **Nothing new enters at 復命.** The chapter is handing a second name to the returning it has just shown you, and then a third, so that a motion you can watch in a field becomes a thing you can know.

So the question is never *what else happens at 復命* — it is **what the returning looks like when you call it by this name.**

### The graph: the two characters, down to the radicals

**復 (*fù*) — a foot on a road it has walked before**

Our vendored 說文解字: **往來也。从彳复聲** — *"going and coming. From 彳 (chì), with 复 (fù) for sound."*

彳 is one half of a walking graph, and the 說文 says so where it defines 行 (*xíng* — to walk): **人之步趨也。从彳从亍** — *"a person's stepping and hurrying. From 彳 and 亍 (chù)."* 行 is a crossroads; 彳 is its left-hand stride.

And 复, the half Xu Shen calls phonetic, is not phonetic only — he glosses it **行故道也**, *"to travel the old road."* Its oracle-bone form sets a **foot beneath a dwelling**: going out from where you live and coming back to it. *(复 is not among the 711 characters the Laozi uses, so the repository's 說文 does not carry it; that gloss comes from outside this repo.)*

**So 復 holds two feet** — one inside 复, and 彳 wrapped around it when the bronze script built the fuller graph. It is the most pedestrian word in the chapter, and **the road it walks is one it knows**.

**命 (*mìng*) — a voice over someone kneeling**

Our 說文: **使也。从口从令** — *"to send. From 口 (kǒu) and from 令 (lìng)."* 使 (*shǐ*) in classical Chinese is both *to send* and *the one sent* — an envoy.

Each part, one level down:

- **口 (*kǒu*)** — 說文: **人所以言食也。象形** — *"what a person speaks and eats with. A pictograph."* A mouth.
- **令 (*lìng*)** — 說文: **發號也。从亼、卪** — *"to issue a call. From 亼 (jí) and 卪 (jié)."*
- **亼 (*jí*)** — the assembling sign: three strokes converging. Read either as an inverted 口, or as a **hand-bell rung to call people in**.
- **卪 (*jié*, also written 卩)** — **a kneeling figure.** *(說文 itself reads it as 瑞信也, "an auspicious tally"; the kneeling-person reading is modern palaeography, and neither component is among the Laozi's 711.)*

**And the two characters were one.** In the oracle-bone script **命 and 令 are the same graph** — the gathering-sign above, the kneeling figure below. A chief sounds a bell to call people in; whoever receives the order kneels to take it. **口 was added during the Western Zhou bronze period**, and by the small seal script the two had separated into 命 and 令.

So the scene inside 命 is complete: a summons, a gathering, someone on their knees, and **a mouth** — the utterance made explicit, which is the whole of what 命 adds to 令.

**Which is why the compound is not a redundancy.** 復 walks a road it already knows. 命 is what was said, out loud, over the one who was sent down it.

**A note on how physical the chapter's returning is.** Two lines above 是謂復命 stands 各復歸其根, and 歸 (*guī*) is 說文 **女嫁也。从止，从婦省** — *"a woman marrying. From 止 (zhǐ — a foot), from an abbreviated 婦 (fù — woman)."* **復歸 carries three feet between them**, and it arrives at 根 (*gēn*), which is 說文 木株也 — a **stump**. Nothing in this passage is abstract until the chapter names it: the returning is walked, and the place walked to is a piece of wood in the ground.

### What the commentators make of it

Both read it as coming back to what one was allotted to be, and both reach for the same compound:

> **王弼 (*Wáng Bì*, d. 249 CE):** 歸根則靜，故曰靜。靜則復命，故曰復命也。復命則得**性命**之常，故曰常也
> *"Returning to the root is stillness, hence 'stillness.' Stillness is 復命, hence '復命.' 復命 is attaining the constancy of 性命 (xìng mìng — inborn nature and allotted span), hence 'the ever-present.'"*

> **河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*, Han):** 言安靜者是為復還**性命**使不死也
> *"The still one is returning to their 性命, so as not to die."*

**Both link 復命 to 常 through constancy** — which is what the next line does too, so the commentary and the text agree on the joint.

**But 性 (*xìng* — inborn nature) has zero occurrences in the Tao Te Ching.** 性命 is the vocabulary of a later philosophical settlement, read back onto a text that does not use it. The reading may be right; the word is theirs. An English that says *nature* here would be translating the commentary. *(`CLAUDE.md`: a commentator's gloss is not the text.)*

### The reading the commentators do not take

**復命 is also standard classical Chinese for an envoy reporting back after completing a commission** — and 說文 glosses 命 with 使, the envoy word itself.

Under that reading the chapter's shape is exact. Things 作 (*zuò* — 說文 起也, *"to rise"*): they are sent out. They come to their fullest. They 復: they return, and what they hand back is the charge they went out with.

Neither commentator takes it. The graph and the idiom do, and the chapter's own 作 → 復 architecture fits it without strain. **This edition records both rather than choosing**, because nothing in the Chinese forces the choice and the difference is real: one is *resuming what you always were*, the other is *discharging what you were given to do*.

### What is set aside

**destiny, fate** — both make 命 a script settled before the actor arrives. 命 is spoken *to* someone, at a moment, and it can be reported back on. *Fate* additionally carries the Greek Moirai and Christian providence into a text with neither.

**mandate** — 天命 (*tiān mìng* — the Mandate of Heaven)'s word, the Zhou warrant-to-rule. **天命 has zero occurrences in this book.** Using it here imports a 天 that grants and withdraws, which is the overlay `tian-天.md` exists to strip.

**"restoring destiny," "the system's command"** — the Source table's literal glosses, and the second is mechanistic in exactly the way `CLAUDE.md` names as this edition's own besetting temptation.

**"returning to the source," "returning to the origin"** — 復命 is not 歸根 restated in cosmic terms. 根 (*gēn*) is 說文 木株也, a **stump**; the chapter has already given the return its concrete name and is now giving it a different one. Collapsing the two throws away the reason there are two.

### Working register

| Form | Chapters | English |
|---|---|---|
| 是謂復命 | 16 | This is called *(the chosen phrase)* |
| 復命曰常 | 16 | *(the same phrase)*, repeated verbatim as the subject |

**The phrase must survive repetition**, because 是謂復命。復命曰常 is the chapter's tail-head device (頂真 *dǐng zhēn*): the last word of one line opens the next. Whatever is chosen is said twice, adjacently, and a phrase that reads well once may not read well immediately again.

### What was set aside, and why it took four tries

***returning to the allotted course*** — a *course* is a path you run, and the chapter's event is a thing **finishing** one, not rejoining it. 命 is not a path: everything the graph gives is a moment — a bell, a gathering, someone kneeling, a mouth. The phrase also sat comfortably in a sermon, which is the hymn test failing.

***returning the charge* · *returning the message*** — both take 復命 **transitively**, handing the commission back, which is the envoy idiom and is genuinely available. But **neither commentator reads it that way**, and `CLAUDE.md`'s tie-breaking order puts the classical commentaries above this edition's ethos and above poetic intuition. Both also need an antecedent the chapter never supplies — *which* charge, *which* message — and *the message* additionally carries the English sense of *the moral*.

***returning to what is*** — the worst of the four, and the reverse check catches it in an unusual form. *What it is* is already **自然 (*zì rán* — of itself)**'s English at ch 25 (道法自然 → *"the Tao models itself on being what it is"*), and 自然 is not merely another term: **chapter 51 sets it against 命 in a single clause** — 夫莫之命而常自然, *"no one 命s it, and it is always 自然."* Rendering 命 with its own antonym's English would collapse the book's antithesis from the inside.

### Left open

**命's verb is unsettled one chapter over.** Ch 51's 夫莫之命而常自然 reads *"no one commands it"* — but *command* is 令 (*lìng*)'s English at ch 32, in the identical 莫之X而 frame, and the two characters were **one graph** before the Western Zhou split them. See `ming-命.md` and `WORKLIST.md` T2-29.

**And the commentators' reading is not the only one the book supports.** 復命 is standard classical Chinese for an envoy reporting back from a commission, and 說文 glosses 命 with 使 — the envoy word. The chapter's 作 → 復 architecture fits that without strain. This edition follows the commentators and records the other reading rather than burying it: one is *resuming what you always were*, the other is *discharging what you were given to do*, and nothing in the Chinese forces the choice.

## 敢 (Gǎn) — The Forward Press to Take

*Say "gahn," dipping. Ten lines across seven chapters, and 不敢 (bù gǎn) is the third of the book's three treasures.*

**Locked: 敢 → "push / venture" — the forward press to take.** *(Never "dare," "dares," "dared," "daring.")*

Every English Tao Te Ching renders 不敢 (*bù gǎn*) as **dare not**. It is the natural English, and it inverts the book.

In modern English, *he did not dare* means **he was afraid**. Chapter 73 says the opposite in six characters:

> 勇於**敢**則殺，勇於**不敢**則活
> *"Courage in 敢 kills. Courage in **not**-敢 lives."*

There is a **courage of not-敢**. Whatever English carries the word must be able to be brave. *Not daring* cannot: it makes the third of Chapter 67's three treasures sound like timidity, in a chapter that two lines earlier says 慈故能勇 — *"tenderness, and so you can be brave."*

### The graph: a hand, a weapon, and a boar

The oracle-bone accounts read 敢 as **a hand holding a hunting implement, going after a wild boar** (豕, *shǐ*). Its oldest sense is *to hunt, to pursue*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* keeps that and abstracts it slightly: 敢，**進取**也 — *"敢 is to advance and take."*

**So 敢 is appetite, not bravery.** It is the forward motion of someone going after a thing in order to have it. Courage may accompany that; it is not what the word means.

**And it may be 爭's cousin.** On one account the bronze-script form of 敢 is built on **爭** (*zhēng* — two hands pulling at a single object), with 甘 supplying only the sound. If that holds, the two characters are relatives — and so are the book's two great refusals. 不爭 declines to pull at a thing two hands already hold. 不敢 declines to go after a thing no hand holds yet. Between them they cover the whole of wanting. *(Scholars differ on the graph; recorded as a resonance, not a proof. See `zheng-爭.md`.)*

### 不敢 is a politeness formula, not a confession

Classical Chinese uses 不敢 the way English once used *I should not presume*:

- 不敢高攀 — *"I could not presume upon your attention."*
- 愧不敢當 — *"I am ashamed, and do not deserve it."*

This is the language of **declining to help yourself to something**. Nobody in these phrases is frightened; they are being well-mannered about appetite.

### The book supplies its own gloss

Chapter 67 names the third treasure as 不敢為天下先, then four lines later says what abandoning it looks like: 舍後且先. 王弼 glosses the particle 且 in three characters — 且猶**取**也, *"且 is like 取, **to grab**."*

So what 敢 does to 先 (*xiān* — the front) is **grab at it**. 不敢 is not-grabbing. The verdict on the person who does grab is 死矣 — *that is death* — which is not a sentence anyone passes on the merely timid.

### Where it stands

| Chapter | Chinese | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 使夫智者**不敢**為也 | and the knowers never push to act |
| 30 | **不敢**以取強 | never pushes on to seize dominance |
| 64 | 而**不敢**為 | and never pushes them |
| 67 | **不敢**為天下先 ×2 | never pushing to be first in the world |
| 69 | 吾**不敢**為主，而為客 · **不敢**進寸，而退尺 | does not venture to act as host · does not venture an inch forward |
| 73 | 勇於**敢**則殺，勇於**不敢**則活 | the load-bearing line |
| 74 | 孰**敢** | who would venture? |

**Seven chapters, and only Chapter 73 uses 敢 affirmatively.** Everywhere else it appears under negation, which it shares with 爭 — see that entry, where all nine occurrences are negated.

### Chapter 69 shows the register

> 吾不敢為主，而為客；不敢進寸，而退尺
> *"I do not venture to act as host, but act as guest; do not venture an inch forward, but retreat a foot."*

Host against guest is a question of **propriety** — who presides, who defers — and it has nothing to do with courage. An inch forward against a foot back is a question of **position**. Both are the vocabulary of someone choosing not to take precedence, which is what 敢 is for.

### What is set aside

**dare, daring** — the fear reading, which reverses Chapter 73 and makes Chapter 67's third treasure a confession of nerves. Forbidden outright. *(If a drafted chapter ever needs it — Chapter 73 is the only candidate, since 勇 stands beside 敢 there and blocks the timid reading — that is a `lock-ok` waiver with its reason stated, not a loosening of the lock.)*

**presume** — the exact word for 不敢, and unavailable: 恃 (*shì*) holds it at Chapters 2, 10 and 51, where 為而不恃 reads *"acts but does not presume."* **That rendering is itself loose** — 恃 means *to rely on, to lean on*, as our own source tables gloss it every time and as Chapter 34's 萬物恃之以生 (*"the countless things rely on it to live"*) requires. If 恃 is ever corrected to *rely*, *presume* comes free and should be reconsidered here. Logged in `WORKLIST.md`.

**fear, afraid, shrink, flinch, hesitate** — all import the timidity the lock exists to remove.

**bold, boldness** — right for affirmative 敢 but positive in English, where the book treats 敢 as the fault.

### Working register

| Form | Chapters | English |
|---|---|---|
| 不敢為, bare | 64 | never pushes them |
| 不敢為 + role or position | 67, 69 | never pushing to be first · does not venture to act as host |
| 不敢 + verb | 30, 69 | never pushes on to seize · does not venture an inch |
| 敢, affirmative | 73, 74 | venture |

**不敢為 is rendered as a unit at Chapter 64.** *"And never pushes them"* carries 敢為 in one verb rather than splitting it, because English *push to handle* will not stand. The chapter's contrast survives intact and is sharper for it: 輔 (*fǔ*) is the spare timber lashed alongside a cart-wheel to brace it, and a brace holds from the side where a push moves from behind. **Support them; do not push them.**

### Left open

**Whether Chapter 73's one affirmative 敢 wants a different word.** Nine of the ten occurrences are negated; the exception is 勇於**敢**則殺，勇於不敢則活 — *"courage in 敢 kills; courage in not-敢 lives."*

There, 敢 is **nominalised** after 於, so it wants a noun and the modal problem disappears — which reopens a candidate the lock otherwise excludes. **Pursue.** *"Courage in pursuit kills; courage in not pursuing lives"* reads better than *courage in pushing*, and it returns the word to its own picture: a hand with a hunting weapon, going after a boar.

Everywhere else *pursue* fails, and for two reasons worth keeping written down. **The grammar:** 敢 is an auxiliary taking a verb — 敢**為**, 敢**進**, 敢**以取** — and English *pursue* is transitive and cannot fill that slot; *"never pursuing to be first"* is not a sentence. **The semantics:** what 敢 reaches for in this book never runs away. The front of the line, the host's seat, an inch of ground, dominance. Pursuit implies quarry; 敢 is helping yourself to what is already there, which is why 不敢 became a formula of manners rather than a term of the chase.

So the boar belongs in this entry and not in the verse — the etymology justifies the reading, it does not supply the English. **The one line where it might supply the English is Chapter 73's, and that is left open until the chapter is drafted.**

**Laozi drives a wedge through a word the language keeps whole.** 勇 (*yǒng* — courage) and 敢 sit together in Chapters 67 and 73, and in ordinary Chinese they join into one compound, 勇敢 (*yǒng gǎn*), which is simply the word for *brave*. This book splits the halves and assigns them opposite values — 慈故能**勇**, *tenderness and so courage*, against 不**敢**為天下先. Chapter 73 states the split as a paradox: 勇於不敢, **courage in not-venturing**.

Whether that distinction was live in Laozi's period or is his own coinage, nothing in this book settles.

**And the sage arrives at the front regardless.** Chapter 7: 後其身而身**先** — *"placing themselves last, the sage is first."* Chapter 66: the world 樂推, gladly pushes them forward. So 不敢為天下先 forbids the **reaching**, not the **arriving** — and whether a refusal that reliably delivers the thing refused is an ethic or a technique is the same question left open at the foot of `zheng-爭.md`. The two entries end in the same place, which is probably not an accident.
entries.render: push / venture — the forward press to take

entries.body:
## 公 (Gōng) — Impartiality

*Say "gong," first tone, level and held. A word English splits into two that have nothing to do with each other: a virtue and a peerage.*

**Locked: 公 → "impartiality" where it names the quality; "lord" or "minister" where it names the office.** *(Never "duke." Reasoning below.)*

Open almost any English Tao Te Ching at Chapter 42 and you will find *dukes*. Open it at Chapter 16 and you will find *fairness*, or *equanimity*, or *the impartial*. Nothing tells the reader these are one word. So the fact the Chinese states plainly — **the office is named after the virtue** — disappears, and with it the quiet judgment the text passes every time it uses the title.

### The graph: a negation, and that is the whole of it

公 is two pieces:

- **八** (*bā*) — two strokes turning away from each other. It is the numeral eight by sound-loan, but the picture is *dividing*, and by extension **turning one's back on**.
- **厶** (*sī*) — a small self-enclosing curl. It is the original form of **私** (*sī* — private, one's own).

So the graph is *turning your back on the self-enclosing*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (~100 CE) glosses it 公，平分也 — **"公 is fair division"** — and then, unusually, names a source: 韓非曰：背厶爲公, *"Han Feizi says: turning your back on 厶 is 公."*

Han Feizi's own sentence, from 五蠹 (*Wǔ dù* — "The Five Vermin"), gives the full form:

> 古者蒼頡之作書也，自環者謂之**私**，背私謂之**公**。
> *"When Cangjie made writing in ancient times, what encircles itself he called **私**, the private; what turns its back on 私 he called **公**."*

**That 公 is a negation and not a positive quality is the finding.** English *impartiality*, *fairness*, *justice* all sound like attainments — things you build up. 公 is what is left when the curl uncurls. You do not acquire it; you stop doing the other thing.

### Why that matters at Chapter 16

Ch 16 puts 公 on a chain where each line begins with the word the last one ended on:

> 知常**容**，**容**乃**公**，**公**乃**王**，**王**乃**天**，**天**乃**道**，**道**乃久
> *knowing the ever-present is capaciousness; capaciousness is impartiality; impartiality is sovereignty; sovereignty is the open sky; the open sky is the Tao; the Tao endures.*

Every rung widens the circle beyond the self, and **公 is where the widening leaves the person.** 容 (*róng* — capaciousness) is still an inner quality, something you have. 公 is the first rung that is not about you at all, because it is defined as facing away from you. Read as *equanimity*, rung two collapses back inside the person and the ascent stalls — which is exactly why that rendering was set aside.

### The counter-term is in the book, twice

Laozi does not use 公 and 私 in one line, but he uses 私 where it counts, and it is the same negation running the other way.

> Ch 7 · 天地所以能長且久者，以其不自生 … 非以其**無私**邪？故能成其**私**。
> *"Sky and earth endure because they do not live for themselves … Is it not because they have no private self? And so they can fulfil their own."*

That is 公 stated as a paradox: the self is completed by facing away from it. And Ch 19 gives the instruction in four characters — 少**私**寡欲, *"reduce the private, diminish desire"* — where 私 sits beside 欲 (*yù* — desire) as one of the two things to thin out.

### The office, and the judgment hidden in it

Chinese titles are often meaning-transparent in a way English peerage is not. English has one good parallel: *justice* is both the virtue and the person who holds the office — Justice Roberts. Nobody hears *fair division* in **duke**.

That transparency does work in Chapter 42:

> 人之所惡，唯孤、寡、不穀，而**王公**以為稱。
> *"What people most hate is to be called orphaned, meagre, unworthy — yet kings and lords take these very words as their titles."*

The chapter is about rulers naming themselves with words of **lack**. A title that means *turned away from the private* belongs in that sentence, and the joke is sharper for it: the rank itself already says *not for yourself*, and the chapter is telling rulers to live up to their own letterhead.

And in Chapter 62 the manuscripts hand us an argument. Where the received text reads 三**公**, the Mawangdui silks write 三**鄉**, which editors read as a loan for 三**卿** (*sān qīng* — the three high ministers). **The oldest witness names the office with the plain word for a minister of state** — not with a rank. *Minister* is therefore not a modernization; it is the older reading's own word.

### What is set aside

**"Duke."** Rejected outright. It imports the European feudal ladder — duke, marquess, earl — an entire social order the Zhou did not have and did not resemble, and it severs the office from its meaning. A reader who meets *duke* in 42 and *impartiality* in 16 has no way to know they read the same character.

**"Equanimity."** Inner calm. It puts rung two of Ch 16's ladder back inside the person, halting a climb whose whole motion is outward. 公 is a direction of facing, not a state of nerves.

**"Justice."** A legal and moral frame, concerned with **desert** — what a person is owed. 公 is concerned with **whose interest** — it asks who you are facing, not who deserves what. The distinction is the difference between a courtroom and a horizon.

**"The public"** as a noun. A modern civic abstraction with a nineteenth-century shape, and it makes 公 a body of people rather than a way of standing.

*"Fairness"* is not forbidden, and it is not wrong — only thinner. Fairness is a **procedure**; 公 is a **direction**. You can execute a fair procedure while facing entirely inward.

### Working register

| The grammar | Where | Render |
|---|---|---|
| the quality, as a noun in the ladder | 16 (容乃公) | **impartiality** |
| the quality, as an adjective | — | **impartial** |
| the office, compounded with 王 | 42 (王公) | **lords** |
| the office, the three highest of state | 62 (三公) | **the three ministers** |

### Left open

**The two senses cannot take one English word, and this entry does not force them to.** Every available rendering for the office severs it from the root, so a reader of Chapter 62 will not hear what a reader of Chapter 16 hears. That is a real loss, and the glossary can only partly repair it: the entry can say *the office is named after the virtue*, but the verse cannot.

Whether that is worth a translator's note in the finished edition, or whether the loss should simply be borne, is not settled here.

**And 私 has its own drift.** It reads *"selfish"* at Ch 7 and *"the self"* at Ch 19 — and Chapter 7's paradox, 故能成其私, *"and so they can fulfil their own,"* has vanished from the English altogether, which takes the sting out of a line built to sting. 私 may want an entry of its own rather than shelter under this one.
entries.render: impartiality / impartial (the quality) · lord / minister (the office)

entries.body:
## 谷 (Gǔ) — The Valley

*Say "goo," dipping and lifting. Ten lines in seven chapters. One of the text's plainest images, and the one it trusts with the dark female.*

**Locked: 谷 (*gǔ*) → "valley," in every line, and a noun in chapter 6, as Wang Bi reads it.** *(Not "reservoir" or "basin," which hold the water a valley lets go. Not "hollow," "the void" or "emptiness," which name the gap instead of the land. Not "ravine," which belongs to 谿 (xī — a watercourse with no outlet); see* What no rule can enforce.*)* *(Not Heshang Gong's "to nourish" in chapter 6; see* Chapter 6: two commentators, two grammars. *Shalom's call, 2026-10-25.)*

### The graph: water half seen, coming out of an opening

> 谷，泉出通川爲谷。从水半見，出於口。
> *"Valley: where a spring comes out and runs through to a river is a valley. From 水 (shuǐ — water) half seen, coming out of 口 (kǒu — an opening)."* — the *Shuowen Jiezi* (the Han dictionary)

**The picture is water at the moment it comes out of the land.** In the oracle bones and the bronzes the graph is the same: broken strokes of water above, and an opening below. The broken strokes are water not yet a stream, a spring just out of the hill, and the opening is the valley's mouth (the *Ziyuan*, quoted by *Handian*). The Shuowen reads it the same way: 水半見 (*shuǐ bàn jiàn* — "water half seen"), 出於口 (*chū yú kǒu* — "coming out of an opening").

**The Shuowen defines the valley by where its water goes.** The definition has three verbs, 出 (*chū* — to come out), 通 (*tōng* — to run through) and 川 (*chuān* — a river) as the place it runs to. The character directly after it in the dictionary is its opposite:

> 谿，山瀆無所通者。从谷奚聲。
> *"Ravine: a mountain watercourse with no way through. From 谷 (gǔ — valley), with 奚 (xī, used here only for its sound)."*

A 谿 (*xī* — "ravine") is a valley closed at the bottom. Both are land that water runs down, and the Shuowen separates them only by whether the water gets out. **So a valley is not where water is held. It is where water passes.**

**Xu Shen's definitions run downhill in a chain.** 川 (*chuān* — a river) is 貫穿通流水也, *"water that cuts through and flows on."* 海 (*hǎi* — the sea) is 天池也，以納百川者, *"the pool of the sky, which takes in the hundred rivers."* Spring, valley, river, sea: the receiving happens at the bottom, and the dictionary gives it to the sea. The text gives it to the sea too (below).

**The valley stands in other characters, and in one of them it holds.** 容 (*róng* — to hold) is 盛也。从宀、谷, *"to hold, as a vessel holds; from 宀 (mián — a roof) and 谷 (gǔ — valley),"* a roof over a valley. In 欲 (*yù* — to want), 俗 (*sú* — custom) and 卻 (*què* — to step back), the valley character is only the sound. Chapter 15's valley-people have 不欲盈 (*bù yù yíng* — "no wish to be full"), so the valley's sound stands in the line about it, but that is sound, not evidence, and the entry rests nothing on it.

### Ten lines, and the valley is land in every one

> *The spirit of the valley is deathless.*
>
> 谷神不死
>
> — chapter 6

> *Open, like a valley.*
>
> 曠兮其若谷
>
> — chapter 15

> *serve as the world's valley.*
> *Serve as the world's valley, and the ever-present integrity is enough at last.*
>
> 為天下谷。
> 為天下谷，常德乃足
>
> — chapter 28

> *The Tao in the world is like small valleys to the river and the sea.*
>
> 猶小谷之與江海
>
> — chapter 32

Chapter 32 reads with Guodian and silk B here. Our base text has 川谷 (*chuān gǔ* — streams and valleys).

> *The valley received the one, and so became full.*
> *The valley with no way to be full is likely to run dry.*
>
> 谷得一以盈
> 谷無以盈，將恐竭
>
> — chapter 39

> *The highest integrity seems a valley.*
>
> 上德若谷
>
> — chapter 41

> *Rivers and seas can rule the hundred valleys*
> *because they are masterful at staying below them.*
> *That is how they come to rule the hundred valleys.*
>
> 江海所以能為百谷王者，
> 以其善下之，
> 故能為百谷王。
>
> — chapter 66

**In chapters 32 and 66 the valley is not the lowest place.** Small valleys run down to the river and the sea, and it is the river and the sea that stay below. Heshang Gong (Han dynasty) on chapter 66: 江海以卑，故衆流歸之, *"rivers and seas are low, so the many streams return to them."* The oldest witness says it more plainly still. Guodian (~300 BCE) reads 以其能為百谷下 (*yǐ qí néng wéi bǎi gǔ xià* — "because they can be below the hundred valleys"). Wang Bi (d. 249) on chapter 32: 川谷之求江與海，非江海召之，不召不求而自歸者, *"streams and valleys seek the river and the sea, but the river and the sea do not summon them; unsummoned and unsought, they return of themselves."* Heshang Gong on the same line uses the Shuowen's own verb: 如川谷與江海相流通也, *"as streams and valleys and the river and the sea flow through to one another."*

So the valley's lowness is a slope's lowness. It is low because it is on the way down. That is why the valley gives water and the sea takes it in.

**In chapter 39 the valley fills, and the line after warns against wanting to stay full.** The verb is the vessel's, not the valley's: the Shuowen defines 盈 (*yíng* — full) as 滿器也, *"a full vessel."* Wang Bi: 清不能為清，盈不能為盈，皆有其母以存其形, *"clearness cannot make itself clear, fullness cannot make itself full; each has its mother, by which its form is kept."* Heshang Gong reads the warning line as a paradox: 谷當有盈縮虛實，不可但欲盈滿無已時，將恐枯竭不為谷, *"a valley must have filling and shrinking, emptiness and fullness; it cannot only want to be full without end, or it will dry out and stop being a valley."* A valley full the whole year is a lake. Chapter 15 says the same of the people it is likened to: 保此道者不欲盈, *"those who keep the Tao safe like this do not want to be full."*

**In chapter 15 the valley is wide and open to the sky.** The Shuowen defines 曠 (*kuàng* — wide, bright) as 明也，从日廣聲, *"bright; from 日 (rì — the sun), with 廣 (guǎng — broad) for sound."* Heshang Gong: 曠者寬大，谷者空虛，不有德功名，無所不包也, *"'Wide' means broad and large; 'valley' means empty. It claims no integrity, achievement or name, and there is nothing it does not enfold."* *Open* carries the width and the light together.

**In chapter 41 the valley keeps nothing to itself.** Wang Bi on 上德若谷 (*shàng dé ruò gǔ* — "the highest integrity seems a valley"): 不德其德，無所懷也, *"it does not count its integrity as integrity; there is nothing it holds close."* 懷 (*huái* — to hold to the breast) is what the valley does not do. What comes into it goes on.

### The valley's company: the soil, and no shame in it

**The valley stands beside 辱 (*rǔ* — soiling, disgrace) twice.** Our base text reads chapter 28 as 知其榮，守其辱，為天下谷 (*zhī qí róng, shǒu qí rǔ, wéi tiān xià gǔ* — "know the glory, hold to the disgrace, serve as the world's valley"). In chapter 41 the line after the valley is 大白若辱 (*dà bái ruò rǔ*), rendered "the whitest white seems soiled." The verse now reads *soiled* in both, for the reason below.

**The graph of 辱 (*rǔ*) is a hand working a field.** The Shuowen explains it with farming: 恥也。从寸在辰下。失耕時，於封畺上戮之也。辰者，農之時也, *"shame. From 寸 (cùn — a hand) beneath 辰 (chén — a farming blade; the farming season). Whoever missed the ploughing season was punished on the field's boundary. Chén is the season of farming."* The oracle-bone graph is older than that story. It shows a hand holding the blade, which many paleographers read as a shell used to cut weeds, and its first sense was *to weed* or *to till*, later written 耨 (*nòu* — to hoe) (*Handian*; *Dong Chinese*). The sources differ on what tool the blade was. They agree that the hand is in the soil. The shame is a later meaning, laid over a farmer's work.

**Both times, Heshang Gong reads the valley's *rǔ* as dirt, and says the valley is not ashamed of it.** On chapter 28: 辱以喻汚濁 … 如是則天下歸之，如水流入深谷也, *"Rǔ figures the dirty and the murky … do this and the world returns to you, as water flows into a deep valley."* On chapter 41: 上德之人若深谷，不恥垢濁也, *"the person of highest integrity is like a deep valley, and is not ashamed of grime and murk."* The Shuowen defines 垢 (*gòu* — grime) as 濁也，从土, *"murky; from 土 (tǔ — earth)."* 恥 (*chǐ* — shame) is the word the Shuowen uses to define *rǔ* itself. The commentator is saying that the valley does not take the soil as the thing it is supposed to mean.

**The older witnesses change chapter 28's pair.** Both Mawangdui silks read 知其白，守其辱，為天下浴 (*zhī qí bái, shǒu qí rǔ, wéi tiān xià yù* — "know the white, hold to the soiled, serve as the world's valley"). The pair is 白 (*bái* — white) and *rǔ*, not 榮 (*róng* — glory) and *rǔ*. Beside white, *rǔ* is a mark on a surface, as it is in chapter 41. Beside glory, it is a judgment in other people's eyes. The *Zhuangzi* quotes the stanza the same way, ravine first and then the valley with white, and goes on in the same breath: 受天下之詬 (*shòu tiān xià zhī gòu* — "take on the world's reviling"; one edition reads 垢, grime). *(Corrected 2026-10-25: this quoted the variant 垢 (*gòu* — grime) as the text. The *Zhuangzi*'s main text reads 詬 (*gòu* — reviling, shame), and records 垢 as another edition's reading.)* Wang Bi reads chapter 41 straight into chapter 28: 知其白守其黑，大白然後乃得, *"know the white, hold to the black; only then is the great white attained."* The verse follows the silks: *"Know the white, hold to the soiled, / serve as the world's valley"* (Shalom's call, 2026-10-25). `sources/variants.yaml` and `notes/manuscript.md` have the facts, and `DISCOVERIES.md` §8 the question behind the call.

In both readings *rǔ* is the valley's company, and in neither is the valley ashamed of it. The difference is whether the line names a stain or a reputation. Either way, nothing in the valley's own character passes a verdict. The valley is made of earth, and earth is not a fault.

### Chapter 6: two commentators, two grammars

**Wang Bi reads the character as a noun, and makes it nothing.** 谷神，谷中央無谷也。無形無影，無逆無違，處卑不動，守靜不衰, *"The valley's spirit is the middle of the valley, where there is no valley. It has no form and no shadow, it opposes nothing and resists nothing; it stays low and does not move, keeps still and does not fail."* The valley's spirit is the empty center between the slopes.

**Heshang Gong reads it as a verb, and the valley leaves the line.** 谷，養也。人能養神則不死也, *"Gǔ means to nourish. If a person can nourish the spirit, they do not die."* 神 (*shén* — spirit) for him is the spirits of the five organs. The dark female is the nose and the mouth, and the gate is where breath comes and goes.

**Ruled: Wang Bi's grammar, and not his emptiness.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-10-25.)* *The spirit of the valley is deathless* keeps 谷 (*gǔ* — valley) a noun. Five reasons:

- **The other nine lines.** Everywhere else in the book the character is a valley, and no one reads it otherwise.
- **The silks spell chapter 6 as they spell the land.** Both Mawangdui silks write 浴 (*yù* — to bathe) in chapter 6, the same graph they write in chapters 28, 32, 39 and 66. Those lines have rivers and seas in them, so the bathing graph there can only spell the valley (below). The scribes heard one word in all of them.
- **Heshang Gong gives no reason for 養 (*yǎng* — to nourish).** His gloss works only if 谷 (*gǔ* — valley) is heard as a different word that sounds the same, and the likeliest is 穀 (*gǔ* — grain), the book's own word in 不穀 (*bù gǔ* — "unworthy," literally "not good grain," ch 39). That is an inference, and the silks do not support it. The *Huainanzi* (139 BCE) does show the hearing was available: quoting chapter 28, it spells the valley 穀 (*gǔ* — grain). That proves the two graphs could stand for each other in the Han, which is not the same as proving chapter 6 means *nourish*.
- **A commentator's gloss is evidence, not a rendering.** Heshang Gong's breath is a reading of the Han dynasty, and a coherent one: 綿綿若存 (*mián mián ruò cún* — "unbroken, as if barely there") fits breath very well. It is still his reading, not the line.
- **The pointing test.** A valley can be pointed at. "The middle of the valley, where there is no valley" cannot, and neither can a nourished organ-spirit. Wang Bi's grammar can be kept without his metaphysics: what he does say in plain terms, 處卑不動 (*chǔ bēi bù dòng* — "it stays low and does not move"), is true of the land. The slopes stay. The water goes through.

**What Wang Bi's grammar costs.** Heshang Gong's reading gives chapter 6 a body that breathes, and the English loses that body. It also loses the one reading in which 用之不勤 (*yòng zhī bù qín* — "use it, and there is no strain") describes something a person does. A reader who wants the breath reading has it in Heshang Gong; the verse cannot carry both.

### 浴 (yù — to bathe) in the silks: a spelling, not a second word

**The Mawangdui silks write the valley as 浴 (*yù* — to bathe) almost everywhere.** It is 谷 (*gǔ* — valley) with 氵 (*shuǐ* — water) beside it. Both silks have it in every valley line that survives, with one exception: silk B writes plain 谷 (*gǔ* — valley) in chapter 39's second valley line.

**It cannot mean bathing.** In chapter 66, 百浴王 (*bǎi yù wàng* — "rule the hundred bathings") stands where every other witness has valleys, and *rivers and seas can rule the hundred bathings* is not a sentence. So the bathing graph is standing in for the valley by sound and shape. **The oldest witness writes the valley plainly.** Guodian has plain 谷 (*gǔ* — valley) in chapters 41 and 66, and 小谷 (*xiǎo gǔ* — "small valleys") in chapter 32. It does not carry chapters 6, 28 or 39. The added water may be a scribe's habit or a scribe's hearing, and no reading is built on it.

### 谿 (xī — ravine)

**The ravine stands in one chapter, twice.** Chapter 28's first stanza reads 知其雄，守其雌，為天下谿 (*zhī qí xióng, shǒu qí cí, wéi tiān xià xī* — "know the rooster, hold to the hen, serve as the world's ravine"). Its third stanza reads 為天下谷 (*wéi tiān xià gǔ* — "serve as the world's valley"). The chapter sets the closed watercourse and the open one in the same template, and the English keeps them apart with two words. It cannot keep the Shuowen's reason for the difference, which is the outlet, and so this section exists.

**The stanzas may answer each other.** The ravine's line ends 常德不離 (*cháng dé bù lí* — "the ever-present integrity never leaves you"): nothing leaves a watercourse with no outlet. The valley's ends 常德乃足 (*cháng dé nǎi zú* — "the ever-present integrity is enough at last"). Wang Bi on the ravine: 谿不求物而物自歸之, *"the ravine does not seek things, and things come to it of themselves."* That fit may be an accident of the template. It is a reason to look, and not yet a reason to conclude.

### What is set aside

**"reservoir."** It is a tank that keeps water in, and the Shuowen defines the valley by letting water out. If anything in the book is a reservoir, it is the ravine.

**"basin."** A basin is a vessel, and the vessel enters chapter 39 through 盈 (*yíng* — full, written with 皿 *mǐn*, a dish), not through the valley. The Shuowen's basin is the sea: 天池 (*tiān chí* — "the sky's pool"). A *basin* would put the sea's work on the valley, which is the confusion chapters 32 and 66 rule out.

**"hollow."** It is good English for a small valley, and its weight falls on the emptiness, the scooped-out part. Heshang Gong's 谷者空虛 (*gǔ zhě kōng xū* — "a valley is empty," ch 15) is a commentator's reading, and the land is the thing the line points at. *Hollow* also drifts toward 虛 (*xū* — empty), which has its own entry.

**"the void," "emptiness."** These are Wang Bi's 無谷 (*wú gǔ* — "no valley") made into a noun, and they label an idea where the line has a place. Both are already forbidden for 虛 (*xū* — empty).

**"the Valley."** A capital turns a place into a doctrine, and only the Tao keeps one.

**"to nourish," in chapter 6.** This is Heshang Gong's reading, argued above and set aside. *Nourish* is on the `forbidden:` list: no line where 谷 (*gǔ* — valley) stands prints it for another character.

### Working register

| Where the valley stands | English | Chapters |
|---|---|---|
| a noun, alone | *the valley* | 6 (谷神 *gǔ shén* → *the spirit of the valley*), 39 ×2 |
| counted or qualified | *valleys* | 32 (小谷 *xiǎo gǔ* → *small valleys*), 66 ×2 (百谷 *bǎi gǔ* → *the hundred valleys*) |
| after 為天下 (*wéi tiān xià* — "serve as the world's") | *serve as the world's valley*, the locked English of 為 (*wéi* — to do, to serve as) | 28 ×2 |
| after 若 (*ruò* — like, seems) | *like a valley* in a simile, *seems a valley* in a saying | 15, 41 |

### What no rule can enforce

***Ravine* is ruled out for the valley and cannot go on the `forbidden:` list.** `check_locks.py` fires on a forbidden word wherever its character stands in that chapter's Chinese, and chapter 28 holds both 谷 (*gǔ* — valley) and 谿 (*xī* — ravine). *Ravine* is the second one's English there, twice, so forbidding it for the valley would flag the correct line. Only this entry holds that distinction.

**The lock holds in this book only.** The I Ching vendors these locks as its own, and its 谷 (*gǔ*) is not always land. At its hexagram 48, 井谷 (*jǐng gǔ*) is the bottom of a well shaft, which it renders *the well's hollow*. At its hexagram 30 the character stands where its source text misprints 穀 (*gǔ* — grain). A lock that forbade *hollow* there would flag a deliberate rendering and a typo. So this entry carries `binds: [taoteching]`, and the I Ching rules its own valley.

### Left open

**What chapter 6's ruling costs.** The valley is a noun there, as Wang Bi reads it, without his emptiness. That costs Heshang Gong's breathing body, and the one reading in which the chapter's last line describes something a person does. A reader who wants the breath has it in Heshang Gong.

**What 辱 (*rǔ* — soiling, disgrace) points at.** Chapter 28 now follows the silks and reads *soiled*. Whether the text means the earth, the low place in others' eyes, or both at once is `DISCOVERIES.md` §8, and the character is owed its own entry.

**Chapter 15's valley, which the oldest witness does not have.** Guodian carries the chapter with no valley simile at all. The verse keeps *"Open, like a valley"* on the authority of both silks and every received edition (Shalom's call, 2026-10-25). What the simile adds to a series that once ran without it is a question the evidence cannot settle.

**Full, or passing through.** Chapter 39's valley receives the one and becomes full. Chapter 15's valley-people do not want to be full. The Shuowen's valley is a passage. 盈 (*yíng* — full) is what the line says, and the English keeps it. Whether the valley's fullness is a store or a flow, the water in the valley at the wet time of year and gone at the dry, is the question the image leaves for the reader.

## 廣 (Guǎng) — Broad

*Say "gwahng," dipping. Three times, in two chapters, and both times the breadth looks like its opposite or costs something to have.*

**Locked: 廣 → "broad," and "breadth" where it stands as a noun, in all three lines.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-11-15, setting aside his own call of 2026-09-07, which read "boundless" at chapter 41.)* *(Not "boundless," which takes the walls off a hall that has a roof, and is the infinite that the 極 (jí — the far end) entry forbids as "limitless." Not "reach far," which turns width into distance: "far" is 遠's (yuǎn — far). Not "vast," which is 恢恢's (huī huī — vast) at chapter 73. Not "expansive," which is a mood.)*

### The graph: a great hall, under a roof

> 廣，殿之大屋也。从广黃聲。
> *"廣 is the great hall of a palace. From 广 (yǎn — a roof), with 黃 (huáng — yellow) for sound."* — the *Shuowen Jiezi* (the Han dictionary)

**Breadth begins as a building's.** 广 is the roof, the part that marks a character as a building: it heads 府 (*fǔ* — a storehouse), 庫 (*kù* — an armoury), 廟 (*miào* — an ancestral temple). A 廣 is the widest span one roof can cover, the great hall of a palace. Character dictionaries list the graph from early Western Zhou bronzes, and give no oracle-bone form.

**Where the picture stops.** 黃 (*huáng*) gives the sound, and nothing in the word is yellow. And the hall has a roof. Its breadth is great, and it is not endless. The book's emptiness is bounded in the same way: `xu-虛.md` finds every 虛 (*xū* — empty) a container with its contents gone, *"walls still standing, nobody home."*

### Three lines, and breadth looks like lack, or is bought

> *Broad integrity seems not enough.*
> *Sturdy integrity seems slack.*
> *Substantial truth seems to waver.*
>
> 廣德若不足，
> 建德若偷，
> 質真若渝。
>
> — chapter 41

> *Tenderness, and so you can be brave.*
> *Frugality, and so you can be broad.*
> *Never pushing to be first in the world, and so you can become chief of the vessels.*
>
> 慈故能勇；
> 儉故能廣；
> 不敢為天下先，故能成器長。
>
> — chapter 67

> *Now: to abandon tenderness and grab at courage,*
> *to abandon frugality and grab at breadth,*
> *to abandon the rear and grab at the front.*
> *That is death.*
>
> 今捨慈且勇，
> 捨儉且廣，
> 捨後且先，
> 死矣！
>
> — chapter 67

**The book never offers breadth for free.** In chapter 41, the broad seems to have too little. In chapter 67, breadth is the price frugality pays for, and grabbing it without paying is death. The word names a size every time. It never names a reach, a distance or an infinity.

### Chapter 41: a hall too broad to fill looks empty

> 廣德不盈，廓然無形，不可滿也。
> *"Broad integrity does not fill. Open and formless, it cannot be filled."* — Wang Bi

> 德行廣大之人若愚須不足也。
> *"A person whose conduct of integrity is broad and great seems foolish, as though they had too little."* — Heshang Gong

**Wang Bi's paradox is a matter of capacity.** What is broad cannot be filled, and so it seems not enough. 不盈 (*bù yíng* — not full) is the valley's and the vessel's word in this book: chapter 4's 用之或不盈 (*yòng zhī huò bù yíng* — "used, it never fills") and chapter 15's 保此道者不欲盈 (*bǎo cǐ dào zhě bù yù yíng* — "those who keep the Tao safe like this do not want to be full"). The Shuowen makes 盈 a full vessel (`gu-谷.md`).

**The saying stands beside one that builds.** The next line is 建德若偷 (*jiàn dé ruò tōu* — "sturdy integrity seems slack"), and 建 (*jiàn*) is to erect. `chapters/041.md` sets the two side by side: the span of a hall, and the setting-up of a structure. Each saying pairs a thing with the look of its own lack. *Broad* keeps the hall. *Boundless* gave the line a reason for the paradox, but it had to remove the walls to do it, and the building went with them.

### Chapter 67: breadth is what frugality buys, and it lands on others

All three of the oldest readers make 67's breadth something that spreads beyond the frugal one. For Han Fei the state is broad because the people are many: 民衆則國廣 (*mín zhòng zé guó guǎng* — "when the people are many, the state is broad"). For Wang Bi the world never runs short: 天下不匱，故能廣也 (*tiān xià bù kuì, gù néng guǎng yě* — "the world does not run short, and so it can be broad"). For Heshang Gong the people have enough to live on: 民日用廣矣 (*mín rì yòng guǎng yǐ* — "the people's daily means are broad"). The full passages are in `jian-儉.md`.

**"Broad" leaves open what is broad:** a household, a state, the people's means. *"Reach far"* answered that question wrongly twice. It put the breadth on the frugal one's own range, and it turned width into distance. Distance is 遠's word: 遠曰反 (*yuǎn yuē fǎn* — "going far means returning," 25), 深矣，遠矣 (*shēn yǐ, yuǎn yǐ* — "deep, and far," 65), 不遠徙 (*bù yuǎn xǐ* — "not move far away," 80).

The new line also keeps chapter 67's parallel audible: *"Tenderness, and so you can be brave. / Frugality, and so you can be broad."*

### What is set aside

- **"Boundless."** Chosen for chapter 41 on 2026-09-07 because it explains the paradox: there is no edge to arrive at, so the broad seems not enough. The explanation costs the picture. 廣 is a roofed hall, and Wang Bi's 不可滿 (*bù kě mǎn* — "cannot be filled") is about how much the hall holds, not about a missing edge. *Boundless* is also the infinite that `ji-極.md` keeps out of the book as *limitless* and *infinite*, and it fails the hymn test (*boundless love*). At chapter 67 it fails outright, since frugality makes no one boundless.
- **"Reach far," "reach."** Distance, not width. *Far* is 遠's in three chapters, and *the far end* is 極's. *Reach* stands for other characters in ten lines.
- **"Vast."** 天網恢恢 (*tiān wǎng huī huī* — "nature's net is vast") at chapter 73. Two characters would share it.
- **"Wide."** 疏 (*shū* — loose, wide-meshed) holds it in the same line of chapter 73, *"Its mesh is wide."*
- **"Expansive."** A mood or a manner, and it moves: an expansive thing is spreading. 廣 is a span that stands.
- **"Ample."** The runner-up in September. It means more than enough, which makes chapter 41 a flat contradiction (*"ample… not enough"*), and *"you can be ample"* does not stand at 67.

### Working register

| Where 廣 stands | English | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 廣德若不足 (41) | *Broad integrity seems not enough.* | an adjective on 德 (*dé* — integrity) |
| 儉故能廣 (67) | *Frugality, and so you can be broad.* | a predicate after 能 (*néng* — can), as 勇 (*yǒng* — brave) is in the line before |
| 捨儉且廣 (67) | *to abandon frugality and grab at breadth* | the object of 且 (*qiě* — to grab, in Wang Bi's reading), a noun, as 勇 is *courage* in the same line |

The split between *broad* and *breadth* is grammatical, so it stays in `render:` and nothing goes in `flexions:`.

**曠 (*kuàng* — wide open) is not covered here.** Chapter 15's 曠兮其若谷 (*kuàng xī qí ruò gǔ* — "open, like a valley") is built on 廣, but 廣 is only its sound part there, beside 日 (*rì* — the sun), and `gu-谷.md` reads it as *open*. The part's role in a graph is not a reading of the line.

### Left open

- **Whether chapter 41's paradox survives the plainer word.** The September call held that *broad → not enough* reads as no paradox, and that is a fair worry. The paradox now rests on a picture the reader has to supply: a hall too broad to fill looks empty. Wang Bi supplies it, and the verse does not. One English for one character is paid for at chapter 41.
- **Whose breadth, at chapter 67.** *"You can be broad"* still has the frugal one as its subject, as the Chinese does. The English no longer contradicts the commentators, but it does not say what they all saw, that the breadth spreads outward to the household, the state and the people.
- **曠 has no entry.** Its English, *open*, holds in chapter 15 by the verse and by `gu-谷.md` alone.

## 歸 · 復 · 反 (Guī · Fù · Fǎn) — Return

*Say "gway," level; "foo," falling; "fahn," dipping and rising. 歸 (guī) stands in eleven lines across eight chapters, 復 (fù) in fourteen across eight, 反 (fǎn) in four across four. Three characters for one movement, each drawing a different part of it: the arrival, the going back, the turning over.*

**Locked: 歸 → "return"; 復 → "return," and "go back" where it takes a place; the doubled verb 復歸 → "return," one verb; 反 → "returning."** *(Not "returns again," which counts the doubled verb twice and says "a second time." Not "go home": the Chinese prints no house. Not "revert" or "reversion," a lawyer's and a biologist's words. Not "the Return," whose capital makes a doctrine.)* *(Shalom's calls, 2026-11-01: 歸 keeps "return," and 復歸 reads as one verb. 反 was fixed as "returning" at chapters 25 and 40 on 2026-09-06.)*

*根 (gēn — root), the place chapter 16 returns to, is covered here.*

### The graph: a bride's feet, a step retraced, a hand turning something over

> 歸，女嫁也。从止，从婦省，𠂤聲。
> *"歸 (guī): a woman marrying. From 止 (zhǐ — a foot), from an abbreviated 婦 (fù — wife), with 𠂤 (duī) as its sound."* — the *Shuowen Jiezi* (the Han dictionary)

> 復，往來也。从彳复聲。
> *"復 (fù): going and coming back. From 彳 (chì — a step), with 复 (fù) as its sound."* — the *Shuowen Jiezi*

> 反，覆也。从又，厂反形。
> *"反 (fǎn): to overturn. From 又 (yòu — a hand), with the shape of 厂 (hǎn — a cliff) turned around."* — the *Shuowen Jiezi*

**Three pictures, one movement.** 復 (fù) is a step going back along the way it came. 歸 (guī) is a woman's feet arriving at the house she will live in. 反 (fǎn) is a hand turning something over. Read together, they are the turn, the going back and the coming to rest.

**歸 also names an ending.** The Shuowen defines the dead through it: 鬼，人所歸為鬼 (*guǐ, rén suǒ guī wéi guǐ* — "鬼 (guǐ — the dead): what a person returns to is called 鬼"). So the word that arrives also carries a life's close, and chapter 16, where everything returns to the root and the root is stillness, means it.

**Where the picture stops.** The bride in 歸 (guī) comes from a marriage custom in which a woman left her family for her husband's. The book never uses the word for marriage, and takes it for what everything does: things return to the root, the countless things return to the Tao. In the graph she is the one who moves, but the English carries none of the custom, and no line here says where anyone belongs.

### 復歸: a doubled verb, and one English verb for it

> *Things come to their fullest,*
> *Each returns to its root.*
> *Returning to the root is called stillness.*
>
> 夫物芸芸，
> 各復歸其根。
> 歸根曰靜，
>
> — chapter 16

**復歸 (fù guī) is two verbs, side by side, for one motion with two parts.** 復 (fù) is the going back, the turn of the journey; 歸 (guī) is the arrival where the thing belongs. Classical Chinese often sets two verbs of motion together like this, where English uses one verb, sometimes with a particle: *go back*, *come home*. The compound stands in seven lines: 14, 16, three times in 28, and 52.

**It is not "return return," and it is not "return again."** 復 (fù) can be an adverb elsewhere, *again*, and an English that takes it so writes *"returns again."* But *again* says *a second time*, a repetition, and the commentators read the phrase as a going **back to the beginning**:

> 各返其所始也。
> *"Each goes back to where it began."* — Wang Bi, on chapter 16

> 言萬物無不枯落，各復反其根而更生也。
> *"It says the countless things all wither and fall; each goes back to its root, and lives anew."* — Heshang Gong, on chapter 16

Wang Bi glosses the two verbs with one, 返 (fǎn — go back). Heshang Gong keeps two, and adds the cycle: what goes back down to the root comes up again. Neither reads a second return.

**English "return" is built the way 復歸 is.** It is *re-* (back) and *turn*: a turning back that arrives. One English word holds both beats, so nothing the Chinese says is lost and nothing it doesn't say is added. **What the English drops is the sound of the doubling.** The Chinese strikes twice, and the English once. Spelling both beats out, as in *"each goes back, returns to its root,"* was weighed and declined (Shalom's call, 2026-11-01): faithful, but it breaks the line's music, and in chapter 28's triple it would break it three times.

### Chapter 16 uses every part of the movement in five lines

> *Go totally empty.*
> *Hold steadily to stillness.*
> *The countless things arise together,*
> *Relying upon this, I observe their return.*
>
> 致虛極，
> 守靜篤。
> 萬物並作，
> 吾以觀復。
>
> — chapter 16

The chapter names the whole cycle with 復 (fù) alone: *"I observe their return."* Wang Bi glosses it 以虛靜觀其反復 (*yǐ xū jìng guān qí fǎn fù* — "with emptiness and stillness I watch their going back and coming round"), and then, in his own words, 萬物雖並動作，卒復歸於虛靜 (*wàn wù suī bìng dòng zuò, zú fù guī yú xū jìng* — "though the countless things all stir and act, in the end they return to the empty and still"). Then the chapter's verse moves through the parts in order: 復歸其根, the doubled verb, the going back that arrives; 歸根, the arrival alone, *"returning to the root"*; and 復命, *"returning to what is given"* (`glossary/fuming-復命.md`).

So one English verb runs the length of a chapter in which the Chinese uses three forms. That is a cost, and the reason the distinctions live here rather than in the verse: the motion in chapter 16 is one motion, and the English keeps it whole.

### 歸 alone: arriving, and where a thing comes to rest

| Line | English | What 歸 does |
|---|---|---|
| 歸根曰靜 (16) | *Returning to the root is called stillness.* | arrives at the root |
| 若無所歸 (20) | *as if with nowhere to return* | has no place to arrive |
| 萬物歸焉 (34) | *The countless things return to it.* | the countless things come to the Tao |
| 德交歸焉 (60) | *their integrity converges and returns* | two integrities arrive together |
| 誠全而歸之 (22) | *Return to them.* | see *Left open* |

**The sense of arriving where one belongs is strongest in chapter 20.** The speaker is *"listless, as if with nowhere to return,"* and the commentators hear a homeless person. Wang Bi: 若無所宅 (*ruò wú suǒ zhái* — "as if having no dwelling"). Heshang Gong: 我乘乘如窮鄙，無所歸就 (*wǒ chéng chéng rú qióng bǐ, wú suǒ guī jiù* — "I am adrift, like the poor and lowly, with nowhere to go to and settle"). The verse keeps *return*, because the line prints no dwelling: the commentators' house is their reading of 歸 (guī), and a reading is not a rendering (`process/principles/commentary-is-not-a-rendering.md`). A reader of this entry can carry the dwelling back into the line.

**In chapter 34, 歸 is coming to someone.** 萬物歸焉而不為主 (*wàn wù guī yān ér bù wéi zhǔ* — "the countless things return to it, and it does not act as their master"). Heshang Gong: 萬物皆歸道受氣 (*wàn wù jiē guī dào shòu qì* — "the countless things all return to the Tao and receive breath"). It is the word a people uses for turning to a ruler they trust, and the chapter's point is that the Tao takes no rule from it.

### 復 alone: going back

| Line | English | What 復 does |
|---|---|---|
| 吾以觀復 (16) | *I observe their return* | names the whole cycle, as a noun |
| 復命 (16) | *returning to what is given* | `glossary/fuming-復命.md` |
| 民復孝慈 (19) | *the people return to devotion and tenderness* | goes back to a state |
| 復守其母 (52) | *return and hold fast to our mother* | goes back, then holds |
| 使民復結繩而用之 (80) | *Let the people go back to keeping their records in knotted cord* | goes back to a practice: *go back* |
| 復眾人之所過 (64) | *brings the crowd back from where they have gone too far* | made causative: *bring back* |
| 正復為奇 (58) | *The straight turns crooked* | the adverb, *in turn*, carried by *turns* |

**Chapter 58 is the one line where 復 (fù) is plainly the adverb.** 正復為奇，善復為妖 (*zhèng fù wéi qí, shàn fù wéi yāo* — "the straight in turn becomes crooked, the good in turn becomes monstrous"). The English carries it in the verb, *"turns crooked,"* which is where *in turn* belongs. Elsewhere, 復 (fù) is the going back, and the step in its graph is doing the work.

### 反: the turning over

| Line | English | What 反 does |
|---|---|---|
| 遠曰反 (25) | *going far means returning* | the far point turns back |
| 反者道之動 (40) | *Returning is the Tao's movement;* | the Tao's own motion |
| 與物反矣 (65) | *and turns back together with things* | turns back, alongside |
| 正言若反 (78) | *Words on the mark seem like their opposite.* | a word turned over: *opposite* |

**The hand in the graph is turning something over, and both senses follow from it.** Turned around, a thing goes back the way it came: *returning* (25, 40, 65). Turned over, a thing shows its other side: *opposite* (78). The English follows the grammar. Chapter 25 shows the first in a chain: 大曰逝，逝曰遠，遠曰反 (*dà yuē shì, shì yuē yuǎn, yuǎn yuē fǎn* — "great means departing, departing means going far, going far means returning"). The Tao goes out until it comes round.

### 根 (gēn — root)

> 根，木株也。从木艮聲。
> *"根 (gēn): the stump of a tree. From 木 (mù — tree), with 艮 (gèn) as its sound."* — the *Shuowen Jiezi*

**The root is a stump in the ground, something you could stand on.** It stands in five lines across four chapters: the dark female's gate is *"the root of sky and earth"* (6); things *"return to the root"* (16, twice); *"The heavy is the root of the light"* (26); *"the Tao of deep roots, firm base"* (59). It is covered here because chapter 16 makes it the place the whole movement arrives, and because its one temptation is the same as the family's: to turn something you could point at into an abstraction.

**"The source" is set aside for it.** A source is where water starts, and a principle in English. The root is a stump, the low dark part of a tree that the visible part comes back down to.

### What is set aside

**"Returns again."** It reads 復 (fù) as the adverb and says *a second time*, where both commentators read the doubled verb as going back to the beginning. One English verb, *return*, already carries the turn and the arrival.

**"Go home," "home."** The belonging sense of 歸 (guī) is real: the bride arriving, Wang Bi's *dwelling* at chapter 20. But the Chinese prints no house, and *home* would put one in a line that has only a stump in the ground (Shalom's call, 2026-11-01). The sense stays in this entry, where a reader can find it. *Going home* is also English shorthand for dying in a Christian register, and the line would carry that too.

**"Revert," "reversion."** A legal term for property coming back to an owner, and a biologist's term for a throwback. Both are the wrong kind of return: one a transaction, one a regression.

**"The Return," capitalized.** The capital makes a doctrine of a movement (`CLAUDE.md` standing rule 3).

**"Eternal return."** Nietzsche's phrase, with its whole argument attached. Chapter 16's return is not a recurrence of the same events. It is things going back down to where they began.

**"Cycle."** A label for what the chapter performs. The verse shows things rising, ripening and going back down; naming it a cycle replaces the watching with a concept (`process/principles/perform-dont-label.md`).

**"The source," for 根 (gēn — root).** Above.

### Working register

- **歸 (guī)** → *return*, in every line, as a verb (*"returns to it"*) or a gerund (*"Returning to the root"*).
- **復歸 (fù guī)** → *return*, one verb, in all seven lines: 14, 16, 28 ×3, 52.
- **復 (fù)** → *return* as a verb or noun; *go back* where it goes back to a practice (80); *bring back* where it is causative (64); carried by *turns* where it is the adverb *in turn* (58).
- **反 (fǎn)** → *returning* (25, 40); *turns back* (65); *opposite* (78), where the thing turned over shows its other side.
- **根 (gēn)** → *root*.

### What no rule can enforce

**The forbidden list holds only in 歸 (guī)'s chapters.** The build reads a pairing's chapters from its first character, so *home*, *revert*, *the Return* and the rest are held in chapters 14, 16, 20, 22, 28, 34, 52 and 60. In chapters where only 復 (fù) or 反 (fǎn) stands, 19, 25, 40, 58, 64, 65, 78 and 80, those rulings are held by this entry and by the reader. *Home* could not be forbidden there in any case: chapter 72 prints *homes* for another character.

**"Again" cannot be forbidden.** Other characters print it legitimately, as 又 (yòu — again) does in chapter 1's *"Dark, and dark again."* The ruling against *"returns again"* for 復歸 (fù guī) is held here.

### Left open

- **反 (fǎn) at chapter 40 may be reversal as well as return.** 反者道之動 (*fǎn zhě dào zhī dòng*) reads *"Returning is the Tao's movement,"* and the graph's turning over supports a second reading: things turn into their opposites, as chapter 58 says, *"The straight turns crooked."* The English chose *returning* on 2026-09-06, and chapter 25's *"going far means returning"* supports it. The other reading is real, and the line holds both.
- **Chapter 22's 誠全而歸之 (*chéng quán ér guī zhī*)** reads *"Return to them,"* an instruction to the reader. The Chinese may say that wholeness truly *returns to* the one who bends: *"truly whole, and it returns to them."* `glossary/quan-全.md` has the argument; the line has not been revisited with this entry.
- **Heshang Gong's cycle and Wang Bi's beginning are two readings of chapter 16.** In Heshang Gong, things go back to the root *and live anew*; in Wang Bi, they go back to where they began. The verse's *return* holds both, and the entry leaves them both standing.
- **The witnesses for the family's lines are unrecorded** in `sources/variants.yaml`, beyond chapter 16's 觀其復 (*guān qí fù* — "observe their return") and chapter 19's 民復孝慈 (*mín fù xiào cí* — "the people return to devotion and tenderness"). The Guodian bamboo carries chapter 16's first couplet only, so the silks are the oldest witnesses for its return.

## 貴 & 賤 (Guì, Jiàn) — Prized & Cheap

*Say "gway," falling, and "jyen," falling. 貴 stands twenty-two times across fifteen chapters; 賤 three times, always beside it. Two words off a price list, and the book uses them to price people, bodies, the Tao, and itself.*

**Recommended: 貴 → "prize" as a verb · "prized" as a state · 賤 → "cheap," and "cheapen" as a verb.** *(Not "noble" and "humble," which moralize a price. Not "precious," which belongs to 貨 (huò — goods)'s forbidden list and makes the book's own prizing sound like the jewels it refuses. Not "honor," which is 尊 (zūn — honor)'s, covered here.)* **One flexion:** *status* in 富貴 (fù guì — wealth and rank) at chapter 9. **Covered:** 尊 → *honor*.

### The graph: two cowries, and a price

> 貴，物不賤也。从貝，臾聲。
> *"貴: a thing that is not cheap. From 貝 (bèi — a cowry shell), with 臾 (yú) for the sound."* — Shuowen (說文, *Shuōwén* — Xu Shen's dictionary, c. 100 CE)

> 賤，賈少也。从貝，戔聲。
> *"賤: small in price. From 貝 (bèi — a cowry shell), with 戔 (jiān) for the sound."* — Shuowen

**Both characters stand on the cowry, the shell that was money.** The Shuowen defines each by the other and by the market: 貴 is *not cheap*, 賤 is *a low price*. Neither carries a moral. Before they were said of people they were said of goods on a stall, and that is the ledger this book keeps open. When it calls rulers 貴 and their root 賤, it is pricing them, not praising and blaming.

### Twenty-two lines, and what the book prices

**Goods, which the sage refuses to price.** 不貴難得之貨 (*bù guì nán dé zhī huò*) at chapters 3 and 64, *"does not prize rare goods"* (`glossary/huo-貨.md`).

**The body, which the sage prices highest.** Chapter 13's 貴大患若身 (*guì dà huàn ruò shēn* — "prize great trouble as your own body") and 貴以身為天下 (*"one who prizes their body as a way to serve the world"*); chapter 75's 貴生 (*guì shēng* — "to prize life").

**The Tao, and the mother.** 貴食母 (*guì shí mǔ* — "I prize feeding from the mother," 20); 尊道而貴德 (*"honor the Tao and prize integrity,"* 51); 貴此道 (*"prize this Tao,"* 62).

**People, high and low.** 侯王無以貴高 (*"rulers with no way to be prized and high,"* 39); 則我者貴 (*"those who pattern themselves on me are prized,"* 70); 不自貴 (*"does not prize themselves,"* 72).

> *So the prized takes the cheap as its root,*
>
> 故貴以賤為本，
>
> — chapter 39

> *neither honor nor debase them.*
> *And so, they become the most honored in the world.*
>
> 不可得而貴，不可得而賤。
> 故為天下貴。
>
> — chapter 56

**Chapter 56 is the hardest line, and it decides the English.** Those who have the dark sameness cannot be made near or far, benefited or harmed, 貴 or 賤, and so they become the world's 貴. The chapter takes the price scale off them and then prices them highest. Wang Bi says why the two halves of the line go together: 可得而貴，則可得而賤也, *"whatever can be prized can be made cheap."* To be beyond pricing is to be beyond cheapening, and the only English that shows the scale is a price word on both sides:

> *You cannot prize them nor cheapen them.*
> *And so they are the most prized in the world.*

*Honor* and *debase* break the scale into two vocabularies, one of rank and one of coinage, and they hand the second line's 貴 an English, *honored*, that chapter 62 needs for 尊.

### What the commentators did with it

**Heshang Gong makes chapter 39's root a body of work.** 言必欲尊貴，當以薄賤為本，若禹稷躬稼，舜陶河濵，周公下白屋也, *"it says: if you must want to be honored and prized, take the thin and cheap as your root, as Yu and Ji farmed with their own hands, Shun made pots on the riverbank, and the Duke of Zhou bowed to men in thatched houses."* The cheap is not a humility to be felt. It is the work the founders did.

**At chapter 13 the commentators split, and the English takes Wang Bi.** Wang Bi: 無以易其身，故曰貴也, *"having nothing to trade one's body for: that is why it says 貴."* Prizing is refusing to sell. Heshang Gong reads the character as a different word: 貴，畏也, *"貴 means to fear,"* and the line becomes *fear great trouble as your own body*. The verse's *prize* follows Wang Bi and the price graph; Heshang Gong's fear is recorded here, not lost (`process/principles/divergence-stays-open.md`).

**On chapter 72 Wang Bi says what self-prizing does.** 自貴則物狎厭居生, *"prize yourself, and things crowd in and weary of dwelling and living."* The ruler who prices themselves high presses on the people's houses to be seen doing it (`notes/reading.md`, chapter 72).

### 尊 (zūn — honor)

> 尊，酒器也。从酋，廾以奉之。
> *"尊: a wine vessel. From 酋 (qiú — matured wine), with 廾 (gǒng — two hands) raising it."* — Shuowen, which goes on to name the six 尊 of the *Rites of Zhou* used *"in the rites of sacrifice and of receiving guests."*

**尊 is a wine vessel lifted in both hands to an ancestor or a guest.** The honor is a gesture: raising something up to someone. 貴 is a price; 尊 is a lifting. 尊 stands three times. Chapter 51 sets the two side by side, 萬物莫不尊道而貴德 (*"the countless things all honor the Tao and prize integrity"*) and 道之尊，德之貴 (*"this honoring of the Tao, this prizing of integrity"*). Chapter 62's 美言可以市尊 (*měi yán kě yǐ shì zūn* — "fine words can buy honor") makes it a thing traded at market, the book's own irony on the vessel.

**It lives in this entry because chapter 62 needs it kept apart from 貴.** The same chapter that says fine words *buy honor* (尊) says the Tao is 為天下貴, the world's most prized. Our English gave both *honor*, in one chapter, and the chapter's point, that what can be bought is not what the world truly prizes, went flat. *Revere* at chapter 51 also sat a step toward the hymnal; *honor* is plainer and fits the vessel raised in both hands.

### What is set aside

**"Noble" and "humble."** The moralized pair: a price turned into a rank of soul. Chapter 39 read *"the noble is rooted in the humble"* until 2026-09-05, and the line became a sermon on humility where the Chinese is a ledger. *Humble* is also the virtue-word this edition refuses for 後 (*hòu* — behind) (`glossary/xian-hou-先後.md`).

**"Lowly."** The same moral pricing as *humble*, in a softer coat.

**"Precious."** On 貨's forbidden list, because it makes chapter 3's line circular (*"do not treasure the precious"*). Spent on 貴 at chapters 70, 72 and 75, it also makes the sage's prized few and prized life sound like jewels. Those three chapters hold no 貨, so no check sees it; the ruling holds by argument (see below).

**"Honor," "honored," for 貴.** 尊's word. At chapters 56 and 62 it broke the price scale and collided with 尊 in the same chapter.

**"Value," "valuing."** An abstraction off the same root as *valuable*, and a third verb where *prize* serves. Chapter 51's *value integrity* beside *revere the Tao* made the pair sound like two kinds of regard; the Chinese makes it one regard and one gesture.

**"Debase."** Coinage, but of metal clipped and alloyed: a corruption. 賤 is only a low price, and *cheapen* says so.

**"Esteem."** Polite, abstract, and opinion rather than price.

### Working register

| line | grammar | English |
|---|---|---|
| 不貴難得之貨 (3, 64) · 貴大患 · 貴以身 (13) · 貴食母 (20) · 不貴其師 (27) · 貴左 · 貴右 (31) · 貴德 (51) · 貴此道 (62) · 不自貴 (72) · 貴生 (75) | a verb, with an object | *prize* (51, 62, 72, 75 recommended; 27 Shalom's call, 2026-11-19) |
| 侯王無以貴高 · 故貴以賤為本 (39) · 則我者貴 (70) · 德之貴 (51) | a state | *prized* · *prizing* (51, 70 recommended) |
| 為天下貴 (56, 62) | a state, as a noun | *the most prized in the world* (recommended) |
| 不可得而貴，不可得而賤 (56) | verbs, the scale | *prize… cheapen* (recommended) |
| 以賤為本 (39) ×2 | a state | *the cheap* |
| 富貴 (9) | a fixed pair | *wealth and status* — flexion |
| 貴言 (17) | a verb | *prize their words* (Shalom's call, 2026-11-19) |
| 尊道 · 道之尊 (51) · 市尊 (62) | 尊 | *honor* · *honoring* (51 recommended) |

### What no rule can enforce

***Precious* is ruled out for 貴, and cannot be forbidden yet.** Chapters 70, 72 and 75 print it now, and forbidding it would report all three at once. Once they change, it can join this list.

***Honor* is ruled out for 貴, and can never be forbidden here.** 尊 shares chapters 51 and 62 with 貴 and legitimately prints it. The distinction lives in this entry and in the reader.

***Value* and *debase* likewise**, while chapters 51 and 56 still print them.

***Noble* is ruled out for 貴, and can never be forbidden here.** 君子 (*jūn zǐ* — the noble one) reads *the noble* at chapter 31, which also holds 貴 (貴左, 貴右).

### Left open

**Nine lines would change, and each is Shalom's call.** (Chapter 27 took *prize* on 2026-11-19.) 51 ×2 (*revere… value* → *honor… prize*; *reverence… valuing* → *honoring… prizing*); 56 ×2 (*honor nor debase* → *prize nor cheapen*; *the most honored* → *the most prized*); 62 ×2 (*honor this Tao* → *prize this Tao*; *the most honored* → *the most prized*); 70 (*precious* → *prized*); 72 (*hold themselves precious* → *prize themselves*); 75 (*hold life precious* → *prize life*).

**Heshang Gong's fear at chapter 13 is a real reading.** 貴，畏也 makes the line a warning, *fear great trouble as you fear for your body*, and the rest of the chapter, which is about shock at favor and disgrace, can carry it. The verse follows Wang Bi and the price. A reader of the chapter should know the line has two faces.

**The book prices the sage's few (70) by the inference it refuses for goods (3, 64).** Scarcity confers value on understanding and not on jade. `glossary/huo-貨.md` holds this tension, and the English should not resolve it: *prized* at 70 and *does not prize rare goods* at 64 now use one verb, so a reader can see the book doing both.
