## 和 (Hé) — Harmony

*Say "huh," rising. Eight appearances across seven chapters in our base text, and a ninth in chapter 55's verse, which follows the older copies there. The word for different things sounding together, and in this book it can be heard: in sound and tone, in a breath, and in an infant who cries all day.*

**Locked: 和 → "harmony," and as a verb "harmonize"; "settle" at chapter 79.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-11-18.)* *(Not "dim" at chapters 4 and 56, which is a commentator's word for the line, not the line's. Not "peace," a stillness, where 和 is a sound. Not "balance," two weights held level, where 和 is many voices. Not "blend," which ends where the parts can no longer be told apart, and that is the work of 同 (tóng — the same), the word the book sets beside it.)* **Settled within it:** chapter 55 follows Guodian and silk A, *"Harmony is called the ever-present"* (Shalom's call, 2026-11-01), and chapter 79 reads *settle*.

### The graph: pipes in tune, a mixing pot, and a mouth that answers

**Three graphs wrote one word, and each pictures a different way of bringing differences together.**

**The oldest is 龢**, which stands on the oracle bones and on Western Zhou bronzes: 龠 (yuè — a set of bamboo pipes bound side by side) with 禾 (hé — a grain stalk) for its sound. Zhou bells call themselves 龢鐘 (*hé zhōng* — "harmonious bells"). The *Shuowen* defines it by tuning:

> 龢，調也。从龠禾聲。讀與和同。
> *"龢: to tune. From 龠 (yuè — pan-pipes), with 禾 for sound. Read the same as 和."* — the *Shuowen Jiezi* (the Han dictionary)

**The second is 盉**, a bronze vessel for mixing drink, with 皿 (mǐn — a vessel) for meaning: 盉，調味也 (*hé, tiáo wèi yě* — "盉: to blend flavors"). The same 調 (tiáo — to tune, to adjust) defines both: pipes brought into tune, flavors brought into one taste.

**The third is the graph the book writes**, 口 (kǒu — a mouth) with the same 禾 for sound:

> 和，相譍也。从口禾聲。
> *"和: to answer one another. From 口 (kǒu — mouth), with 禾 for sound."* — the *Shuowen Jiezi*

譍 is an old form of 應 (yìng — to answer, to respond). **The mouth is a reply, and 相 (xiāng — one another) makes it a reply in both directions.** 和 needs at least two: a voice and the voice that answers it.

**Where the picture stops.** 禾 is in all three graphs for its sound, so there is no harvest or grain in the meaning. And the dictionary's *answer* is a voice answering a voice in song, not one person answering another's question; ch 73's 善應 (*shàn yìng* — "masterful at answering") is where the book uses 應 itself.

### Eight lines, and the harmony in them can be heard

> *Sound and tone harmonize each other,*
> *Front and back follow each other.*
>
> 音聲相和，
> 前後相隨。
>
> — chapter 2

> *When kin are out of harmony, devotion and tenderness appear.*
>
> 六親不和，有孝慈；
>
> — chapter 18

> *The countless things carry yin on their backs and embrace yang with their arms, and the breath within makes harmony.*
>
> 萬物負陰而抱陽，沖氣以為和。
>
> — chapter 42

> *It cries all day and never goes hoarse — this is harmony at its utmost.*
> *Harmony is called the ever-present.*
> *Knowing harmony is called clear-seeing.*
>
> 終日號而不嗄，和之至也。
> 知和曰常，
> 知常曰明。
>
> — chapter 55

The second and third lines follow Guodian and silk A, which read 和曰常，知和曰明 (*hé yuē cháng, zhī hé yuē míng*); the Chinese above is our base text (`notes/manuscript.md`).

> *Settle a great grudge*
> *and some grudge always remains.*
> *How could that count as masterful?*
>
> 和大怨，
> 必有餘怨；
> 安可以為善？
>
> — chapter 79

And twice, in chapters 4 and 56, 和其光 (*hé qí guāng* — "harmonize its light"), quoted in its own section below.

**Where 和 stands without an object, it is something heard or breathed.** In chapter 2 it is sound and tone. In chapter 42 the breath makes it. In chapter 55 it is an infant's crying, and Heshang Gong says what makes the cry harmony:

> 赤子從朝至暮啼號聲不変易者，和氣多之所致。
> *"The newborn wails from dawn to dusk and its voice does not change: an abundance of harmonious breath brings this about."* — Heshang Gong, on chapter 55

The graph's pipes are breath brought into tune, and its mouth is a voice that answers. That the book's own lines keep landing on breath and voice is a reason to keep an English with music in it, not proof that every 和 is music: chapter 18's is a household, and chapter 79's is a grudge.

### Chapter 55: harmony is the ever-present, and it is a voice that does not strain

**In the oldest reading, harmony is not a step on the way to the ever-present. It is the ever-present.** And the harmony named is the one just shown, an infant who cries all day and never goes hoarse. The chapter does not reach for a cosmic principle. It points at a voice that is used all day and never forced.

**Wang Bi read the received chain and collapsed it into the same claim:**

> 物以和為常，故知和則得常也。
> *"Things take harmony as their ever-present; so to know harmony is to gain the ever-present."* — Wang Bi, on chapter 55

**The chapter then shows harmony's opposite**, two lines on: 心使氣曰強 (*xīn shǐ qì yuē qiáng* — "when the heart drives the breath, that is called strong"). Heshang Gong describes the loss: 和氣去於中，故形體日以剛強也 (*hé qì qù yú zhōng, gù xíng tǐ rì yǐ gāng qiáng yě* — "the harmonious breath leaves the middle, and so the body grows harder and stronger by the day"). **Harmony is the breath left undriven**, and *strong* is what the breath becomes when it is pushed (`glossary/qi-氣.md`, `glossary/qiang-強.md`).

### Chapters 4 and 56: the light is harmonized, not dimmed

> *It blunts the sharpness, untangles the knots,*
> *harmonizes its light, is the same as the dust.*
>
> 挫其銳，解其紛，
> 和其光，同其塵。
>
> — chapter 4

> *Blunt the sharpness, untangle the knots.*
> *Harmonize your light, be the same as the dust.*
> *This is called profound sameness.*
>
> 挫其銳，解其紛。
> 和其光，同其塵。
> 是謂玄同。
>
> — chapter 56

**These are the only two lines in the book where 和 takes an object, and the English keeps the book's word in both.** The tradition's English has long said *dim* or *soften* here, and so did this translation until 2026-11-18. *Dim* was considered at length and decided against (Shalom's call), so that a commentator's word does not stand in for the character and warp what the line says.

**Dim comes from Heshang Gong, and his own gloss shows how it got into the line:**

> 雖有獨見之明，當和之使闇昧，不使曜亂。
> *"Though one has the clarity of seeing alone, one should harmonize it, making it dark and dim, and not let it dazzle and confuse."* — Heshang Gong, on chapter 56

**He keeps 和 as the verb and gives the dimming as its result**, with 使 (shǐ — to make, to cause): harmonize it, and so make it dim. To render the line *dim* is to keep his result and drop the verb. On chapter 4 he says the same, 當知闇昧 (*dāng zhī àn mèi* — "one should know how to be dark and dim").

**Wang Bi does not dim the light at all:**

> 和光而不汙其體，同塵而不渝其真。
> *"It harmonizes with the light and does not soil its substance; it is the same as the dust and does not alter its truth."* — Wang Bi, on chapter 4

> 無所特顯則物無所偏争也。
> *"When nothing is specially displayed, things have nothing to contend over."* — Wang Bi, on 和其光, chapter 56

**For Wang Bi the light is not lessened. It is no longer set apart from the light around it.** Chapter 4's verse takes his subject, the Tao, for these four lines (`chapters/004.md` → Notes). *Dim* would have given the Tao Heshang Gong's verb, an instruction he wrote for a person.

**Why *dim* was set aside:**

- **It is a commentator's word in the verse** (`process/principles/commentary-is-not-a-rendering.md`). One commentator gives it as a result, and the other does not give it.
- **It carries a verdict the Chinese does not.** *Dim* judges the light as too much and lessens it. 和 describes a relation between the light and what is around it (`process/principles/no-verdict-the-chinese-lacks.md`).
- **It cut chapter 55 from chapter 56.** Chapter 55 ends: knowing harmony is called 明 (míng — clear-seeing). The next chapter says 和其光, harmonize the 光 (guāng — outward light), and 光 and 明 are the pair chapter 52 sets side by side (`glossary/ming-明.md`). In the Chinese, two chapters in a row bring harmony to light. With *dim*, chapter 55's clear-seeing was followed by an order to go dark.
- **It hid one word of a pair.** 和其光 and 同其塵 are harmony and sameness side by side (the next section), and *dim* left the reader only the second.

*Own*, which stood in both lines, went with *dim*: it was there to steer it, and 其 (qí — its, your) is enough.

**The cost, paid openly.** *Harmonize* is a long Latinate word beside *blunt* and *untangle*. The plain instruction *dim* gave at once, do not outshine, is now something the reader has to think through. *Harmonize your light* can sound like the language of a wellness retreat, the hymn test's modern cousin. Both commentators read the line toward not standing out, and the English keeps that only by implication.

### 和 and 同: the book puts side by side a pair others set against each other

**Before the Han, 和 and 同 (tóng — the same) were already a known contrast.** In the *Zuozhuan*, Duke Jing of Qi says that only his favorite is in harmony with him, and his minister Yanzi answers that the man is only the same:

> 和如羹焉。水火醯醢鹽梅，以烹魚肉。
> *"Harmony is like a soup: water, fire, vinegar, pickled meat, salt and plums, to cook fish and meat."* — the *Zuozhuan*, Duke Zhao, year 20

> 若以水濟水，誰能食之？若琴瑟之專壹，誰能聽之？同之不可也如是。
> *"If you add water to water, who could eat it? If the zithers played a single note, who could listen? That is why sameness will not do."* — the *Zuozhuan*, Duke Zhao, year 20

The soup is 盉's picture, and the zithers are 龢's. The *Analects* puts the same pair into one line: 君子和而不同，小人同而不和 (*jūn zǐ hé ér bù tóng, xiǎo rén tóng ér bù hé* — "the noble person harmonizes and is not the same; the small person is the same and does not harmonize").

**The Laozi does both, in order, and names the whole by the second word:** 和其光，同其塵。是謂玄同 (*hé qí guāng, tóng qí chén. shì wèi xuán tóng* — "harmonize the light, be the same as the dust. This is called profound sameness"). Wang Bi reads the two halves as a matched pair: do not stand out above, do not hold yourself apart below. Whatever the book means by putting the two words together, the English can show the pair only if both words are visible, and with *harmonize* they are.

### What the commentators did with it

**Heshang Gong reads chapter 2's 相和 as call and answer:** 上唱下必和也 (*shàng chàng xià bì hè yě* — "when the one above sings, the one below must sing in answer"). That is the *Shuowen*'s 相譍, and later dictionaries give this sense its own reading, *hè*, falling: to join in a song, to answer it. *Harmonize each other* holds both a call and its answer and two notes sounding at once.

**Wang Bi reads chapter 18's harmony as something that happens without being made:** 若六親自和，國家自治，則孝慈、忠臣不知其所在矣 (*ruò liù qīn zì hé, guó jiā zì zhì, zé xiào cí, zhōng chén bù zhī qí suǒ zài yǐ* — "if the six relations were in harmony of themselves, and the state in order of itself, then devotion, tenderness and loyal ministers would not know where they were"). The virtues appear only once the harmony is gone.

**Heshang Gong reads chapter 79's 和 as an answering of accounts:** 殺人者死，傷人者刑，以相和報 (*shā rén zhě sǐ, shāng rén zhě xíng, yǐ xiāng hé bào* — "whoever kills dies, whoever wounds is punished: so they answer and repay each other"). His 相和 is the dictionary's 相譍 again, this time between a wrong and its penalty. That is the ledger *settle* stands inside (`notes/translation.md` → *Ch 79 · 和 → "settle"*).

### What is set aside

**"Peace."** A stillness, where 和 is a sound: the infant in chapter 55 is crying all day. *Peace* also carries the modern compound 和平 (*hé píng* — "peace"), and fails the hymn test outright: *the peace that passes understanding*.

**"Balance."** Two weights held level on a scale. It is the reading most often laid over chapter 42's yin and yang, and the line does not say that yin and yang counterweigh. It says the breath makes harmony. 和 holds many things, the soup's six flavors and the band's many notes, not two. Levelling is 均 (jūn — to even out) at chapter 32 (`chapters/032.md` → Notes).

**"Blend."** Yanzi's cook does blend, and *blends its light* would be good idiomatic English for not standing out. It is set aside because a blend ends where the parts can no longer be told apart, which is 同's work, and chapters 4 and 56 put 同 in the next three words: *blends its light, is the same as the dust* would say one thing twice where the Chinese says two. The glossary has also set *blend* aside twice already, for 混 (hùn — mixed) and for 沖 (chōng — empty), as a cook's word for something done on purpose (`glossary/hun-混.md`, `glossary/chong-沖.md`).

**"Union," "unity," "oneness."** These are what 和 is not. The *Zuozhuan* defines harmony against sameness, and a harmony made one has lost its voices. *Union* is also the English of 合 (hé — to join), the same sound in chapter 55: 牝牡之合 (*pìn mǔ zhī hé* — "the union of female and male").

**"Concord" and "accord."** Latinate, and both are agreements between parties. *Accord* was set aside for 順 (shùn — to run with the current) at chapter 65 for being bilateral where the Chinese is not (`notes/translation.md` → *Ch 65 · 大順*). 和 is not an agreement reached. It is a sound.

**"Reconcile" and "reconciliation" at chapter 79.** More literal than *settle*, and they step out of the ledger the chapter is built from: grudge, remainder, tally, score.

**"Dim" and "soften" at chapters 4 and 56.** Heshang Gong's result, given as the verb, with a verdict on the light the Chinese does not carry (above).

**"Gentle."** Heshang Gong's compound 和柔 (*hé róu* — "harmonious and soft") pulls 和 toward a manner. *Gentle* is already set aside for 柔 (róu — soft) as a material quality made into praised conduct (`glossary/rou-柔.md`), and 和 is not a manner at all.

### Working register

| Line | English | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 音聲相和 (2) | *Sound and tone harmonize each other* | a verb, made mutual by 相 (xiāng — each other) |
| 六親不和 (18) | *When kin are out of harmony* | the negated state, as a noun |
| 沖氣以為和 (42) | *and the breath within makes harmony* | the noun, what the breath makes |
| 和之至也 (55) | *this is harmony at its utmost* | the noun |
| 和曰常，知和曰明 (55, after Guodian and silk A) | *Harmony is called the ever-present. / Knowing harmony is called clear-seeing.* | the noun, named and known |
| 和其光 (4, 56) | *harmonizes its light* (4), *Harmonize your light* (56) | the verb with an object |
| 和大怨 (79) | *Settle a great grudge* | the verb with an object, inside the ledger; recorded as a flexion |

**No adjective is needed.** The book never uses 和 to describe a thing as *harmonious*; it names harmony or does it.

### What no rule can enforce

**"Union" and "unite"** are ruled out for 和 and cannot go on the `forbidden:` list: 合 (hé — to join) stands in chapter 55, and *union* is its English there.

**"The same," "one" and "oneness"** belong to 同 (tóng — the same) at chapters 4 and 56 and to 一 (yī — one) at chapter 42, which share chapters with 和.

**"Soften"** is ruled out for 和 at chapters 4 and 56, and cannot be forbidden because 柔 (róu — soft) and 弱 (ruò — yielding) stand in chapter 55, where a verb from them may one day print it. The gate keys on which characters are in a chapter, and cannot tell these apart (`process/principles/ruling-and-enforcement-are-two-facts.md`).

### Left open

- **Whether the Laozi answers the *Zuozhuan*'s ranking.** The book sets 和 and 同 side by side and names the practice by 同, the word Yanzi and the *Analects* rank below 和. That may be an answer to them, or two common words that fell together. The dates of the *Analects* and the *Zuozhuan* are not settled closely enough to say which way any influence ran, and this entry claims only the pairing.
- **Chapter 2 hears a chord where Heshang Gong hears a reply.** *Harmonize each other* can hold call and answer, but an English reader will most likely hear two notes sounding at once. 應 (yìng — to answer) is spoken for at chapter 73, so the more exact *answer each other* is not free.
- **How the old copies write 和** at chapters 2, 18, 55 and 56, whether with the pipes, the mouth, or another graph, is not recorded in `sources/variants.yaml`. Nothing in the English turns on it, but a 龢 in the Guodian slips at chapter 2 would put the pipes in the book's oldest copy of its sound-and-tone line.
- **The *Shuowen*'s line for 龢 was read online**, since the vendored selection holds only the characters the Laozi prints. One transcription gives it as 謂也 (*wèi yě* — "to call") for 調也 (*tiáo yě* — "to tune"), likely a copying slip, since 調 is the word 盉's line shares. Duan Yucai's edition would settle it.
- **Chapter 55's Source table keeps the base text**, 知和曰常，知常曰明, while the verse follows Guodian and silk A. A reader of the Chinese alone meets the chain; the oldest reading lives in the verse and the notes (`notes/manuscript.md` → Ch 55).

flexions.why: the chapter is one ledger, grudge to surplus to tally to score, and settle is the verb for 和 that stays inside it

## 混 (Hùn) — Mixed

*Say "hoon," falling. Three lines across three chapters, and every one of them describes the Tao or the people who kept it.*

**Locked: 混 → "mixed," and as a verb "mix."** *(Not "chaos" or "chaotic," not "undifferentiated," not "blend" or "merge." Not "muddy" either, which is 濁's, but that ruling no check can hold. See the last section but one.)*

The book never uses 混 for a mess. Three things that cannot be seen, heard or touched mix into one (14). The ancients who were masterful in service were mixed, like muddy water (15). Something mixed and complete was there before sky and earth (25). Each time, 混 is praised. It is how the Tao is, and how those who held to it were.

### The graph: a river in flood

> 混，**豐流也**。从水昆聲。
> *"混 is an abundant flow. From 水 (shuǐ — water), with 昆 (kūn) for the sound."* — 說文解字

A river in flood carries everything along with it: silt, leaves, branches, whatever it has picked up on the way. The mixing is what a full flow does, not a fault in it. 混 is a water word, and ch 15 makes that visible by setting it beside 濁 (*zhuó* — muddy water).

**Two other spellings of the same word stand in the witnesses.** Both Mawangdui silks write the bare sound element, 昆, at ch 25. 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*)'s text prints 渾 (*hún*) at ch 15, and 說文 defines 渾 by 混: 渾，**混流聲也**, *"渾 is the sound of a 混 flow."* Both are recorded in `sources/variants.yaml` as variants of spelling, not of meaning. 渾 also stands in our own base, once, at ch 49.

### What the book does with it

**Ch 14 — three become one.** 視之不見…聽之不聞…搏之不得…此三者不可致詰，故混而為一, *"Look, but you cannot see it… Listen, but you cannot hear it… Reach, but you cannot touch it… These three defy comprehension. Therefore, they mix into one."* 河上公 glosses the verb plainly: **混，合也**, *"混 means to join."* 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) gives the reason they cannot be pulled apart: 無狀無象，無聲無響, *"no shape, no image, no sound, no echo."* What has no edges cannot be kept separate.

**Ch 15 — the last of seven likenesses.** The ancients were careful, hesitant, dignified, loosening, solid, open, and 混兮其若濁, *"Mixed, like muddy water."* 王弼 on all seven: 凡此諸若，皆言其容象不可得而形名也, *"every one of these 'like's says that their bearing cannot be given a shape or a name."* The likeness is the point: 若 (*ruò* — like) holds 混 and 濁 apart even as it sets them side by side. 河上公 reads 濁 as a manner, not a state of the water: 濁者不照然也，與衆合同，不自尊, *"濁 is not shining; joining with the crowd, being the same as them, not holding oneself high."*

**Ch 25 — mixed, and already whole.** 有物混成，先天地生, *"Something mixed and complete, born before sky and earth."* 混成 is a paradox in two characters: undivided, and finished. 王弼: 混然不可得而知，而萬物由之以成，故曰混成也, *"mixed, it cannot be known, and yet the countless things are completed through it; so it says 混成."* 河上公: 謂道無形，混沌而成萬物, *"it means the Tao: formless, 混沌 (hùn dùn — mixed and unbroken), it completes the countless things."*

**What the three lines share is unknowability.** Mixed is why the three of ch 14 defy comprehension, why the ancients of ch 15 cannot be read, and why ch 25 goes on to say 吾不知其名, *"I do not know its name."* A thing whose parts cannot be told apart cannot be named. The book does not count that as a defect.

### Is 混 the opposite of 清?

**No. The book's opposite of 清 (*qīng* — clear) is 濁, and 混 stands beside 濁 rather than being it.** Ch 15 runs a single turn across two lines: 混兮其若濁。孰能濁以靜之徐清, *"Mixed, like muddy water. Who can be muddy, and by stilling it slowly come clear?"* 混 is likened to the muddy water, and the muddy water, left still, comes clear. 混 stands at the start of the turn and 清 at its end, but nothing in the book makes them rivals.

**The book praises both ends.** 混 is one of the seven likenesses for the ancients. And 河上公, glossing ch 25, the chapter of 混成, calls the same Tao clear: 道清淨不言, *"the Tao is clear and clean, and does not speak."* He holds it mixed and clear in one chapter.

**Two chapters put them in sequence.** 混 is how the three become one (14: 混而為一), and the one is what makes the sky clear (39: 天得一以清, *"Sky received the one, and so became clear"*). A pattern across chapters is a reason to look, not a ruling (`process/principles/distribution-locates.md`), but it points the same way as ch 15: clear is what mixed becomes when it is left still, not what defeats it. See `glossary/qing-清.md`.

### What is set aside, and why

**"chaos" and "chaotic"** are the strongest pull, and 河上公's 混沌 (*hùn dùn*) invites them. They fail twice. Chaos is a cosmology, Hesiod's void before creation, and this book's beginning is not a void: it is full, a river in flood. And chaos is disorder, where 混 is abundance, and a full river is not disordered. `glossary/luan-亂.md` refuses *chaos* for 亂 (*luàn* — disorder) on its own grounds.

**"undifferentiated"** is a philosopher's word for a river's word, and it names an absence: *un-*, the differences missing. 豐流 names a presence, the flow full of everything. It also fails the pointing test. Laozi could point at a flooded river, not at the undifferentiated.

**"blend"** is something someone does on purpose, a cook's word or a tea merchant's. 混 happens of itself, the way a flood mixes. *Blend* is set aside for 沖 (*chōng*) at ch 42 too, for want of any witness behind it (`glossary/chong-沖.md`).

**"merge"** fits ch 14, where three become one, and nothing else: at ch 15 and ch 25 there is nothing being merged into anything. It also loses the water.

**"muddy"** is 濁's. Ch 15 says 混 is *like* muddy water, not that it is muddy water.

### Working register

| Chinese | English | form |
|---|---|---|
| 故混而為一 (14) | *Therefore, they mix into one* | verb |
| 混兮其若濁 (15) | *Mixed, like muddy water* | adjective, one of seven single-word likenesses |
| 有物混成 (25) | *Something mixed and complete* | adjective, paired with 成 (*chéng* — complete) |

### What no rule can enforce

**"muddy" is ruled out for 混 and cannot go on its `forbidden:` list.** 濁 stands beside 混 in ch 15 and prints *muddy* there twice.

### Left open

**渾 at ch 49.** 為天下渾其心 reads *"for the sake of the world, they let their heart go muddy."* 渾 is 混's own word, by 說文 and by 河上公's text of ch 15, but *muddy* is 濁's English. The chime with ch 15 is real in the Chinese, and it runs through 混, not through 濁. Whether ch 49 should carry *mix* rather than *muddy* is open (`WORKLIST.md` T2-63).

**The emperor without openings.** The 莊子 (*Zhuāngzǐ*) tells of 渾沌 (*Hùndùn*), emperor of the center, who had none of the seven openings everyone has for seeing, hearing, eating and breathing. The emperors of the two seas, repaying his kindness, bored one a day, and on the seventh day he died. It is the most famous story about this word, and it says exactly what this book's three lines say: what is whole and mixed is not improved by being opened up. It is also a later book's story, and this edition does not read it into the verse.

## 貨 (Huò) — Goods

*Say "hwaw," falling. Five appearances across five chapters — 3, 12, 44, 53, 64. Three of them are the same four-character phrase, and that phrase carries one of the book's sharpest political arguments.*

**Locked: 貨 → "goods." · 難得之貨 → "rare goods."** *(Not "treasure," not "the precious," not "wealth.")*

---

### Scarcity is a fact; the value is conferred

Chapter 3 says 不貴難得之貨，使民不為盜 — *"do not prize 難得之貨, and the people do not become thieves."* The line is a causal claim about **what a ruler does**, and the standard English quietly destroys it:

> *"By not valuing **the precious**, no one becomes a thief."*

If the goods are *already precious*, the advice is circular. **Do not prize the prized.** It shrinks to a shrug about austerity, and the ruler drops out of the sentence — which is the one place the sentence is pointing.

The Chinese does not say the goods are precious. It says they are **難得** (*nán dé* — hard to obtain), which is a fact about **acquisition**, not a verdict about **worth**. The argument runs:

> **the goods are hard to get → the ruler prizes them → people steal.**

The scarcity is a fact about the world. **The value is conferred by the prizing.** 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*, d. 249 CE) states the causation in four characters and then follows it to its end: 貴貨過用，貪者競趣，穿窬探篋，沒命而盜 — *"prize goods **beyond their usefulness**, and the greedy race for them: they tunnel through walls, rifle chests, and steal at the cost of their lives."* 貴貨過用 (*guì huò guò yòng*) is the cause, and its subject is the ruler.

河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*, Han) supplies the image, on chapter 64: 聖人不眩為服，不賤石而貴玉 — *"the sage is not dazzled into adorning themselves; does not despise stone and prize jade."* **賤 (*jiàn* — to hold cheap) and 貴 (*guì* — to prize) are both things a person does.** Stone and jade differ in what someone does about them.

---

### The graph: a shell that changes hands

貨 is 貝 (*bèi* — a cowrie shell) with 化 (*huà*) above it. 說文解字 (*Shuōwén Jiězì*, c. 100 CE): **財也。从貝化聲** — *"property. It follows 貝, with 化 as the sound."*

**貝 is a drawing of a cowrie shell**, and it is not a metaphor. Cowries were currency in the Shang and early Zhou, strung and counted, and they are why the whole vocabulary of value in Chinese is built on this one radical.

**化 is two people, one of them upside down.** 說文: 教行也。从𠤎从人 — *"teaching put into practice. It follows 𠤎 and 人."* 人 (*rén*) is a person standing; 𠤎 is the same figure inverted. The graph is **a body turning over** — transformation, one state becoming another. It is the 化 of 自化 (*zì huà* — "transform of themselves"), which chapter 37 and chapter 57 make the whole point of good government.

So even taken as a pure sound-element, 化 sits over the shell in a word for **things that circulate**. 貨 is money in motion. Goods that change hands.

### The three 貝 characters, and why English has three words for them

The book uses three characters built on the cowrie, and our English had been shuffling them.

| | 說文 | what it is | our word |
|---|---|---|---|
| **貨** (*huò*) | 財也 — *"property"* | 貝 + 化: a shell that **changes hands** | **goods** |
| **寶** (*bǎo*) | 珍也 — *"a precious thing"* | 宀 (*mián* — a roof) over 王 (jade) and 貝 (cowrie): **a hoard that does not move** | **treasure** |
| **貴** (*guì*) | 物不賤也 — *"a thing that is not cheap"* | a **position on a price scale**, paired against 賤 (*jiàn* — cheap; 說文 賈少也, *"small in price"*) | **precious · prize** |

**貨 moves, 寶 sits still, 貴 is a rating someone assigns.** They are not three words for the same idea, and the differences are exactly what chapter 3 is arguing about. Giving 貨 the word for a hoard (*treasure*) or the word for a rating (*precious*) collapses the very distinction the line depends on.

---

### Where it appears

**Three of the five are one stock phrase**, 難得之貨, always under a verb of prizing or in a list of what disables a person:

> 不貴**難得之貨**，使民不為盜 (3) — *not prizing rare goods, the people do not become thieves.*
> **難得之貨**，令人行妨 (12) — *rare goods hinder people's conduct.*
> 是以聖人欲不欲，不貴**難得之貨** (64) — *so the sage wants the not-wanting, and does not prize rare goods.*

**The other two are ordinary and concrete.** Chapter 44 sets it against the body: 身與貨孰多 — *"the self or goods, which is worth more?"* Chapter 53 puts it at the end of a list of a ruler's excesses: 財貨有餘 — *"wealth and goods in surplus"*, where 財 (*cái* — property) and 貨 form a bound compound and each keeps its own English.

**What the goods actually are** is not left to guessing. 河上公 names them on chapter 3: 好珎寶，黃金棄於山，珠玉捐於淵 — *"fine treasures; gold left in the mountain, pearls and jade abandoned in the deep."* Gold, pearls, jade. **Nobody needs jade.** That single fact decides several of the rejected renderings below.

### The thief was drooling

說文 on 盜 (*dào* — thief), the word chapter 3 says the ruler creates: **私利物也。从㳄，㳄欲皿者** — *"to take private profit from a thing. It follows 㳄 (*xián* — drool), the drooling of one who wants the dish."*

A thief, in the oldest analysis of the graph, is **someone salivating over a vessel.** The theft begins in the wanting, and chapter 3's third line says where the wanting begins: 不見可欲，使民心不亂 — *"do not display what can be desired, and the people's hearts are not thrown into disorder."* Display, then appetite, then theft. The chapter blames the first link, and the character agrees with it.

---

### What is set aside, and why

**"precious" — it is 貴's word, and it makes the line circular.** 貴 renders *precious* at chapters 70, 72 and 75, and *prize* as a verb at 20 and 64. In chapters 3 and 64 貴 is the verb standing directly over 貨, so *"do not prize precious goods"* puts one character's English on top of another and argues in a circle. **Forbidding it here is safe**: 貴 occurs in chapters 3 and 64 *only* inside 不貴, verbal both times, so no legitimate claimant for *precious* exists in either chapter.

**"treasure" / "treasures" — it is 寶's word.** 寶 has chapters 62, 67 and 69 and never shares a chapter with 貨, so the words can be kept apart cleanly. And the senses genuinely differ: 寶 is a hoard under a roof, the three 寶 of chapter 67 that one 持而保之 (*chí ér bǎo zhī* — "holds and keeps safe"). 貨 is the opposite motion.

**"scarce" — it imports a shortage the chapter denies.** *Scarce* is relational: not enough of a thing for what is wanted. But nobody needs jade. Call the goods scarce and the people's wanting becomes **natural, a real shortfall honestly felt** — and then the ruler cannot be blamed for it, which unmakes the whole stanza. Chapter 12 says the same from the other end: 腹 (*fù* — belly), the organ that **can** be satisfied, against 目 (*mù* — eye), the one that cannot. Scarcity is a fact about bellies. These chapters are about eyes. *(Secondarily: scarcity is the founding term of modern economics and drags that apparatus into a Warring States line.)*

**"wealth" — it belongs to 富 (*fù*), and to 財 in the one chapter they share.** 富 carries *wealth · wealthy · enrich* at chapters 9, 33 and 57. Chapter 44 had 貨 wearing that word and it has been swept to *goods*.

**"hard to get" / "hard to come by" — blocked, and instructively.** These are the literal sense of 難得, and they cannot be used: **"hard" is 堅 (*jiān* — rigid)'s word**, settled across chapters 36, 43, 76 and 78, where 堅強 (*jiān qiáng*) is what a corpse is. And 難's own English elsewhere is *difficult* (chapters 2, 63, 73), which will not go attributive in verse without grinding. Both routes close.

**"luxuries," "rarities," "coveted," "costly" — each puts the verdict back in the noun.** *Luxury* is Latin *luxuria*, excess, and it does the chapter's work for it: Laozi's claim is that these are ordinary goods that prizing turns into objects of theft, not that they are inherently excessive. *Coveted* collides directly with 可欲 (*kě yù* — what can be desired), which is *the desirable* two lines below in chapter 3's own triad. *Costly* is a price, and a price is conferred value.

---

### Working register

**貨 → "goods," in all five places, with no flexions** — and that, not *rare goods*, is what the frontmatter locks. **"Rare" is not 貨's rendering**; it renders 難得 (*nán dé* — hard to obtain), which as the closing section says renders no character at all. Putting *rare goods* in the `render:` field would overstate the lock and would push an unglossed Chinese phrase into the generated CSVs. Chapter 53's 財貨 is a bound compound and reads *"wealth and goods,"* 財 keeping its own word.

**難得之貨 → "rare goods," as a unit.** The phrase is lexical in classical Chinese — a **category of thing**, not a fresh description — so it takes a category name in English rather than a relative clause. That also restores something chapter 3 had lost: its three objects are 賢 (*xián* — the talented, one character), 難得之貨 (four), and 可欲 (two), so **the middle line is deliberately the heaviest**, and an English triad of neat two-word abstractions had flattened it.

**貴 keeps *prize* as its verb here.** Chapters 3 and 64 both open the phrase with 不貴, and both now read *does not prize*, matching 貴食母 (*guì shí mǔ* — "prize feeding from the mother") at chapter 20.

---

### Left open

**"Rare" renders no character.** This is the honest cost of the lock and it should not be smoothed over. 難 (*nán* — difficult) simply goes unspoken in these three lines: *rare* is a fact about **quantity**, 難得 is a fact about **acquisition**. The causal chain still runs — rare, therefore hard to obtain honestly, therefore stolen — but it runs as an inference the reader makes, not as something the line says. 王弼's thieves 穿窬探篋，沒命而盜, tunnelling through walls at the cost of their lives, are no longer visible in the English. Their labour mirrored the trader's, and that mirror is gone.

**It is gone because English will not carry it.** There is **no one-word English adjective meaning "difficult to obtain" that is not also a value word** — because in English, difficulty of acquisition is simply *how we say* a thing is valuable. That gravitational pull is what dragged three separate renderings of one phrase toward *the precious*, *rare treasures* and *precious goods*, independently, in three different chapters. **Rare** is the last word on that slope that stops before the verdict. It is not the whole of 難得, and no available word is.

**The book uses the scarcity-makes-value inference elsewhere, and does not disown it.** Chapter 70 puts the two characters in one couplet: 知我者**希**，則我者**貴** (*zhī wǒ zhě xī, zé wǒ zhě guì* — "those who know me are few; those who pattern themselves on me are precious"). 河上公 draws the link explicitly: 希，少也…惟達道者乃能知我，故為貴也 — *"希 means few… only those who have reached the Tao can know me, and therefore it is precious."*

So **the same commentator who has the sage refuse to let rarity confer value on jade (64) lets rarity confer value on understanding (70).** That is not obviously a contradiction — one is a ruler setting a price that other people will steal to meet, the other is a plain observation about how few readers there are — but the machinery is identical, and the book never says where the line falls. Anyone reading 貨 as a straightforward critique of valuing scarce things has to account for chapter 70. *(See `希` in `glossary/TRIAGE.md`, still owed an entry; whatever English it takes must not be *rare*, which is spent here.)*

**And one word here is doing a job the book does elsewhere with a whole chapter.** 貨 is goods **in circulation** — the shell that changes hands. Chapter 80 imagines a state where 有舟輿，無所乘之 (*yǒu zhōu yú, wú suǒ chéng zhī* — "there are boats and carts, and no occasion to ride them") and neighbours grow old without visiting. That is a world with no 貨 in it, because nothing is moving. Whether the book is against **prizing** goods or against **circulating** them is not settled by this character, and the two readings pull the political chapters in different directions.

## 極 (Jí) — The Far End

*Say "jee," rising. Six lines across five chapters, and the graph beneath it is a standing body.*

**Recommended: 極 → "the far end" — the point at which a thing runs out.** *(Not "limitless," not "the Absolute," not "the Ultimate," not "infinite," not "extreme," not "utmost." The compound 無極 → "the endless.")* *Two lines remain unsettled; see the close.*

極 is the late graph. The original is **亟 (*jí*)**, and in the oracle-bone script 亟 is a standing person with one horizontal stroke above the head and one below the feet — traditionally read 極于頂 (*jí yú dǐng* — "the pole at the crown") and 極于踵 (*jí yú zhǒng* — "the pole at the heel"). A figure drawn between the two things a body can touch: what is over it, and what it stands on. Bronze forms add 口 (*kǒu* — a mouth) and 又 (*yòu* — a hand).

There is no fence in the graph. There is a person at full extension, and the two places their reach runs out.

Then 木 (*mù* — wood) was added, and the same idea became a building. 說文解字 (*Shuōwén Jiězì*, c. 100 CE) on 極: **棟也。从木亟聲** — *"the ridgepole. From 木, with 亟 for sound."* The 棟 (*dòng*) is the topmost beam of a roof, the timber the rafters lean into from both slopes. Not an ornament set on top of the house: **the last structural member, the one past which there is no more house.**

A body at full stretch; a roof at its topmost beam. Both are terminal points of something extended. Both are finite, because the thing that reached them is. And neither is a boundary imposed from outside — which is what separates 極 from every English word for a limit.

### The commentators gloss it with one word, seven times

Wherever 極 appears, 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*, d. 249 CE) and 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*, Han) reach for **窮 (*qióng* — to exhaust, to use up)**:

| Chapter | Line | The gloss |
|---|---|---|
| 28 | 復歸於無極 | 王弼: 不可窮也 — *"it cannot be exhausted"* |
| 28 | 復歸於無極 | 河上公: 歸身於無窮極也 — *"return the body to what has no exhausting 極"* |
| 58 | 孰知其極 | 河上公: 禍福更相生，誰能知其窮極時 — *"disaster and fortune give birth to each other in turn; who can know the time of their exhausting 極?"* |
| 59 | 莫知其極 | 王弼: 道無窮也 — *"the Tao is inexhaustible"* |
| 59 | 莫知其極 | 河上公: 莫有知己德之窮極也 — *"no one knows the exhausting 極 of their own integrity"* |
| 25 | on 自然 | 王弼: 窮極之辭也 — *"an expression of the exhausted 極"* |
| 36 | on 柔弱 | 王弼: 柔弱同通，不可窮極 — *"the soft and the yielding alike run through; they cannot be run out to the 極"* |

Seven instances, one word. **極 is not how far a thing extends. It is where a thing runs out** — a claim about supply, not about size.

That is also what 無極 (*wú jí*) says at chapter 28. Not a thing of unbounded extent: a thing you cannot use up. A roof with no topmost beam.

### The hardest line: 致虛極

致 (*zhì* — to send all the way there) 虛 (*xū* — empty) 極 (*jí*) invites an objection that turns out to be instructive. If emptiness has no measure, then reaching its 極 is reaching the limit of the limitless.

**The objection dissolves, because 虛 in this book is never boundless.** Every occurrence is a container with its contents gone — a heart at chapter 3, a bellows at 5, hollow words at 22, a granary at 53. 說文 makes 虛 a settlement-mound, a unit of surveyed land. *(See `xu-虛.md`.)*

**And the graph closes the question. The 極 in 致虛極 does not belong to emptiness. It belongs to the person doing the emptying** — the standing body, crown to heel, at the end of its reach. The line does not measure the hollow. It measures how far you go into it.

What is left is a better difficulty, and a real one. **The verb is a travelling and the method is a subtraction.** 致 is 夊 (*suī* — a dragging foot) beneath 至 (*zhì* — to arrive); 說文: 送詣也, *"to send all the way there."* You go on foot. But 河上公 says how you go: 得道之人捐情去欲，五內清淨，至於虛極 — *"one who has gained the Tao sheds feeling and casts off desire; the five viscera are clear and still; and so arrives at 虛極."* Chapter 48 gives the same movement in the same grammar: 損之又損，以至於無為 — *"reduce, and reduce again, until arriving at non-doing."*

**You travel by taking away.** The only way to reach the far end of a hollow is to keep removing until there is nothing left to remove.

### What is set aside

**limit** — the word English reaches for first, and the reason the rest of the list is needed. A limit is a fence: a stop set from outside, marking where you are not allowed to go. 極 is the far point of a reach, measured by the reacher. The two are opposite kinds of word, and only one of them has a person in it.

**limitless** — the wrong axis. It answers *how big*, where every commentator answers *how much is left*.

**the Absolute, the Ultimate** — 極 is the load-bearing beam of a specific roof. Both import a metaphysical absolute the graph does not hold, and *the Ultimate* additionally drags in 太極 (*tài jí* — "the supreme ridgepole"), Song-dynasty cosmology reading its own system back into a Warring States word. The failure has the same shape as 一 (*yī* — one) rendered *the One*.

**infinite** — a ridgepole is finite, a body's reach is finite, and 說文 offers no other picture.

**extreme** — belongs to 甚 (*shèn* — excessive), which carries it at chapters 29 and 44. English *extreme* also means immoderation, a verdict 極 does not pass.

**utmost** — belongs to 至 (*zhì* — to arrive at), which carries it twice in chapter 55: 精之至也 and 和之至也, *"vital essence at its utmost," "harmony at its utmost."*

### Working register

**極 flexes by grammar, and the flexions are not interchangeable.**

| Form | Chapters | English |
|---|---|---|
| 無極, the compound | 28 | the endless |
| 知其極, the far point of a process | 58, 59 | where it ends |
| 極 after a verb and its object | 16 | the terminal degree of the verb, not a noun |
| 古之極, the far point of a practice | 68 | *(unsettled — see below)* |

**The line-final position at chapter 16 is grammatical, not decorative.** 致虛極 and 守靜篤 (*shǒu jìng dǔ* — "hold to stillness, 篤") are the same three-beat shape twice: verb, object, terminal degree word. 篤 (*dǔ* — steady; 說文 馬行頓遟, *"a horse's gait, halting and slow"*) cannot be a noun head — nobody arrives at the thickness of stillness — so 極 in the matching slot is doing the same adverbial work. 王弼 confirms it from the other side by binding the two into a single compound across both lines: 言致虛，物之極篤 — *"reaching emptiness is things' 極篤"* — and again 是物之極篤也. He can only pair them if they are the same kind of word.

### Left open

**Chapter 68's 古之極 is the one appearance this entry cannot place.** 是謂配天，古之極 — *"this is called being 配 (pèi — matched, as one of a pair) with 天 (tiān — sky), the 極 of the ancients."* It is not a process whose end is unknowable, and it is not adverbial. It reads as *the far point the ancients reached*, which is exactly the graph — but that line is already contested at 配天, and settling one half would settle both. *(See `tian-天.md`.)*

**And the book reaches a 極 exactly once.** Chapter 16 is the only imperative: go there. Everywhere else the word is denied — unknowable at 58 and at 59 twice, negated outright at 28. Four refusals and one instruction, and the instruction is the one addressed to a person rather than to a process. Whether that is the text distinguishing what a body can do from what a world does, or a word used loosely across a compiled book, the six lines do not say.

flexions.why: the compound 無極, where the negation turns the limit into its absence

entries.render: the far end — where a thing runs out

entries.body:
## 儉 (Jiǎn) — Frugality

*Say "jyen," dipping. Three times in eighty-one chapters, all of them in chapter 67, where it is the second of the book's three treasures. Too small for any count to find, and half of the chapter's argument.*

**Locked: 儉 → "frugality," in all three lines.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-11-15.)* *(Not "economy," which now names a nation's markets. Not "thrift," which saves and puts by, the granary's work and 嗇's (sè — conserving). Not "austerity," which spends nothing and so can broaden nothing. Not "simplicity," which is forbidden for 樸 (pǔ — the uncarved) and names a style of life, not a way of spending. Not "moderation" or "restraint," which hold back an impulse where 儉 holds back an outlay. Not "conservation," whose verb is 嗇's at chapter 59.)*

### The graph: a person, and a cord wound round

> 儉，約也。从人僉聲。
> *"儉 is 約 (yuē — to bind). From 人 (rén — person), with 僉 (qiān) for sound."* — the *Shuowen Jiezi* (the Han dictionary)

> 約，纏束也。从糸勺聲。
> *"約 is to wind round and tie. From 糸 (mì — silk thread), with 勺 (sháo — a ladle) for sound."* — the *Shuowen Jiezi*

**The Shuowen defines frugality with a picture of cord wound round a bundle.** 儉 is a person, and 約, the word Xu Shen explains it by, is thread tied tight. What is frugal is held in, the way a bundle is held together: not thrown away, and not let spill.

**Where the picture stops.** The graph itself pictures only the person. 僉 (*qiān* — "all, together") is its sound, on the Shuowen's account, and reading *gathering everything in* out of it would be making a meaning from a sound part. The cord is in the definition, not in the character.

### Three lines, and in each one frugality buys breadth

> *I have three treasures. I hold them and keep them safe.*
> *The first is tenderness.*
> *The second is frugality.*
> *The third is never pushing to be first in the world.*
>
> 我有三寶，持而保之：
> 一曰慈，
> 二曰儉，
> 三曰不敢為天下先。
>
> — chapter 67

> *Tenderness, and so you can be brave.*
> *Frugality, and so you can be broad.*
> *Never pushing to be first in the world, and so you can become chief of the vessels.*
>
> 慈故能勇；
> 儉故能廣；
> 不敢為天下先，故能成器長。
>
> — chapter 67

> *Now: to abandon tenderness and grab at courage,*
> *to abandon frugality and grab at breadth,*
> *to abandon the rear and grab at the front.*
> *That is death.*
>
> 今捨慈且勇，
> 捨儉且廣，
> 捨後且先，
> 死矣！
>
> — chapter 67

**In each line 儉 is never a lack for its own sake: it is what something wide is bought with.** The second line names the purchase, 儉故能廣 (*jiǎn gù néng guǎng* — "frugal, and so able to be broad"). The third names the failure: keeping the breadth and dropping its price. Wang Bi reads 且 (*qiě* — and, about to) as 取 (*qǔ* — to grab), 且猶取也, *"且 is like 取,"* so 捨儉且廣 is reaching straight for the wide thing without the frugality that would have paid for it.

### The middle treasure: a small thing that buys a wide one

**The three treasures share one shape, and 儉 is what shows it is a shape.** Each is a small thing that yields a large one: tenderness yields courage, frugality yields breadth, staying behind yields leadership. Each failure is the same failure: grabbing the large thing directly. 慈 (*cí* — tenderness) and 勇 (*yǒng* — courage) could be read as a paradox about the heart, and 先 (*xiān* — first) and 後 (*hòu* — behind) as a paradox about rank. **With 儉 and 廣 (*guǎng* — broad) between them, it is plainly arithmetic.** Spend little, and what you have goes far. The middle term makes the other two legible as one claim.

That is why an entry for 慈 alone left the chapter half-argued. Three occurrences put 儉 below every frequency threshold, the same way three occurrences hid 全 (*quán* — whole) until it turned out to be chapter 22's whole argument (`quan-全.md`).

### Han Fei: frugality is winter, and the breadth is the spring

Han Fei, who died in 233 BCE, is the oldest reader of this line, and his reading is seasonal before it is economic:

> 周公曰：「冬日之閉凍也不固，則春夏之長草木也不茂。」天地不能常侈常費，而況於人乎？……是以智士儉用其財則家富，聖人愛寶其神則精盛，人君重戰其卒則民衆，民衆則國廣。是以舉之曰：「儉，故能廣。」
> *"The Duke of Zhou said: 'If winter's closing-in and freezing is not firm, the growing of grass and trees in spring and summer will not be lush.' Sky and earth cannot always be lavish and always spending; how much less can people? … So when a person of good sense is frugal in using their wealth, the household grows rich; when the sage cherishes and treasures their spirit, their vital essence flourishes; when a ruler is grave about sending soldiers to war, the people are many, and when the people are many, the state is broad. Hence it is put: 'Frugal, and so able to be broad.'"* — the *Han Feizi*, 解老 (*jiě lǎo* — "Explaining Laozi")

**Frugality here is the closed ground in winter that makes the spring lush.** It passes the pointing test as few virtues do: you can point at a frozen field. It also says what 儉 spends sparingly, which is anything that can be spent: wealth, the spirit, 神 (*shén* — spirit), with its vital essence, 精 (*jīng* — vital essence), and soldiers. And Han Fei's 廣 is literal breadth: the state is broad because the people are many.

### Two commentators, two purses

> 節儉愛費，天下不匱，故能廣也。
> *"Sparing and frugal, careful of expenditure, so the world does not run short: that is how it can be broad."* — Wang Bi, on 儉故能廣

> 賦儉若取之於己也。
> *"Taxing frugally, as though taking it from oneself."* — Heshang Gong, on 二曰儉

> 天子身能節儉，故民日用廣矣。
> *"When the son of heaven can be frugal in their own person, the people's daily means are broad."* — Heshang Gong, on 儉故能廣

**Wang Bi keeps the household's purse, and Heshang Gong the ruler's,** and his frugality is a restraint on what is *taken*: tax levied as if it came out of the ruler's own pocket. Neither is ascetic. Heshang Gong also carries the word past money: two of his chapter titles are built on it, 儉武 (*jiǎn wǔ* — "frugal with arms") for chapter 30 and 儉欲 (*jiǎn yù* — "frugal with desire") for chapter 46. That is Han Fei's list again: wealth, soldiers, and what the spirit wants.

**He also names 儉's opposite, and the book has already rendered it.** On 捨儉且廣 he writes 舍其儉約，但為奢泰, *"they let go of frugal restraint and practise only extravagance and grandeur."* 奢泰 (*shē tài* — extravagance and grandeur) are the two things the sage lets go of in chapter 29:

> *Therefore the sage lets go of excess, lets go of extravagance, lets go of grandeur.*
>
> 是以聖人去甚，去奢，去泰。
>
> — chapter 29

So the English already holds the word frugality is set against, and the two chapters answer each other: the sage of chapter 29 lets go of what the grabbers of chapter 67 grab.

### 嗇 (sè — conserving) stores the harvest, and keeps its own English

> *When governing people and serving nature, nothing compares to conserving.*
> *Only conserving is called accepting early,*
>
> 治人事天，莫若嗇。
> 夫唯嗇，是謂早服；
>
> — chapter 59

**嗇 is 儉's nearest kin in the book, and a different picture.**

> 嗇，愛濇也。从來从㐭。來者，㐭而藏之。故田夫謂之嗇夫。
> *"嗇 is to cherish and hold back. From 來 (lái — wheat) and 㐭 (lǐn — granary): the wheat comes in, and the granary stores it. That is why a field-hand is called a 嗇夫 (sè fū — 'the one who stores')."* — the *Shuowen Jiezi*

Wang Bi opens chapter 59 the same way: 嗇，農夫, *"嗇 is the farmer."* Han Fei defines it by the arithmetic he uses for 儉: 多費之謂侈……少費之謂嗇, *"spending much is called 侈 (chǐ — lavishness) … spending little is called 嗇."* Heshang Gong gives it the same opposite, 治國者當愛民則不為奢泰, *"one who governs a state should cherish the people, and so not practise extravagance and grandeur."*

**So the two words share an opposite and keep separate pictures:** 嗇 is the harvest put away, 儉 the bundle tied tight. They also do different work. 嗇 is the way to govern, in a chain that runs to deep roots. 儉 is a treasure, and it is spent to buy breadth. *Conserving* is the granary's English, and it stands in chapter 59's verse. *Frugality* is 67's. One English for both would join two lines the book never puts side by side.

The family has a third member, and it is a different kind of word. 知足 (*zhī zú* — knowing you have enough) is a *knowing*: it knows where the line is. 嗇 stores, and 儉 spends little. `zhizu-知足.md` sets aside *content with little* for exactly this reason: it turns knowing enough into frugality.

### What is set aside

- **"Economy."** Once exact: the Greek word is the management of a household, which is Wang Bi's reading. In English now it names a nation's markets, and *"the second is economy"* reads as fiscal policy.
- **"Thrift."** The root is good (*thrift* is what makes you *thrive*), but the word saves and puts by: the savings bank, the thrift society, the self-improvement sermon. Putting by is the granary's work, which is 嗇's. 儉 in chapter 67 is not a reserve. It is a way of spending that makes what is spent go far.
- **"Austerity."** Self-denial for its own sake, the hair shirt and the budget cut. It fails the hardest line outright: austerity spends nothing, so it can broaden nothing, and 儉故能廣 says frugality is how you become broad. All three commentators read 儉 as economy, never as a discipline of the body.
- **"Simplicity."** Forbidden for 樸 (*pǔ* — the uncarved), whose plainness the book argues in its own chapters. And simplicity is a style of life, where 儉 is a way of spending.
- **"Moderation."** The mean between too much and too little, a Greek doctrine. 儉 is not a midpoint: it leans toward less, and the chapter sets it against grabbing, not against having too little.
- **"Restraint."** The nearest English to the Shuowen's cord: to restrain is to hold back with a tie. In English, though, restraint holds back an *impulse*, which makes it a moral self-control and a sermon word, and it drops the purse all three commentators find. 儉 holds back an *outlay*.
- **"Conservation," "conserving."** The source table's alternative gloss. *Conserving* is 嗇's in chapter 59, and *conservation* now names nature reserves.
- **"Sparing."** The commentators' own sense (節, *jié* — to be sparing, to measure out), but it is an adjective or a verb. The chapter counts its treasures as nouns, and *"the second is sparing"* does not stand.

**Why "frugality" holds.** It passes the hardest line, and in its own idiom: frugality is what makes a little go a long way, which is 儉故能廣 said in English. Its root is a harvest word as well. Latin *frugalis* comes from *frux*, "fruit, produce," and the frugal are those who make the crop last. That root keeps it a word about goods, not about the soul.

### Working register

| Where 儉 stands | English | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 二曰儉 | *The second is frugality.* | the name of a treasure, counted as a noun |
| 儉故能廣 | *Frugality, and so you can be broad.* | the condition, standing as topic, as 慈 does in the line before it |
| 捨儉且廣 | *to abandon frugality and grab at breadth* | the object of 捨 (*shě* — to let go of) |

One English, a noun every time. The three treasures stand in parallel three times over, and the English repeats as the Chinese does, so nothing goes in `flexions:`. **It is never *be frugal*:** an imperative would turn a treasure the speaker holds into advice to the reader, and the chapter never advises.

### Left open

- **Whose breadth.** All three of the oldest readings put the breadth on *other people*: Han Fei's household grows rich and his state broad with people, Wang Bi's world never runs short, and Heshang Gong's people have broad daily means. *"And so you can be broad"* keeps the frugal one as subject, as 能 (*néng* — can) does in the Chinese. It no longer turns the breadth into the frugal one's own range, but it does not say what every commentator saw: frugality's breadth goes outward, and in Heshang Gong it is the powerful sparing what they take (`guang-廣.md`).
- **The oldest graphs, and the silks.** The oracle-bone and bronze record for 儉 has not been checked for this entry. Chinese Wikisource's collated text of the Mawangdui silks reads 二曰檢 (*èr yuē jiǎn*), writing 儉's sound part with 木 (*mù* — wood) in place of 人, and 茲 (*zī*) for 慈. Neither reading is confirmed against a printed edition or recorded in `sources/variants.yaml`, so nothing here rests on them (`WORKLIST.md` T2-80).
- **嗇 has no entry.** Its English, *conserving*, holds in chapter 59 by the verse alone. A `covers:` line here would lock it beside 儉, and that is a ruling for Shalom, not for this entry (`glossary/TRIAGE.md`).

entries.body:
## 精 (Jīng) — Vital Essence

*Say "jing," level and light. Only three appearances, in two chapters — and one of the smallest footprints in this glossary hides one of its clearest inversions.*

**Locked: 精 → "vital essence" / "essence."** *(Not "primordial mass," not "soul," not "spirit," not "energy.")*

Chapter 21 rendered 其中有精 as *"within its dark depths lies the primordial mass of creation."* That is not a loose translation; it is the **precise opposite** of the character. 精 is what remains when the mass is taken **away**.

### The graph: hulled rice

精 is 米 (*mǐ* — rice) beside 青 (*qīng*), which supplies the sound and lends a sense of *fresh, pure*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (~100 CE) glosses it in a single word: **擇也** — *to select, to sift.*

The picture is **grain that has been hulled and winnowed**: the husk beaten off, the chaff blown away, the broken and the empty discarded, and what is left is the small heavy edible heart of the thing. 精 is the *result of subtraction*. Everything bulky has been removed.

That is why "primordial mass" fails so completely. **Mass is exactly what 精 is not** — mass is the husk and the chaff, the undifferentiated bulk that sifting removes. The rendering also imports Big Bang cosmology, a different overlay from the mechanistic one but the same family of anachronism, and it fails the pointing test flatly: Laozi could point at a bowl of polished rice. He could not point at a primordial mass.

Every good English sense of the word follows from the winnowing: *refined*, *concentrated*, *choice*, *precise*, *potent*. In modern Chinese 精 still carries all of them, and 精米 is still polished rice.

### The evidence — both chapters are about undiminished potency

**Chapter 55, the newborn.** 未知牝牡之合而朘作，精之至也 — *not yet knowing the union of female and male, yet quickening with life; this is 精 at its utmost.* The infant has the most 精 of anyone in the book, and has spent none of it. Nothing has been dissipated, nothing performed, nothing sought. The concentration *is* the vitality.

The same chapter then draws the line that keeps 精 from meaning merely "energy": 心使氣曰強 — *when the heart drives the 氣, that is forcing.* **氣** (*qì*) is breath-energy in motion, and it can be driven, pushed, mismanaged. 精 cannot be driven; it can only be kept or squandered. One is a current, the other a reserve. A translation that renders both as "energy" loses the whole distinction Chapter 55 is built on — and it is the distinction that makes 益生曰祥 (*to force life to increase is an ill omen*) legible.

**Chapter 21, the source.** 窈兮冥兮，其中有精；其精甚真，其中有信 — *deep and dim, and within it there is 精; its 精 is utterly real, and within it there is trust.* Here the sifting image does its cosmological work: at the bottom of the indistinct there is not a mass but a **concentrate** — the small dense real thing left when everything vague has been winnowed off. The chapter's whole descent is a sifting: through 象 (*xiàng* — image), 物 (*wù* — thing), 精, 信 (*xìn* — trust), each finer than the last.

### What is set aside, and why

**"Primordial mass"** inverts the character, as above, and dates the text to the twentieth century.

**"Soul"** is on the overlay watchlist for exactly this word. Chinese has a vocabulary for souls — 魂 (*hún*, the ethereal soul) and 魄 (*pò*, the corporeal one) — and Laozi never uses 魂 and uses 魄 once, at chapter 10, for the body's own **aliveness** (`po-魄.md`). Rendering 精 as "soul" imports a separable immortal self into a book with no such thing, and makes Chapter 55's newborn a vessel for something rather than simply a creature brimming.

**"Spirit"** carries the same freight and collides with 神 (*shén* — spirit), a different character that the text does use (6, 29, 39, 60).

**"Energy"** collapses 精 into 氣, as Chapter 55 forbids. It is also the vaguest word available in English for the most precise word in the family.

*Energy* is ruled out for 氣 (qì — breath) as well (`glossary/qi-氣.md`), so no character in chapters 21 and 55 can claim it, and the build holds the ruling. The general rule is that **a forbidden rendering must be a word no other character in those same chapters can legitimately claim**; it is what keeps *integrity* off 信's list, since 德 shares its chapters (see `glossary/xin-信.md`).

**"Semen"** deserves naming, because it is a real reading and not a foolish one: in later Daoist and medical literature 精 unambiguously means seminal essence, and Chapter 55's line about the infant's arousal invites it. We decline it for two reasons. The specialized sense is **later** than this text, and taking it here would make the passage a claim about one organ in one sex, where the point is a whole small body full of unspent life. The male-default is the text's, not the argument's. *(See the Chapter 55 manuscript note on 朘 / 全, where the same question arises in the source text itself.)*

### Working register

精 barely flexes — three occurrences, two grammatical positions:

- as the thing present in something → **vital essence** (其中有精 → "within it there is vital essence")
- when already named and referred back to → **essence** (其精甚真 → "its essence is utterly real")
- at its extreme → **vital essence at its utmost** (精之至也)

**Never** "primordial mass," "soul," "spirit," "energy," "life force."

### Left open

**Is it one word here, or two senses?** Chapter 55's 精 is unmistakably **bodily** — an infant's undissipated vitality, sitting in a line about genitals and grip strength. Chapter 21's 精 is **cosmological** — what is found at the bottom of the indistinct, before anything has a name. English "vital essence" covers both, which is convenient and may be a cheat.

The winnowing image is what argues they are one word: in both places 精 is *the concentrate left after everything loose is removed*, whether the sifting is done to grain, to a body, or to the visible world. But it is worth admitting that Laozi may simply be using a household word for *the good part* in two unrelated ways, and that our unified reading is tidier than his usage.

We leave it single, and note the seam here rather than smoothing it in the verse.

## 靜 (Jìng) — Stillness

*Say "jing," falling. Ten appearances in nine lines across seven chapters. Water that has stopped moving, so the silt goes down: the book's stillness is something that works.*

**Recommended: 靜 → "still" and "stillness," and "still" as a verb (to make still).** *(Not "tranquil" or "serene," the spa and the hymnal. Not "meditation" or anything built on it, which turns a state of water into a practice. Not "passive" or "inert," which this edition refuses for the female the book makes still at chapter 61.)* **Covered:** 躁 (zào — restless), its opposite, → *restless* and *restlessness* (Shalom's call, 2026-11-19).

### The graph: the green of new growth, and a word for contending

> 靜，審也。从青，爭聲。
> *"靜: to settle and examine closely. From 青 (qīng — the green of new growth), with 爭 (zhēng — to contend) for the sound."* — Shuowen (說文, *Shuōwén* — Xu Shen's dictionary, c. 100 CE)

**The Shuowen defines stillness as 審, close and settled attention**, the look you can give a thing only when nothing is moving: water that has cleared enough to see into. Its meaning part is 青, the color of a fresh shoot and of deep clear water, the same 青 that gives 清 (*qīng* — clear) its sound (`glossary/qing-清.md`). The two words meet twice in the book, and both times the stillness comes first and the clearness follows: 濁以靜之徐清 (*"by stilling it, slowly come clear,"* 15) and 清靜 (*"clear stillness,"* 45).

*A calibration.* 爭 is the sound part, and the Shuowen says nothing more of it. A reader of this book, whose sage *does not contend* (不爭), may notice the word for contending sitting inside the word for stillness. We do not claim the scribes meant it.

**The silks spell it by its sound.** In the collated silk text, chapters 15 and 16 write 情 (*qíng* — feeling, 青 with 心 (*xīn* — the heart)), and chapter 61 writes 靚 (*jìng* — 青 with 見 (*jiàn* — to see)). Each keeps 青 and changes the rest, the way a scribe writes a word by its sound.

### Nine lines, and stillness always does something

> *Who can be muddy, and by stilling it slowly come clear?*
>
> 孰能濁以靜之徐清？
>
> — chapter 15

> *Hold steadily to stillness.*
>
> 守靜篤。
>
> — chapter 16

> *The female always overcomes the male by stillness.*
> *By stillness she is underneath.*
>
> 牝常以靜勝牡，
> 以靜為下。
>
> — chapter 61

**In every line, stillness is a cause.** It clears muddy water (15). It is what returning to the root is called (16). It rules the restless (26). It lets the world right itself (37, 57). It overcomes heat (45). It is how the female overcomes the male (61). Nowhere is it a mood to be enjoyed or a retreat from things. Heshang Gong on chapter 15 says how it works: 誰能知水之濁止而淨之，徐徐自清也, *"who can know the water's muddiness, stop it and still it, so that slowly it comes clear of itself?"* You do not clean the water. You stop stirring it.

**Chapter 16 makes stillness the root itself.** Heshang Gong: 靜謂根也。根安靜柔弱，謙卑處下，故不復死也, *"stillness means the root. The root is calm, still, soft and yielding, low and beneath, and so it does not die again."* Wang Bi: 歸根則靜，故曰靜。靜則復命, *"returning to the root is stillness, hence 'stillness.' Stillness is returning to the given"* (`glossary/fuming-復命.md`).

### Chapter 26: what does not move governs what moves

> *The heavy is the root of the light.*
> *Stillness is the ruler of the restless.*
>
> 重為輕根，
> 靜為躁君。
>
> — chapter 26

**Wang Bi reads the pair as mechanics.** 不行者使行，不動者制動，是以重必為輕根，靜必為躁君也, *"what does not go makes things go; what does not move governs what moves. So the heavy must be the root of the light, and the still the ruler of the restless."*

**Heshang Gong gives it two animals.** 龍靜故能變化，虎躁故夭虧也, *"the dragon is still, and so it can transform; the tiger is restless, and so it dies young."* And for the ruler: 王者行躁疾則失其君位，治身躁疾則失其精神也, *"a king who acts in restless haste loses his throne; one caring for the body in restless haste loses their vital spirit."* That is the chapter's last line, 躁則失君 (*zào zé shī jūn* — "restlessness loses the ruler").

### 躁 (zào — restlessness)

> 躁，疾也。从走，喿聲。
> *"躁: hasty. From 走 (zǒu — to run), with 喿 (zào) for the sound."* — Shuowen

**躁 is a body running, in a hurry.** Its sound part draws three mouths over 木 (*mù* — a tree), and the whole graph looks like the thing it names: legs going and a racket overhead. It stands three times, all against 靜, and it lives in this entry because it never appears without stillness set against it.

**Outside this book, 躁 is someone who cannot wait.** Three early texts use it, and all three describe a person moving of their own accord, too soon and too much:

> 侍於君子有三愆：言未及之而言，謂之躁。
> *"Attending on a noble person, there are three faults. To speak before your turn has come is called 躁."* — Analects 16.6

> 吉人之辭寡，躁人之辭多。
> *"The fortunate person's words are few; the 躁 person's words are many."* — the Commentary on the Appended Phrases (繫辭, *Xìcí*), part 2

> 君子齊戒，處必掩身，毋躁。
> *"The noble fasts and keeps vigil, keeps the body covered wherever they are, and does not rush about."* — Book of Rites, Monthly Ordinances (禮記·月令), at midsummer, when 陰陽爭 (*yīn yáng zhēng* — "yin and yang contend")

**Speaking out of turn, talking too much, rushing about.** The Xici's line is this book's own pair from the other side: chapter 23's 希言 (*xī yán* — sparse speech) and chapter 5's 多言 (*duō yán* — much speech). And the midsummer rite sets 躁 against the season's heat, as chapter 45 does.

**English *agitation* means two things, and 躁 is neither.**

- ***Agitate* in its first sense is to stir or shake something**, Latin *agitare*, to drive, to set going: a solution in a flask, the water in a washing machine. That sense is transitive. Something agitates the water, and the water is moved. **躁 is not moved by anything.** The person who speaks before their turn, the tiger, the ruler who rushes off ahead of the baggage wagons: each moves itself. *The agitated*, in chapter 26, quietly makes the restless one a victim of some outside stirring, and the chapter makes them the cause of their own loss.
- ***Agitated* in its common sense is upset**: anxious, irritated, worked up. That is a mood, and in modern Chinese 躁 can carry it, in 煩躁 (*fán zào* — fretful) and 暴躁 (*bào zào* — hot-tempered). **The early texts do not.** The Analects' 躁 is not angry; it is impatient. The Xici's 躁 person is not upset; they talk too much. Read *agitated* as *upset*, and chapter 26 says that a ruler who is irritable loses the throne, a narrower and different claim.

**What 躁 is, then, is restlessness**: the want of rest, in the body and in the temper at once, moving because one cannot keep still. *Restless* is the plain English antonym of *still*, built on the same idea, and it carries both halves of the early usage, the bodily rushing and the impatience. Wang Bi already reaches for it at chapter 61: 雄躁動貪欲, *"the rooster is restless and greedy."* You can point at a restless horse, a restless child, a restless sleeper.

> *Restlessness overcomes cold; stillness overcomes heat.*
> *Clear stillness brings order to the world.*
>
> 躁勝寒，靜勝熱。
> 清靜為天下正。
>
> — chapter 45

**Chapter 45 read 躁 as *movement* until 2026-11-19, and neither commentator does.** Wang Bi: 躁罷然後勝寒，靜無為以勝熱。以此推之，則清靜為天下正也。靜則全物之真，躁則犯物之性, *"only when restlessness is spent does it overcome cold; stillness, not doing, overcomes heat. Reason from this, and clear stillness is the world's standard. Stillness keeps things whole and genuine; restlessness violates their nature."* Heshang Gong reads the first clause as a season: 春夏陽氣躁疾於上，萬物盛大，極則寒，寒則零落死亡也。言人不當剛躁也, *"in spring and summer the yang breath rushes overhead and the countless things grow great; at its height it turns to cold, and with cold they fall and die. It says a person should not be hard and restless."* For both, 躁 is still chapter 26's, a thing that wins a little and costs much. *Movement* was neutral where they are not, and it cut the tie to chapter 26.

**Settled, in all three lines (Shalom's call, 2026-11-19):**

> *Stillness is the ruler of the restless.* (26)
> *Restlessness loses the ruler.* (26)
> *Restlessness overcomes cold; stillness overcomes heat.* (45)

The physical sense at chapter 45 survives, since a body that cannot keep still keeps warm, and the reader hears chapter 26 again.

### What is set aside

**"Tranquil," "tranquility," "serene," "serenity."** The register of the spa brochure and the evening prayer, and both are moods. The book's stillness is a cause, and it clears water.

**"Meditation," "meditative," "meditate."** A practice imported from later Buddhist and modern usage. Chapter 16's *hold steadily to stillness* is not a sitting instruction; Heshang Gong's stillness is the root's.

**"Quietude."** A Quaker and Romantic word, and a sound word: stillness heard, not stillness seen. 靜 is first of all water not moving.

**"Quiet."** Sound, which belongs to 希 (*xī* — barely heard). In modern Chinese 安靜 means *quiet*; in this book, 靜 stills water. It can stay plain English elsewhere.

**"Passive," "inert," "inactive."** For chapter 61's female, this edition's first standing rule refuses any English that makes her place an assignment, and *passive* by name (`CLAUDE.md`; `glossary/pin-牝.md`). Stillness in this book overcomes; *inert* cannot overcome anything.

**"Calm."** Not wrong, and kept for other characters: 安 (*ān* — at rest) and 恬 (*tián* — placid) need it. 靜 keeps one word.

**"Movement," "motion," for 躁.** Neutral where the character is hasty, and 動 (*dòng* — to move) is the book's word for moving (5, 8, 15, 40, 50). *Movement* also cannot be forbidden, since 動 shares the 靜 chapters.

**"Agitation," "agitated," for 躁.** Forbidden, and wrong in both its senses, as argued above. As stirring, it makes the restless one moved by something else; as upset, it makes 躁 a mood. The early texts' 躁 is neither: it is impatience, too many words, rushing about.

**"Haste," "hasty," "hurry."** The Shuowen's own sense, 疾也, and right at the Analects. But haste is speed, and the book's pair is stillness against its want; *haste* has *slowness* for its opposite, not *stillness*. *Hurry* is also spoken for: *unhurried* reads 繟 (*chǎn* — easy, slack) at chapter 73. Kept for notes.

**"Impatient," "rash," "impetuous."** Each catches one half, the temper without the body, and *rash* adds recklessness the texts do not.

### Working register

| line | grammar | English |
|---|---|---|
| 濁以靜之 (15) | a verb, with an object | *by stilling it* |
| 守靜篤 · 歸根曰靜 (16) · 靜為躁君 (26) · 靜勝熱 (45) · 我好靜 (57) · 以靜 ×2 (61) | a noun | *stillness* |
| 不欲以靜 (37) | a state, after 以 | *still* |
| 清靜 (45) | a noun, with 清 | *clear stillness* |
| 靜為躁君 (26) | 躁, the restless | *the restless* |
| 躁則失君 (26) | 躁, a noun | *restlessness* |
| 躁勝寒 (45) | 躁, a noun | *restlessness* |

### What no rule can enforce

***Calm* and *movement* are ruled out for 靜 and 躁, and cannot be forbidden.** 安 (*ān* — at rest) stands in chapter 15 beside 靜 and may print *calm*; 動 (*dòng* — to move) stands there too and prints *move*.

***Quiet* is held by argument.** It is plain English the verse may need for other things, and no line of the 靜 chapters prints it now.

### Left open

**Chapter 37's line was rebuilt with the 欲 entry** (2026-11-19): *"Not desiring, and so still, the world will right itself."* 靜's English did not change.

**Chapter 26's couplet mixes its forms.** *The heavy is the root of the light* keeps both halves adjectival; *stillness is the ruler of the restless* makes one a noun and one an adjective. The Chinese is four bare characters on each side. Noted, not worth a rewrite on its own.

**The silks' 情 at chapters 15 and 16.** 情 is *feeling*, and the silk reading *"holding to feeling"* would be a different chapter. Read as a sound spelling of 靜, which is how both commentators' texts print it, it changes nothing; recorded here because a reader of the silks will meet it.
