entries.body:
## 咎 (Jiù) — Fault

*Say "jyo," falling. Two lines, in two chapters, and both times it is self-inflicted.*

**Locked: 咎 → "fault."** *(Not "blame," which is 尤's. Not "calamity," which is 殃's. Not "disaster" either, but that is a ruling no check can hold; see below.)*

### The graph: a person at odds

> 咎，**災**也。从人从各。各者，相違也。
> *"Disaster. From 人 (rén — a person) and 各 (gè — each, apart). 各 means being at odds."* — 說文解字 (*Shuōwén Jiězì*, the Han dictionary)

The graph holds two things: **a person at odds, and the disaster that follows.** 說文 defines 各 on its own as 異辭也 (*"words of difference"*), a mouth and a foot that 有行而止之，不相聽也 — *"set out, and are stopped: they do not heed one another."* The falling-out is in the picture; the falling is in the definition.

### Two lines, both self-inflicted

- **Ch 9** — 富貴而驕，自遺其咎 (*fù guì ér jiāo, zì yí qí jiù* — "wealthy, high and arrogant, one leaves oneself one's own 咎") → *Grow arrogant with wealth and status, and you leave yourself the fault.*
- **Ch 46** — 咎莫大於欲得 (*jiù mò dà yú yù dé* — "no 咎 greater than wanting to get") → *No greater fault than craving to acquire.*

**自遺 (*zì yí* — to leave to oneself) is the character's grammar.** Nobody hands you 咎. The arrogant leave it to themselves at ch 9, and at ch 46 it is the craving's own. 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) on ch 9 names what is left: 而反驕恣，必被禍患也 — *"if instead they are arrogant and unrestrained, they will surely suffer disaster and trouble."* 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) gives it a time limit: 不可長保也 — *"it cannot be kept long."*

### What is set aside

**"disaster"** is 說文's own word, and the book will not let 咎 have it. Ch 46 sets two characters in a parallel couplet, 禍莫大於不知足 / 咎莫大於欲得 (*"no greater disaster than discontent / no greater fault than craving to acquire"*), and the couplet only reads if the two differ. 禍 (*huò*) takes *disaster*.

**"calamity"** belongs to 殃 (*yāng*), at ch 52's 無遺身殃 (*"leave no calamity for the body"*). 說文 makes the two near-twins, defining 殃 as 咎也. The same verb, 遺 (*yí* — to leave behind), stands in both lines: at ch 9 you leave yourself 咎, at ch 52 you leave the body no 殃. The English keeps the verb the same and the nouns apart.

**"blame"** belongs to 尤 (*yóu*), at ch 8, and it points the wrong way. Blame is what other people do to you; 咎 is what you do to yourself. See `you-尤.md`.

### What no rule can enforce

***"disaster"* is ruled out for 咎 but is not on the `forbidden:` list, because it cannot be.** Ch 46 holds both 咎 and 禍, and *disaster* is 禍's word on the line just above. A rule keyed to 咎 would fire on 禍's own line. The couplet is held by the entries and by the reader.

### This lock stays in this book

**The I Ching renders 咎 *blame*, and both rulings are intended.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-10-20.)* There 咎 is the verdict word, 无咎 (*wú jiù* — "no blame") ninety-two times, set against 譽 (*yù* — praise) at its hexagrams 2 and 28. *Blame* and *praise* are English's own pair, and *fault* is kept free there for 過 (*guò* — to overstep). The Laozi is a different context and may use the word differently. So this entry carries `binds: [taoteching]`, and the I Ching, which vendors this glossary's locks as its own, does not inherit it.

### Left open

**The cost of *fault* is the disaster half.** English *fault* says *the failing is yours*. The character says *the trouble is yours*, and 說文 and 河上公 both weight the trouble. *Fault* keeps the person at odds and the self-inflicting grammar, and loses the fall. The misfortune words, 禍 · 凶 (*xiōng* — ill-omened) · 咎 · 殃 · 患 (*huàn* — trouble), are still being sorted as a family (`WORKLIST.md` T2-53), and 咎's English could move with them.
entries.shuowen: Disaster. From 人 (rén — a person) and 各 (gè — each, apart); 各 means being at odds.

entries.body:
## 可 (Kě) — Can Be

*Say "kuh," dipping and then rising. Thirty-six appearances across twenty chapters, two of them in the book's first six characters.*

**Locked: 可 → "can be"** (before a verb, the subject is what the verb is done to) **/ "can"** (as 可以, the subject does the verb) **/ "cannot"** (不可, for what the situation does not allow). *(Not "must not" or "should not" for a plain 不可; see* Cannot, not must not *below. No check can hold that ruling; see* What no rule can enforce.*)*

可 says what a situation allows. It is not a person's strength or skill; that is 能 (*néng*), its partner, treated below. 可 is the gap in the world through which a thing can happen, and 不可 is a world with no such gap. The book uses it most often in the negative, and almost always about the Tao or about the world, saying what cannot be done to them.

### The graph: a mouth, and a breath getting out

**Our vendored 說文解字 (*Shuōwén Jiězì*): 𦘫也。从口丂，丂亦聲** — *"to consent. From 口 (kǒu — mouth) and 丂 (kǎo), and 丂 also gives the sound."*

- **口 (*kǒu*)** is a mouth. 說文: 人所以言食也, *"what a person speaks and eats with."*
- **丂 (*kǎo*)** is drawn as a breath pushing up against a line. 說文 describes it as breath that wants to come out and is held back from above. In 可 it does two jobs: it is the sound, and it is the breath leaving the mouth.

**The oldest sense is permission, not possibility.** 𦘫 is the old form of 肯 (*kěn* — to be willing, to agree). So for Xu Shen 可 is the mouth saying *yes*: *all right, it may be done.* Some modern scholars propose an even older sense, *to sing*, since 可 written twice is 哥, and 歌 (*gē* — song) is built on it. That is a tentative proposal. What is certain is that the word began as someone **allowing** something, and *possible* is that permission read off the world instead of a person. 可 is in the Shang oracle bones, already in this shape.

That sense never left. 朝聞道，夕死**可**矣 (論語 4.8) is *"hear the way in the morning, and in the evening you **may** die."* And modern Chinese still answers *yes, fine* with 可以.

### Two constructions, two voices

This is the grammar the English must keep, and the first line depends on it.

**可 + verb: the subject receives the action.** 道可道 is *"the Tao that **can be** made a way."* 名可名 is *"the name that **can be** named."* The Tao is not doing the *dào*-ing. It is what would be *dào*-ed. The same construction gives 可欲 (3), *"what can be desired,"* which English has as one word: **the desirable.**

**可以 + verb: the subject acts.** 可以 is 可 with 以 (*yǐ* — by means of), *"has the means to."* 可以長久 (44, 59) — *"you **can** last long."* 可以有國 (59) — *"you **can** have the state."* 美言**可以**市尊 (62) — *"fine words **can** buy honor."*

**With an intransitive verb, 可 is simply *can*.** 大道汎兮，其可左右 (34) — *"the great Tao overflows. It can go left or right."* 左右 (*zuǒ yòu*) is used as a verb with nothing to act on, so there is no one to receive the action and the subject just *can*.

**One 可以 in our base is a copying error.** 知止可以不殆 (32) stands alone against every other witness, which read 所以 (*suǒ yǐ* — that by which): knowing when to stop *is how* you come to no danger. We follow 所以 (`notes/manuscript.md`, Ch 32), so the line carries no *can*.

The line can be checked by swapping the forms: 道可以道 would mean *the Tao can make a way*. The book does not say that.

| Construction | Voice | English | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| 可 + verb | the subject receives | **can be** | 道可道 (1), 可名為大 (34) → *"it can be named great"* |
| 不可 + verb | the subject receives | **cannot be** | 不可名 (14) → *"it cannot be named"*; 不可為也 (29) → *"it cannot be handled"* |
| 可以 + verb | the subject acts | **can** | 可以長久 (44) → *"you can last long"* |
| 可欲 | a fixed noun | **the desirable** | 不見可欲 (3) → *"by not displaying the desirable"* |
| 不可不 + verb | cannot-not | **must** | 不可不畏 (20) → *"what people fear must be feared"* |

### Cannot, not must not

不可 has two readings, and English has to choose between them every time:

- **cannot**: the situation does not allow it, so trying fails.
- **must not**: you are forbidden to.

The book means the first. The pattern is clearest at chapter 29, the line that matters most:

> 天下神器，不可為也，不可執也。為者敗之，執者失之。
> *"The world is a sacred vessel. It cannot be handled. It cannot be grasped. Those who handle it ruin it. Those who grasp it lose it."*

The next sentence gives the reason, and the reason is a result, not a rule: handle it and it breaks. **王弼 (*Wáng Bì*)** reads it exactly that way: 萬物以自然為性，故可因而不可為也，可通而不可執也。物有常性而造為之，故必敗也 — *"the countless things take being so of themselves as their nature. So they can be followed and cannot be handled, can be passed through and cannot be grasped. Things have their own nature, and to manufacture them is to ruin them, surely."* 必 (*bì* — surely, without fail) is a prediction. **河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*)** agrees: 以有為治之則敗其質性, *"govern it by handling, and you ruin its nature."* *Must not* would turn a description of how the world works into a commandment. That is a verdict the line does not carry (`process/principles/no-verdict-the-chinese-lacks.md`).

The other lines run the same way. 不可致詰 (14), *it cannot be questioned through to the end*. 善閉無關楗而不可開 (27), *masterful security uses no locks, yet cannot be breached*. 不可得而親 (56), *you cannot draw them near*. 王弼's gloss on 56 is a logic, not a law: 可得而親，則可得而疏也, *"if they could be drawn near, they could be held off."*

**不可不 is the one place *must* belongs.** 人之所畏，不可不畏 (20) is *cannot not fear*, and English says that as **must**: *"What people fear must be feared."* This *must* is still necessity rather than a command. 王弼 reads it in the first person: 人之所畏，吾亦畏焉, *"what people fear, I fear too."*

### 能, the partner: a bear

**能 (*néng*)** is the other English *can*: ability, what an agent is able to do. It appears thirty-three times across seventeen chapters, often as 孰能 (*who can…?*) and 莫能 (*no one can*).

Our 說文: 熊屬。足似鹿。从肉㠯聲。能獸堅中，故稱賢能；而彊壯，稱能傑也 — *"a kind of bear, with feet like a deer's. From 肉 (ròu — flesh), with 㠯 (yǐ) for sound. The 能 beast is solid at its core, and so the able are called 賢能; and it is strong, and so the outstanding are called 能傑."* The graph is a **bear**: two paws, and a head with an open mouth. The word for the animal later took 火 (fire, here four dots for the feet) and became 熊 (*xióng*). Xu Shen's account of how a bear came to mean *able* is a commentator's story, but the picture is right for the word: 能 is strength in a body.

**The voice keeps them apart in English.** 可 is *can be*, the situation's allowance. 能 is *can* or *is able to*, someone's power. 莫之能守 (9) — *"no one can guard them"* — is a failure of ability. 不可長保 in the same chapter — *"it will not keep for long"* — is the world not allowing it. Where both stand together, the book is saying something about each. At 70: 吾言甚易知，甚易行…天下莫能知，莫能行 — *"my words are very easy to know, very easy to follow. In all the world, no one can know them. No one can follow them."* The words *can be* known. People *cannot* know them. The fault is in the agents, not the words.

### What is set aside

- ***must not / should not*** for a plain 不可 — puts a commandment where the book describes a consequence (above). Chapter 36 is the case where it came closest to fitting, and *cannot* holds there too (below).
- ***may*** — the oldest sense, and fine in 論語, but in modern English *may* means *perhaps* as often as *is permitted*. *"The Tao that may be made a way"* would read as a guess.
- ***is possible to / is able to be*** — accurate and wooden. 可 is a small word and wants a small English word.
- ***-able*** suffixes (*nameable*, *graspable*) — compact, but they turn a statement about the world into a property of the thing. *"It is ungraspable"* says what the Tao is like. *"It cannot be grasped"* says what happens when you try. The book means the second. *The desirable* (3) is the one exception, because 可欲 is a fixed noun and English has the noun.

### Chapter 36, the hardest line

> 魚不可脫於淵，國之利器不可以示人。
> *"A fish cannot leave deep water. / A state's tools of advantage cannot be shown."*

**The two clauses are one parallel, and the English keeps it.** Both read *cannot* (Shalom's call, 2026-10-14).

**Why *cannot* for both:**

- **王弼 reads both halves as one consequence:** 魚脫於淵則必見失矣。利國器而立刑以示人，亦必失也 — *"a fish that leaves the deep is surely lost. To set up punishments as the state's tools and show them to people, that too is surely lost."* 亦 (*yì* — also) ties the two clauses together, and 必 makes both predictions.
- **The fish line is plainly not advice.** A fish is not forbidden to leave the water. It dies. The second line borrows the first's logic.
- **The chapter keeps its *musts* for the four 必固 lines** (*"you must first stretch it out…"*), where 必 (*bì*) prints them.

**What it costs:** 河上公 hears advice: 治國權者不可以示執事之臣也, *"the authority that governs the state must not be shown to the ministers who run affairs."* 韓非 (*Hán Fēi*) reads the whole chapter as counsel to a ruler: rewards and punishments, the state's 利器, 在君則制臣，在臣則勝君, *"held by the lord they control the ministers; held by the ministers they overcome the lord."* And 可以 rather than 可 marks the second clause slightly differently from the first. On their reading the line is a warning to rulers, and *must never* would be honest to it. That reading is set aside, not refuted.

### What no rule can enforce

***Must not* and *should not* are ruled out for a plain 不可, and they cannot go on `forbidden:`.** *Must* is 不可不's English at 20, and chapter 36 prints *must* four times for 必 (*bì*), in the same chapter as two 不可. The checker keys on chapter presence, so forbidding *must* would flag correct lines. The reader holds this one: **不可 is *cannot*; *must* belongs to 必 and to 不可不.**

### Left open

**Chapter 35's *never* is softer than the Chinese.** 用之不可既 is *"use it, and it cannot be used up."* *"It never runs out"* reports a record, where 不可 says the world doesn't allow it. The *never* is declared as a flexion because the line sounds right, but it is a small loss.

**English *can* serves both characters.** The voice usually keeps them apart (*can be* against *can*), but where 可以 makes the subject act, 可以 and 能 land on the same English. 可以有國 (59), *"you can have the state,"* and 能守之 (32), *"able to hold to this,"* are different claims, an opening and a capacity. English barely shows it.

flexions.why: 可欲 is a fixed phrase, what can be desired, and English has the word
不可不 is cannot-not, which English says as must
不可既, cannot be used up, said as it never runs out

entries.render: can be (可 + verb) / can (可以 + verb) / cannot (不可)
entries.shuowen: To consent. From 口 (kǒu — mouth) and 丂 (kǎo), and 丂 also gives the sound.

entries.body:
## 亂 (Luàn) — Disorder

*Say "lwahn," falling. Four lines across four chapters, and the dictionary defines it as its own opposite.*

**Locked: 亂 → "disorder."** *(Never "chaos," never "chaotic.")*

### The graph: a tangle with hands in it

> 亂，**治**也。从乙，**乙，治之也**；从𤔔。
> *"亂 is to bring to order. From 乙 (yǐ), and **乙 is what orders it**; and from 𤔔 (luàn)."* — 說文解字

Read that twice, because it says the opposite of what the character is used to mean. **說文's headword gloss for 亂 is 治 — to govern, to put in order** — and it then singles out one component and names it *the thing that does the ordering*. The tool is inside the graph.

𤔔 is the rest of it: a hank of **silk** with a hand above and a hand below. 說文 draws both hands in our own corpus — 爪, **覆手曰爪**, *"a covering hand,"* reaching down; 又, **手也**, a hand, reaching up. The bronze forms show the threads on a frame, one hand holding, one working a shuttle through.

**And the hands are untangling, not tangling.** This is the fact that reorders the whole entry, and the dictionary states it twice. Besides 亂，治也, 說文 defines the 𤔔 element outright — in the entry for a character **this book uses**:

> 辭，訟也。从𤔔，**𤔔猶理辜也。𤔔，理也。**
> *"辭 (cí) is pleading a case. From 𤔔, because 𤔔 is like **putting right** (理) a wrong. **𤔔 means 理 — to put in order.**"*

辭 stands at chapter 34 — 萬物恃之以生而不**辭**, *"the countless things rely on it to live, yet it refuses none."* So the Laozi already contains one 𤔔-character, and the dictionary explains it as sorting out a dispute.

*A divergence, recorded rather than settled: a minority reading takes the bronze graph as silk on a loom that* cannot *be sorted — the hands present but defeated. Either way the hands are at work on the tangle, not making it.*

**So 亂 does not name a mess. It names a mess somebody has their hands in.** That is why chapter 64 can say 治之於未亂 at all: the tangle is addressable, and the counsel is to get to it early.

### Where it stands, and what it is set against

| ch | line | set against |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 不見可欲，使民心不**亂** | 聖人之**治** three lines later, and 無不**治** at the close |
| 18 | 國家昏**亂**，有忠臣 | 昏 (*hūn* — clouded) beside it; loyal ministers as the symptom |
| 38 | 忠信之薄，而**亂**之首 | 忠信 (*zhōng xìn* — loyalty and trust), worn thin |
| 64 | 為之於未有，**治**之於未**亂** | **治 itself, in the same clause** |

**Chapter 3 shows what it does to a person.** 亂 there is something done **to** the heart from outside, not a state it generates: 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) glosses the line 心無所亂也, *"the heart has nothing to be disordered by"* — remove the display and the disordering has no purchase. 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) pairs it with 惑 (*huò* — led astray): 不惑亂也. Both read it as agitation rather than as misunderstanding, which is why *confused* is wrong for it: that word puts the damage in the knowing, and this chapter has just spent two lines separating knowing from the heart. *(This was established during the ch 3 rebuild of 2026-08-31 and is recorded in `notes/translation.md` → Ch 3.)*

**Chapter 64 prints the pair the dictionary describes** — *"Order it before it falls into disorder."* Two of the four chapters set 亂 directly against 治, and the English keeps them visibly related, which *chaos* could not do.

**王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) reads 64 as a matter of scale, not of kind**: 治之於未亂 gets the gloss 謂㣲脆也, *"this refers to what is faint and brittle."* The disorder is not a different condition arriving from outside. It is the same thing, further along — a thread or two before it is a knot.

### The 反訓, and why the verse does not show it

A character that faces both ways is called a 反訓 (*fǎnxùn*), and 亂 is the standard example: the tangle and the untangling in one graph. It is the most interesting thing about the word. **It is also not what this book does with it.**

All four of Laozi's lines sit on the disorder side — a heart stirred by what it was shown (3), a state come apart (18), where the rot starts (38), the thing to catch early (64). **The 治 sense is the dictionary's, not the text's**, and an English that reached for it would be rendering a fact about the character over a fact about the sentence. The graph belongs in this entry; the verse says what the verse says. Same arrangement as 萬 (*wàn*), which is a scorpion here and *the countless things* on the page.

### What is set aside

**"chaos"** was the rendering at chapter 18, and it is the one to refuse.

It is a **cosmological** word in English — Hesiod's Χάος, the void before creation, *chaos and old night* — and it points at the wrong end of this book's cosmology. Where Laozi does describe an undifferentiated beginning he uses 混成 (*hùn chéng*, ch 25), rendered *"something mixed and complete"* (`glossary/hun-混.md`). 亂 is not that. It is **political and domestic**: a state coming apart, a household out of harmony, a heart stirred up.

And it is the wrong shape for the graph. **Chaos is a condition with nobody in it.** 亂 has two hands in it. You cannot catch chaos early; you can catch a tangle early, which is the whole of chapter 64.

**"unravelled"** is the near miss, and it is worth the paragraph.

It **performs the graph** — silk coming undone — and in English it faces both ways exactly as 亂 does, since one unravels a mystery and a plan unravels. It would carry the 反訓 natively, with no help from this entry. *"Order it before it unravels"* (64) and *"the people's hearts do not unravel"* (3) are both better lines than the locked ones.

It fails at **chapter 38**, and the failure is structural rather than a matter of taste. 亂之**首** is *the head of* 亂, and *"the head of the unravelling"* is not English. The obvious repair — *"where the unravelling begins"* — spends 首 (*shǒu*) on *begins*, and **首 and 始 (*shǐ*) were separated in that exact couplet during Pass D**, 而亂之首 against 而愚之始, because they had been sharing one English. Restoring that collision to gain a better line elsewhere is a bad trade. One chapter should not decide four, but a rendering that breaks in one of four is not a lock.

**"untangled"** is the opposite error, and naming it is the point. *Untangle* is the **治 half** of the 反訓 — the hands succeeding — and that is the half this book never uses. Put it in any of the four lines and the meaning inverts: chapter 18 would have nations becoming *untangled* as loyal ministers appear, which reverses the chapter's whole argument. It is the rendering the **graph** supports and the **text** forbids, which is a useful thing for a reader to see stated rather than left as a puzzle.

**"turmoil"** is better than *chaos* and still wrong: a word about agitation and feeling, so it carries the heart at ch 3 and drops the constitutional sense at 18 and 38. It has no relation to *order*.

### Working register

- as the state a thing falls into → **disorder** (亂之首 → "the head of disorder")
- as what a thing is kept out of → **thrown into disorder** (使民心不亂 → "the people's hearts are not thrown into disorder")
- beside 治 → keep the two English words visibly related (治之於未亂 → "order it before it falls into disorder")

**Never** "chaos," "chaotic," "untangled."

### Settled alongside

**治 (*zhì*) was locked on 2026-09-23** — *govern*, with a declared flexion to *order* at chapters 8 and 64 — so the pairing this entry rests on is now held at both ends. `zhi-治.md`. 說文 files 治 as **a river**, which is the other half of this entry's picture: 亂 is the tangle, 治 is what you do to a watercourse, and 王弼 says what that consists of at ch 60 — **不擾也**, *"it is not to disturb."*

**正 (*zhèng* — upright) stays out of it.** *Order* is also worn by 正 at chapter 45 — 清靜為天下正, *"clear stillness brings order to the world"* — and 正 is one of the calls Shalom has deferred (`WORKLIST.md` T4-2, 正/奇). It is named here so that a reader who notices the third claimant knows it was seen and left alone.

## 民 (Mín) — The People

*Say "meen," rising. Thirty-two appearances across thirteen chapters, nearly all of them in the book's political half.*

**Locked: 民 → "the people,"** always with the article, **and "the people" belongs to 民 alone.** *(Not "the masses," "the multitude," "the populace," "subjects," "citizens," "commoners," "peasants," or "the governed." That 人 (*rén* — a person) must not wear "the people" is a ruling no check can hold; see* What no rule can enforce *below. 百姓 (*bǎi xìng*), the other word for the population, is locked to "everyone": `baixing-百姓.md`.)*

民 is the people **as seen from the seat of government**: the population a ruler governs, taxes, frightens, loves, or leaves alone. The word is never neutral about who is looking. In every line but one, someone stands across from 民: a sage, a ruler, a state, those over them. Laozi's whole political teaching is addressed to that someone, and 民 is the name for the ones on the other side of the address.

### The graph: sprouts, or a blinded eye, and nobody knows

**Our vendored 說文解字 (*Shuōwén Jiězì*, c. 100 CE): 眾萌也。从古文之象** — *"the many sprouts. From the shape of its ancient form."*

萌 (*méng*) is a shoot breaking the soil. Xu Shen defines the people as **a field coming up**: numerous, low, alive, and not yet anything in particular. 段玉裁 (*Duàn Yùcái*, 1815) defends the reading against editions that print 氓 (*méng* — the common folk) in its place. 萌 is the original, he says, and the ancients called the people 萌, with many examples in Han writing. 林義光 (*Lín Yìguāng*, 1920) arrived at the same picture from the bronze graphs, which he read as a plant pushing up out of the ground.

**The other reading is the one that circulates, and it is a theory.** 郭沫若 (*Guō Mòruò*, 1930s) read the bronze graph as **an eye pierced by a blade**: captives blinded in one eye and set to work, so that 民 began as a word for slaves. 白川靜 (*Shirakawa Shizuka*) and 藤堂明保 (*Tōdō Akiyasu*) took it up. Its critics, 永澤要二 (*Nagasawa Yōji*) and 加納喜光 (*Kanō Yoshimitsu*), point out that nothing supports it beyond the shape. The oracle-bone graphs once claimed for 民 are themselves disputed, and the form securely identified as 民 begins with the bronzes. Guo was building a Marxist history of ancient China, and a blinded slave fit the slave society that history required. The reading may be right. But it is one scholar's argument, made inside a framework, and it should not be quoted as the meaning of the graph.

**What the two readings share is position.** A sprouting field and a captive labourer are both **low, numerous, and acted upon**. Whichever picture is true, the graph does not draw a person standing upright, as 人 does. It draws a mass seen from above.

### The evidence: 民 always has someone across from it

The pattern is the argument, and it is complete enough to read as a table.

| Ch | Line | Who stands across |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 使民不爭 · 使民不為盜 · 使民心不亂 · 常使民無知無欲 | the sage who governs (聖人之治) |
| 10 | 愛民治國 | the one asked *can you* |
| 19 | 民利百倍 · 民復孝慈 | the ruler told to cut off and abandon |
| 32 | 民莫之令而自均 | the rulers who could hold to the Tao (侯王) |
| 57 | 民彌貧 · 民自化 · 民自正 · 民自富 · 民自樸 | 我 (*wǒ* — I), the sage speaking |
| 58 | 其民淳淳 · 其民缺缺 | 其政 (*qí zhèng* — its government) |
| 65 | 非以明民 · 民之難治 | the ancients who were masterful at the Tao |
| 66 | 欲上民 · 欲先民 · 民不重 · 民不害 | the one who would rise above them |
| 72 | 民不畏威 | the authority they stop fearing |
| 74 | 民不畏死 · 若使民常畏死 | the one who would kill to frighten them |
| 75 | 民之飢 · 民之難治 · 民之輕死 | 其上 (*qí shàng* — those over them), three times |
| 80 | 小國寡民 · 使民重死 · 使民復結繩 · 民至老死 | the small state that *lets* them |

**Chapter 57 shows the relation working.** The sage speaks four times in the first person, and each time 民 answers in the reflexive: *I do not do, and the people transform themselves.* 民 is defined by being on the receiving end of rule. The teaching is that the best rule gives them nothing to receive.

**Chapter 75 names the direction outright.** 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) comments on the whole chapter in one sentence: 言民之所以僻，治之所以亂，皆由上，不由其下也，民從上也 — *"this says that the reason the people go astray, and the reason order falls into disorder, all comes from above and not from below. The people follow those above."* Hunger, unruliness, and the cheapness of life are all traced upward. 民 is the word for the people as the ones it happens to.

### The witnesses draw the line too

The copying tradition let 民 and 人 change places three times, and each change falls where the distinction is being drawn.

| Ch | Our base | The older reading | A ruler in the line? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 57 | 人多利器 | **民**多利器: Guodian, and the lemmas of both 王弼 and 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) | yes: *the state grows benighted* |
| 60 | 聖人亦不傷人 | 聖人亦不傷**民**: 韓非 (*Hán Fēi*) | yes: the chapter is governing a large state |
| 64 | 民之從事 | **人**之敗也: Guodian, bundle C | no: anyone's affairs |

**In every case the oldest reading puts 民 where a ruler is present and 人 where none is.** Three cases is a pattern worth noticing and too few to rest on alone, but it agrees with the thirty-two lines above. And chapter 57 at Guodian sets the two side by side, a line apart: **民**多利器，而邦滋昏；**人**多智，而奇物滋起. The people's weapons trouble the state; *someone's* cleverness breeds strange contrivances. 河上公 makes that second 人 the rulers themselves, 人謂人君百里諸侯也 (*"人 here means the rulers, the lords of a hundred li"*), while 王弼 glosses it as the people's cleverness. They disagree about who 人 is. Neither treats it as 民.

### What is set aside, and why

**"The masses."** Nineteenth-century class politics, and it is the word the blinded-slave etymology was built to support. It makes 民 a bloc, a demographic, an object of history. Chapter 80's villagers who *find their food sweet, their clothes fine* are not the masses. `zhong-眾.md` rejects the word for the same reason.

**"The multitude."** King James English. It fails the hymn test outright, and it belongs, if anywhere, to 眾 (*zhòng* — the crowd), which is a plurality and not a relation.

**"The governed."** The most accurate label, and the most tempting. It says exactly what the table above shows. That is the problem: it states as a definition what the lines *show* by putting a ruler across from 民 every time. *"I do not do, and the governed transform themselves"* turns a line about people into a line about administration, and *"the governed go hungry"* takes the hunger away. The Chinese performs the relation. It does not name it. `process/principles/perform-dont-label.md`.

**"Subjects," "citizens."** Each brings a constitution with it. *Subjects* have a sovereign, *citizens* have rights, and 民 has neither in this sense. Both carry a theory of the state the book does not share.

**"The populace," "the population."** Census words. They count where 民 is a relation.

**"Commoners," "peasants."** They name a rank and an occupation. Some 民 were peasants. The word does not say so, and chapter 80's people keep records, own boats, and wear fine clothes.

### Working register

- the default, with the article → **the people** (愛民 → "loving the people"; 民之難治 → "the people are hard to govern")
- possessive → **the people's** (使民心不亂 → "the people's hearts are not thrown into disorder")
- under a number word, the article drops by English grammar → **people** (小國寡民 → "a small state, few people")
- **ch 64 alone → people**, bare: 民之從事 → *"people always ruin their affairs."* It is the one 民 in the book with no ruler in sight, and Guodian reads 人 there. The flexion records the line as it reads and why.

### Its neighbours

| | Graph | What it names | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| **民** | sprouts, or a disputed eye | the people across from a ruler | *the people* |
| **人** (*rén*) | a person standing, in profile | a human being, anyone | *people · a person · others* |
| **眾** (*zhòng*) | figures under the sun or an eye | the many, the crowd | *the crowd · the many* (locked) |
| **百姓** (*bǎi xìng*) | 百 a hundred, 姓 a clan name, from 女 (*nǚ* — woman) and 生 (*shēng* — birth) | the whole population, named from among themselves | *everyone* (locked, `baixing-百姓.md`) |

### What no rule can enforce

**人 must not render as "the people," and the checker cannot say so.** A `forbidden:` entry works by chapter presence, and chapter 57 holds both characters: 民 five times, legitimately *the people*, and 人 twice. Any ban on *the people* would flag 民's own lines. The ruling is for the reader: **in a chapter with 民, *the people* is 民's, and 人 takes *people*, *a person*, or *others*.** Chapter 57's *"the more sharp weapons the people have"* is not a breach: it renders the 民 that every witness but our base prints, a fork recorded in `sources/variants.yaml`.

**百姓 is held by its own entry.** It is locked to *everyone*, and it forbids *the people*, which the checker can enforce because none of its chapters (5, 17, 49) holds 民.

### Left open

**Chapter 60 fits the pattern, and we keep our base against it.** 韓非 reads 聖人亦不傷**民**, which is exactly where the pattern above would put 民. But both transmitted commentators read 人 in both clauses, and 王弼 builds the next line on the symmetry: 神不傷人，聖人亦不傷人…故曰兩不相傷也, *"the numinous does not harm people, the sage also does not harm people… therefore it says the two do not harm each other."* The couplet needs the same object twice. 韓非 is explaining the line in his own terms, and an explanation can sharpen a distinction the text left flat.

**"The people" has its own echoes.** *We the People*, *a people's republic*, *let my people go*. English hears popular sovereignty, revolution, or a covenant in the phrase, and 民 carries none of them. It is the plainest English the word has, and it fails the hymn test less badly than anything else. But it is warmer and prouder than 民 is, and the reader who hears *the people* as the sovereign hears the opposite of chapter 75, where the people are the ones a sovereign eats.

flexions.why: the one 民 with no ruler in the line, and the oldest witness reads 人 there

entries.shuowen: The many sprouts. From the shape of its ancient form.

entries.body:
## 名 (Míng) — Name

*Say "ming," rising. Twenty-four times in twenty-two lines, across ten chapters. The word the book opens its second line with, and the one it keeps setting against the Tao.*

**Locked: 名 → "name," in every line: a noun, and a verb where it takes an object.** 無名 and 有名 are *nameless* and *named*, and 可名 and 不可名 are *can be named* and *cannot be named*. *(Not "reputation" or "fame" in chapter 44, which spend a second English on one word and hide the chapter's link to chapter 32. Not "description" or "designation," which turn a spoken name into an account of a thing. Not "be called," which is 謂's (wèi — "is called"); see* What no rule can enforce.*)*

### The graph: a mouth calling out at dusk

> 名，自命也。从口从夕。夕者，冥也。冥不相見，故以口自名。
> *"Name: to name oneself. From 口 (kǒu — mouth) and 夕 (xī — dusk). 夕 means 冥 (míng — the dark). In the dark people cannot see one another, so they name themselves with the mouth."* — the *Shuowen Jiezi* (the Han dictionary)

**The picture is someone calling out who they are, after dark.** The oracle bones already write 名 with the same two parts: 夕, a crescent moon, beside 口, a mouth. Where the two sit varies in the oracle-bone graphs and settles in the bronzes, but the parts never change. Xu Shen reads them as a scene: two people who cannot see each other at dusk, and a voice saying *it's me*.

**So in the oldest account of the word, a name is what you reach for when sight fails.** That is not a gloss laid over the book. It is what the book does with the word, twice, in so many characters (below).

**Where the picture stops.** The Shuowen's 自命 (*zì mìng* — "to name oneself") is a person naming themselves. In this book nobody does: things are named, and the Tao is named by force. The reflexive scene is the graph's, not the book's.

### Twenty-two lines: a name is given where sight fails, and forced on the Tao

> *The name that can be named is not the ever-present name.*
> *The nameless is the beginning of sky and earth.*
> *The named is the mother of the countless things.*
>
> 名可名，非常名。
> 無名，天地之始；
> 有名，萬物之母。
>
> — chapter 1

> *Look, but you cannot see it — its name is the invisible.*
>
> 視之不見，名曰夷；
>
> — chapter 14

> *I do not know its name.*
> *Forcing a label on it, I call it the Tao.*
> *Forcing a name on it, I call it great.*
>
> 吾不知其名，
> 強字之曰道，
> 強為之名曰大。
>
> — chapter 25

> *When the carving begins, there are names.*
> *Since names already exist, one must know when to stop.*
>
> 始制有名，
> 名亦既有，夫亦將知止，
>
> — chapter 32

> *Therefore, the sage knows without venturing,*
> *names without seeing,*
>
> 是以聖人不行而知，
> 不見而名，
>
> — chapter 47

**In these lines a name stands where seeing cannot, or where the Tao will not be held.** Chapter 14 is the Shuowen's scene, word for word: you look and cannot see, so a name is given (視之不見，名曰夷, three times over, for sight, hearing and touch). Chapter 47 prints the definition as an instruction, 不見而名, *"names without seeing."* Chapter 25 says what it costs: the name has to be forced (強, *qiǎng* — "to force"). 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) gives the reason in four characters, 名以定形, *"a name fixes a form,"* and the mixed-and-complete has no form to fix.

**The Tao is named three ways in the book, and each is an admission.** It is 無名 (*wú míng* — "nameless," 1, 32, 37, 41), it 不可名 (*bù kě míng* — "cannot be named," 14), and when it is named at all the name is forced (25). Chapter 21 then says the opposite of all three in one line, 自古及今，其名不去, *"From ancient times until today, the Tao's name has never been erased,"* and reads the beginning of things *in* that name. The book never reconciles the two, and the English does not either.

### Names and knowing when to stop: chapters 32 and 44

> *Since names already exist, one must know when to stop.*
> *Knowing when to stop, you come to no danger.*
>
> 名亦既有，夫亦將知止，
> 知止可以不殆。
>
> — chapter 32

> *Your name or your body — which is dearer?*
>
> 名與身孰親？
>
> — chapter 44

**Two chapters put names beside knowing when to stop, and they close on the same words.** Chapter 32 reaches 知止可以不殆 from names; chapter 44 opens with a name weighed against the body and ends 知止不殆, *"Know when to stop, and you come to no danger."* In chapter 32 the names are the ones carving makes, the uncarved cut into vessels with functions. In chapter 44 the name is the one a person makes. **They are the same word, and the book treats them as the same danger**: a name is where you stop, or fail to.

**This is why chapter 44 reads *name*.** English *name* carries the person's sense natively, *a good name*, *to make a name for yourself*, and so it can hold chapter 44 without leaving chapter 1. The commentators keep the one word as well. 王弼 on chapter 44: 尚名好高其身必疏, *"whoever exalts a name and loves height, their body must grow distant."* 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*): 名遂則身退也, *"when the name is achieved, the body withdraws."*

### What the commentators did with chapter 1: the same word, two readings

At the book's second line the two commentators read 名 differently, and the difference is the one between chapters 32 and 44.

- **王弼:** 可道之道，可名之名，指事造形，非其常也, *"the Tao that can be made a way and the name that can be named point at affairs and make forms; they are not the ever-present."* A name is a cut, as it is in chapter 32.
- **河上公:** 名可名：謂富貴尊榮高世之名也, *"the name that can be named means the name of wealth, rank, honor and glory that stands high in the world."* A name is a standing, as it is in chapter 44.

**The English keeps both open by keeping one word.** Had chapter 44 read *reputation*, chapter 1 would have had to choose between them, or a reader would never learn there was a choice.

### 名 as a verb: chapters 34 and 47

Twice 名 takes an object and is a verb, and it is *name* both times.

> *The work is done, and it does not name it its own.*
>
> 功成而不名有。
>
> — chapter 34

**河上公 reads the line with the word itself:** 有道不名其有功也, *"having the Tao, it does not name the merit as its own."* The opening, *the work is done*, is the one 功成 (*gōng chéng*) takes in chapters 2 and 77, so the three lines open alike, as they do in the Chinese.

Chapter 47's 不見而名 is the received reading, against silk A's 明 (*míng* — "clear," the same sound), and both commentators print 名: 王弼, 雖不見而是非之理可得而名也, *"though it does not see, the principle of right and wrong can be got and named"* (`sources/variants.yaml`).

### What is set aside

- **"Reputation," "fame," "renown."** The conventional English for chapter 44 (Legge: *"Or fame or life, which do you hold more dear?"*). Each is a true sense of 名, and each is a second English for one word, which hides what the chapter shares with chapter 32 and what chapter 1's first line may already mean (河上公). *Fame* adds a size the line does not have: chapter 44 weighs any name against the body, not a famous one.
- **"Description."** A description is an account of what a thing is like. A 名 is a word spoken for it, and in chapter 25 the whole argument is that no account is possible, which is why the name has to be forced. *Description* there makes the line say the Tao was described.
- **"Designation."** Exact for 王弼's 稱 (*chēng* — "designation"), which he uses of 字 (*zì*) in chapter 25, and bureaucratic. It fails the pointing test: you can point at someone calling out in the dark.
- **"The Name," capitalized.** The divine-name overlay, which turns chapter 1 into a sermon on an ineffable Name. Lowercase, as everything but the Tao.
- **"True name."** Chapter 25's 吾不知其名 is *I do not know its name*. A *true* name invents one existing somewhere out of reach, and turns a claim about formlessness into one about the speaker.

### Working register

| Form | Lines | English | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| a noun | 1, 14, 21, 25, 32, 44 | **name** | 吾不知其名 → *"I do not know its name"* (25) |
| 名曰 X | 14 ×3 | **its name is** | 名曰夷 → *"its name is the invisible"* |
| 異名 | 1 | **differ in name** | 同出而異名 → *"emerge together, but differ in name"* |
| 無名 / 有名 | 1, 32, 37, 41 | **nameless / named** (*names* where 有 is "there are") | 道常無名 → *"the Tao is ever nameless"* (32); 始制有名 → *"there are names"* (32) |
| 可名 / 不可名 | 1, 14, 34 | **can be named / cannot be named** | 可名為大 → *"it can be named great"* (34) |
| a verb, with an object | 34, 47 | **name** | 不見而名 → *"names without seeing"* (47) |

The split is grammatical, not by chapter, so it stays in prose and nothing goes in `flexions:`. **可 + 名 is always passive** (`ke-可.md`): the Tao is what gets named, never what names.

### What no rule can enforce

- **"Be called" belongs to 謂 and 曰 (*yuē* — "to call"), not to 名.** 可名 must read *can be named*, never *can be called*, but *called* cannot go on the forbidden list: 謂 stands in chapters 1 and 14 (同謂之玄, 是謂), and 曰 in chapter 25 (*"I call it great"*), all three of them 名 chapters. A reader, and `concordance.py --english "called"`, are the only check.
- **"Label" belongs to 字 (*zì* — "a courtesy name"), once, in chapter 25.** 王弼 keeps the two apart, 名以定形，字以稱可言, *"a 名 fixes a form; a 字 designates what can be spoken,"* and so does the English: *"Forcing a label on it, I call it the Tao. / Forcing a name on it, I call it great."* *Label* cannot be forbidden here, because chapter 25 holds both characters.

### Left open

- **Chapter 21 against the rest.** Everywhere else the Tao is nameless, cannot be named, or is named by force, and in chapter 21 its name has never been erased and the beginning of things is read in it. 王弼 resolves it by reading the name as namelessness itself, 以無名說萬物始也, *"it is by the nameless that the beginning of the countless things is told"* (`fu-父.md`). The English leaves the contradiction standing, as the Chinese does.
- **Chapter 34's fork.** The Yongle encyclopedia's text of 王弼 reads 而不居 for 不名有, which would turn the line back into chapter 2's 功成而弗居 and take 名 out of the chapter's first half. Our base keeps 不名有. The fork is noted in `chapters/034.md` and not yet recorded in `sources/variants.yaml`.
- **Chapter 9's longer reading.** Every edition the Siku editors knew reads 功成名遂身退 (*gōng chéng míng suì shēn tuì* — "the work done, the name achieved, the body withdraws"), and our base prints the shorter 功遂身退. Adopting it would add a 名 line, and the name and the body would stand together in chapter 9 as they do in chapter 44 (`sources/variants.yaml`, our call: base).
- **The mouth in the graph.** 說文 makes a name something said aloud, and the book distrusts speech: 不言之教 (*bù yán zhī jiào* — "the teaching without words," 2, 43). Whether the book's suspicion of names is its suspicion of speech is a question for the 言 (*yán* — speech) entry, still owed (`glossary/TRIAGE.md`).
entries.shuowen: To name oneself. From 口 (kǒu — mouth) and 夕 (xī — dusk). Dusk means the dark: in the dark people cannot see one another, so they name themselves with the mouth.

entries.body:
## 命 (Mìng) — What You Were Sent With

*Say "ming," falling. Three lines in two chapters, and one of them is the hinge of Chapter 16's chain toward clear-seeing.*

**Recommended, not yet locked: 命 → the allotted course — what is spoken over a thing and sent with it.** *(Never "mandate," never "destiny," never "fate," never "decree." Chapter 16's line and Chapter 51's verb are both still open; see the close.)*

說文解字 (c. 100 CE): **使也。从口从令** — *"命 is 使 (shǐ — to send; also, an envoy). From 口 (kǒu — a mouth) and 令 (lìng)."*

Each part, one level down:

- **口 (*kǒu*)** — 說文: **人所以言食也。象形** — *"what a person speaks and eats with. A pictograph."* A mouth.
- **令 (*lìng*)** — 說文: **發號也。从亼、卪** — *"to issue a call. From 亼 (jí) and 卪 (jié)."*
- **亼 (*jí*)** — the assembling sign, three strokes converging. Read either as an inverted 口, or as a **hand-bell rung to call people in**.
- **卪 (*jié*, also written 卩)** — **a kneeling figure.** *(說文 itself reads it as 瑞信也, "an auspicious tally"; the kneeling-person reading is modern palaeography. Neither component is among the Laozi's 711 characters, so the repository's 說文 does not carry them.)*

**And 命 and 令 were one graph.** In the oracle-bone script they are the same character — the gathering-sign above, the kneeling figure below. A chief sounds a bell to call people in; whoever receives the order kneels to take it. **口 was added during the Western Zhou bronze period**, and by the small seal script the two had separated.

**So the graph stacks up into a scene**: a summons, a gathering, someone on their knees, and a mouth. 命 is 令 with the utterance made explicit — and the dictionary defines the whole with 使, the word for *sending* and for *the person sent*.

**命 is what is spoken over you, and then you go.** Not a plan, not a fate written in advance: an instruction handed to someone at the moment they are dispatched. Everything below follows from that being a **speech act with a destination**, rather than a decree of the universe.

### 天命 is not in this book

天命 (*tiān mìng* — the Mandate of Heaven) is the compound this character is famous for: the Zhou dynasty's founding political theology, in which a ruler holds power by warrant from 天 (*tiān* — sky) and forfeits it by misrule. It is the single most consequential thing 命 does in classical Chinese.

**It has zero occurrences in the Tao Te Ching.**

So *mandate* imports a warrant-to-rule the book never invokes, and *destiny* and *fate* import a Greek and a Christian freight on top of it. All three make 命 a plot written in advance. The character describes a thing said out loud to someone who then leaves the room.

### 令 is in the book, and the two collapse in English

令 runs eight lines across four chapters, and the book puts the two characters in the **same frame** one chapter apart:

> ch 32 — 民莫之**令**而自均 — *"the people, with no one 令-ing them, even out of themselves"*
> ch 51 — 夫莫之**命**而常自然 — *"with no one 命-ing it, it is always so of itself"*

Identical construction 莫之X而, different character — **and the two were one graph before the Western Zhou split them**, which is why they are so easy to collapse and so worth keeping apart. The graphs separate them cleanly: **令 is the order as issued** — impersonal, and the book uses it that way (ch 12's 五色令人目盲, *"the five colours make people's eyes blind"*; ch 57's 法令, *"laws and decrees"*). **命 is the order as given to someone who is then sent.** One is the decree; the other is the commission.

### The commentators agree, in a word the text does not have

**王弼 (*Wáng Bì*, d. 249 CE):** 歸根則靜，故曰靜。靜則復命，故曰復命也。復命則得**性命**之常，故曰常也 — *"returning to the root is stillness, hence 'stillness.' Stillness is 復命, hence '復命.' 復命 is attaining the constancy of 性命 (xìng mìng — inborn nature and allotted span), hence 'the ever-present.'"*

**河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*, Han):** 言安靜者是為復還**性命**使不死也 — *"the still one is returning to their 性命, so as not to die."*

Both reach for **性命**. And **性 (*xìng* — inborn nature) has zero occurrences in the Tao Te Ching.** It is the vocabulary of a later settlement — 性 becomes a central term after this text, and both commentators are reading it back.

Their reading may still be right. But it is not the book's own word, and an English that says *nature* at Chapter 16 would be translating the commentary rather than the line. *(`CLAUDE.md`: a commentator's gloss is not the text.)*

### 復命 has its own entry

The compound at Chapter 16 — 是謂復命，復命曰常 — is treated in **`fuming-復命.md`**, including the two readings the book supports (the commentators' *return to what one was allotted*, and the idiom's *an envoy reporting back*), and the three candidate renderings with their costs.

### What is set aside

**mandate** — 天命's word, and 天命 is absent from this book. It imports the Zhou warrant-to-rule, and with it a 天 that grants and withdraws, which is precisely the overlay this edition strips from 天 (see `tian-天.md`).

**destiny, fate** — both make 命 a script settled before the actor arrives. 命 is spoken *to* someone, at a moment, and it can be reported back on. *Fate* additionally carries the Greek Moirai and the Christian providence in a text that has neither.

**decree, law** — 令's territory, and the book uses 法令 (*fǎ lìng*) for exactly that at ch 57.

**command** — 令 already carries it at ch 32, in the identical 莫之X而 frame. If 命 takes it too at ch 51, the pair the book distinguishes collapses into one English word. *(This is the open question below, not a settled prohibition — ch 51 currently reads* commands*.)*

**"the system's command"** — the Source table's literal gloss, and mechanistic in the way `CLAUDE.md` names as this edition's besetting temptation.

### Working register

| Form | Chapters | English |
|---|---|---|
| 命 as a negated verb | 51 (莫之命) | *(unsettled — must not be* command*, which is 令's at ch 32)* |
| 復命, the compound | 16 ×2 | *(unsettled — see below)* |

### Left open

**Chapter 16's line is settled.** 是謂復命，復命曰常 → *"returning to what is given"* — present tense, giver present but unnamed. The four candidates it beat, and why, are in `fuming-復命.md`.

**Chapter 51's verb**, 夫莫之命而常自然, reads *"no one commands it"* — 令's English, in 令's own construction.

**And Chapter 51 has a variant.** Our vendored 王弼 carries 命並作爵 — *"命 is written 爵 (jué — to confer a noble rank) [in other editions]"* — under a collation note flagging the line as probably an editorial gloss mistaken for Wang Bi's own comment: 〔案此句疑係命字下原校注語誤作弼注〕. If 爵, the line reads *"no one ennobles it."* That is the conferral sense of 命 showing through in a second character, and it argues that whatever is happening at ch 51 is a **granting**, not an ordering.

**令 is owed an entry of its own.** Eight lines, four chapters, and at least three Englishes — *makes* (12), *command* (32), *laws* (57).

entries.body:
## 明 (Míng) — Clear-Seeing

*Say "ming," rising like a question. Thirteen appearances across twelve chapters. Conventionally "enlightenment" — a word that points the reader in exactly the wrong direction.*

**Locked: 明 → "clear-seeing" / "clarity" / "sees clearly."** *(Not "enlightenment," not "illumination," not "brilliance.")*

Render 明 as *enlightenment* and you hand the reader a whole cosmology they did not ask for: transcendence, ascent, a higher state attained, light breaking in from somewhere else. Every one of those is foreign to what Laozi does with this word. 明 is not a state you rise into. It is what is left when you stop obstructing your own sight.

The early draft of this glossary put it better than most translations manage: **"You don't ascend; you just stop being blind."** That instinct was right, and the evidence supports it overwhelmingly.

### The graph: moonlight through a window

In its modern form 明 is 日 (*rì* — sun) beside 月 (*yuè* — moon): the two lights of the world, together. A satisfying image, and not wrong.

But it is not the oldest one. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (~100 CE) heads this entry not with 明 but with the older form **朙** — and that form is 月 (moon) beside **囧** (*jiǒng*), a **window**: a lattice or opening in a wall. The picture is **moonlight coming through a window into a dark room.**

Hold that against "enlightenment" and the difference is the whole entry. This is not the sun blazing at noon. It is not revelation, or radiance, or a light that transfigures. It is the **modest, sufficient light by which you can finally make out what is actually in the room with you.** Nothing has been added; nothing is transformed. You can simply see.

### The proof — Chapter 52 uses two different words

The decisive evidence sits in a single line:

> 用其光，復歸其明
> *Use its light; return to its clarity.*

**光** (*guāng*) is outward light — radiance, glare, the light a thing **emits**. It is the light chapters 4 and 56 bring into harmony (和其光 — *harmonize its light*, `glossary/he-和.md`) and to hold without dazzling in Chapter 58 (光而不耀 — *bright but not dazzling*). **明** is what you **return** to.

If 明 meant "illumination," this line reads *"use its light, return to its light"* — a tautology. The chapter is drawing a distinction and the translation must keep it: 光 is **emission**, 明 is **reception**. One is the light you shine; the other is the seeing you come home to. "Illumination" names the wrong half.

### What 明 actually attaches to

Follow it through the text and it is perceptual every time — and strikingly modest in what it perceives.

**It sees small things.** 見小曰明 (52) — *seeing the small is called clarity.* Not the infinite, not the divine. The small. Enlightenment does not help you notice what is minute and near; clear sight does.

**It sees the self.** 知人者智，自知者明 (33) — *knowing others is cleverness; knowing yourself is clear-seeing.* The pairing is exact: 智 (*zhì*) is the outward-facing smartness that sizes up other people; 明 is turned around, and Laozi ranks it higher.

**It is blocked by self-display.** Here Laozi puns, because 見 means both *to see* and *to show oneself*:

> 不自見，故明 (22) — *they do not display themselves, therefore they see clearly.*
> 自見者不明 (24) — *one who displays themselves does not see clearly.*

The one who is busy being seen cannot see. Clarity is not something acquired; it is what returns when the performing self gets out of the light.

**It sees what does not change.** 知常曰明 — *knowing the ever-present is called clear-seeing* — stands in **16**, and in the received text of **55**. Chapter 55's verse follows Guodian and silk A instead, which read 知和曰明 (*zhī hé yuē míng* — "knowing harmony is called clear-seeing"): there, clear-seeing is knowing harmony itself (`notes/manuscript.md`).

**And it is quiet, not brilliant.** 是謂微明 (36) — *this is called subtle clarity.* 明道若昧 (41) — *the clear Tao seems murky.* The word for the highest seeing is repeatedly qualified as faint, subtle, easily mistaken for dullness. No tradition that meant "brilliance" would keep saying so.

### What is set aside: why not "enlightenment" or "illumination"

**"Enlightenment"** imports a Buddhist and New Age structure — *awakening*, ascent, a threshold crossed, a self transformed into a higher kind. Laozi has no such architecture. There is no attainment, no realized state, no before-and-after. There is a person who has stopped displaying themselves and can therefore see the small thing in front of them. The word also carries the European Enlightenment as a second ghost — reason, progress, the dispelling of superstition — which is if anything further off.

**"Illumination"** fails on the evidence: Chapter 52 sets 光 and 明 side by side, and "illumination" collapses them. It also names emission where the text names reception.

**"Brilliance," "brightness," "radiance"** — all three describe how a thing *appears to others*, which is precisely the 光 that Laozi keeps from standing apart: harmonized in chapters 4 and 56, bright but not dazzling in chapter 58. And they contradict 微明 (subtle clarity) and 明道若昧 (the clear Tao seems murky) directly.

**"Wisdom"** is the conventional English of a different character, 智 (*zhì* — cleverness), which Chapter 33 explicitly ranks *below* 明. This edition uses it for neither (`glossary/zhi-智.md`).

### Working register

明 flexes by grammar; keep it inside one image — *sight that is unobstructed*:

- as the named state → **clear-seeing** (知常曰明 → "knowing the ever-present is called clear-seeing")
- as a noun → **clarity** (用其光，復歸其明 → "use its light, return to its clarity"; 微明 → "the hidden clarity"; 襲明 → "clarity worn covered")
- as predicate or verb → **sees clearly / does not see clearly** (不自見，故明; 自見者不明), except at ch 33, below
- as a modifier → **clear** (明道 at 41 → "the clear Tao")
- 明白四達 (10) → **"clarity reaching the four quarters"**

**Never** "enlightened," "illuminated," "brilliant."

*Why this stays prose in `render:` and is not a `flexions:` entry.* The variation here is **grammatical, not chapter-scoped** — 明 takes the predicate form wherever it predicates, which happens at 22 and 24 (47 left 明 for the received 名 on 2026-09-24), and would take it in a chapter nobody has written yet. **Chapter 33 is the declared exception, and its licence is the chapter, not the grammar.** Its eight lines share one frame, and six of their predicates are a single bare word, 智 (*zhì* — clever), 明, 強 (*qiáng* — strong), 富 (*fù* — wealthy), 久 (*jiǔ* — lasting) and 壽 (*shòu* — long-lived), which the English sets as *is* + one word through its first three couplets: 自知者明 → *"one who knows themselves is clear-seeing."* *(Shalom's call, 2026-10-30; the chapter's notes.)* `flexions:` exists for a licence tied to a named place, and its `flexion-chapter` rule checks exactly that; pinning a grammatical form to a chapter list would assert a condition the language does not have. See `process/skills/glossary-entry/SKILL.md` §4.


### Left open

One chapter uses 明 against everything above, and honesty requires flagging it rather than smoothing it.

**Chapter 65**: 古之善為道者，非以明民，將以愚之 — *those anciently masterful at the Tao did not use it to make the people 明, but meant to make them 愚 (yú — the fool's simplicity).* Here 明 is not sought but done **to** a populace, and the masters decline to do it.

**The lock holds here, and the verse reads *"did not use it to make the people see clearly."*** *(Shalom's call, 2026-11-16: "We shouldn't gloss over this actual usage of 明 for the sake of an easier translation, or because this usage may create some discomfort.")* It reverses the call of 2026-09-24, under which ch 65 read *clever*. Every witness that has the line reads 明 — Wang Bi's text, Heshang Gong's, silk A, and silk B before its damage — and nothing in the line qualifies it: 非以明民 and 將以愚之 are two causatives in parallel, sharing one object. *Clever* came from Wang Bi's gloss, 明謂多見巧詐蔽其樸也 — *"明 here means seeing too much, craft and deceit, which covers over their simplicity"* — and a gloss is evidence for a reading, never a word for the line (`process/principles/commentary-is-not-a-rendering.md`). It also put two characters under one English, since 智 (*zhì* — cleverness) follows four lines later.

**What the line says, read by the book's own grammar.** Everywhere else 明 is arrived at by oneself: 自知者明 (33), 不自見，故明 (22), 見小曰明 (52), 知常曰明 (16). Chapter 65 is the one place anyone sets out to make others 明, and the masters do not. Clear-seeing that is administered is not the clear-seeing of chapter 33, and what administering produces is the next line's cleverness. The book uses one word for a thing found and the same thing imposed, as a book that says *the straight turns crooked* (58) would: even clarity curdles when it is administered rather than arrived at.

**The cost, stated.** Read alone, the line says the ancient masters did not make the people see clearly, and that is the sentence quoted to call Laozi an authoritarian. The edition prints it rather than translating around it. `notes/reading.md` → *Ch 65* is where a reader finds the case against that reading, and with 愚 as *fools* (`glossary/yu-愚.md`) the pair lands as hard as the Chinese does.

Either way the entry's core holds. 明 is what you see with when nothing is in the way — including, in Chapter 65, the well-meaning hand of someone trying to enlighten you.

flexions.why: ch 33 sets its six bare predicates as *is* + one word, and 明 stands among them; the chapter's shape is the licence (Shalom's call, 2026-10-30)

entries.render: clear-seeing / clarity — *see clearly* in predicate position, *clear* as a modifier

## 母 (Mǔ) — The Mother

*Say "moo," the third tone — it dips and then lifts. One of the Tao's truest names, and the one translators most often flinch from.*

Here, for once, the plain English word is exactly right. 母 is *mother*, and no cleverness improves on it. So the danger in this entry is not mistranslation — it is **abstraction**. For centuries, uneasy with a cosmos that has breasts and nurses its young, translators have quietly cooled 母 into "the Source," "the Origin," "the Matrix," "the Ground of Being" — each of them a way of holding the warmth and the body at arm's length. The work of this entry is the opposite of clever. It is to refuse the flinch and let her stay what she is: a mother. Bodily, generative, nursing — and, this is the hardest part, utterly unsentimental.

### The graph

Set the character beside its neighbor. 女 (nǚ) is *woman* — the old graph draws a figure kneeling, arms folded across the body. 母 is that very same figure, with **two dots added at the breast**. That is the entire difference. The mark that turns *woman* into *mother* is the breasts: 母 is specifically the one who has borne a child and *feeds it from her own body*. The character will not let you forget the body. Before "mother" is an idea, it is milk. Whatever cosmology we raise on this word, it rests on a nursing woman.

### What 母 does in the Daodejing

The Tao's oldest and warmest name is not "the Way." It is **the mother**. She is 萬物之母, the mother of the countless things (1); 天下母, the mother of the world (25) — "mixed and complete, born before sky and earth," and able to bear it all. In Chapter 20 the sage marks themselves off from everyone precisely by *how they feed*: while the crowd gorges on the world's spectacle, 我獨異於人，而貴食母 — "I alone differ from others: I prize **feeding from the mother**." The image is exact and unembarrassed — the sage as an infant at the breast, drawing sustenance straight from her, while the world feasts on noise. And in Chapter 59 she is the **root**: 有國之母，可以長久 — "Have the mother of the state, and you can last long": "the Tao of deep roots, firm base, long life."

### The return — womb and refuge (52)

Her deepest chapter is the fifty-second, and it is the most consoling movement in the whole book. 天下有始，以為天下母 — "The world has a beginning, which serves as the mother of the world." 既得其母，以知其子；既知其子，復守其母，沒身不殆 — *"Find our mother, and you know her children. Know her children, return and hold fast to our mother, and to the end of your days, no danger will find you."* Here she is not only where you came *from*; she is where you go *back to*. The countless things are her children (子), the whole manifest world her brood — and the movement of wisdom is to turn from the children back toward the one who bore them: to return, and hold, and rest. Womb and refuge at once — origin and destination, the mother you were born from and the mother you can always come home to. No danger, to the end.

### 始 (shǐ — beginning)

*Say "shr," dipping. Eight lines across seven chapters. Locked: 始 → "beginning," and "begin" as a verb.* *(Shalom's call at chapter 52, 2026-11-19, the one line that read otherwise.)*

> 始，女之初也。从女，台聲。
> *"始: the beginning of a woman. From 女 (nǚ — woman), with 台 (tái) for the sound."* — Shuowen (說文, *Shuōwén* — Xu Shen's dictionary, c. 100 CE)

**The beginning is filed under the same kneeling woman as the mother.** 母 is 女 with two dots at the breast; 始 is 女 with a sound beside her. What exactly the Shuowen means by *a woman's beginning* is not certain, and this entry does not guess. What the graph shows is enough: the book's word for *beginning* and its word for *mother* are both built on a woman, and the book sets them side by side twice.

> *The nameless is the beginning of sky and earth.*
> *The named is the mother of the countless things.*
>
> 無名，天地之始；
> 有名，萬物之母。
>
> — chapter 1

> *The world has a beginning, which serves as the mother of the world.*
>
> 天下有始，以為天下母。
>
> — chapter 52

**A beginning is a moment. A mother is a body that stays.** Wang Bi reads chapter 1's couplet as two times in one life: 凡有皆始於無，故未形無名之時，則為萬物之始；及其有形有名之時，則長之育之亭之毒之，為其母也, *"all that is begins in what is not. So in the time before form and name, it is the beginning of the countless things; when there is form and name, it grows them, raises them, settles them, matures them: it is their mother."* His four verbs are chapter 51's own (*"grows and raises them, settles and matures them"*). The beginning happens once. The mother goes on feeding.

**Chapter 52 joins the two in one line**, and the joint is 以為 (*yǐ wéi* — "takes as," "serves as"): the world has a beginning, and that beginning serves as its mother. The moment is taken up into a body. That is why the next lines can say *return*: no one goes back to a moment, but you can go back to a mother. Wang Bi: 母，本也；子，末也, *"the mother is the root; the children are the branch tips."* Heshang Gong reads the beginning itself as presence: 始有道也, *"the beginning is: there is the Tao."*

**Everywhere else 始 is a plain beginning, and it never takes a capital or a cosmos.** Chapter 14's 古始 (*gǔ shǐ*) is *the ancient beginning*; chapter 38's 愚之始 (*yú zhī shǐ*) is *the beginning of foolishness*; chapter 64 has it twice, *the thousand-mile journey begins beneath your feet* and 慎終如始 (*shèn zhōng rú shǐ* — "be as careful at the end as at the beginning"), where it stands against 終 (*zhōng* — end). As a verb it is chapter 32's 始制有名 (*shǐ zhì yǒu míng* — "when the carving begins, there are names") and chapter 2's *the sage does not begin them*.

**Set aside, for 始:**

- **"origin."** Chapter 52's English until 2026-11-19. It is the cooling this entry refuses for 母, *the Origin* without its capital: a word with no arms, standing in the same line as the mother it is meant to become. And it breaks the echo. Chapter 52 sets down the same two characters chapter 1 does, and *beginning* lets a reader hear chapter 1 again; *origin* hides it.
- **"in the beginning."** Genesis 1:1, and John 1:1, whose Logos the Chinese Union Bible renders 道 (太初有道). Already refused at chapter 39 (`notes/translation.md`).
- **"the primordial," "genesis," "dawn."** The first was this edition's chapter 14 until it was taken out (`WORKLIST-CLOSED.md` T1-11). The other two are the same move in other coats, a beginning turned into an epoch.

### What is set aside

So we keep every warm and bodily thing the tradition has tried to abstract away. We do not render 母 as "the Source" (a word with no body), "the Origin" (a word with no arms), or "the Ground of Being" (a phrase that has never nursed anything). We keep the breasts the character draws. We keep the milk of 食母. We keep the womb of 玄牝 (the dark female, 6) and the children of 子. The Tao is not an impersonal principle a translator has dressed, for warmth, in a mother's robe. Laozi says the reverse: reach for the truest name you have for what bears all things and clings to none — and the word that comes is *mother*.

### Fierce, not fond

And now the hard honesty, without which this entry becomes a greeting card. **The cosmic mother is not sentimental.** The same book that calls her the mother of the world also says 天地不仁 — sky and earth are *not concerned with humaneness*, not doting; they treat the countless things as straw dogs (5). Her love, if we call it that, is not the hovering fondness we pour into the word "mother." It is 生而不有 — she gives birth and does not possess; she bears you, nurses you, and *lets you go*. She does not cling, does not coddle, does not shield you from the weather. Her tenderness is the fierce, impartial, inexhaustible giving of one who pours out life to all and keeps none of it. That is a deeper tenderness than sentiment — the love that can release what it made. To nurse from *this* mother is to be fed, and then set free.

### Left open

**On the capital, which she does not take.** *(Decided 2026-08-11, after argument; this entry had capitalized her for months without a ruling.)* She is rendered **mother**, lowercase, throughout. Chapter 25 offers her as a role — 可以為天下母, *"it can serve as the mother of the world"* — and then says in the next breath 吾不知其名, *"I do not know its name,"* before coining 道 under protest. All seven occurrences are genitive, possessive, or governed by 為 (*serve as*); she is never addressed and never stands as a bare subject. Heshang Gong makes it a simile outright — 如母之養子, *"like a mother nourishing her child."* And the capital would work against her: in English it confers institutional status rather than intimacy, lifting her out of the nursing body that the graph's two dots exist to draw. 道 keeps its capital because *"Tao"* is transliterated, not translated; every English word here is lowercase. *(Full reasoning in `notes/translation.md` → Typography.)*

**Chapter 2's 始 is a reading, not the received text.** Our base prints 萬物作而弗始 (*wàn wù zuò ér fú shǐ* — "the countless things arise, and the sage does not begin them"), which is the silks' reading. Wang Bi's text and Heshang Gong's both print 萬物作焉而不辭 (*wàn wù zuò yān ér bù cí* — "the countless things arise, and the sage does not refuse them"), with no 始 at all. Nothing in `sources/variants.yaml` records the choice yet (`WORKLIST.md` T2-87).

**The silks put 始 and 母 on the same object.** At chapter 1 both read 無名萬物之始也 (*"the nameless is the beginning of the countless things"*), so the beginning and the mother both belong to the countless things, and Wang Bi's own comment says 萬物之始 too. Our base keeps 天地之始, *of sky and earth* (`WORKLIST.md` T2-80).

Is she a metaphor, or the thing itself? Laozi hedges on purpose. The Tao *can be called* the mother of the world (可以為天下母) — and in nearly the same breath (1) he warns that no name holds it. So the mother is a name that points *truly* without *caging*: the most maternal thing we know, aimed at what has no name. We hold her the way Chapter 52 says to — not gripping the idea, but returning to the reality, and resting there. Her name is not the Tao. But of all the names, it may be the one that loves it best.
