## 牝 (Pìn) — The Female

*Say "peen," falling. Five appearances in three chapters. The book's word for the female as a body: she has a gate, she mates, and she lies beneath.*

**Locked: 牝 (*pìn*) → "the female," in every line, and its partner 牡 (*mǔ*) → "the male."** *(Not "the receptive female," which adds a quality no line names. Not "the feminine," which turns an animal into an abstraction. Not "the Female," since a capital makes her a doctrine.)* *(The English was settled in the verse before this entry, at chapters 6, 55 and 61. The entry argues for it and holds it. That 牝 and 雌 (cí — the hen) get two entries, not one, is Shalom's call, 2026-10-26.)*

### The graph: the mother of the herd

> 牝，畜母也。从牛匕聲。易曰：畜牝牛，吉。
> *"牝: the mother among livestock. From 牛 (niú — cattle), with 匕 (bǐ) as its sound. The Changes says: 'Rearing a cow brings good fortune.'"* — the *Shuowen Jiezi* (the Han dictionary)

**The class is 牛 (*niú* — cattle), and the class is livestock, not the ox alone.** The Shuowen's word is 畜 (*chù* — a reared animal), and the quotation it chooses, from hexagram 30 of the Changes, is a cow being raised. 牝 is the word a herder or a priest choosing an animal for sacrifice would use: the female of the herd.

**The Shuowen defines its partner in matching words.** 牡，畜父也。从牛土聲 — *"牡: the father among livestock. From 牛 (niú — cattle), with 土 (tǔ) as its sound."* And it defines the book's other pair the same way, among birds: 雌 (*cí* — the hen) is 鳥母 (*niǎo mǔ* — "the mother among birds") and 雄 (*xióng* — the rooster) is 鳥父 (*niǎo fù* — "the father among birds"). So the Han dictionary holds two pairs of words for mother and father, one for animals that walk and one for birds, and the Tao Te Ching uses both pairs. This entry is the first. `glossary/` owes the second its own.

### Three chapters, and she is a body in each

> *The spirit of the valley is deathless.*
> *This is called the dark female.*
> *The dark female's gate —*
> *this is called the root of sky and earth.*
>
> 谷神不死，
> 是謂玄牝。
> 玄牝之門，
> 是謂天地根。
>
> — chapter 6

> *They do not yet know the union of female and male, yet their whole being quickens with life — this is vital essence at its utmost.*
>
> 未知牝牡之合而全作，精之至也。
>
> — chapter 55

> *the confluence of the world, the female of the world.*
> *The female always overcomes the male by stillness.*
> *By stillness she is underneath.*
>
> 天下之交，天下之牝。
> 牝常以靜勝牡，
> 以靜為下。
>
> — chapter 61

**In each line she is something you could point at.**

- **Chapter 6: she gives birth.** She has a gate, and sky and earth come out of it. Wang Bi: 門，玄牝之所由也 — *"the gate is where the dark female comes from."* The Chinese names her twice, so the gate is hers, and the verse keeps the repeat (`chapters/006.md`).
- **Chapter 55: she mates.** 牝牡之合 (*pìn mǔ zhī hé* — "the joining of female and male") is what the newborn does not yet know. Heshang Gong moves the animal words onto people: 赤子未知男女之合會而陰作怒者，由精氣多之所致也 — *"the newborn does not yet know the joining of man and woman, yet its hidden part rises; this comes of abundant vital essence and breath."* 男女 (*nán nǚ* — man and woman) is his word. The book's is the herder's.
- **Chapter 61: she lies beneath.** The female overcomes the male by stillness, and by stillness she is below. That is a posture, and the chapter builds a politics on it: the large state should be the downstream flow, the place everything runs to. Wang Bi on 天下之牝 (*tiān xià zhī pìn* — "the female of the world"): 靜而不求，物自歸之也 — *"still and seeking nothing, things come home to her of themselves."*

### Described, never asked

**In all five lines, the female is spoken about.** No line tells the reader to be her, to hold to her, or to become her. She is named (6), she is half of a joining (55), she is a likeness for a state (61).

**雌 (*cí* — the hen) is the opposite.** It stands in two lines, and in both it is asked of you: 守其雌 (*shǒu qí cí* — "hold to the hen," ch 28) and 能為雌乎 (*néng wéi cí hū* — "can you be the hen?," ch 10). 守 (*shǒu* — to hold to) is a post you are answerable for (`glossary/shou-守.md`), and 為 (*wéi* — to be, to serve as) is a part you play. So the book has one word for the female as a body and another for the female as a place a person can stand. That pattern is a reason to look, not a proof (`process/principles/distribution-locates.md`). Looking, it holds in every line, and it is why the two characters have separate entries.

### What the commentators did with her

**Both commentators turn the female into qualities, and both merge her with the hen.**

- **Wang Bi on chapter 61 glosses her with the other word:** 牝，雌也。雄躁動貪欲，雌常以靜，故能勝雄也 — *"the female is the hen. The rooster is restless and greedy; the hen is always still, and so can overcome the rooster."* The text's 牡 (*mǔ* — the male) becomes 雄 (*xióng* — the rooster), and the line is retold among birds.
- **Heshang Gong on chapter 10 joins the two in one phrase:** 治身當如雌牝安靜柔弱 — *"in caring for the body, be like the hen and the female: calm, still, soft and yielding."*
- **Heshang Gong on chapter 6 makes her earth and the mouth:** 玄，天也，於人為鼻；牝，地也，於人為口 — *"the dark is sky, and in a person the nose; the female is earth, and in a person the mouth."* In the same note, 魄者雌也 — *"the bodily soul is the hen."*
- **Heshang Gong on chapter 61 calls her yin:** 牝者陰□也，柔謙和而不昌也 — *"the female is yin [one graph lost]: soft, humble, harmonious, and does not lead off."* The printed graph is 昌 (*chāng* — to flourish). His note on chapter 10 says the same thing with 唱 (*chàng* — to lead the singing): 和而不唱 (*hé ér bù chàng* — "harmonious, and does not lead off").

**The text does none of this.** It keeps her an animal, and it keeps 牝 and 雌 apart. 陰 (*yīn*) stands once in all 81 chapters, in chapter 42 beside 陽 (*yáng*), and never names the female (`notes/reading.md`). The commentaries are evidence that readers have always heard stillness and softness in her, and they are right to: chapter 61 says stillness outright. But the stillness is what she does, and the line keeps the animal that does it.

### 牡 (mǔ — the male)

**The male stands in two lines, and never without her.** 牝牡 (*pìn mǔ* — "female and male," 55) and 牝常以靜勝牡 (*pìn cháng yǐ jìng shèng mǔ* — "the female always overcomes the male by stillness," 61). Both times the female comes first in the Chinese, and the English keeps the order: *"the union of female and male,"* not the habitual *male and female*. The male has no line of his own in the book.

### What is set aside

**"the receptive female," "receptive."** No line says she receives. 受 (*shòu* — to receive) is not in any of them. The adjective tells the reader how to feel about her, so that they never have to meet the animal. It also borrows the I Ching's later convention for its hexagram 2, whose judgment praises 牝馬之貞 (*pìn mǎ zhī zhēn* — "the steadiness of a mare").

**"the feminine."** It turns a creature into a quality, which is the move both commentators make and the move the mother entry refuses: `glossary/mu-母.md` keeps every warm and bodily thing the tradition has tried to abstract away. The female in chapter 61 lies beneath the male. *The feminine* cannot lie beneath anything.

**"the Female."** A capital makes her a principle. Only the Tao keeps one.

**"the mother."** 母 (*mǔ* — mother) is another character, with its own entry. Chapter 6's dark female gives birth, but the line calls her 牝, and in chapters 55 and 61 she has borne nothing. Calling her *mother* would spend 母's English where 母 does not stand.

**"mare," "cow," "doe."** The line names no species. 牛 (*niú* — cattle) is the graph's class, and the Shuowen's gloss is the female of any reared animal.

### Working register

| Where 牝 (*pìn*) stands | English | Chapters |
|---|---|---|
| a noun, named | *the dark female* | 6 (玄牝 *xuán pìn*, twice) |
| a noun, in a pair, before 牡 (*mǔ* — the male) | *female and male* | 55 |
| a noun, in apposition | *the female of the world* | 61 (天下之牝 *tiān xià zhī pìn*) |
| the subject, with 牡 as object | *the female … the male* | 61 |

**Her pronoun is *she*.** Chapter 61 reads *"By stillness she is underneath."* Standing rule 1 forbids *he* for the sage: the Chinese never says whether the sage is a woman or a man, and *he* would make the male the default. 牝 says she is female, and the line is about her.

### What no rule can enforce

***Yin* is ruled out and cannot go on the `forbidden:` list.** The checker matches strings, not words, and *yin* is inside words the verse prints. It is held here and by the reader.

***Hen* is 雌's English, and cannot be forbidden here for the same reason:** *hen* is inside *when* and *then*. The two characters never share a chapter, so nothing in the book tests it.

***Mother* is ruled out above and left off the list.** A forbidden word fires wherever 牝 or 牡 stands, and the ruling is against borrowing another character's English, which this entry and `glossary/mu-母.md` already argue.

**The lock holds in this book only.** The I Ching vendors these locks as its own, and its 牝 names species: 牝馬 (*pìn mǎ* — a mare) in hexagram 2, and 牝牛 (*pìn niú* — a cow) in hexagram 30, the line the Shuowen quotes. Its hexagram 2 is also conventionally called *the receptive*, so a lock forbidding *receptive* there would flag a name rather than a rendering. So this entry carries `binds: [taoteching]`, and the I Ching rules its own female.

### Left open

**The graph's older story.** The Shuowen reads 匕 (*bǐ*) as sound only. Whether the oracle bones write the female with 匕 beside more animals than cattle, which would make 匕 a mark of the female, and whether that 匕 is the one that writes 妣 (*bǐ* — ancestress), has not been checked against a printed collection. If both hold, chapter 6's root of sky and earth has an ancestress in its graph. Until someone checks, it is a question.

**What *the female* loses.** In English *female* is a word from biology and from forms. In the Chinese it is a farmyard word, and the farmyard does not survive the translation. The entry carries it, on the same principle as 心 (*xīn* — heart) and 物 (*wù* — things).

**Whose stillness wins in chapter 61.** The commentators read it as a virtue: humility, softness, yielding. The line reads it as a posture: she is still, she is below, and she overcomes. Whether the chapter is teaching a quality or describing what an animal does, and then building a state on it, is left to the reader. The English keeps the animal so that both readings stay open.

refs.locator: Hexagram 2, Judgment, the mare

entries.shuowen: The mother among livestock. From 牛 (niú — cattle), with 匕 (bǐ) as its sound. The Changes says: 'Rearing a cow brings good fortune.'

## 魄 (Pò) — Aliveness

*Say "paw," falling. One appearance in the whole book, in the first line of chapter 10.*

**Locked: 魄 → "aliveness."** *(Never "soul," never "spirit," never "life force." Not "breath," "energy" or "life" either, but those three are rulings no check can hold. See the last section but one.)*

*The line is* 載營魄抱一，能無離乎 *: "Housing your aliveness and embracing the one, can you keep these from parting?" 營 (yíng — a walled dwelling), the character beside it, is covered here as "housing."*

### The graph: a ghost, and the moon's pale light

> 魄，**陰神**也。从鬼白聲。
> *"魄 is the yin spirit. From 鬼 (guǐ — a ghost), with 白 (bái — white) for the sound."* — 說文解字

**鬼** is the same character chapter 60 renders *ghosts*. In the oracle bones it is a figure with an outsized head, usually read as a mask: the dead, or someone standing in for them. **白**'s original picture is unknown. A thumb (郭沫若, *Guō Mòruò*), a container and a human head have all been proposed, and none has won. 說文 counts it as sound alone.

**The graph is young, and the word is old.** 魄 has no oracle-bone or bronze form. The word does: Western Zhou bronzes date events by the moon's phases, and they write *pò* as **霸**, a moon (月) with a sound part. 既生霸 is *"after the light is born,"* 既死霸 *"after the light has died."* 說文 under 霸: 月始生，霸然也, *"the moon first coming to life, pale and bright."* 段玉裁 (*Duàn Yùcái*) notes the hand-over, 後代魄行而霸廢矣, *"in later ages 魄 took over and 霸 fell out of use"*. The moon sense survived inside it: 李軌 (*Lǐ Guǐ*), on the 法言, has 魄，光也, *"魄 is light,"* and 孟康 (*Mèng Kāng*) has 魄，月質也, *"魄 is the moon's body."*

**So 白 may be more than a sound.** A Han apocryphal text quoted by 孔穎達 (*Kǒng Yǐngdá*) puns the two outright: 魄，白也…白，明白也, *"魄 is white… white is brightness."* 說文 does not say 白亦聲 (*"白 also gives the sound"*), its usual mark for a part that carries meaning and sound at once, and the atlas reports 說文. This entry records that Han readers heard more.

*A calibration: we do not claim Laozi heard the moon in this word. By his time 魄 was a word for a part of a living person, and the evidence for that is what decides the English.*

### What 魄 is: the life that clings to the form

The locus classicus is 子產 (*Zǐ Chǎn*) in the 左傳 (*Zuǒ Zhuàn*), explaining how a man eight years dead could walk as a ghost:

> 人生始化曰魄，既生魄，陽曰魂。用物精多，則魂魄強。
> *"When a person first comes into being, that is called 魄. Once the 魄 is born, its yang side is called 魂 (hún). Draw on much 精 (jīng — vital essence) and the 魂 and 魄 grow strong."*

The commentators read it as plainly bodily, and the readings agree:

| source | says | in English |
|---|---|---|
| 杜預 (*Dù Yù*), on the 左傳 | 魄，**形**也 | *"魄 is the form"* |
| 孔穎達, on the same line | **附形之靈**為魄，附氣之神為魂 | *"the life clinging to the form is the 魄; the spirit clinging to the breath is the 魂"* |
| 孔穎達, continuing | 初生之時，**耳目心識，手足運動，啼呼為聲**，此則魄之靈也 | *"at birth, the ears, eyes and heart taking things in, the hands and feet moving, the crying that is its voice: this is the life of the 魄"* |
| 鄭玄 (*Zhèng Xuán*), on the 禮記 | **耳目之聰明**為魄 | *"the sharpness of ear and eye is the 魄"* |
| 白虎通 (*Báihǔ Tōng*) | 魄者迫也，猶迫迫然**箸於人**也 | *"魄 means pressed close: it clings tightly to a person"* |
| 禮記, 郊特牲 | 魂氣歸于天，**形魄歸于地** | *"the 魂 and the breath return to the sky; the form and the 魄 return to the earth"* |

Five things follow. 魄 is **first**, the life a person has before anything else. It is **bodily**, attached to the form and not to the breath. It is **sensing and moving**, and 孔穎達's example is a newborn. It **clings**. And it comes **in degrees**, strong or weak, as the 左傳 says.

王弼 (*Wáng Bì*), whose commentary this edition reads beside the text, puts 魄 on the same side in his own vocabulary. At chapter 4 the earth is 形魄, *"form and 魄,"* against the sky's 精象, *"essence and image"*: 地雖形魄不法於天則不能全其寧, *"the earth, though it is form and 魄, cannot keep its rest unless it models itself on the sky."* At chapter 25: 形魄不及精象, *"form and 魄 do not reach essence and image."*

### Chapter 10: the breath beside it

> 載營魄抱一，能無離乎
> 專氣致柔，能如嬰兒乎
> *"Housing your aliveness and embracing the one, can you keep these from parting?*
> *Gathering the breath to softness, can you be an infant?"*

**The couplet names the two halves of a living person that the 禮記 pairs.** 祭義: 氣也者，神之盛也；魄也者，鬼之盛也, *"breath is the fullness of spirit; the 魄 is the fullness of ghost."* Aliveness stands in the first line and breath in the second. The infant the second line asks for is 孔穎達's picture of the 魄 itself.

**魂 (*hún*), the 魄's usual partner, never appears in the book.** 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) supplies it anyway: 營魄，魂魄也…魂在肝，魄在肺, *"營魄 is the 魂 and the 魄… the 魂 in the liver, the 魄 in the lungs."* The pairing is older than he is. It is in the 左傳 above, and in 韓非子 (*Hán Fēizǐ*)'s own commentary on chapter 60, 魂魄去而精神亂, *"when the 魂 and 魄 leave, essence and spirit fall into disorder."* What is Han is the **organ map**. In five-phase medicine the lungs are metal, autumn and white, and that is the second road by which whiteness reaches 魄. It runs through a system this text does not use. Michael Brashier has argued that even the two-soul scheme was a scholars' model, and that Han grave inscriptions set the 魂 and 魄 together at the tomb against the 神 (*shén* — spirit) at the shrine.

**Who houses whom.** 王弼: 載猶處也。營魄，人之常居處也…言人能處常居之宅, *"載 is like 'to dwell.' 營魄 is a person's constant dwelling… a person who can dwell in the house where they always live."* For him the 營魄 is the house and the person lives in it. ***Housing* takes the other direction**: the person holds the 魄. That is 王逸 (*Wáng Yì*)'s reading of the same phrase in the 楚辭 (*Chǔ Cí*), 載營魄而登霞兮, *"bearing my 營魄 I climb the rosy clouds,"* glossed 抱我魂靈而上升也, *"embracing my soul I rise."* It is also 河上公's, 當愛養之, *"you must cherish and nourish it."* The verb stands on 營's graph, 說文 營，市居也, *"a walled residence."*

**The witnesses.** The Mawangdui silk B text reads 戴營魄抱一，能毌離乎, with 戴 (*dài* — to carry on the head) for 載. The Peking University Han slips read 載**熒**魄, with 熒 (*yíng* — a glimmer) for 營. That is one witness, and it is a reason to look rather than a reading, but it puts the moon's pale light back into the line. Guodian has no chapter 10.

### Why "aliveness"

- **It is the body's own.** Nothing in it leaves the body or lives elsewhere, and *housing* already says where it is kept.
- **It carries the senses.** English *alive to* means sensitive to, which is 鄭玄's sharp ear and eye. *Vigor* had motion only.
- **It comes in degrees.** You can be more or less alive, as the 左傳's 魄 grows strong.
- **It is the infant.** 孔穎達's newborn, eyes open, limbs moving, crying, is aliveness you could point at, and chapter 10 asks for the infant one line later.
- **It brings nothing in.** No theology, no breath, no energy and no sex.

### What is set aside, and why

**"soul"** is what every English translation prints: Waley *the physical-soul*, Lau *the bodily soul*, Lynn *the earthbound soul*, Legge *the animal soul*, and plain *soul* in Henricks, Mair and Ivanhoe. Each qualifier is an attempt to take back what the noun imports, a separable, immaterial self, and the qualifiers are the evidence that it does. Already refused for 精 (*jīng*) and 身 (*shēn*) on the same grounds.

**"the corporeal soul"** is the accurate label, and it is right in a note. In the verse it is a technical term for the overlay; see `process/principles/perform-dont-label.md`.

**"spirit"** is 神's (6, 39, 60), and 神 is the half the 禮記 sets against the 魄.

**"life force"** and **"life-energy"** are the popular English for 氣 (*qì* — breath), which is the other half, and *energy* is ruled out for 氣 as well (`glossary/qi-氣.md`).

**"vitality"** shares its root with 精's locked *vital essence* (21, 55). The 左傳's definition would then read *"draw on much vital essence and the vitality grows strong,"* and the distinction it draws is lost.

**"vigor"** leans toward virility, and the sexual vitality in this book is 精's, at chapter 55's 朘作.

**"the animating part"** sends 魄 the wrong way. *Anima* is breath, and breath is 氣's, in the next line.

**"the quick"** is the creed's *the quick and the dead*, and chapter 55 already *quickens*.

**"body"** and **"flesh"**: *body* is 身's (13, 54, 76), and *flesh* is Pauline, Romans 8, the hymn test.

### Working register

One occurrence, a noun, the object of 載 (*zài* — to carry, to ride, to dwell in). The two characters before it are rendered together by one verb:

| Chinese | English | renders |
|---|---|---|
| 載營 | *housing* | 營's graph, a walled dwelling, with 載's carrying |
| 魄 | *your aliveness* | 魄. *Your* is supplied, as English needs a possessor |

### What no rule can enforce

**"breath" and "life" are ruled out for 魄 and are not on the `forbidden:` list, because they cannot be.** 氣 stands in chapter 10 and prints *breath* there. 生 (*shēng*) stands in chapter 10 too (生之畜之), and *life* is its word elsewhere. `check_locks.py` gates on whether a character is present in the chapter, and both characters are. So *soul*, *spirit*, *life force*, *vigor* and *energy* are held by the build; *breath* and *life* are held by this entry and by the reader. See `process/principles/ruling-and-enforcement-are-two-facts.md`.

### Left open

**The ghost.** Aliveness ends at death; the 魄 does not. 子產's whole point is that a strong 魄 can outlast the person: the 禮記 sends it into the ground with the body, and it is what lingers at the tomb. The English keeps the living half of the word and drops the half that goes into the earth, and it has to, because the only English that keeps both is *soul*. Laozi's line is about a living person keeping two things from parting, so the ghost is offstage. It is not gone.

**Whether 白 carries meaning.** 說文 says sound. The 霸 word family and a Han pun say more. 明白 (*míng bái* — clarity) stands four lines below in this chapter, and that compound is bound, to *clarity* (`glossary/ming-明.md`; `WORKLIST-CLOSED.md` T2-23). Whether the chapter hears 魄 and 明白 together is a reason to look and not a reading (`process/principles/distribution-locates.md`).

**The direction of 載.** 王弼 has the person inside the 營魄; 王逸 and 河上公 have the person holding it. The verse follows the second. 王弼 is the commentator this edition most often follows, and here it does not.
entries.shuowen: The yin spirit. From 鬼 (guǐ — a ghost), with 白 (bái — white) for sound.

entries.body:
## 樸 (Pǔ) — Uncarved Wood

*Say "poo," dipping and lifting. Eight appearances across six chapters — 15, 19, 28, 32, 37, 57. Perhaps the most concrete image in the book, and the one most often turned into an abstraction.*

**Locked: 樸 → "uncarved wood" / "the uncarved."** *(Lowercase. Not "simplicity," not "the Uncarved Block" as a capitalized proper noun.)*

樸 is a piece of timber that has not yet been made into anything. That is the whole word, and its power is that it stays a piece of wood. The temptation — and most translations succumb — is to lift it into a virtue: *simplicity, purity, primal innocence*. But an abstraction cannot be **split**, and splitting is precisely what Chapter 28 does to it. Keep the wood, and the argument survives.

### The graph

樸 is built on **木** (*mù*) — a tree, the oldest and plainest graph for wood — with a phonetic element beside it. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it 木素也: *wood in its 素 state*, where **素** (*sù*) is **undyed silk** — cloth still the color it was when it came off the worm.

So the character's own definition reaches for its twin. And Laozi puts them side by side, once, in **Chapter 19**:

> 見素抱樸
> *See the undyed; embrace the uncarved.*

Two materials, one condition: **before human working.** Silk before the dye-vat, timber before the chisel. Not innocent, not sacred — just not yet turned into something for us.

### Chapter 28 — the block and the vessels

The central passage, and the reason the wood must stay wood:

> 樸散則為器
> *When the uncarved is split up, it becomes vessels.*

**器** (*qì*) is a vessel, a tool, an implement — a thing with a **function**. And here is the whole idea in one motion: the block has no function. Carve it, and you get a bowl, a wheel, a handle — each useful, each *named*, each now only one thing. What the block loses in becoming useful is **everything it might otherwise have been.**

Note where this lands in the chapter's architecture. Chapter 28 is built of three parallel triads, each closing on 復歸於 — *return to*: return to **the infant** (嬰兒), return to **the limitless** (無極), return to **the uncarved** (樸). All three name the same direction: back toward what has not yet been made particular.

And 器 in Chinese is not only pottery. It is also what a **person** amounts to — 成器 means *to become someone useful, to amount to something*. So 樸散則為器 reads, without strain, as a sentence about people: society takes the whole raw human and carves them into a function. A role. A job title. Useful, named, and no longer able to be anything else.

### Why the uncarved is nameless

Two chapters bind 樸 to 無名 (*wúmíng* — namelessness), and the link is exact rather than poetic:

> 道常無名，樸。(32) — *The Tao is ever nameless, uncarved.*
> 吾將鎮之以無名之樸。(37) — *I will settle them with the nameless uncarved.*

**Carving is naming.** A shaped thing can be named because it is now one determinate thing — *this is a bowl*. The block resists naming for the same reason it resists use: it is not yet any particular thing. Chapter 1's nameless (無名) and Chapter 28's uncarved (樸) are one condition described in two materials — one in language, one in wood.

Which explains the strangest line of the group:

> 樸雖小，天下莫能臣也。(32)
> *Though the uncarved is small, nothing in the world can make it a subject.*

**臣** (*chén*) is a vassal, a servant, one who serves under. You cannot subordinate the uncarved — because to subordinate is to assign a function, and to assign a function is to carve. What has no use cannot be put to use. Its smallness is not weakness; it is the reason nothing can get a grip on it.

### The resolution — 大制不割

Chapter 28 does not leave us with a prohibition on all shaping, which would be unlivable. It closes:

> 聖人用之，則為官長，故大制不割。
> *The sage uses them, and so becomes chief of officials — therefore the greatest shaping does no cutting.*

**制** (*zhì*) is to tailor, cut out, regulate, govern. **割** (*gē*) is to sever. So: *the great carving does not sever.* The sage does not refuse to govern, and does not pretend the world contains no vessels. What they refuse is the **cut** — the severing that turns a whole person into an instrument. Shape without severing; use without reducing. That is the practical form of 無為 (*wúwéi* — non-doing) applied to people.

### The far echo — Chapter 41

One more line belongs to this cluster, and its manuscript fork makes it sharper: 大器晚成 (41), which the older witnesses read as 大器**免**成 — *the great vessel is **never** completed.* This edition follows the manuscript reading.

Set it beside Chapter 28 and it snaps into place. If a vessel is made by cutting, then the **greatest** vessel is the one never finished being cut — which is to say, the block itself. The great vessel is never completed because completion is exactly what would ruin it.

### What is set aside

**"Simplicity."** The most common rendering and the most costly. It is abstract, it sounds like a lifestyle preference, and it cannot be split into vessels. Chapter 28's argument becomes unreadable.

**"Purity," "innocence," "primal wholeness."** These import moral and spiritual value the wood does not carry. An uncut log is not virtuous. It is simply uncut — which is a fact about its history, not its character.

**"The Uncarved Block," capitalized.** The initial capitals turn a log into a doctrine, and this is exactly the devotional typography the overlay audit warns against: in English, capitals confer deity. Laozi's word is small and homely — 樸雖小, *the uncarved is small*. Keep it lowercase.

**"Raw material," "unprocessed material."** Correct in denotation, industrial in feel, and they imply the thing is *awaiting* processing — which inverts the value.

**Leaving it untranslated as *pu*.** The image is fully available in English. Transliterating would mystify a piece of wood.

### Working register

- as noun → **uncarved wood**, or **the uncarved** where the sentence needs it to act as a subject (樸散則為器 → "when the uncarved is split up, it becomes vessels")
- in simile → **like uncarved wood** (敦兮其若樸 → "solid, like uncarved wood")
- bound to namelessness → **the nameless uncarved** (無名之樸)
- predicative, of people → **plain** — a licensed flexion, see below
- **器** as its counter-term → **vessel** where the thing is a container, **tool** or **instrument** where the point is function

**On "plain" at Chapter 57.** 我無欲，而民自樸 is rendered *"I am desireless, and the people become plain of themselves"* — and it should stay. The line sits in a four-part refrain (transform / right / enrich / ——), each member a short predicate ending in 自 (*of themselves*); "become uncarved of themselves" would stall it, and "plain" carries 樸's core sense exactly. This is a deliberate flexion, not a drift: the plain people of Chapter 57 and the uncut wood of Chapter 28 are the same image at two scales.


### Is there a paradox inside the word? — the "block" question

A tempting reading holds that 樸 is *self-contradictory by construction*: to have a **block**, someone must already have felled, squared, and sawn the timber — so the "uncarved block" is always already carved. It is an elegant thought. It does not survive the evidence, and it is worth showing why, because what replaces it is better.

**The lexicography.** The *Shuowen* defines 樸 as 木素 — *plain wood, unworked lumber.* Not a block. Not a blank. A **state**, not a shape.

**The word-family.** 樸 is 木 (wood) + the phonetic 菐. Change the material radical and you get **璞** (*pú*) — 玉 (jade) + the same 菐 — meaning **uncut jade still in the rock**, the stone as it comes out of the mountain. The shared phonetic carries the sense *raw, pre-worked*, and jade-in-the-matrix is unambiguously a natural object that no hand has touched. Whatever 菐 means, it is not "prepared stock."

**The company it keeps.** Chapter 28's architecture is decisive. Three parallel triads, each closing on 復歸於 — *return to*:

> 復歸於**嬰兒** — return to the **infant**
> 復歸於**無極** — return to the **endless**
> 復歸於**樸** — return to the **uncarved wood**

Three slots, one grammar, one category. An infant is not a prepared material; neither is the limitless. 樸 sits among *original natural conditions*, not processed intermediates.

**The syntax.** Chapter 32 reads 道常無名。樸雖小 — *the Tao is ever nameless; though [it is] uncarved and small…* Here 樸 attaches to **the Tao itself**. The Tao is not a piece of squared timber awaiting a chisel.

So the "block" is **English**, not Chinese — a noun supplied by translators to give an adjective a body. Scholars have said so directly: Pas and Leung note that the addition of "block" is an *interpretation* rather than a translation of the original sense of plain wood. This is a further argument for our lock: **"uncarved wood," never "uncarved block."** The block imports a paradox Laozi did not write — and worse, by satisfying the appetite for paradox, it hides the three real ones.

### The paradoxes that are actually there

**1. You are told to return to a state that cannot be recovered.** 復歸於樸 (28). Wood does not un-carve. Once the block is vessels, no craft on earth makes it a block again. Yet the instruction stands, three times over, in parallel with returning to infancy and to the limitless — both equally irreversible. Either the instruction is impossible, or *returning* means something other than reversal: not restoring a former shape but ceasing to identify with the shape you were cut into. The text does not explain. It simply keeps pointing backward along a road that only runs forward.

**2. The great carving does not cut.** 大制不割 (28) — Laozi's own explicit paradox, placed in the very passage where the block becomes vessels. 制 is to tailor, cut out, govern; 割 is to sever. The greatest shaping does no severing. Not a refusal to shape — a shaping that leaves nothing cut.

**3. The un-usable is used.** Chapter 32 insists that nothing in the world can make the uncarved a subject — 天下莫能臣也 — because it has no function to be pressed into. Then Chapter 37: 吾將鎮之以無名之樸 — *I will settle them with the nameless uncarved.* The ruler **deploys** it. The thing defined by having no use is picked up and used, and the paradox is exactly the point: what settles a grasping world is the one thing that cannot be grasped.

**And one more, structural.** Chapter 32 says 始制有名 — *when the carving begins, there are names.* Naming **is** carving. Which means every word in this book is a cut, including the word 樸 — Laozi is using chisels to point at the uncut log. He seems to know it: 道可道，非常道 (1), and 知者不言 (56). The book is a carving that argues against carving.

That is the honest shape of the thing. The paradox is not buried in the etymology; it is in what Laozi *does* with a perfectly ordinary word for raw timber. Which is more interesting, and more his.

### Left open

The obvious objection: bowls are good. Wheels are good. A world of uncut logs is a world with nothing to eat from. Laozi knows this — Chapter 11 is a hymn to the usefulness of vessels, and Chapter 28 has the sage *using* the carved things and governing with them.

So this is not a counsel to remain unformed. It is closer to a warning about **which way the traffic runs.** Everything in the book moves toward the uncarved — return to the infant, return to the limitless, return to the block — while the world moves the other way, cutting and naming and assigning, until nothing whole is left. The instruction is directional, not absolute: know that you were a block before you were a tool, and that the tool is the smaller thing.

What the text will not say is how much carving a life requires. It offers only 大制不割 — *shape without severing* — which is less a rule than a discipline of the hand, and, like most of this book's central instructions, easier to recognize than to follow.

## 器 (Qì) — Vessel

*Say "chee," falling. Twelve appearances across nine chapters. A concrete object that abstraction keeps reaching for — and the one word in this glossary that the mechanistic overlay attacks directly.*

**Locked: 器 → "vessel" / "tool" / "implement."** *(Not "system," not "mechanism," not "machine.")*

Chapter 29 read 天下神器 as *"the world is a sacred system."* That single substitution costs the chapter its argument, because the next clause is 不可執也 — *it cannot be grasped* — and then 執者失之, *those who grasp it lose it.* **You can grasp at a vessel and break it. You cannot grasp a system.** The image and the warning are one gesture, and abstraction severs them.

The danger runs the other way too. Chapter 11's whole case depends on 器 staying a **pot**: 埏埴以為器 — *knead clay to make a vessel* — and the vessel is useful only because of the hollow. Let 器 drift toward "structure" or "function" and the argument evaporates, because a structure has no inside.

### The graph: a dog guarding the crockery

器 is four 口 (*kǒu* — mouth, opening) around 犬 (*quǎn* — dog). The *Shuowen Jiezi* (~100 CE) is unusually plain about it:

> 皿也。象器之口，犬所以守之。
> *A vessel. It depicts the mouths of containers, with a dog to guard them.*

The picture is a **yard of open pots with a dog watching over them.** It is worth sitting with, because it says two things at once. 器 is a *made* thing — fired, shaped, owned. And it is a thing **worth guarding**: valuable enough that you set an animal on it.

That second half is what makes 神器 (*shén qì*) in Chapter 29 land. In the late Zhou a 神器 was concrete: the **ritual bronzes**, above all the 九鼎 (*jiǔ dǐng* — the nine cauldrons), whose possession was the visible warrant of the mandate to rule. The chapter opens on 將欲取天下 — *wishing to seize the world* — and answers that the world is a sacred vessel and cannot be grasped. To a contemporary ear that is not a metaphor. It is a sentence about reaching for the cauldrons. *(See the Reading Note at Chapter 29.)*

### The evidence — 器 is what wholeness becomes

**The fall from the uncarved.** Chapter 28: 樸散則為器 — *when the uncarved wood is broken up, it becomes 器.* This is the hinge of the whole 樸 argument. 器 is the **plural, specialized, useful** state on the far side of a loss: one log becomes many tools, each good for something and none good for everything. The word is not an insult, but it names a diminishment.

**And yet 器 is exemplary.** Chapter 11 makes a clay pot one of three proofs that emptiness is what works — 有器之用, *there is the use of the vessel* — alongside the wheel's hub and the room's windows. The vessel here is not fallen; it is the teacher.

**And weapons are 器.** Chapter 31 says it three times: 夫佳兵者，不祥之器 · 兵者不祥之器 · 非君子之器 — *fine weapons are implements of ill omen; weapons are implements of ill omen; they are not the implements of a person of quality.* Chapter 57's 人多利器，國家滋昏 (*the more sharp implements among the people, the darker the state grows*) and Chapter 36's 國之利器不可以示人 (*the sharp instruments of the state must not be displayed*) run the same way. Here "implement" or "instrument" serves better than "vessel," and the flexion is licensed.

**And a person can be one.** Chapter 41's 大器晚成 — in our base text *"the great vessel is completed late,"* and in the Mawangdui and Guodian witnesses 免成 / 曼成, *never completed*, which we follow. Classical Chinese applies 器 to people as **capacity** — the size of what someone can hold — and the idiom survives in modern Chinese as *a person of great capacity matures slowly*. Chapter 67's 故能成器長 (*and so can become the elder of the vessels*) uses the same personal sense.

### What is set aside, and why

**"System"** is the mechanistic overlay, and this project's own besetting temptation. It abstracts a fired clay pot into a set of relations, breaks Chapter 29's grasping image, and empties Chapter 11's hollow. It also fails the pointing test twice over: Laozi could point at the pot and at the dog.

**"Mechanism," "machine," "apparatus"** import moving parts and a designer. 器 has neither. A pot does nothing; that is the point of Chapter 11.

**"Utensil"** is not wrong so much as small and domestic — it makes 神器 (the world) and 不祥之器 (weapons of ill omen) faintly absurd. Keep it out of the register.

**"Organ"** is a real classical sense of 器 and is right to leave unused here: nothing in these nine chapters is anatomical.

**"Vessel" everywhere** would also be an error. Chapter 31's weapons are not vessels, and Chapter 28's carved tools are not vessels. The lock is a small family — *vessel, tool, implement* — held together by being **made, concrete, and usable**, and it flexes by what the chapter has in hand.

### Working register

- containers, and the world as one → **vessel** (有器之用 → "the use of the vessel"; 神器 → "a sacred vessel"; 大器 → "the great vessel")
- what the uncarved becomes → **tools** (樸散則為器 → "when the uncarved wood is carved, it is made into tools")
- weapons and sharp things → **implement / instrument** (不祥之器 → "implements of ill omen"; 利器 → "sharp instruments")
- of a person → **capacity** (器長 → the elder among them; 大器晚成 and its variants)

**Never** "system," "mechanism," "machine," "utensil."

### Left open

**Is 器 fallen or exemplary?** The text will not say.

Chapter 28 makes 器 the **result of breaking wholeness**: the uncarved log scattered into specialized tools, and the chapter's whole movement is a call to 復歸於樸 — *return to the uncarved.* On that reading 器 is a diminishment, and the sage's task is to be the log and not the chisel.

Chapter 11 makes 器 the **model of how anything works at all**, and Chapter 29 makes it **sacred**. On that reading being a vessel is not a fall but the condition of usefulness, and the hollow at the centre is the same emptiness the Tao is praised for.

Both are in the book, unreconciled, and we do not reconcile them. The nearest thing to a resolution is that Chapter 28 objects to being **one** tool — 樸散, *scattered*, made plural and partial — while Chapter 11 admires the vessel for **what it lacks**. A pot is not a specialized blade. But that reading is ours, and the text does not state it.

## 氣 (Qì) — Breath

*Say "chee," falling. Three appearances, one in each of three chapters. The book's word for what moves in a living body and between the halves of things: in its plainest sense, a breath, the kind you can see on a cold morning.*

**Locked: 氣 → "breath," in all three lines.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-11-01.)* *(Not "energy" or "vital energy," which bring physics and a twentieth-century register into a book about bodies. Not "vital breath," because* vital *is 精 (jīng — vital essence)'s word, and chapter 55 needs the two kept apart; that ruling no check can hold, see the last section but one. Not "life force," and not "qi" left in pinyin.)*

*精 (jīng — vital essence) is its counterpart, and has its own entry: chapter 55 sets the two against each other, a reserve against a current, and one entry for both would blur the distinction the chapter is built on (`glossary/jing-精.md`).*

### The graph: three spellings, three pictures, one word

The word was written three ways before the modern character settled, and each spelling draws something different.

**Cloud, in the Shuowen's reading.** The Han dictionary keeps two characters where the book prints one:

> 气，雲气也。象形。
> *"气 (qì): cloud vapor. A picture."* — the *Shuowen Jiezi* (the Han dictionary)

> 氣，饋客芻米也。从米气聲。
> *"氣 (qì): fodder and grain presented to guests. From 米 (mǐ — rice), with 气 (qì — cloud vapor) as its sound."* — the *Shuowen Jiezi*

Duan Yucai, its great Qing commentator, draws the line from the picture to the word: 气本雲气，引伸爲凡气之偁 (*qì běn yún qì, yǐn shēn wéi fán qì zhī chēng* — "气 is first cloud vapor, and is extended to name every kind of 气").

**But the cloud is a reading of the shape, not a use anyone recorded.** The oracle-bone graph is three horizontal strokes, the outer two later bent so it wouldn't be read as 三 (sān — three). In the oracle bones it is used almost only as a function word: an adverb, "in the end," and sometimes a preposition, "until." In bronze it writes 乞 (qǐ — to pray for) and 訖 (qì — to end). The vapor and the breath are not attested in either. They appear in the Warring States texts, the century of the oldest Laozi. The picture of layered cloud is Xu Shen's analysis, five centuries after the bronzes, and it may be right. The earliest record doesn't show it.

**Grain, in the standard spelling.** 氣 (qì) began as a different word, the gift of grain to a guest, built from 米 (mǐ — rice) with the vapor graph lending its sound. The Shuowen cites the commentary on the Spring and Autumn: 齊人來氣諸侯 (*qí rén lái xì zhū hóu* — "the people of Qi came and presented grain to the lords"). The vapor word took over the grain character, and the gift moved to 餼 (xì — a gift of grain), with 食 (shí — food) added. **So the rice in 氣 is not steam over a rice pot.** It belongs to the guest's provisions and came into the vapor word through a borrowed spelling.

**Fire, in the oldest Laozi.** The Guodian slips, copied around 300 BCE, write the word with 既 (jì — already) for its sound, in all of the roughly ten places it stands in that tomb. The graph in chapter 55's line is transcribed with 火 (huǒ — fire) as its meaning part. So the scribes who wrote the earliest copy of this book spelled 氣 (qì) with fire, the warm vapor that rises from heat. It's the one spelling of the three that draws something Laozi could have pointed at in these lines: the warm breath of a body.

**Where the pictures stop.** None of the three is the word's sense in the book. Cloud and fire are outside a body, and grain is a spelling. In the book, 氣 is what moves in a body, and between yin and yang.

### What the manuscripts print

Every witness that survives agrees on the character in all three lines. The words around it fork.

| Line | Guodian, c. 300 BCE | Mawangdui silk A, c. 200 BCE | Mawangdui silk B, c. 175 BCE | Wang Bi, received |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | not among the slips | lost to damage | 專氣至柔 (*zhuān qì zhì róu* — "gathering the breath, reaching softness") | 專氣致柔 (*zhuān qì zhì róu* — "gathering the breath to softness") |
| 42 | not among the slips | 中氣以為和 (*zhōng qì yǐ wéi hé* — "the breath within makes harmony") | lost to damage | 沖氣以為和 (*chōng qì yǐ wéi hé* — "the 沖 breath makes harmony") |
| 55 | 心使氣曰強 (*xīn shǐ qì yuē qiáng* — "when the heart drives the breath, that is called strong"), in Chu spellings | the same | the same | the same |

**Chapter 55's line is the best attested 氣 (qì) in the book.** It stands in all four witnesses, and the Guodian bamboo carries it a century before the silks. It is also the hardest of the three, so the evidence is strongest where the decision matters most.

**Silk B's 至 (zhì — to reach) for 致 (zhì — to bring to) in chapter 10** is one word in two spellings, 致 being the causative of 至. In silk B's spelling, the softness arrives rather than being brought about, and the English "gathering the breath to softness" reads either way.

**Silk A's 中 (zhōng — middle) in chapter 42 is a word, and the verse follows it** (Shalom's call, 2026-11-15). 中 is 沖 (chōng)'s sound part and could be a short spelling of it, but silk A writes 沖 in full at chapter 45, Beida writes 中 here too, and Heshang Gong reads the received 沖 as 中. The line reads *"and the breath within makes harmony,"* so 氣 (qì) is no longer the object of a verb in chapter 42 but the thing that makes the harmony. *Within* holds both readings: yin, yang and the breath between them, the third of 二生三 (*èr shēng sān* — "the two births the three"), or the breath inside each thing. The argument is in `glossary/chong-沖.md`.

### In Laozi's century, 氣 ran from a held breath to the sky

The book's own three lines are a small sample, so the evidence widens to the texts of its time.

- **A held breath.** The Analects describes Confucius entering the hall: 屏氣似不息者 (*bǐng qì sì bù xī zhě* — "holding in his breath as if he were not breathing"). Here 氣 is breath, literally, the thing a person can hold.
- **What fills the body.** Mencius: 夫志，氣之帥也；氣，體之充也 (*fú zhì, qì zhī shuài yě; qì, tǐ zhī chōng yě* — "the will is the commander of the 氣; the 氣 is what fills the body"). And so, he says, 持其志，無暴其氣 (*chí qí zhì, wú bào qí qì* — "hold to your will, and do no violence to the 氣").
- **The empty thing the heart should give way to.** Zhuangzi's fasting of the heart: 無聽之以心而聽之以氣……氣也者，虛而待物者也 (*wú tīng zhī yǐ xīn ér tīng zhī yǐ qì … qì yě zhě, xū ér dài wù zhě yě* — "don't listen with the heart, listen with the 氣 … the 氣 is empty, and waits on things").
- **The weather of the world.** The Zuo commentary: 天有六氣 (*tiān yǒu liù qì* — "the sky has six 氣"), named as yin, yang, wind, rain, dark and light.
- **The sky itself, in the tomb that held the oldest Laozi.** Guodian Tomb No. 1, the grave of an unnamed Chu aristocrat buried around 300 BCE, held the oldest copies of the book, and with them the Taiyi Sheng Shui ("The Great One Gives Birth to Water"), a text found with the Guodian Laozi and written on slips of the same form as its third bundle: 上，氣也，而謂之天 (*shàng, qì yě, ér wèi zhī tiān* — "above, it is 氣, and it is called sky"). In the same tomb, the Xing Zi Ming Chu ("Nature Comes from the Mandate") says 喜怒哀悲之氣，性也 (*xǐ nù āi bēi zhī qì, xìng yě* — "the 氣 of joy, anger, grief and sorrow is one's nature").

**Breath is the word's plain core, and the word was already wider than breath when the book was written.** The cosmic 氣 (qì) is not a later growth. It was buried in the Guodian tomb, beside the oldest copy of the book.

**Chapter 55 takes a side in a live argument.** Mencius puts the will over the 氣 and approves the command, warning only against violence. Laozi says the heart driving the 氣 is 強 (qiáng — strong), the hardness chapter 76 gives the dead. Zhuangzi stands with Laozi: the heart is to give way to the 氣, which is empty and waits. In all three, heart and 氣 are a pair, one that wills and one that moves. The English has to name something a heart can drive, and that, left alone, is empty and moves of itself. Breath does both. Everyone has held a breath under effort, and everyone has felt it go easy when the effort stopped.

### Chapters 10 and 55 are one instruction, given twice

> *Gathering the breath to softness, can you be an infant?*
>
> 專氣致柔，能如嬰兒乎？
>
> — chapter 10

Every witness reads 能嬰兒乎 (*néng yīng ér hū* — "can you be an infant?"), without our base's 如 (*rú* — like), and the English follows them (`notes/manuscript.md`).

> *It cries all day and never goes hoarse — this is harmony at its utmost.*
> *Harmony is called the ever-present.*
> *Knowing harmony is called clear-seeing.*
> *To force life to increase is an ill omen.*
> *When the heart drives the breath, that is called strong.*
>
> 終日號而不嗄，和之至也。
> 知和曰常，
> 知常曰明。
> 益生曰祥。
> 心使氣曰強。
>
> — chapter 55

The second and third lines follow Guodian and silk A, which read 和曰常，知和曰明 (*hé yuē cháng, zhī hé yuē míng*); the Chinese above is our base text (`notes/manuscript.md`).

Chapter 10 asks a person to gather the breath until it comes to 柔 (róu — soft). Chapter 55 says that when the heart drives the breath, that is 強 (qiáng — strong). In that chapter it is the strength of the stiffening thing: "When things reach their prime, they decay," runs the next line, and chapter 76 calls the dead "hard and strong" (`glossary/qiang-強.md`). **The same breath, handled two ways, gives the two outcomes the book cares most about.** Gathered, it ends soft, like an infant. Driven, it ends strong, like the corpse.

Both commentators read chapter 55 this way:

> 心宜無有，使氣則強。
> *"The heart should hold nothing. When it drives the breath, that is forcing."* — Wang Bi, on chapter 55

> 心當專一和柔，而氣實內，故形柔；而反使妄有所為，和氣去於中，故形體日以剛強也。
> *"The heart should be gathered into one, harmonious and soft, with the breath full within, and so the body is soft. If instead it drives the breath recklessly into doing, the harmonious breath leaves the center, and so the body grows hard and unbending by the day."* — Heshang Gong, on chapter 55

Heshang Gong's 專 (zhuān — to gather into one) is chapter 10's verb, so his reading of chapter 55 is chapter 10 in reverse. **And chapter 55 shows what the gathered breath does.** The infant "cries all day and never goes hoarse," and Heshang Gong gives the reason: 和氣多之所致 (*hé qì duō zhī suǒ zhì* — "it comes of abundant harmonious breath"). A voice that lasts all day is a matter of breath, and the line calls it "harmony at its utmost."

In chapters 10 and 55, 氣 is the object of a verb: gathered, 專 (zhuān — to gather, wind onto a core); driven, 使 (shǐ — to make, to drive). In chapter 42 it is the subject, the breath within that makes the harmony. In chapters 10 and 55, every witness agrees: **the breath is what a body does something with.**

### Breath and vital essence, in one chapter, must stay two words

Chapter 55 holds both characters, three lines apart. The infant's 精 (jīng — vital essence) is "at its utmost" because none of it has been spent: it is a reserve, kept or squandered, and nothing drives it. The 氣 is a current, the thing that moves and the thing a heart can push. **The chapter's argument lives in the difference.** The infant is full of the one and easy in the other. The forcing adult is driving the second and spending the first.

So the English needs two words that share nothing. *Vital essence* and *vital breath* share their adjective, and the adjective is what a reader carries away. *Vital essence* and *breath* do not.

### What the commentators did with it

**Heshang Gong fuses what the book keeps apart.** He writes 精氣 (*jīng qì* — "essence-breath") as one compound, again and again, where the book never sets the two characters side by side:

> 專守精氣使不亂，則形體能應之而柔順。
> *"Gather and guard the essence-breath so it is not disordered, and the body can answer it and become soft and supple."* — Heshang Gong, on chapter 10

That is his physiology, the practice of nourishing life. It is real evidence for how the Han read the book, and it is not the book's vocabulary. Laozi keeps 精 (jīng — vital essence) for the reserve and 氣 (qì) for the current, and the English follows Laozi.

**He also hears breath in lines that don't print 氣.** On chapter 10's 天門開闔 (*tiān mén kāi hé* — "the gate of the sky opens and closes"), he writes 治身，天門謂鼻孔 (*zhì shēn, tiān mén wèi bí kǒng* — "in tending the body, the gate of the sky means the nostrils"), and reads its opening and closing as breathing. It is a striking reading, and it stays a reading: the verse renders the sky's gate as the sky's gate (`process/principles/commentary-is-not-a-rendering.md`).

**Wang Bi ties the breath to 自然 (zì rán — of itself).** On chapter 10:

> 專，任也。致，極也。言任自然之氣，致至柔之和，能若嬰兒之無所欲乎。
> *"專 (zhuān) means to entrust oneself. 致 (zhì) means to bring to the utmost. It says: entrusting yourself to the breath that is so of itself, and reaching the harmony of utmost softness, can you be like an infant that wants nothing?"* — Wang Bi

His 專 (zhuān) runs against the graph's spindle whorl, and the verse follows the graph (`notes/translation.md`, chapter 10). His phrase 自然之氣 (*zì rán zhī qì* — "the breath that is so of itself") names what chapter 55's heart overrides, and what Zhuangzi's heart gives way to.

**On chapter 42, Heshang Gong puts the breath in the hollows of things:**

> 萬物中皆有元氣，得以和柔，若胸中有藏，骨中有髓，草木中有空虛，與氣通，故得久生也。
> *"Within each of the countless things there is the original breath, and by it they are harmonious and soft: as the chest has its organs, and the bones their marrow, and grasses and trees their hollows, open to the breath, and so they live long."* — Heshang Gong

Even the plants breathe, through the hollow inside the stem. His image is bodily, like the verse's backs and arms, and it reads 沖 (chōng) as 中 (zhōng — within), the reading the verse follows (`glossary/chong-沖.md`).

### What is set aside

**"Energy" and "vital energy."** *Energy* is a nineteenth-century physicist's word, a quantity that is conserved and converted, and in twentieth-century English it became the house word of wellness and the 1970s paperback. It fails the pointing test: no one can point at energy, and anyone can point at breath. It belongs to the mechanistic overlay this edition strips out, the same family as *source code* and *operating system*. And it empties chapter 55's verdict of anything a body feels. *"When the heart drives the energy"* describes nothing in particular. *"When the heart drives the breath"* describes straining, shouting, a held breath under effort, what a body does when a will takes it over.

**"Vital breath."** The adjective is spoken for. *Vital* is 精 (jīng — vital essence)'s English in chapters 21 and 55, and in chapter 55 the two characters argue against each other (`process/principles/already-spoken-for.md`). *Vital* also adds a word the Chinese doesn't print, and tilts the line toward the gravity of doctrine.

**"Life force."** The popular English for 氣, with Victorian vitalism and the cinema in it. A force is pushed from outside, where breath moves of itself. It sits in the 1971 paperback the imported-register test warns of (`process/principles/imported-register.md`). `glossary/po-魄.md` sets it aside for 魄 (pò — aliveness) for the same reasons.

**"Qi," left in pinyin.** It turns the commonest thing a body does into a foreign technical term, carrying a century of martial arts and acupuncture into the verse. The edition translates, and here the plain English word exists.

**"Spirit."** Taken by 神 (shén — spirit) in the chapters that print it, and set aside for 精 (jīng — vital essence) already. Heshang Gong's own formula 愛氣養神 (*ài qì yǎng shén* — "cherish the breath, nourish the spirit") keeps 氣 and 神 two (`glossary/shen-身.md`).

**"The breath of life."** Never, though *breath* stays. The phrase is Genesis, God breathing into Adam's nostrils, and it fails the hymn test outright. Breath in this book is not given from outside. It moves of itself, and a heart can only interfere with it.

**"Vapor" or "steam."** The pictures in the graph, not the word's sense in these lines. Inside a body, the vapor is breath, and English has the word.

**"Air."** Modern Chinese writes the atmosphere as 空氣 (kōng qì — "empty breath"). That sense is later, and air is not what a heart drives.

### Working register

氣 doesn't flex. It takes one English in three lines, with the article English grammar asks for:

| Line | English | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 專氣致柔 (10) | *gathering the breath to softness* | the object of 專 (zhuān — to gather) |
| 沖氣以為和 (42) | *and the breath within makes harmony* | the subject, after silk A's 中 (zhōng — middle), read as *within* |
| 心使氣曰強 (55) | *when the heart drives the breath* | the object of 使 (shǐ — to drive) |

**The verb *breathe* stands once in the verse, for another character.** Chapter 49's 歙歙 (xī xī — drawing in the breath) reads *"the sage breathes gently."* 歙 (xī) is a verb of the nose and the lungs, and *breathes* is its word there.

### What no rule can enforce

**"Vital" is ruled out for 氣 and cannot go on the `forbidden:` list.** 精 (jīng — vital essence) stands in chapter 55 beside 氣, and prints *vital* there legitimately, so a forbidden *vital* would fire on a correct line. The checker gates on whether a character is present in the chapter, and cannot say *right for 精, wrong for 氣, same chapter*. That distinction is held by this entry and by the reader (`process/principles/ruling-and-enforcement-are-two-facts.md`).

**"Breath" without 氣 is not a breach in chapter 49,** where it renders 歙歙 (xī xī — drawing in the breath) as a verb.

### Left open

- **Breath is the narrowest of the word's senses in Laozi's time.** The book's contemporaries used 氣 for a held breath, for what fills the body, for the weather and for the sky, and the cosmic sense was buried in the Guodian tomb beside the oldest copy of the book. Chapters 10 and 55 sit at the body's end, where breath fits. Chapter 42 is the cosmic line, and asks the most of the English. The bet is that the plain core, carried faithfully, lets the reader feel the wider word through it, where *energy* would replace the word with an idea.
- **The Guodian graph should be checked against the plates.** The fire in the oldest spelling rests on the published transcription of chapter 55's slip and on a study of the tomb's roughly ten occurrences, all with 既 (jì — already) for sound. The glyph itself is the evidence, and the photographs in the 1998 edition are where to see it.
- **The Peking University Han slips are not yet consulted** for chapters 10 and 55. At chapter 42, a secondhand transcription reads 中 (zhōng — middle), still to be checked against the printed edition (`WORKLIST.md` T2-79).
- **The vapor reading of the oracle-bone graph is Xu Shen's,** and the oracle-bone and bronze uses don't confirm it. The entry says *cloud* only as his reading.

## 強 (Qiáng) — Strong

*Say "chyahng," rising. Twenty-one lines across twelve chapters, and the book makes it both the disease and the cure.*

**Locked: 強 → "strong" — *strengthen* where it takes an object, *forcing* where it strains against a thing's nature.** *(Not "mighty," not "forceful," not "brute strength," not "perseverance." 力 (lì) → "force.")*

Chapter 78 forces four words apart — 柔 (*róu* — soft) · 剛 (*gāng* — unbending) · 弱 (*ruò* — yielding) · 強 — and 強 is the one that carries opposite verdicts inside a single frame.

The book's sharpest joke depends on it, and any English that resolves the word makes the joke invisible.

Two chapters use the identical three-character frame **X 曰強** (*yuē qiáng* — "is called 強"):

> 守柔曰強
> *ch 52 — "holding to the soft is called 強"*

> 心使氣曰強
> *ch 55 — "the heart driving the energy is called 強"*

The first is praise. The second is a warning, and the line after it is 物壯則老 (*wù zhuàng zé lǎo* — "things at their prime grow old"). **One word, one frame, opposite verdicts.** A translation that renders the first *strength* and the second *forcing* has answered a question the text deliberately leaves standing — and has spent two English words to hide the fact that Laozi used one.

### The graph, and it is the same instrument as 弱

The character now written 強 is not the original word for strength. Two graphs are involved and the *Shuowen Jiezi* (c. 100 CE) separates them cleanly.

**彊** (*qiáng*) — 弓有力也，从弓畺聲: *"a bow having force"*; 弓 (*gōng* — a bow) with 畺 as phonetic. The image is a stiff bow, one that takes strength to draw.

**強** (*qiáng*) — 蚚也，从虫弘聲: *"the 蚚"*, a weevil in stored grain; 虫 (*chóng* — insect) with 弘 (*hóng*) as phonetic. From the Qin onward this borrowed graph displaced 彊 in the sense of strength, and it is the form our recension carries throughout: 彊 appears nowhere in the base text.

So two things follow, and the second is the one that matters.

**The word we read is a grain weevil borrowed for its sound.** The strength is a phonetic accident, exactly as 萬 (*wàn* — a scorpion) is an accident inside 萬物. Two of this book's load-bearing terms are insects conscripted by rhyme.

**And the word underneath it is a bow.** 彊 is 弓 at the limit of what it will take. 弱 (*ruò* — yielding), which the Shuowen defines as 橈也 (*náo yě* — "to bend"), is what gives under the same load. **They are not opposites in kind. They are one behaviour under load, in two states**, and the images the book builds on the pair show it.

> 木強則折
> *ch 76 — "a tree that is 強 snaps"*

That is wood taken past its give. Ch 76's whole botany is the same figure: 王弼 glosses 強大處下 as 木之本也 (*"this is the trunk"*) and 柔弱處上 as 枝條是也 (*"these are the branches"*). The trunk cannot bend and is nearer the ground; the branches bend and are nearer the light.

### The commentators name the quartet outright

河上公, glossing ch 42's 人之所教，我亦教之 (*"what others teach, I also teach"*), states both curricula in fourteen characters:

> 謂衆人所以教去弱為強，去柔為剛
> *"what the crowd teaches: leave 弱 for 強, leave 柔 for 剛"*

> 言我教衆人使去強為弱，去剛為柔
> *"I teach them: leave 強 for 弱, leave 剛 for 柔"*

A Han commentator, using all four characters, in two matched lines, treating them as a fixed set. This is the strongest evidence in the repository that 柔 · 剛 · 弱 · 強 must take four distinct and stable English words.

**And 王弼 states the paradox directly.** On ch 52's 守柔曰強:

> 守強不強，守柔乃強也
> *"holding to 強 is not 強; holding to the soft is truly 強"*

強 twice in seven characters, with opposite valence, from the fourth-century commentator the recension is named for. Whatever English 強 takes has to survive being said twice in one breath and meaning something different each time. **Strong survives it. Forcing does not, and neither does true strength.**

### Where it flexes, and the flexions are grammatical

The split is marked in the Chinese, so it can be checked rather than argued.

**Transitive, with an object — *strengthen*.** Two lines, and they are the same two lines where 弱 (*ruò* — yielding) is made causative:

- **ch 3** 弱其志，強其骨 — *teaching their ambition to yield and strengthening their bones*
- **ch 36** 將欲弱之，必固強之 — *If you would have it yield, you must first strengthen it*

The symmetry is not a coincidence: it is one grammar taken twice, a stative word made causative. *Strengthen* keeps the root of *strong*, and *yield* keeps the root of *yielding* (`ruo-弱.md`).

**Straining against a thing's nature — *forcing*.** Where 強 modifies a verb of naming or describing, it is the strain of the act, not a quality of anything:

- **ch 15** 強為之容 — *forcing a description of them*
- **ch 25** 強字之曰道，強為之名曰大 — *forcing a style on it, I call it the Tao; forcing a name, I call it the vast*

The tradition heard this as a separate word. 河上公's text at ch 25 carries the phonetic note 強其文反, a *fanqie* spelling giving the third-tone reading *qiǎng* — "to force, to compel" — rather than *qiáng*. (These phonetic notes are later editorial additions to the Heshang Gong text, not the Han commentary itself; they record how the line was read, not what its first reader wrote.)

**Coercing something that is not yours — *force / dominance*.** Ch 30 uses 強 three times against the world and against people, where *strengthen* would be simply wrong: you do not strengthen a country by invading it.

- 不以兵強天下 — *does not use arms to force the world*
- 不敢以取強 — 河上公: 不以果敢取強大之名也, *"does not use boldness to seize the name of 強大"*
- 果而勿強 — 河上公: 果敢勿以為強兵堅甲以侵凌人也, *"succeed, but do not make strong troops and hard armor to trample people"*

**Everywhere else — *strong*.** Chapters 29, 33, 36 (柔弱勝剛強), 42, 52, 55, 76, 78.

### 力 is the plain word, and ch 33 has the pair inverted

強 cannot be settled without 力 (*lì* — a plough or an arm, the ordinary word for physical force), because ch 33 sets them against each other:

> 勝人者有力，自勝者強
> *"those who overcome others have 力; those who overcome themselves are 強"*

王弼: 勝人者有力而已矣，未若自勝者無物以損其力 — *"one who overcomes others merely has 力; unlike one who overcomes themselves, whose force nothing can diminish."* 河上公: 能勝人者不過以威力也 — *"one who can overcome others does so by no more than 威力"* (awe and force).

The couplet is **plain force against achieved strength**, and it rhymes with the line above it, where 智 (*zhì* — cleverness) is the lesser term against 明 (*míng* — clear-seeing). 力 is what you have. 強 is what you become.

**力 takes *force*** — which ch 68 already does (用人之力, *"using people's force"*) — and 強 takes *strong*. Neither needs an adjective; the couplet supplies the comparison.

### What is set aside

**mighty · forceful · brute strength.** All three pre-judge. 強 is the word the book uses for the state it warns against *and* the state it recommends, and an English that carries a verdict cannot do both.

**perseverance** for 強行 (ch 33). 王弼 glosses it 勤能行之，其志必獲 — *"diligently able to practise it, their will surely attains"* — so persistence is the sense. But *perseverance* is a virtue-word that leaves no trace of 強, and it hides the fact that the chapter has just spent two lines distinguishing 力 from 強. Whatever the line takes, the character has to be audible in it.

**And do not let *strong* or *strength* drift onto its neighbours.** Two characters have borrowed 強's English in chapters that contain 強 — 固 (*gù* — firm) at ch 55's 握固, and 壯 (*zhuàng* — in its prime) at 物壯則老 in ch 30 and ch 55. A lock is a claim in both directions, and no checker rule can catch these: 固 and 壯 sit in the same chapters as 強, so the evidence gate that makes the tool trustworthy is exactly what blinds it here. This is a reader's job.

### Left open

**強 is both the disease and the cure, and nothing in the text resolves it.** It is rigor mortis at ch 76, an army that cannot win at ch 76 and ch 30, a roof-beam at ch 42, the heart bullying the breath at ch 55 — and it is also what you are when you overcome yourself at ch 33 and when you hold to the soft at ch 52.

The temptation is to read the good instances as a different word, or as irony. 王弼 refuses that escape: 守強不強，守柔乃強也 puts both on the page at once and lets them stand. The English should be able to say the same sentence.

What is genuinely unsettled is **ch 55's 心使氣曰強**, the one line where the reader most needs help and gets least. Rendered *"when the heart drives the breath, that is called strong,"* it can be misheard as approval for exactly one beat — until 物壯則老 lands in the next line. Whether that beat is a flaw or the point is not a question the Chinese answers.
entries.render: strong — *strengthen* where it takes an object, *forcing* where it strains against a thing's nature

## 勤 (Qín) — Strain

*Say "chin," rising. Three lines in three chapters. In one of them the best people do it, and in the other two the point is not doing it.*

**Locked: 勤 → "strain," and "labor" in ch 41, the one line where it is affirmed.** *(Not "exhausted," which reads a different character into the line. Not "diligence," which praises where the character only describes. Not "toil," which came closest.)*

### The graph: a digging stick, and a word older than its picture

> 勤，**勞**也。从力堇聲。
> *"Labor. From 力 (lì — strength), with 堇 (jǐn) for sound."* — 說文解字 (*Shuōwén Jiězì*, the Han dictionary)

**The word is older than the graph.** Late Western Zhou bronzes write the word with 堇 alone, borrowed for its sound. 力 was added in the Warring States period, to mark which word 堇 was standing for, and the Mawangdui silks still write bare 堇 (漢語多功能字庫, *Multi-function Chinese Character Database*, Chinese University of Hong Kong). So the graph was built to name a word people already used, and the meaning-part is the one that was added.

**力 (*lì* — strength) is a farm tool, not a muscle.** 說文 explains it as 筋也，象人筋之形, *"sinew; it pictures a person's sinews,"* and the dictionary was guessing. The oracle-bone graph is a digging stick: the pointed wooden pole of the earliest farming, grown into a tool for turning soil, with a short crossbar for the foot to press down (裘錫圭 *Qiú Xīguī*, cited in the same database). The strength in 力 is the strength of breaking ground. 說文 keeps a trace of it in its next sentence: 治功曰力, *"the work of setting things in order is called 力."* The book's other 力 words carry it too: 功 (*gōng* — work done), which 說文 defines as 以勞定國也, *"settling the state through labor."*

**堇 (*jǐn*) is only the sound, and its own picture is a drought.** In the oracle bones 堇 shows a person with mouth turned upward, set over fire. It is the same graph as 熯 (*hàn* — to scorch, drought): a victim burned to bring rain. 徐中舒 (*Xú Zhōngshū*) reads the figure as a captive with arms bound; 姚孝遂 (*Yáo Xiàosuì*) reads the graph as 艱 (*jiān* — hardship, calamity). In the bronzes the fire was miscopied as 土 (*tǔ* — earth), and from that miscopy came the seal graph 說文 knew and its gloss, 黏土也, *"sticky clay."* None of that is in 勤's meaning. 堇 was chosen for its sound, as 萬 (*wàn*)'s scorpion was. But the words that sound with it keep company with hardship. 僅 (*jǐn* — barely). 饉 (*jǐn* — famine): 說文 蔬不孰為饉, *"vegetables not ripening."* 殣 (*jǐn*): 說文 道中死人, *"a person dead on the road."* That is a family resemblance in sound, not evidence, and the entry rests nothing on it.

**What the word meant in use: strength spent to the end.** The bronze 叔尸鐘 (*Shū Shī zhōng* — Shu Shi's bell) pairs it with 勞 (*láo* — labor): 堇勞其政事, *"toiled and labored at his affairs of government."* The 中山王鼎 (*Zhōngshān wáng dǐng* — the Zhongshan king's tripod) has 身勤社稷, *"in his own body toiled for the altars of the state."* 杜預 (*Dù Yù*, d. 285), on the 左傳 (*Zuǒ Zhuàn*), defines it outright: 盡心盡力無所愛惜為勤, *"to spend all your heart and all your strength, sparing nothing: that is 勤."* 盡 (*jìn* — to use up) is in his definition. 勤 is not running out. It is spending yourself until you do.

### Three lines, and two of them are a negation

> *Use it, and there is no strain.*
>
> 用之不勤。
>
> — chapter 6

> *Block the openings, close the doors, and to the end of your days you will not strain.*
>
> 塞其兌，閉其門，終身不勤。
>
> — chapter 52

> *Those highest in service hear the Tao and labor to practice it.*
>
> 上士聞道，勤而行之
>
> — chapter 41

Word for word, two of the lines put 不 (*bù* — not) before the character: 用之不勤 (*yòng zhī bù qín* — "use it, and not 勤") and 終身不勤 (*zhōng shēn bù qín* — "to the end of your days, not 勤"). The third, 勤而行之 (*qín ér xíng zhī* — "勤, and practice it"), is what the highest in service do.

**Both commentators read the spending of strength in ch 6, and both read it in ch 52.**

| | 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*, d. 249) | 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*, Han) |
|---|---|---|
| ch 6 | 用而不勞也 — *"it is used, and does not labor"* | 用氣常寬舒，不當急疾懃勞也 — *"use the breath always loose and easy; it should not be hurried or toiling"* |
| ch 52 | 無事永逸，故終身不勤也 — *"no affairs, forever at ease, so to the end of your days you do not strain"* | 人當塞目不妄視，𨳲口不妄言，則終身不勤苦 — *"if a person blocks the eyes from looking wildly and closes the mouth from speaking wildly, then to the end of their days they do not strain and suffer"* |
| ch 41 | 有志也 — *"they have resolve"* | 上士聞道，自勤苦竭力而行之 — *"the highest in service hear the Tao, and of themselves strain and suffer, using up their strength, to practice it"* |

王弼 glosses 勤 with 勞 (*láo* — labor) in ch 6, which is 說文's own word. 河上公 writes 懃 (*qín*), 勤 with 心 (*xīn* — heart) beneath it, and pairs it with 勞 too.

**河上公 names the opposite of 勤 in ch 6, and it is the opposite of strain.** 寬舒 (*kuān shū* — loose and easy), against 急疾 (*jí jí* — hurried, rushed). That is what *strain* means in a body: the breath held tight, the muscle pulled past ease. Labor and toil can be steady and unhurried. Strain cannot.

**The two commentators disagree about whose strain ch 6 means.** For 王弼 it is the thing: what is used never labors. For 河上公 it is the person breathing, who must not force it. *There is no strain* names no one, so it carries both.

### One commentator, one compound, both ways

河上公 uses the same compound in ch 41 and ch 52. 勤苦 (*qín kǔ* — "strain and suffer"). In ch 41 the highest people do it: they hear the Tao and spend themselves, using up their strength. In ch 52 the person who closes the openings is spared it to the end of their days.

So the book holds both. The best student labors at the Tao. The Tao itself, used, does not strain, and neither does the one who stops chasing what the eyes and mouth want. An English that praised the first (*diligence*) and pitied the second (*exhaustion*) would be two words with two opposite verdicts.

### Why ch 41 reads *labor*

**Negated, *strain* is the thing avoided. Affirmed, it is a fault.** In chs 6 and 52, *there is no strain* and *you will not strain* describe ease, and the word's edge, forcing past what is easy, is exactly what the line rules out. In ch 41 nothing is ruled out. *Strain to practice it* would say the best students overreach, and neither commentator says that: 王弼 hears resolve, and 河上公's suffering is the cost of their effort, not a mistake in it. So the line takes a flexion.

***Labor* is the character's own definition.** 說文's 勞也 is the word, and 王弼 glosses ch 6 with the same 勞. The bronze bell pairs them, 堇勞. *Labor* is honest strength spent, neither praised nor faulted, and *labor to* still carries a little of the difficulty the line may hold (below). The word is set aside in ch 6 for a reason ch 41 does not have: there is no gate of the dark female beside it to turn it into childbirth.

**The cost is the echo.** The book now says *labor* in ch 41 and *strain* in chs 6 and 52, where the Chinese says one character three times. The two words are neighbors, and labor is what strain is the excess of, so a reader can still hear the best student's effort against the ease of the other two lines. But it is a near echo, not the same word.

### What is set aside

**"toil," narrowly.** It came closest, and for a while it was the recommendation. It is plain, it is old, and it carries what 勞 carries: long work and the tiredness after it. It fits all three lines. It lost on the hardest one: in ch 6, *strain* names what 河上公 sets against 勤, the breath that is hurried instead of loose and easy, and *toil* does not. What *toil* has and *strain* loses is duration: toil goes on all day, and strain can be a moment.

**"exhausted," "inexhaustible."** These read 勤 as if it were 盡 (*jìn* — to use up). 盡 is near the word, in 杜預's definition, and the line before ch 6's already says the thing is 綿綿 (*mián mián* — unbroken, unbroken). But running out is where 勤 ends, not what it is. 說文 says labor, both commentators say labor, and ch 52's 終身不勤 cannot mean *to the end of your days you are not used up*. *Inexhaustible* is also the hymn's word: it sits well in a sermon about grace.

**"diligence," "diligent," "diligently."** These are a virtue, and English hears approval in them. 勤 describes strength being spent. 王弼 reads the ch 41 line as resolve and 河上公 as suffering, and neither is praise.

**"effort."** It is close, and lighter than *strain*. It has no cost in it, where 杜預's definition is all cost: *sparing nothing*. It also fails ch 52: *you will make no effort* sounds like idleness, where the line describes ease.

**"labor," outside ch 41.** 說文's own gloss, and the best evidence for the sense, which is why it is ch 41's flexion. In ch 6, though, *no labor* beside the gate of the dark female becomes a birth without labor pains. The line does not say that. Ch 52 follows ch 6, so the two negated lines keep one word.

**"heavy labor," "labored."** Two words for one character, and *heavy labor* is a sentence handed down by a court. *Labored* is good English for a breath, and it is an adjective, which ch 41's verb cannot take.

**"work hard."** Both words are spoken for. *Work* is 功 (*gōng* — work done) in seven lines, *"the work is done, and the sage does not stay in it"* (2, 77), so the best students would be doing what the sage lets go of. *Hard* is the *hard and strong* that ch 76 calls the followers of death, and 難 (*nán* — difficult) in *hard to govern* (65, 75).

### Working register

| Grammar | English | Where |
|---|---|---|
| negated predicate, 不勤 | *there is no strain* / *will not strain* | 6, 52 |
| verb before 而 + verb, affirmed | *labor to* (do it) | 41 |

### Left open

**Ch 41 may not be about effort at all.** The highest in service labor at the Tao, the middling keep some and forget some, and the lowest laugh. The received text reads the first line as effort, and both commentators do. Some readers take the line as saying the Tao is hard to carry out, so that even the best can only just manage it. *Labor to practice it* leans toward effort and keeps some of the difficulty. But the line where the best people labor sits oddly in a book whose ideal is not straining, and that oddness may be the point, or it may be a sign of a misread graph.

**What strain loses.** In modern English *strain* has drifted toward stress, the mind's tightness more than the arm's. The digging stick in 力 is the older sense, and the English word has both. A reader who hears only stress hears half.

flexions.why: affirmed rather than negated, so strain would fault the effort, a verdict the Chinese does not pass
