entries.body:
## 清 (Qīng) — Clear

*Say "ching," level. Four lines across three chapters.*

**Locked: 清 → "clear."** *(Not "pure" or "purity," and not "clarity," which is 明's noun. Not "settled," which is 寧's, or "still," which is 靜's, but those rulings no check can hold. See the last section but one.)*

*濁 (zhuó — muddy), its opposite, stands twice in ch 15 and is covered here.*

清 is the clearness of water after the silt has gone down, and of sky without cloud. The book never tells anyone to make something clear. It asks who can let muddy water be still, and wait: 孰能濁以靜之徐清, *"Who can be muddy, and by stilling it slowly come clear?"* (15). The clearing is slow, and it happens of itself. Elsewhere the sky receives the one, and so becomes clear (39), and clear stillness brings order to the world (45).

### The graph: water that has settled

> 清，**朖也。澂水之皃**。从水青聲。
> *"清 is bright. The look of water that has settled. From 水 (shuǐ — water), with 青 (qīng) for the sound."* — 說文解字

澂 (*chéng*) is 澄, to let water stand until the sediment sinks. The dictionary's picture is a process, and it is ch 15's process exactly: muddy, then still, then clear. **Nothing is taken out of the water.** The silt is still in the pool, on the bottom. Clear water is water that has stopped being stirred.

The first gloss, 朖 (*lǎng* — bright), is a light word, and the sky line of ch 39 can bear it. 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) reads 天得一以清 as 垂象清明, *"the sky hangs its images clear and bright."* English *clear* holds both senses: clear water, clear sky.

**青 gives the sound, and it stands in 靜 (*jìng* — stillness) too.** 說文 files 靜 under 青: 靜，審也。从青爭聲. The two words meet twice in the book, 濁以靜之徐清 at ch 15 and 清靜 at ch 45. In 清 the 青 is only sound, so this is a resemblance and not a pun the text was built on.

### 清 and 濁: the one opposite the book gives it

**說文 does not define 濁 as muddy.** It gives a river: 濁，水。出齊郡厲嬀山，東北入鉅定, *"濁 is a river. It rises at Mount Lìguī in Qí commandery and flows northeast into Jùdìng."* The muddy sense comes from use, and the book uses it twice, both in ch 15: 混兮其若濁, *"Mixed, like muddy water,"* and the line that turns it, 孰能濁以靜之徐清.

**Both commentators read the turn as a passage, not a fight.** 河上公: 誰能知水之濁，止而淨之，徐徐自清也, *"who can know the water's muddiness, stop it and let it be clean? Slowly, slowly it clears of itself."* 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) sets it inside a series: 夫晦以理物則得明，濁以静物則得清，安以動物則得生，此自然之道也, *"dim, to order things, and gain bright; muddy, to still things, and gain clear; at rest, to move things, and gain life. This is the way of things being so of themselves."* And he adds why the line asks *who can*: 孰能者言其難也，徐者詳慎也, *"'who can' speaks of how hard it is; 'slowly' means with care."*

**Clear is not where the chapter stops.** The next line runs the other way: 孰能安以動之徐生, *"Who can be at rest, and by moving it slowly come to life?"* The person ch 15 describes can let the stirred settle and stir the settled. The muddy state is no failure. It is one of the seven likenesses the chapter praises.

### 清 and 混

**混 (*hùn* — mixed) is not 清's opposite.** Ch 15 likens it to 濁, *"like muddy water,"* and 若 (*ruò* — like) keeps the two apart. 混 stands at the start of the chapter's turn and 清 at its end. 河上公 calls the Tao clear in ch 25, the chapter where it is 混成, *mixed and complete*: 道清淨不言, *"the Tao is clear and clean, and does not speak."* And across chapters, 混 is how three become one (14), and the one is what makes the sky clear (39). Clear is what mixed becomes when it is left still. See `glossary/hun-混.md`.

### Clear is not the goal: ch 39

天得一以清，地得一以寧, *"Sky received the one, and so became clear. Earth received the one, and so became settled."* And then the same lines turned round: 天無以清，將恐裂, *"Sky with no way to be clear is likely to split."*

**Both commentators refuse to let clear stand on its own.** 王弼: 用一以致清耳，非用清以清也。守一則清不失，用清則恐裂也, *"it is by using the one that it comes clear, not by using clearness to be clear. Hold to the one and the clearness is not lost; use the clearness, and it may split."* And further: 清不能為清…故清不足貴, *"clear cannot make itself clear… so clear is not worth prizing."* 河上公 goes further still: 天當有隂陽施張，晝夜更用，不可但欲清明無巳時，將恐分裂不為天, *"the sky must have yin and yang unfolding, day and night taking turns. It cannot want only to be clear and bright without end, or it may split apart and stop being sky."*

A sky that is only clear, with no night in it, breaks. The book prizes clear and will not let anyone grasp at it.

### Why "clear"

**It is the first English sense of the word.** Water you can see the bottom through, sky with nothing in it. It passes the pointing test: Laozi could point at a pool after the rain has stopped.

**One English word does all four lines.** *Come clear* (15), *became clear* (39), *to be clear* (39), *clear stillness* (45). The verb, the predicate and the modifier are all native English for this one word.

### What is set aside, and why

**"pure" and "purity"** are the overlay to refuse. 清淨 (*qīng jìng* — clear and clean) became, in later Daoist and Buddhist Chinese, the word for a monk's or a temple's purity, and English *purity* is moral and ritual. *"Purity and stillness are the standard of the world"* would sit comfortably in a sermon. And settled water has not been purified: nothing was removed from it.

**"clarity"** is 明's noun, in five lines (10, 27, 36, 52 twice). 明 (*míng*) is light, the moon through a window. 清 is water and air. 王弼's ch 15 comment keeps them on two axes, dim to bright and muddy to clear, and the English keeps them apart by keeping 清 off 明's noun. 明 and 清 share no chapter, so the build can hold this one.

**"settled"** is 說文's own picture, and it is 寧 (*níng*)'s, in the same chapter: 地得一以寧, *"Earth… became settled"* (39).

**"limpid"** is a poet's word, and **"lucid"** is a mind's. **"transparent"** is about glass.

**"still"** is 靜's.

### Working register

| Chinese | English | form |
|---|---|---|
| 孰能濁以靜之徐清 (15) | *by stilling it slowly come clear* | verb, to become clear |
| 天得一以清 (39) | *Sky received the one, and so became clear* | verb, to become clear |
| 天無以清，將恐裂 (39) | *Sky with no way to be clear is likely to split* | predicate |
| 清靜為天下正 (45) | *Clear stillness brings order to the world* | modifier, with 靜 |
| 混兮其若濁 (15) · 孰能濁以靜之徐清 (15) | *like muddy water* · *Who can be muddy* | 濁, covered |

### What no rule can enforce

**"settled" is ruled out for 清 and cannot be forbidden.** 寧 stands beside 清 in ch 39 and prints *settled* twice.

**"still" and "stillness" are ruled out and cannot be forbidden.** 靜 stands beside 清 in ch 15 and ch 45.

**Bare *clear* is also 明's, once.** 明's English is built on the same root, *clear-seeing*, *clarity*, *see clearly*, and at ch 41 it takes *clear* bare: 明道若昧, *"The clear Tao seems murky."* No rule can tell the two apart, since they never share a chapter. A reader holds it: bare *clear* is 清's in four lines and 明's in one.

### Left open

**Ch 41 reads like 清 and 濁, and the Chinese is 明 and 昧.** *"The clear Tao seems murky"* sets a clear thing against a murky one, and an English reader hears water. The Chinese pair is light: 明 against 昧 (*mèi* — dim). That is the distinction 王弼 draws at ch 15, 晦以理物則得明，濁以静物則得清, light on one axis and water on the other. The cost of keeping it is real, and so is the cost of removing it. *Bright*, the plain light word, is already worn by three characters: 皦 (*jiǎo*) at 14, 昭 (*zhāo*) at 20 and 光 (*guāng*) at 58. And 河上公 himself glosses 清 with 清明, *clear and bright*, so the two characters overlap in the commentary too. Ch 41 keeps *clear*.

**清淨 in the commentary.** 河上公 calls the Tao 清淨 at ch 25 and reaches for the word elsewhere. That is the compound that later became *purity*, and it is the commentator's, not the book's. The book's own pairing is 清靜, *clear stillness*, at ch 45.
entries.shuowen: Bright. The look of water that has settled. From 水 (shuǐ — water), with 青 (qīng) for sound.

entries.body:
## 全 (Quán) — Whole

*Say "chwen," rising. Three occurrences in eighty-one chapters, all of them in Chapter 22, and the word English keeps reaching for is a repair verb.*

**Locked: 全 → "whole" — as an outcome, *stay whole*; as a transitive act, *keep whole*.** *(Never "complete," never "perfect," never "flawless," and never any verb of repair.)*

### The live problem: English wants to fix something

Chapter 22 opens 曲則全 (*qū zé quán* — "bend, then whole") and closes 誠全而歸之. Four drafts of that closing line, in this repository, reached for a verb of restoration — *makes you whole*, *restores your wholeness* — and every one of them smuggled in **a breakage the Chinese never concedes.**

The chapter is not about being mended. It is about **not getting broken in the first place.** 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) says so in five characters, glossing 曲則全:

> 曲己從眾，不自專，則**全其身**也
> *"Bend yourself and follow the crowd, do not act on your own authority, then you **keep your body whole**."*

全其身 — **全 as a transitive verb meaning *keep intact***. Not *make whole*. The sense is attested straight through the lexical tradition: *to preserve, to keep whole or intact*. Preservation, never repair.

To *restore* is to bring something back to a former condition, which presupposes the loss. It is *make whole* with better manners. Under this lock, neither can stand.

### The graph: a piece of jade brought in whole

全 is **入** (*rù* — to enter, to bring in) over **玉** (*yù* — jade), written 王 with its dot dropped. The picture is **a piece of jade carried in unbroken.**

The *Shuowen Jiezi* (~100 CE) glosses it 完也 (*wán* — intact), and the tradition attached to the graph reads **純玉曰全** — *"pure jade is called 全."* Not jade that has been polished into perfection: jade that arrived without a crack in it.

That single image carries the whole lock. **You cannot repair jade.** A cracked piece is not restorable; it is a different, lesser object. Wholeness in jade is not an achievement, it is a survival — which is exactly the claim Chapter 22 is making about a person who bends.

> **A caution specific to this repository.** The component at the bottom of 全 is **玉 (*yù* — jade), not 王 (*wáng* — ruler)**, though the two are written alike once 玉 loses its dot. There is no king inside *whole*. Given how much work `DISCOVERIES.md` §4 does to get a throne out of 王, it is worth saying plainly that this graph never had one.

### The evidence — a closed system, and a quotation

**全 occurs three times, all in Chapter 22:** 曲則全, the verbatim quote-back 古之所謂「曲則全」者, and the closing 誠全而歸之. **曲** (*qū* — bent) does the same: twice, both in Chapter 22, both bound to 全. Neither character appears anywhere else in the book.

That seals the pair inside one chapter and makes it a self-contained argument. It also raises a question the chapter answers itself — see the open tension at the foot of this entry.

**The material vocabulary around it, none of which is 全's word.**

| Character | Picture | Where | Rendered |
|---|---|---|---|
| **瑕** (*xiá*) | a **flaw in jade** | 27 · 善言無瑕謫 | *flawless* — already spent |
| **缺** (*quē*) | a **chipped jar** (缶 *fǒu*, an earthen vessel) | 45 · 大成若缺 · 58 | *deficient* |
| **散** (*sàn*) | scattered, broken up | 28 · 樸散則為器 | *carved* |
| **成** (*chéng*) | brought to completion | 14 chapters | *complete* |

The book thinks about integrity in **objects** — jade, jars, timber. 全 belongs in that company and should be rendered from it.

### What is set aside, and why

**"Complete"** belongs to **成** (*chéng*), which runs through fourteen chapters, and the two are not synonyms. *Complete* means **finished**; 全 means **undamaged**. A thing can be whole and unfinished — Chapter 41 insists on it: 大器晚成 (*dà qì wǎn chéng* — *"the great vessel is never completed"*). The book is openly suspicious of completion. It is not suspicious of wholeness.

**"Perfect"** imports an ideal, and usually a moral one. 全 is physical integrity, not attainment. Fails the hymn test on contact: *"bend, and you shall be made perfect."*

**"Flawless"** is the right semantic field and **the wrong chapter** — it is already carrying 瑕 (*xiá* — a flaw in jade) at Chapter 27, 善言無瑕謫, *"masterful speaking is flawless."* Two jade words in one book, and English has one good adjective for them. 瑕 got there first, and *flawless* also drifts toward **appearance**, where 全 is about **condition**.

**"Restore," "make whole," "heal"** — the repair family, rejected above. They concede the damage the chapter denies.

**"Preserved,"** as in the familiar *"yield and you will be preserved,"* fails on **voice**. The English passive hands the preserving to an unnamed outside agent. 全其身 has the person doing it themselves — which is the point of a chapter about what your own bending accomplishes.

**"Unbroken"** is not wrong, and was this edition's first rendering (*"Yield and remain unbroken"*). It was set aside for defining by negation: the jade is not merely *not shattered*, it is **whole and worth something**. The positive value is in the stone.

**"Intact"** is the most exact one-word gloss of the sense and is not used in the verse, because it is clinical — a word for shipping crates and evidence bags. It is the right word for the *definition* and the wrong register for the *poem*, and that gap is worth knowing when reading this entry against the line.

### 曲 (*qū* — bend), treated here

曲 is a picture of something **bent** — the older graph is read as a curved or notched implement, a bamboo frame or bent vessel. It is the ordinary word for *crooked, curved, bent aside*.

**Render it *bend*, and never *yield*.** *Yielding* is the locked English for **弱** (*ruò*), which the Shuowen defines as 橈也 (*náo yě* — "to bend"). This edition's earlier Chapter 22 read *"Yield and remain unbroken,"* which borrowed 弱's locked word for a character that is not 弱 and does not appear in that chapter. The two ideas are cousins; the two words are not interchangeable.

*Bend* also keeps the physical gesture the chapter needs, because the four opening lines are all bodily: bent, wronged-and-straightened, hollowed, worn out.

### Working register

- as the outcome of the 則 (*zé* — then, thus) construction → **stay whole** (曲則全 → *"Bend, and stay whole"*)
- as a transitive act, chiefly in the commentaries → **keep whole** (全其身 → *"keep their body whole"*)
- as a bare predicate → **whole**
- 曲 → **bend** / **bent**, never *yield*

**Never** *complete*, *perfect*, *flawless*, or any verb that implies the thing was broken first.

### Left open

**Why does a word this load-bearing appear in one chapter and nowhere else?**

全 is the whole argument of Chapter 22 — it opens the poem, it is quoted back, it closes the poem. And in the other eighty chapters, silence. So does 曲. A vocabulary that central ought to recur, and it does not.

**The chapter may be telling us why.** It marks the line as borrowed: 古之所謂「曲則全」者 — *"what the ancients called 'bend, then whole'."* If Chapter 22 is commentary on an older proverb, then **the 曲/全 vocabulary arrived with the quotation** and was never Laozi's own. That would explain the distribution exactly, and it would make this chapter a rare thing in the book: not a teaching, but a defence of somebody else's.

It also leaves a second question genuinely unanswered. **Whole *what*?** 河上公 supplies 身 (*shēn* — the body) and reads the closing line as returning that body to one's parents unharmed — the filial register of his self-cultivation reading, and a Han import this edition declines. The text itself never says. It writes 全, bare, three times, and lets the reader carry it.

We keep it bare too.

## 仁 (Rén) — Humaneness

*Say "run," rising, with the tongue curled back. Eight lines across five chapters, and it is the first thing chapter 5 says sky and earth are not.*

**Locked: 仁 → "humaneness."** *(Not "benevolence," not "charity," not "goodwill.")*

**Benevolence** is the word this character wears in nearly every English Tao Te Ching, and it is a translation of the Latin, not of the Chinese. *Bene-volens* is a **disposition of the will**: to wish well. It names something happening inside one person.

仁 names something happening **between two**. The graph says so, and so does the earliest dictionary.

The cost of the Latin word is not vagueness. It is that the book's argument stops making sense. Ch 5 says 天地不仁 — and if 仁 is well-wishing, the line reads as cosmic indifference, a universe that does not care. That is not what either classical commentator thought it said, and it is not what the chapter goes on to do.

### The graph

**仁 is 人 (*rén* — a person) beside 二 (*èr* — two).** Two people, and the relation between them. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (c. 100 CE) glosses it in one word:

> 仁，親也。从人从二
> *"仁 is 親 (qīn — kinship, closeness). From 人 and from 二."*

Not a feeling one person has. **A closeness that exists only in the space between two.** Bronze forms write it with 人 over 二 or with 千 over 心; the constant is the pair.

**Humaneness** keeps 人 audible in the English, which is exactly what the character does. That is the whole argument for it, and it is enough.

### What the commentators actually say, and it rescues ch 5

The hardest line in the book for this character is 天地不仁，以萬物為芻狗 — *"sky and earth are not 仁; they treat the countless things as straw dogs."* A 芻狗 (*chú gǒu*) is a dog plaited out of straw for a sacrifice: dressed and honoured through the ceremony, thrown away after.

Read with *benevolence*, that is a cold universe. **Neither commentator reads it that way.**

王弼 says what 仁 would require:

> 仁者必造立施化，有恩有為
> *"the 仁 one must construct and impose transformation; there is 恩 (ēn — favour, obligation) and there is 為 (wéi — doing)."*

So 不仁 is not the absence of care. It is the absence of **management with a debt attached** — 恩, the favour that expects to be remembered.

河上公 is more explicit still, and says the quiet part:

> 天施地化，不以仁恩，任自然也
> *"sky bestows and earth transforms, not by 仁恩 (humane favour), but by leaving things to be of themselves."*

> 聖人愛養萬民，不以仁恩，法天地行自然
> *"the sage **loves and rears** the people — not by humane favour, but modelling sky and earth in acting so of themselves."*

**愛養 — loves and rears.** The sage in ch 5 is not indifferent. The straw dog is not contempt; it is 不貴望其報也, *"expecting no repayment."* 仁 is care that keeps accounts, and the chapter is refusing the accounts, not the care.

### Why the book attacks it, and how little that is about goodness

仁 is never attacked alone. It arrives bonded to 義 (*yì* — duty) as 仁義, the Confucian virtue-pair, and always at the moment something else has already failed:

> 大道廢，有仁義
> *ch 18 — "the great Tao is discarded, and there is humaneness and duty"*

> 失德而後仁，失仁而後義
> *ch 38 — "integrity lost, then humaneness; humaneness lost, then duty"*

河上公 draws the consequence exactly: 大道之時，家有孝子，戶有忠信，**仁義不見也** — *"in the time of the great Tao, every family had devoted children and every household loyalty and trust, and humaneness and duty **were not visible**."* Not absent. **Invisible**, because nothing had gone wrong that would make anyone name them.

**王弼 goes further and refuses to call them evils at all.** Glossing ch 19's three severed pairs:

> 聖智，才之善也；仁義，人之善也；巧利，用之善也
> *"sagehood and knowing are the best of talent; humaneness and duty are the best of persons; cunning and profit are the best of use."*

Three pairs of **goods**, said to be insufficient as 文 (*wén* — cultural form). The chapter is not an attack on kindness. It is a claim that the named virtues arrive too late.

**And the oldest witness does not make the attack at all.** At Guodian (~300 BCE) the passage corresponding to ch 19 carries neither 仁 nor 義 nor 聖; the pairs severed there are different ones. See `notes/manuscript.md` · Ch 19 and `sources/variants.yaml`.

### What is set aside

**benevolence.** A Latin will-word for a Chinese relation-word, and the standard English carries a whole missionary lexicon behind it — Legge's Tao Te Ching came out of the London Missionary Society, and this is one of the words that came with him.

**charity · goodwill.** Both are almsgiving words: they run in one direction, from the one who has to the one who lacks. 仁 runs between two who are simply near each other.

**kindness and love are not forbidden here, because they are not free** — 慈 (*cí* — tenderness) holds that ground and shares two chapters with this character. See `glossary/ci-慈.md`.

### Left open

**仁 is the only word in this book that the text attacks and the commentators defend.** 王弼 calls it 人之善也, the best of what a person can be, in the middle of glossing a chapter that says to cut it off. 河上公 says it becomes invisible when things go well, which is praise disguised as dismissal.

So the English has to be sayable in two tones — as the thing that arrives when the Tao has already been discarded, and as the thing a decent person is. *Humaneness* manages it, barely, and mostly because it is flat enough not to editorialise. **Whether flatness is the right answer to a word this warm is not settled**, and ch 8's 與善仁 is where it presses hardest: there 仁 is not a symptom of decline but one of seven things water is good at.

## 柔 (Róu) — Soft

*Say "roe," rising. Eleven lines across seven chapters.*

**Locked: 柔 → "soft."** *(Not "supple," "pliant," "flexible," "gentle" or "tender," which is 慈's. Not "yielding" either, which is 弱's, but that ruling no check can hold. See the last section but one.)*

*剛 (gāng — unbending), its opposite, stands only twice in the book and is covered here.*

The book never praises 柔 for being kind. It praises it for **winning**. The soft and yielding **overcome** the unbending and strong (36). The softest thing in the world **gallops through** the hardest (43). Holding to the soft is called **strong** (52). The soft and yielding are **followers of life** (76). Nothing is softer than water, and nothing does better against the hard (78). Every line is about what happens when soft meets hard, and in every line soft is still there at the end.

### The graph: wood that bends and comes back

> 柔，**木曲直也**。从木矛聲。
> *"柔 is wood bending and straightening. From 木 (mù — wood), with 矛 (máo — a spear) for the sound."* — 說文解字

段玉裁 (*Duàn Yùcái*) spells out what the four characters mean: 凡木曲者可直，直者可曲，曰柔, *"any wood that, when bent, can be made straight, and when straight, can be bent, is called 柔."* The spear on top gives only the sound, so the meaning is all in the 木 (*mù* — wood) beneath.

**The phrase is older than the dictionary.** The 尚書 (*Shàngshū*)'s 洪範 (*Hóng Fàn*), the oldest list of the five phases, gives each its nature. Water soaks down, fire flames up, and 木曰曲直, *"wood is called bending-and-straightening."* The commentary attributed to 孔安國 (*Kǒng Ānguó*) glosses it 木可以揉曲直, *"wood can be 揉 into bent or straight."* 揉 (*róu*) is the same word with a hand added, and it belongs to the woodworker. In the 周易 (*Zhōu Yì*)'s 繫辭 (*Xì Cí*), the ancient sages 揉木為耒, *"bent wood to make the plough handle."* In the 考工記 (*Kǎogōng Jì*), the wheelwright's 揉輻必齊, *"the spokes he bends must match,"* which 鄭玄 (*Zhèng Xuán*) explains as working the wood over fire.

So the picture behind 柔 is a carpenter's: a length of green or heated wood taking a curve without splitting. It passes the pointing test. Laozi could have pointed at a plough handle.

**The word is older than the graph.** The 柔-and-矛 form is not known from the oracle bones. The word is already in Western Zhou bronze, in the formula 柔遠能邇, *"to 柔 the far and make able the near"*, cast on the 大克鼎 (*Dà Kè dǐng*) and the 番生簋 (*Pān Shēng guǐ*) lid. The 詩經 (*Shījīng*) and the 尚書 repeat it, and the 毛 (*Máo*) commentary glosses it 柔，安也, *"柔 is to settle."* That is the word as a verb, *to make soft*: to settle a distant people the way a woodworker settles a curve into wood. Laozi never uses it that way. In this book 柔 is always a quality and never takes an object.

### What the book does with it

**Water.** 天下莫柔弱於水，而攻堅強者莫之能勝, *"In all the world nothing is softer and more yielding than water, yet at attacking the hard and the strong nothing overcomes it"* (78). On ch 43, 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) names the two ends of the scale: 至柔者水，至堅金石。水能貫堅入剛，无所不通, *"the softest is water, the hardest metal and stone. Water can pierce the hard and enter the unbending; there is nowhere it does not get through."*

**The tongue.** On ch 78's 柔之勝剛, *"the soft overcomes the unbending,"* 河上公 answers with the body: 舌柔齒剛，齒先舌亡, *"the tongue is soft, the teeth are unbending; the teeth go first."*

**The infant.** 骨弱筋柔而握固, *"their bones are yielding and their muscles soft, yet their grip is firm"* (55). 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) says the softness is the reason for the grip: 以柔弱之故，故握能周固, *"because it is soft and yielding, its grip can close all the way round and hold."* A hard hand cannot wrap around a thing. Ch 10 asks for the same body from inside: 專氣致柔，能如嬰兒乎, *"gathering the breath to softness, can you be an infant?"* 王弼 there: 致至柔之和, *"reaching the harmony of the utmost softness."*

**What is alive.** 人之生也柔弱，其死也堅強。萬物草木之生也柔脆，其死也枯槁, *"In life a person is soft and yielding; in death, hard and strong. In life the countless things, the grasses and trees, are soft and fragile; in death, withered and dry"* (76). Rigor mortis and dry stalks are the argument. Softness is how you tell that something is alive.

**The paradox.** 守柔曰強, *"holding to the soft is called strong"* (52). 王弼 states it in two short clauses: 守強不強，守柔乃強也, *"holding to the strong is not strong; holding to the soft is truly strong."*

**Why it wins.** 王弼 on ch 43 gives the mechanism, and it is the 說文's wood again: 至柔不可折, *"the utmost soft cannot be snapped."* What bends does not break. Ch 76 states the other side, in our base text: 木強則折, *"a strong tree snaps."*

### 柔 and 剛: bending against not bending

剛 (*gāng*) appears twice, both times opposite 柔: 柔弱勝剛強 (36) and 柔之勝剛 (78).

> 剛，彊斷也。从刀岡聲。
> *"剛 is strong enough to cut. From 刀 (dāo — a knife), with 岡 (gāng — a ridge) for the sound."* — 說文解字

**剛 is *unbending*, not *hard*, and a third character is why.** 堅 (*jiān*) also wants *hard*: 至堅 (43), 堅強 (76, twice), 攻堅強 (78). Ch 78 holds both a few lines apart, *"attacking **the hard** and the strong"* for 堅 and *"the soft overcomes **the unbending**"* for 剛. 說文 defines each by the other's neighbour, 堅，剛也 (*"堅 is 剛"*). 堅 is solid hardness, and it keeps *hard*, in twice the lines. 剛 is the edge that will not give, and *unbending* is exactly what 說文's 柔 is not. **The book's contest is bending against not bending, and the pair holds the 說文's picture between them:** 柔 is the wood that bends, 剛 the blade that will not. *(Shalom's call, 2026-10-14.)*

**Ch 78 needs four English words, not two:** 弱之勝強，柔之勝剛, *"the yielding overcomes the strong; the soft overcomes the unbending."* 柔 **soft** · 剛 **unbending** · 弱 (*ruò*) **yielding** · 強 (*qiáng*) **strong**. Where 柔 and 弱 stand together, 柔 comes first every time (36, 76 three times, 78), and the English keeps the order: *the soft and yielding*. The argument for keeping the two apart is in the 弱 entry.

**The I Ching holds the same pair the other way.** Its commentaries, the Wings, make 剛柔 (*gāng róu*) their central pair, with 剛 nearly a hundred times and 柔 nearly seventy, and treat the two as equal: each is right in its own place, and a 剛 line where 剛 belongs is correct. Laozi has 剛 twice, never writes 剛柔 as a compound, and both times takes the side of 柔. The I Ching's 文言 (*Wényán*) has the same superlative as ch 43, 坤至柔而動也剛, *"坤 (kūn — earth, the carrying hexagram) is soft to the utmost, yet in moving it is unbending."* The I Ching's usual English for the pair is *firm / yielding*, and this book can use neither word: *firm* is 固's (55, 59, 67) and *yielding* is 弱's.

### Why "soft"

- **It is the book's own images.** Water, a tongue, an infant's grip, new grass are all soft. None of them is *supple*.
- **It is English's own opposite to hard.** Ch 43's 至柔 against 至堅 is *the softest thing* against *the hardest*, and no other English pair is that plain.
- **It describes and does not praise.** *Soft* is how a thing meets pressure, whether that is a virtue or not. The book supplies the verdict itself (勝, 強, 生之徒), so the word must not supply one first.
- **The bending is carried by the pair.** The 說文's wood that bends and straightens is held in the seam between *soft* and *unbending*, which is where the book puts it.

### What is set aside, and why

**"supple," "pliant," "pliable," "flexible"** are the 說文's picture taken literally, and the strongest rivals. They name a trained or worked capacity, a gymnast's spine or a cane under the woodworker's hand, and they fail on the book's central image: water is not supple. They also cost ch 43 its plain opposites, since *the most supple thing gallops through the hardest* sets two unrelated scales against each other.

**"gentle"** and **"gentleness"** turn a material quality into a manner of conduct, and a manner that English praises. 河上公 reads 柔 that way more than once: 和柔謙讓, *"harmonious, soft, humble, deferring"* (on ch 3), and 柔順, *"soft and compliant"* (on ch 10). That is a commentator's ethics, which is evidence for a reading and not a rendering. The verse lines are about water and bones.

**"weak"** names a lack. It was removed from 弱 for that reason, and it would bring the same deficiency back in through 柔.

**"yielding"** is 弱's. Ch 78 sets the two in separate clauses.

**"tender"** is 慈's (*cí*, *tenderness*, the first of ch 67's three treasures). 慈 shares no chapter with 柔, so the build can hold this one.

### Working register

柔 never takes an object in this book. It describes a state, or names the thing in that state.

| Chinese | English | form |
|---|---|---|
| 骨弱筋柔 (55) · 人之生也柔弱 (76) · 草木之生也柔脆 (76, *soft and fragile*) | *soft* | predicate |
| 守柔 (52) · 柔弱勝剛強 (36) · 柔之勝剛 (78) · 柔弱者生之徒 · 柔弱處上 (76) | *the soft* | a quality named as a thing |
| 天下之至柔 (43) | *the softest thing in the world* | 至 (zhì — utmost), superlative |
| 莫柔弱於水 (78) | *nothing softer and more yielding than water* | comparative |
| 專氣致柔 (10) | *gathering the breath to softness* | the end point of 致 (zhì — to bring to the utmost) |

### What no rule can enforce

**"yielding" is ruled out for 柔 and is not on its `forbidden:` list, because it cannot be.** 弱 stands beside 柔 in chapters 36, 55, 76 and 78 and prints *yielding* in every one of them.

**"hard" is ruled out for 剛 and cannot be forbidden either.** A `covers:` character carries a rendering but no `forbidden:` list, and 堅, whose English *hard* is, stands in ch 43, 76 and 78. The reader holds this one: in ch 78, *hard* is 堅's and *unbending* is 剛's. See `process/principles/ruling-and-enforcement-are-two-facts.md`.

### Left open

**English *soft* has idioms that point the wrong way.** *Gone soft*, *soft-headed*, *soft on crime*: as a judgement of a person, English *soft* means lacking, which is exactly why 弱 lost *weak*. *Soft* survives here because its first sense is material, to the touch, and the book's images keep it there: water, tongue, sinew, grass. But ch 78 turns from water to whoever takes on the shame of the state, and a reader who hears *soft* as a judgement of character will hear the deficiency there. No English word for 柔 avoids this. *Supple* and *gentle* avoid it only by losing the image.

**The return.** 說文's wood bends **and straightens**. Its 柔 is not only something that gives way under pressure but something that comes back afterwards, and English *soft* does not say that. Bending and coming back is the motion of 反 (*fǎn*) and 復 (*fù*), *return*, which ch 40 calls the movement of the Tao. Whether the book hears that in 柔 is a reason to look and not a reading (`process/principles/distribution-locates.md`).

**The verb.** The oldest use of the word is political: 柔遠, *to settle the far*, to bring distant peoples round the way wood is brought round. This book never uses 柔 as a verb, but ch 78 does turn from water to the ruler of the state in the same breath. The verse keeps 柔 a quality, and the political sense stays in the background.

## 弱 (Ruò) — Yielding

*Say "rwaw," falling. Ten lines across six chapters, paired throughout with 柔 (róu — soft).*

**Locked: 弱 → "yielding," and the verb *yield* where it makes something so.** *(Not "weak," not "weaken," not "frail," not "feeble," not "feebleness," not "powerless.")*

**Weak** is the dictionary's first word for 弱, and it is a deficiency word in English. It names an absence — of force, of health, of resolve. Put it in the Tao Te Ching and the book acquires a doctrine it does not hold: that the way to prevail is to *lack* something.

That is not how this book uses the character, and it is not how the commentators read it where the book holds it up. They knew the plain sense. Heshang Gong writes 羸弱 (*léi ruò* — lean and feeble) at ch 29 and 脆弱 (*cuì ruò* — brittle) at ch 64, and Wang Bi writes 民强則國家弱 (*mín qiáng zé guó jiā ruò* — "when the people are strong, the state is weak") at ch 57. So 弱 can mean weak. The claim is narrower: what the book prizes as 弱 is never a lack.

### The graph

**The graph does not settle this.** Three readings are on record, and none of them is decisive:

- **A bending, in the Shuowen (c. 100 CE).** 橈也 (*náo yě* — "to bend"). 上象橈曲，彡象毛氂橈弱也 (*shàng xiàng náo qū, shān xiàng máo lí náo ruò yě* — "the top depicts bending; the 彡 (*shān* — fine strokes) depicts fine hair, bending and pliant"). 弱物并，故从二𢎥 (*ruò wù bìng, gù cóng èr* — "pliant things go together, so it is made of two of the bent element"). Xu Shen names no bow.
- **A bow, in popular etymologies,** because the modern form looks like two 弓 (*gōng* — bow). Wiktionary gives this with 彡, and reads it as "a decorative bow that is functionally inferior," which is itself a deficiency reading.
- **Two people urinating,** in Dong Chinese, which lists Ji Xusheng's *Shuowen xinzheng* among its sources. On this reading the word for weakness is a sound loan, and the graph says nothing about the meaning. We have this secondhand and have not read the book.

**So the case rests on how the word was understood and how the book uses it, not on a picture.** The Shuowen is good evidence for the first: a Han reader defined 弱 by how a thing behaves under load. The word's family points the same way. Wiktionary reports it as probably cognate with 柔 (*róu* — soft), citing STEDT, and reports Schuessler and Hill comparing Tibetan *nyog nyong*, "soft, weak."

### What the commentators actually say

Where the book holds 弱 up, the commentators read capacity, and none of them reads deficiency.

**Wang Bi on ch 40** (弱者道之用 — *"弱 is the Tao's use"*):

> 柔弱同通不可窮極
> *"Soft and 弱 alike **pass through**; they cannot be exhausted."*

通 (*tōng*) is to penetrate, to get through, to be unobstructed. This is a gloss about **capacity**, and about inexhaustibility — the opposite of the thing "weak" names.

**Heshang Gong on ch 78**, where the text splits the compound into two clauses and he answers each with an image:

> 弱之勝強 — 水能滅火
> *"The 弱 overcomes the strong — water can put out fire."*
> 柔之勝剛 — 舌柔齒剛，齒先舌亡
> *"The soft overcomes the hard — the tongue is soft, the teeth are hard; the teeth go first."*

**Heshang Gong on ch 36** (柔弱勝剛強):

> 柔弱者久長，剛強者先亡也
> *"The 柔弱 endure long; the hard and strong perish first."*

Water and a tongue are not weak. They are things that do not resist, and therefore do not break, and therefore are still there afterwards. **Yielding** is the English for that.

**Heshang Gong on ch 3,** on 弱其志 (*ruò qí zhì* — "teach their ambition to yield") itself:

> 和柔謙讓不處權也
> *"Gentle and soft, modest and giving way, not holding on to power."*

讓 (*ràng*) means to give way. This is the only gloss any commentator gives on the causative in ch 3, and it reads yielding, not diminishing.

**The same words are for rulers.** At ch 42 he says rulers and lords 處謙卑，法虛空，和柔 (*chǔ qiān bēi, fǎ xū kōng, hé róu* — "dwell modest and low, model on empty space, gentle and soft"). What ch 3 gives the people is what the sage practices, and 弱者道之用 (*ruò zhě dào zhī yòng* — "Yielding is the Tao's use") at ch 40 is where it comes from.

### Making something yield

Two of the ten lines make something yield, with an object:

- **ch 3** 弱其志，強其骨 — *teaching their ambition to yield and strengthening their bones*
- **ch 36** 將欲弱之，必固強之 — *If you would have it yield, you must first strengthen it*

**弱 here is a stative word made causative,** as its neighbours in ch 3 are: 虛 (*xū* — empty) gives *emptying*, 實 (*shí* — full) gives *filling*, 強 (*qiáng* — strong) gives *strengthening*. Each keeps its root, and so does 弱. English has no one-word causative of *yield*, so each line takes a helper verb. The helper belongs to the construction and not to the character, and it is where the two lines differ: the sage **teaches**, and the strategist **has**.

**Ch 3 reads *teaching their ambition to yield*.**

- ***Yielding their ambition*** fails: with an object, *yield* means produce or surrender, and *produce* reverses the line.
- ***Making*** is accurate, but *make them yield* is the language of force, which is the fault `process/principles/collocation-carries-a-verdict.md` names.
- ***Letting*** undersells a real causative.
- ***Teaching*** is the commentators' own account. Heshang Gong on ch 42: 言我教衆人使去強為弱，去剛為柔 (*yán wǒ jiào zhòng rén shǐ qù qiáng wéi ruò, qù gāng wéi róu* — "I teach the many, so that they leave the strong and become yielding, leave the unbending and become soft"). Wang Bi on the same line: 我之非强使人從之也，而用夫自然 (*wǒ zhī fēi qiáng shǐ rén cóng zhī yě, ér yòng fū zì rán* — "it is not that I force people to follow; I use what is so of itself"). The Shuowen defines 教 (*jiào* — teach) as 上所施下所效也 (*shàng suǒ shī xià suǒ xiào yě* — "what those above give out and those below take after"). And ch 2, just before this line, has named the teaching without words, which Heshang Gong glosses 以身師導之也 (*yǐ shēn shī dǎo zhī yě* — "teaching and guiding them with one's own body").

**The costs:** *teaching* is not in the line, and a commentator's gloss at another chapter is not the text. It says the paternalism outright, and the couplet loses its run of four single verbs.

**Ch 36 reads *have it yield*.**

- ***Make it yielding*** fails: yielding is the state the book prizes, so the strategist would be doing the object a favor. All four clauses diminish something, and every commentator reads an undoing. Heshang Gong's lemma has an explicit 使 (*shǐ* — cause), with the gloss 先強大之者欲使遇禍患 (*xiān qiáng dà zhī zhě yù shǐ yù huò huàn* — "making it strong and great first means wanting it to meet disaster").
- ***Make it yield*** puts a fist in the sage's vocabulary.
- ***Have*** keeps the causative without the force, and sits close to Wang Bi's 因物之性令其自戮 (*yīn wù zhī xìng lìng qí zì lù* — "following things' nature, causing them to bring themselves down"), where the thing undoes itself.

**The costs:** *have* undersells a real defeat, and it has an older sound, though the chapter's *If you would* frame already does.

Everywhere 弱 describes a state or a quality — ch 40, 55, 76, 78, and 36's own 柔弱勝剛強 — it reads **yielding**.

### The story Han Fei tells

Chapter 36 uses the character twice, and the English repeats it:

> *If you would have it yield, you must first strengthen it.*
> *The soft and yielding overcome the unbending and strong.*
>
> 將欲弱之，必固強之；
> 柔弱勝剛強。
>
> — chapter 36

Han Fei, the oldest commentary there is, does not gloss these lines. He tells a story, and both uses are in it:

> 越王入宦於吴，而觀之伐齊以弊吳。吳兵既勝齊人於艾陵，張之於江、濟，強之於黄池，故可制於五湖。
> *"The king of Yue went into service in Wu, and steered it into attacking Qi, to wear Wu out. Once Wu's army had beaten the men of Qi at Ailing, it stretched itself out along the Yangtze and the Ji and made itself strong at Huangchi, and so could be subdued at the Five Lakes."*

He quotes the line right there, 將欲弱之，必固強之, and closes the passage with the other:

> 處小弱而重自卑損，謂「弱勝強」也
> *"To dwell in the small and yielding and make much of humbling oneself: this is what 'the yielding overcomes the strong' means."*

**Yue yields, and Wu is had to yield.** Yue serves its enemy and lets it grow. Wu, swollen, is subdued. One character, two parties, one story. So the four second verbs of the chapter, *stretch out, strengthen, raise up, give to*, may themselves be ways of giving way, and line 6 may name what "you" were practicing all along while line 2 names what befalls the other side. That is our reading. The story fits it, and no commentator states it.

**What this leaves open.** A word the book gives the sage, and the Tao at ch 40, stands here in a calculating sentence. In Han Fei's hands it is plainly a tactic. Wang Bi hears something closer to how things go. The chapter calls it 微明 (*wēi míng* — the hidden clarity) and does not choose, so neither does the English.

### 柔 and 弱 are two words, and ch 78 proves it

The compound 柔弱 is so common that it is tempting to treat the halves as one idea. **Ch 78 refuses:**

> 弱之勝強，柔之勝剛
> *"The yielding overcomes the strong; the soft overcomes the unbending."*

Two clauses, two pairs, no overlap. That line is the constraint every rendering has to satisfy, and it needs four distinct English words:

| | |
|---|---|
| 柔 (*róu*) | **soft** |
| 剛 (*gāng*) | **unbending** |
| 弱 (*ruò*) | **yielding** |
| 強 (*qiáng*) | **strong** |

So 柔 keeps **soft** and does not get *yielding*, which it had borrowed in ch 52 (守柔曰強) before this entry existed.

**剛 (*gāng*) is *unbending*, not *hard*,** because 堅 (*jiān*) holds *hard* a few lines away in the same chapter. The case is made in the 柔 entry, `rou-柔.md`, with the rest of 柔's.

### Why this matters for ch 76

Chapter 76 works by spending the **admiring** word on a corpse: 堅強 (*jiān qiáng* — hard and strong) is rigor mortis, and four lines later it is an army. That ambush is on 強 alone. An earlier draft of this entry's reasoning claimed the chapter *also* provokes by calling the living state weak — it does not, and translating to protect that invented second provocation is what put **weak** into the verse. Caught by Shalom, 2026-08-26.

### Working register

- **yielding** — ch 36 (柔弱勝剛強), 40, 55, 76, 78
- **yield**, with a helper verb — ch 3 (弱其志), *teaching their ambition to yield*; ch 36 (將欲弱之), *have it yield*

### What is set aside

**weak · weaken · weakness.** The dictionary's plain English, and it costs the book three things. It says *less force* where 弱 says *gives*, which brings back the doctrine that the way to prevail is to lack something. At ch 36 it splits one character into two unrelated English words in six lines, so a reader cannot hear the close answering the opening. At ch 3 it cuts the line off from *Yielding is the Tao's use*, and turns the sage's own practice into a ruler reducing the people. It also spares the sage's word the stratagem of ch 36, which is a comfort the Chinese does not offer.

**frail · feeble · powerless.** All three name a lack. 弱 names a response.

**For ch 3: soften · gentle · bend · surrender · invite · inspire.** *Soften* and *gentle* are 柔's ground, and *gentle* is forbidden there. *Bend* is 曲 (*qū* — bent)'s word (`quan-全.md`), and *bending their ambition* reads as redirecting it. *Surrender* brings in defeat. *Invite* and *inspire* make optional what the Chinese makes causative, and no commentator uses them.

Also never let 柔 take *yielding* — see the four-word table above. That ruling is held by the reader, not the build; `rou-柔.md` says why.

## 善 (Shàn) — Masterful

*Say "shahn," fourth tone, falling. Forty-five lines in eighteen chapters — one of the largest words in the book, and the one that decides whether Laozi reads as a moralist.*

**Locked: 善 → "masterful," or "masterful at," wherever it names skill. "Good" only where the text is naming *good* as a category — which it does in order to criticize it.**

Render 善 as *good* throughout, as the English tradition does, and you produce a Laozi who divides people into the good and the bad, prizes goodness, and counsels being nice to the wicked. Almost none of that is in the Chinese. **Roughly thirty of the forty-five occurrences mean skilled at something**, and where the word *is* used as a moral category, the book's move is to warn you against the category.

### The graph: a sheep, and it has two siblings

The *Shuowen Jiezi* gives the old form 譱 and glosses it: 吉也。从誩，从羊。**此與義、美同意** — *"auspicious; from 誩 and 羊; this has the same sense as 義 and 美."*

- **羊** (*yáng*) — a sheep, seen head-on: the horns, the face. The sacrificial animal.
- **誩** (*jìng*) — two 言 (*yán* — speech): two people speaking in turn, weighing a matter.

And the Shuowen's own cross-reference is the finding: **善 belongs to a family of three, and all three wear the sheep.**

| | Built from | Became |
|---|---|---|
| **美** (*měi*) | 羊 over 大 (a big person) — a large sheep | **beauty** |
| **義** (*yì*) | 羊 over 我 (a weapon, then *I*) | **duty, right conduct** |
| **善** (*shàn*) | 羊 over speech | **good** |

Its oldest sense survives in the character 膳 (*shàn* — the prepared dish, the meat offering), which is 善 with the flesh radical added back. **So 善 begins as *fit for the altar*: well-made, sound, up to standard, good of its kind.** Not morally good — **good at being what it is.**

That is precisely the sense Laozi uses, over and over.

### What the text actually does with it

**Thirty occurrences are 善 + a verb — skilled at doing something**, and they are the book's most concrete lines:

> Ch 27 · 善行無轍跡，善言無瑕謫，善數不用籌策，善閉無關楗而不可開，善結無繩約而不可解
> *masterful travelling leaves no tracks · masterful speech is flawless · masterful reckoning uses no counting rods · masterful shutting uses no bolts, yet cannot be opened · masterful tying uses no rope, yet cannot be untied*

A traveller, a speaker, an accountant, a locksmith, a knot-tier. **Five trades in five lines.** **Chapter 8 is the showcase: nine occurrences in thirteen lines**, more concentrated than anywhere else in the book — 上善, 善利, then the seven couplets 善地, 善淵, 善仁, 善信, 善治, 善能, 善時: masterful at ground, at depth, at giving, at speech, at governing, at what can be done, at timing. Chapter 68 gives four: the masterful officer is not martial, the masterful fighter does not rage, the masterful conqueror does not engage, the masterful user of people puts themselves below. Chapter 73 gives three more of the Tao itself: 不爭而**善**勝，不言而**善**應 — *does not contend yet masterfully prevails; does not speak yet masterfully answers.*

**None of that is ethics. All of it is craft.**

### Where 善 *is* moral, the book is attacking the category

Six occurrences use 善 as an abstract quality — and in the most important of them, Laozi is not recommending it. He is pointing at what happens when it becomes a name.

> Ch 2 · 天下皆知**美**之為美，斯惡已；皆知**善**之為善，斯不善已。
> *"When all the world knows beauty as beauty, ugliness arises; when all know good as good, the not-good arises."*

**He puts the two sheep-words side by side** — 美 and 善, beauty and good, the pair the *Shuowen* says share a sense — and shows both curdling at the moment they are made into categories. The not-good is not a pre-existing evil the good opposes. It is **manufactured by the act of naming the good.**

Chapter 58 finishes the thought: 正復為奇，**善**復為妖 — *the straight turns crooked, the good turns monstrous.* And Chapter 20 sets 善 against 惡 (*è* — bad) only to ask 相去若何, *what is the distance between them?*

So the book's two uses of 善 are not in tension. **They are one argument: be good at things, and be wary of Goodness.**

### Why this decides three chapters

Chapters 27, 49 and 62 make one claim in three vocabularies — nobody gets thrown away (see the Thread in `notes/reading.md`) — and **the rendering of 善 decides what kind of claim it is.**

Held as *good* and *bad*, Chapter 62 becomes a doctrine of grace: the Tao shelters sinners, and 罪 (*zuì* — **crime**) three lines later completes the gospel. Held as **masterful** and **unmasterful**, it becomes an argument about **use**:

> Ch 27 · 故善人者，不善人之師；不善人者，善人之**資**。
> *"So the masterful are the teacher of the unmasterful, and the unmasterful are the masterful's **資** (zī — raw material, working stock)."*

That is not mercy. It is a claim that **nobody is discarded because nobody is waste** — which is why the chapter puts it beside a locksmith and a knot-tier, and why 不貴其師，不愛其資 (*failing to value the teacher or love the raw material*) is called 大迷, great confusion.

### What is set aside

**"Virtuous," "righteous," "saintly."** Each turns a sheep fit for the altar into a person fit for heaven. 義 (*yì* — duty) is a different character and gets its own treatment; **benevolent** belongs to 仁 (*rén* — humaneness), which Chapter 8's 與善仁 uses in the same line as 善 and must stay distinguishable from it.

**"Good" used everywhere.** Not forbidden — it is right in Chapters 2, 20 and 58, where the category is the subject. But applied to 善行 or 善結 it flattens a locksmith into a saint.

**"Skilful" and "expert."** Accurate and bloodless. *Masterful* holds the register the trades give it, and it is what makes 善人 / 不善人 read as **the adept and the inept** rather than the righteous and the wicked.

### Working register

| The grammar | Where | Render |
|---|---|---|
| 善 + verb — skilled at | 8, 15, 27, 30, 41, 50, 54, 65, 66, 68, 73 | **masterful at** |
| 善人 / 不善人 — the kind of person | 27, 49, 62 | **the masterful / the unmasterful** |
| 善 as the named category | 2, 20, 58 | **good** — because the category is the target |
| 上善 — the superlative | 8 | **the most masterful** (settled 2026-09-02, below) |
| 善 as a verb, "to reckon as 善" | 49 | **count as masterful** |

### Chapter 49 — decided, and it follows Wang Bi

*(settled 2026-08-14.)* 善者，吾善之；不善者，吾亦善之 uses 善 four times in two lines — twice for the kind of person, twice as a **verb**, *to reckon as 善*. It now reads **"The masterful, I count as masterful; the unmasterful, I count as masterful too."**

**Wang Bi reads the chapter in Chapter 27's own vocabulary**, which is what decided it. His gloss on the couplet is 各**因**其**用**，則善不失也 — *"go along with each according to their **use**, and then 善 is not lost."* His gloss on the tag 德善 is three characters — **無棄人也**, *"there are no discarded people"* — which is Chapter 27's own line, 故無棄人, quoted here. And he closes the chapter with 能者與之，**資**者取之, *"those with ability, go along with; those who are **raw material**, take them up"* — 資 (*zī*) being the exact character Chapter 27 gives the unmasterful.

**Heshang Gong reads it morally** and it stays on the record: 百姓雖有不善者，聖人化之使善也 — *"though some of the people are not good, the sage transforms them and makes them good."*

**The English cost, named.** *Count as masterful* is heavier in the mouth than *am good to*. What it buys is the actual claim: 善之 is **appraisal**, not kindness. The sage is not being nice to the incompetent — they are **refusing to run the grading**, which is the same move as 何棄之有 (62) and 無棄人 (27), and a sharper thing to say.

**What it commits.** Ch 79 (常與善人) and Ch 81 (善者不辯，辯者不善) are undrafted and now inherit this: *"the masterful do not argue; arguers are not masterful."* Stranger than *"the good do not argue,"* and consistent with the rest.

### Chapter 8 — decided 2026-09-02, and it settles the grammar for the whole entry

**上善若水 now reads "The most masterful are like water."** *(Shalom's call.)* 上 (*shàng* — highest) is settled at ch 38, where 上德 / 上仁 / 上義 / 上禮 all read *the highest*, so *"supreme"* was the outlier. **The category reading is unavailable here**: *good* is reserved for chapters 2, 20 and 58, where the book attacks the category, and using it at ch 8 would make this chapter endorse what ch 2 dismantles. 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) reads 上善 as a **person** — 上善之人如水之性, *"the person of the highest 善 is like the nature of water"* — which is this entry's own 善人 (*shàn rén* — the masterful). **The cost:** the plural person decides something the Chinese leaves open, since 上善 could be the quality itself. ***The highest excellence*** was rejected as bloodless and as Legge's phrase; ***true mastery*** was rejected because 真 (*zhēn* — genuine) is a live character in this book (21, 41, 54) and 上 is a graded rank word whose middle rung is printed at ch 41 (上士/中士/下士).

**善 governs a verb — eighteen times out of eighteen, and this is the proof the entry has been asserting without evidence.** The *Working register* table above claims a "善 + verb" grammar. Ch 8 is the only place in the book where the claim could fail, because its seven couplets are the only 善 + X where X could pass for a noun, and X善Y admits both parses in classical Chinese: 善 as a verb taking Y (*masterful **at** Y*), or 善 as an adjective modifying Y (*masterful Y*).

Everywhere else, X is a verb:

> 善行 *travel* · 善言 *speak* · 善計 *reckon* · 善閉 *shut* · 善結 *tie* (27) · 善救 *rescue* ×2 (27) · 善為 *handle* (15, 65) · 善貸 *give* (41) · 善攝 *nurture* (50) · 善建 *establish* · 善抱 *embrace* (54) · 善下 *go below* (66) · 善戰 *fight* · 善勝 *overcome* ×2 (68, 73) · 善用 *use* (68) · 善應 *respond* · 善謀 *plan* (73)

**Eighteen verbs, zero nouns.** And ch 8 sets the pattern inside its own chapter, four lines above the stanza: 水善**利**萬物, where 利 (*lì* — to benefit) is unambiguously verbal. The adjectival parse fails on its own terms as well — it yields *masterful order*, *masterful ability*, *masterful timing*, which read, and *masterful ground*, *masterful depth*, *masterful humaneness*, *masterful trust*, which do not. **A reading that survives three of seven loses to one that survives all seven.**

The seven now run in one shape: *In settling, masterful at ground. In the heart, masterful at depth. In giving, masterful at humaneness. In speech, masterful at trust. In governing, masterful at order. In affairs, masterful at what can be done. In moving, masterful at timing.*

**能 (*néng* — able) took *what can be done* rather than *ability***, because 能 has 32 lines in the book and 31 are the plain modal *can*; ch 8's is the only noun. Building the English out of *can* keeps it in the book's own vocabulary and removes the abstract-noun stack beside *masterful*. The cost is a slight drift of the capacity from the agent to the situation.

### Left open


**淵 (*yuān* — a deep pool), inside ch 8's stanza, is not yet settled** and reads three ways across the book: *fathomless* (4), *depth* (8), *the deep abyss* (36). 說文解字 makes it banked water — 回水也…左右，岸也, *"swirling water… left and right are the banks"* — so *limitless*, which stood at ch 8 until 2026-09-02, was precisely backwards. Tracked as `WORKLIST.md` T2-24; not this entry's term, but it sits inside this entry's showcase chapter.
entries.render: masterful / masterful at · the masterful & the unmasterful (of people) · good (only where the text names the category)

entries.body:
## 神 & 靈 (Shén, Líng) — Spirit, and Spirit at Work

*Say "shun," rising, and "ling," rising. 神 stands eight times in seven lines across four chapters; 靈 twice, both in chapter 39, and both times as what 神 becomes. Neither is ever a god.*

**Recommended: 神 → "spirit" · Settled: 靈 → "potent"** (Shalom's call, 2026-11-19, at chapter 39). *(Not "God," "the divine" or "deity," which the missionaries put into 神. Not "holy," which is 聖 (shèng — the sage)'s overlay. Not "soul," which leaves the body. Not "numinous," a theologian's word for the holy that no one could point at.)* **One flexion:** *sacred* at chapter 29, where 神 qualifies a made thing. **Covered here:** 鬼 (guǐ — ghost) → *ghost*, its partner at chapter 60.

### The graph: lightning at an altar, and a shaman wearing jade

> 神，天神，引出萬物者也。从示，申聲。
> *"神 is the spirits of the sky, which draw out the countless things. From 示 (shì — the altar), with 申 (shēn — lightning) for the sound."* — Shuowen (說文, *Shuōwén* — Xu Shen's dictionary, c. 100 CE)

**申 is lightning.** Its oldest graph is a bolt branching from the sky, and it is the parent of two characters: 電 (*diàn* — lightning), which took the rain radical, and 神, which took the altar. In the oracle bones and in some bronzes the spirit is written with the lightning alone; 示 (*shì* — the altar) was added later, to say which sense was meant. The Shuowen's own line for 示 says what the altar is for: 天垂象，見吉凶，所以示人也, *"the sky hangs down signs, showing good fortune and ill, and so it shows people."*

**So the picture is a flash from the sky, received at an altar.** A spirit, in this graph, is not a person sitting somewhere. It is a force that shows itself, and a place where people meet it.

> 𩆜巫，以玉事神。从玉，霝聲。
> *"靈: a shaman, who serves the spirits with jade. From 玉 (yù — jade), with 霝 (líng — drops of rain) for the sound."* — Shuowen, under 𩆜, the old form of 靈

**The Shuowen files 靈 under jade, and the bronzes could not agree on what to put beneath it.** Over a constant 霝 (*líng* — drops of rain falling), the lower half is 玉 (*yù* — jade) in the Shuowen, 巫 (*wū* — a shaman) in the form we print, and 心 (*xīn* — the heart) or 示 (*shì* — the altar) in older bronzes. Four answers to one question: where does spirit arrive? In a precious stone, in a dancer, in a heart, at an altar.

*A calibration.* 霝 counts as sound in the Shuowen, and the rain in it may be only that. The popular reading of 靈 as a rain-shaman is attractive and unproved, and this entry does not lean on it. The silks point the same way: in the collated silk text, chapter 39 writes 神得一以霝 (*shén dé yī yǐ líng*), the bare sound part with nothing beneath it, which is how a scribe writes a word by its sound. What the graph does show is a person, or a thing, through which the spirits are served.

### The word before the book: falling rain, a good end, a spirit made bright

The Shuowen gives the graph. The word is older, and its early uses, gathered in the Kangxi Dictionary (康熙字典, *Kāngxī Zìdiǎn*, 1716), say what it meant before Laozi used it.

**霝, the top of the graph, is rain coming down in drops.** The Shuowen's own entry for it, as the Kangxi quotes it: 霝，雨零也。从雨，𠱠象零形, *"霝: rain falling. From 雨 (yǔ — rain); the three mouths picture the falling drops."* In the 靈 entry the Shuowen counts 霝 as sound; in its own entry it is a picture. The Book of Odes has 霝雨其濛 (*"the falling rain drizzles"*), and the Stone Drums have 霝雨.

**The oldest written 靈 here is a blessing on how a life ends.** The 逑盤 (*Qiú pán*), a Western Zhou bronze basin, closes its prayer 永令、霝冬, *"a lasting mandate, and a 霝 end,"* which its transcribers read as 靈終 (*líng zhōng* — a 靈 ending). Elsewhere the same wish is 令終 (*lìng zhōng*), *a good end*, and 令 (*lìng*) and 靈 trade places by sound.

**In the Odes, 靈 is good, and it is rain.** 靈雨既零 (*líng yǔ jì líng* — "the 靈 rain has fallen," 鄘風 (*Yōng Fēng*), *Dìng zhī fāng zhōng*), and Zheng Xuan's gloss: 靈，善也, *"靈 means good."* The rain the farmers prayed for, fallen when it should. The *Guangyun* (廣韻, *Guǎngyùn*) adds 福也, *"blessing,"* and 巫也, *"a shaman."*

**In the Documents and the Odes' commentary, 靈 is spirit at its brightest.** 惟人萬物之靈 (*wéi rén wàn wù zhī líng* — "humankind alone is the 靈 of the countless things," *Shàngshū*, *Tài Shì*), glossed 靈，神也, *"靈 is spirit."* On King Wen's 靈臺 (*líng tái* — the 靈 terrace), Mao's commentary: 神之精明者稱靈, *"what is most essential and bright in spirit is called 靈."*

**The Dadai Liji pairs it with 神 as two halves:** 陽之精氣曰神，陰之精氣曰靈, *"the essence-breath of yang is called 神; the essence-breath of yin is called 靈."* That is the pairing this entry is built on, already made in the Han.

**And 靈 belongs to the dead as much as the living.** The posthumous-name rules: 死見神能曰靈, *"one who shows spirit-power after death is called 靈."* The *Liji*'s 芻靈 (*chú líng*) are straw figures buried with the dead; the later 靈柩 (*líng jiù*) is the coffin and 靈位 (*líng wèi*) the spirit tablet.

**One thread runs through all of it: spirit where it takes effect and shows.** Rain that falls when it is prayed for. An end that comes out right. A shaman the spirit enters. A spirit bright enough to answer, before death or after it. 靈 is not life, and it is not the stuff of life. It is the moment the unseen acts on the seen.

### Seven lines, and 神 is never a god in any of them

> *The spirit of the valley is deathless.*
>
> 谷神不死，
>
> — chapter 6

> *The world is a sacred vessel. It cannot be handled. It cannot be grasped.*
>
> 天下神器，不可為也，不可執也。
>
> — chapter 29

> *Spirit received the one, and so became potent.*
>
> 神得一以靈；
>
> — chapter 39

> *Spirit with no way to be potent is likely to cease.*
>
> 神無以靈，將恐歇；
>
> — chapter 39

> *Oversee the world with the Tao, and the ghosts lose their potency,*
> *not only do ghosts lose their potency, their potency causes no harm to people,*
> *not only does their potency do no harm, the sage, too, does no harm to people.*
>
> 以道莅天下，其鬼不神；
> 非其鬼不神，其神不傷人；
> 非其神不傷人，聖人亦不傷人。
>
> — chapter 60

**In every line, 神 is something in the world, and nothing above it.** At chapter 6 it belongs to a valley. At chapter 39 it stands in a list with the sky, the earth, the valley, the countless things and the rulers, and like each of them it needs the one, or it stops. At chapter 60 it belongs to the ghosts, and the Tao reaches it the way it reaches the people. A god who needs something else in order not to cease is not God, and the book never asks 神 to be one.

### Chapter 39 is the hardest line: 靈 is what 神 is when the one is in it

Chapter 39 gives each thing the one, and each comes into its own quality:

| the thing | with the one | without it |
|---|---|---|
| 天 (*tiān* — sky) | 清 (*qīng*) — *clear* | 裂 (*liè*) — *split* |
| 地 (*dì* — earth) | 寧 (*níng*) — *settled* | 發 (*fā*) — *burst* |
| **神** (*shén* — spirit) | **靈** (*líng*) — ? | **歇** (*xiē*) — *cease* |
| 谷 (*gǔ* — valley) | 盈 (*yíng*) — *full* | 竭 (*jié*) — *run dry* |
| 萬物 (*wàn wù* — the countless things) | 生 (*shēng*) — *come to life* | 滅 (*miè*) — *die out* |
| 侯王 (*hóu wáng* — rulers) | 貞 (*zhēn*) — *the standard* | 蹶 (*jué*) — *topple* |

**Every other quality is one you could point at.** A clear sky, settled ground, a full valley, a sprouting field. Each failure is the visible end of its own quality: the clear sky splits, the full valley runs dry. So 靈 must be the quality that belongs to spirit as clearness belongs to sky, and its failure is 歇 (*xiē* — to stop, to rest, to breathe out and not breathe in). **A spirit that is 靈 works. A spirit that is not, stops.**

**The early texts say what working means.** The *Songs of Chu* (楚辭, *Chǔ Cí*), in Wang Yi's commentary, use 靈 for both ends of the rite:

> 靈，巫也。楚人名巫為靈子。
> *"靈 is a shaman. The people of Chu call a shaman a 靈 child."* — Wang Yi, on 靈連蜷兮既留 (*líng lián quán xī jì liú* — "the 靈 sways and lingers")

> 靈，謂雲神也。
> *"靈 means the spirit of the clouds."* — Wang Yi, later in the same song, on 靈皇皇兮既降 (*líng huáng huáng xī jì jiàng* — "the 靈, resplendent, has come down")

**The word names the dancer and the spirit who comes down into the dance.** A 靈 is spirit made present and effective: the rite answered, the rain fallen, the medicine working. The later language keeps exactly this sense in 靈驗 (*líng yàn* — efficacious, proved by its result) and 靈藥 (*líng yào* — a remedy that works).

**Heshang Gong reads the line as change:**

> 言神得一故能変化無形
> *"It says: spirit received the one, and so it can transform without form."*

> 言神當有王相囚死休廢，不可但欲靈無巳時，將恐虚歇不為神也
> *"It says: spirit must have its seasons of rising and falling. It cannot want only to be 靈, without end, or it may empty and cease and no longer be spirit."*

His seasons, 王相囚死休廢 (*wàng xiàng qiú sǐ xiū fèi* — thriving, ascending, confined, dead, resting, spent), are the vocabulary of the five-phase cycle, which this book never uses. Where the picture stops: the five phases are his. What he adds that holds is that 靈 is an activity, which can wear out. Wang Bi says only 各以其一致此清寧靈盈生貞, *"each by its one arrives at this: clear, settled, 靈, full, alive, the standard."*

**So the English wants a quality that shows in its effect, and whose failure is to stop.** *Potent* is that word. A potent remedy is one that works, and a spirit that is no longer potent goes quiet. It passes the pointing test the way 清 does: you point at the effect, as you point at the sky to show it is clear.

> *Spirit received the one, and so became potent.*
> *Spirit with no way to be potent is likely to cease.*

### Chapter 60: the spirit and the sage, and which two do no harm

Chapter 60 puts 神 into motion. It is a verb in 其鬼不神 (*qí guǐ bù shén* — "its ghosts do not 神") and a noun in 其神 (*qí shén* — "their 神"), twice. The commentators agree on the Tao and divide on the spirit.

**Heshang Gong makes it the ghosts' own force, held back:**

> 以道德居位治天下，則□不敢見其精神以犯人也
> *"Ruling the world from one's seat with the Tao and integrity, the ghosts do not dare show their vital spirit to trouble people."*

> 其□非无精神也
> *"It is not that the ghosts lack vital spirit."*

*(□ is the Song print's 鬼, written in a variant its transcribers could not encode. The rest of the second comment, 非不八正不能傷自然之人, is corrupt as printed, and this entry does not mend it.)*

**Wang Bi makes 神 a party of its own, set beside the sage:**

> 神不害自然也。物守自然，則神無所加；神無所加，則不知神之為神也
> *"Spirit does not harm what is so of itself. When things keep to what is so of themselves, spirit has nothing to add; and when spirit has nothing to add, no one knows spirit as spirit."*

> 神不傷人，聖人亦不傷人……故曰兩不相傷也。神聖合道，交歸之也
> *"Spirit does not harm people, and the sage does not harm people either… so it says the two do not harm each other. Spirit and sage join the Tao, and both return to it."*

For Wang Bi, *the two* of 兩不相傷 (*liǎng bù xiāng shāng* — "the two do not harm each other") are the spirit and the sage. For Heshang Gong they are the ghosts and the sage. Han Fei, the oldest reader, makes them the people and the ghosts: 治世之民，不與鬼神相害也, *"the people of a well-ruled age do no harm with ghosts and spirits,"* and he says plainly what a ghost's harm is, 鬼祟也疾人之謂鬼傷人, *"a ghost haunting a person and making them ill: this is called a ghost harming people."*

**One English for 神 across the chapter keeps all three readings open.** *Spirit* can be the ghosts' own force, which is Heshang Gong, or a power standing by the sage, which is Wang Bi, and the reader can find *the two* either way. *Potency* can only be the first: a quality the ghosts have, never a party who could stand beside the sage. Wang Bi's best sentence on the chapter, that the height of the Tao is 使不知神聖之為神聖, *"to bring it about that no one knows spirit and sage as spirit and sage,"* needs 神 to be someone. This is why the entry recommends *spirit* at chapter 60 too. The line rewrite it needs belongs with the chapter's larger repair (see *Left open*).

### Chapter 29: a vessel for the spirits

神器 (*shén qì*) is the one place 神 qualifies a made thing, and the thing is concrete. In the late Zhou a 神器 was a **ritual bronze**, above all the nine cauldrons whose possession was the warrant to rule (`glossary/qi-器.md`, and the reading note at chapter 29 in `notes/reading.md`). It was a vessel in which food was offered to the spirits, its inscription cast on the inside, facing them.

The commentators each read 神 here through the word's own sense. Wang Bi: 神，無形無方也。器，合成也。無形以合，故謂之神器也, *"spirit has no form and no fixed place; a vessel is something put together. The formless, joined in something put together: so it is called a spirit-vessel."* Heshang Gong: 人乃天下之神物也。神物好安靜，不可以有為治, *"people are the world's spirit-things, and spirit-things love calm and cannot be governed by doing."*

***Sacred* is what English calls a thing set apart for the spirits**, and it is the exact word for a bronze made to feed them. *Spirit vessel* reads in English as a bottle with a spirit in it, a genie's lamp, an urn. The flexion is grammar: a noun becomes the adjective English needs. The character has not changed.

### 鬼 (guǐ — ghost)

> 鬼，人所歸爲鬼。从人，象鬼頭。鬼陰气賊害，从厶。
> *"鬼: what a person returns to is a 鬼. From 人 (rén — a person), picturing a ghost's head. Ghosts are yin breath that does harm, hence 厶 (sī — the crooked)."* — Shuowen

In the oracle bones 鬼 is a figure with an outsized head, usually read as a mask: the dead, or someone standing in for them (`glossary/po-魄.md`). The Shuowen defines it by a pun, 鬼 (*guǐ*) as 歸 (*guī* — to return), which `glossary/gui-fu-fan-歸復反.md` cites as 歸's naming of an ending. **And the Shuowen says what ghosts do: 賊害, harm.** Chapter 60 is the case where they do not. A ghost is a person who has died, and in this book nothing worse.

鬼 stands twice in the book, both in chapter 60, and it lives in this entry because it never appears without 神: its whole part in the chapter is to be the thing whose spirit is held from harm. **Chapter 60 ends 故德交歸焉** (*gù dé jiāo guī yān* — "so their integrity converges and returns"), and the Shuowen would hear its 歸 in the 鬼 at the chapter's start. We do not claim Laozi meant the chime. The Shuowen's ear heard it.

### What is set aside

**"God," "a god," "the gods."** The Term Question was the missionaries' long argument over which Chinese word would be made to mean the Christian God, and 神 was one of the two candidates; the Chinese Union Bible was printed in a 神 edition and a 上帝 (*shàng dì* — the ancestor-lord above) edition because the parties never agreed (`process/overlay-audit.md`, `glossary/di-帝.md`). Read back into Laozi, *God* turns chapter 39 into nonsense, a God who would cease without the one, and turns chapter 60 into a theodicy. Forbidden lowercase, so it catches *gods* and *godlike* as well.

**"The divine," "divine."** An abstract noun of essence where the Chinese has a force at an altar. It is also the word the watchlist names for 神.

**"Deity."** It names a person with a cult and a name. 谷神 (*gǔ shén*) as *the valley deity* makes chapter 6 a shrine to a goddess; the line prints a valley and its spirit.

**"Holy."** 聖 (*shèng*)'s overlay, already forbidden there. In modern Chinese the Holy Spirit is 聖靈 (*shèng líng*), so the Bible spent both 聖 and 靈 on its third person (`glossary/sheng-聖.md`). That is a second reason 靈 cannot simply be *spirit*: the word had been made to say *Spirit* with a capital.

**"Soul."** The thing that leaves the body. Heshang Gong does put 神 in the body, 心藏神, *"the heart stores the spirit,"* one of his five organ-spirits at chapter 6, but even there it is housed and nourished, never a separable immortal self. Already forbidden for 精 (*jīng* — vital essence) and 魄 (*pò* — aliveness).

**"Numinous," for 靈.** Latin *numen*, a nod of the head, the assent of a god, and then a god's power. Rudolf Otto made *the numinous* the word for the holy as it is felt, in *Das Heilige* (1917), translated as *The Idea of the Holy* (1923). It fails both tests at once. It is a theologian's word for the holy, and no one could point at it. Forbidden since chapter 39 took *potent*.

**"Alive," "come alive," "living."** Three reasons, and the first is the etymology. **靈 is not life.** It belongs to the dead as readily as to the living: the posthumous 靈 who shows spirit-power after death, the straw 靈 in the grave, the spirit tablet. *Alive* would deny it to half the beings it names. **Second, chapter 39 needs *alive* for another word.** Its list gives six things six qualities, and Wang Bi names them as six, 清寧靈盈生貞; 靈 and 生 (*shēng* — to live) are two of them, two lines apart. *Spirit… became alive* above *the countless things… came to life* would make spirit and the countless things receive the same gift, and erase the difference the list exists to make. **Third, the word is spoken for twice over:** 生 prints *live* and *alive* in nine lines (7, 33, 34, 39, 50, 73, 75), and 魄 (*pò*) holds *aliveness* at chapter 10 (`glossary/po-魄.md`).

**"Vital."** The strongest rival, and the Dadai Liji gives it its case: 陰之精氣曰靈, 靈 is the *essence-breath* of yin. But that line defines 靈 by its kind, the way a dictionary names a genus, and giving 靈 the genus's English is rendering a gloss (`process/principles/commentary-is-not-rendering.md`). **The English is also taken**: *vital essence* is 精 (*jīng*)'s locked English (21, 55), and `glossary/po-魄.md` already set *vitality* aside for that collision. **And *vital* has the double meaning *agitation* had.** It means *full of life*, and it means *essential*, as in *vital to*. *Spirit received the one, and so became vital* reads first as *became necessary*. Neither sense is 靈's: not life, and not importance.

**"Blessed," "good."** The Odes' 靈，善也 and the *Guangyun*'s 福也 are real senses. *Blessed* fails the hymn test outright; *good* is right for the rain and empty for a spirit.

**"Quick."** The old English sense is exact, *alive and responsive*, and it is the King James Bible's: *the quick and the dead*. It fails the hymn test, and a modern reader hears *fast*.

**"Awake," "awakened."** Buddhist awakening, the 1971 paperback on consciousness. The register imports a doctrine the chapter does not hold.

**"Present," "presence."** *Presence* is 有 (*yǒu*)'s English, in its locked pairing with 無 (*wú*). And the shaman's sense it would catch, the spirit come down, is the one this entry already admits it loses (see *Left open*).

**"Efficacious," "effective."** The right sense in the wrong register: an apothecary's label, and a mechanism's. *Potent* is the same claim in a word a person says.

**"Responsive."** An abstraction about a relation, and it tells you nothing you could see.

**"Potency," for 神.** A quality, not a party: it can be the ghosts' force but never Wang Bi's spirit standing beside the sage. And once 靈 is *potent*, *potency* for 神 would give two characters one root, in two chapters that never meet, where no check could see it.

**"Demons," "devils," for 鬼.** Christian demonology. A 鬼 is a dead person, and the Shuowen says it does harm, not that it is evil. Chapter 60 is about the harm stopping, which a devil's would not.

**"Spirit vessel," "divine vessel," "sacred system," at chapter 29.** The first is a genie's bottle, the second the watchlist's word, the third the mechanistic overlay `glossary/qi-器.md` set aside.

### Working register

| line | the character's work | English |
|---|---|---|
| 谷神不死 (6) | 神, noun, the valley's | *the spirit of the valley* |
| 天下神器 (29) | 神, qualifying a made thing | *a sacred vessel* — the declared flexion |
| 神得一以靈 (39) | 神, subject in the list · 靈, its quality | *spirit… potent* |
| 神無以靈，將恐歇 (39) | the same, negated | *spirit with no way to be potent* |
| 其鬼不神 (60) | 神, a verb: the ghosts do not act as spirits | *spirit*, carried by a verb the line supplies (recommended) |
| 其神不傷人 (60), ×2 | 神, noun, the ghosts' or a spirit's own | *their spirit* (recommended) |
| 其鬼 (60), ×2 | 鬼, noun | *ghosts* |

**The verb at chapter 60 needs scaffolding.** English cannot say *the ghosts do not spirit*, so the line will supply a verb, as Heshang Gong's 見 (*xiàn* — to show) does. Whatever verb the line takes, it is the construction's, not 神's, and it stays out of `render:` (`process/principles/supplied-verb-is-scaffolding.md`).

### What no rule can enforce

***Alive* is ruled out for 靈, and cannot be forbidden.** Chapter 39 holds 生 (*shēng*), whose English is *come to life* and *live*, two lines from 靈. A rule keyed to 靈's presence would fire on 生's lines.

***Present* is ruled out for 靈, and cannot be forbidden either.** Chapter 6 holds 存 (*cún* — to be there, to last), in 綿綿若存 (*mián mián ruò cún* — "unceasing, as if there"), and 存 may legitimately print *present*.

***Spirit* is held for 神 by three other entries**, which forbid it for 身 (*shēn* — body), 精 (*jīng* — vital essence) and 魄 (*pò* — aliveness). 神 shares no chapter with 身, so the build can never see those two meet; `concordance.py --english "spirit"`, run by hand, is the only check.

***Potency* cannot go on this list yet**, for the reason in *Left open*: chapter 60 prints it, and a forbidden word in a chapter where 神 stands is an error the build would report on the spot.

### Left open

**Chapter 60's English waits on chapter 60's grammar.** Its 非 (*fēi*) reads *not only* in our English, where Heshang Gong's 其□非无精神也 (*"it is not that the ghosts lack vital spirit"*) reads it *it is not that*, and the chapter contradicts itself as it stands. That is `WORKLIST.md` R6, the back-translation audit's deepest finding, and it is Shalom's call. The choice between *spirit* and *potency* for 神 belongs in the same rewrite, because the line has to be rebuilt either way.

**Chapter 39 keeps *Spirit*, singular, capitalized only by position** (Shalom's call, 2026-11-19). The Shuowen's 天神 (*tiān shén* — the spirits of the sky) is plural beings, and *The spirits received the one* would end the capital and match it. The list's other members are a sky, an earth and a valley, and the chapter's rhythm runs on singular nouns; the rhythm was kept. A reader who hears the creed's capital in *Spirit* should know the Chinese has none.

***Potent* keeps the effect and loses the descent.** Wang Yi's 靈 is a spirit that has *come down* into a dancer; *potent* says it works, not that it has arrived. The rite's half of the word, the shaman, has no English in the verse and lives only here. The word also has a sexual edge in English, *potent* against *impotent*, which a spirit should not carry; it is faint next to *spirit*, and it was weighed before *potent* was chosen (Shalom's call, 2026-11-19).

**Heshang Gong's organ-spirits are lost at chapter 6.** His 谷神 is the spirit nourished in the body's five organs, and the verse follows Wang Bi's valley. That cost is recorded in `glossary/gu-谷.md`, where the valley was chosen.
