## 虛 (Xū) — Empty

*Say "shü," level. Five occurrences across five chapters, and four of them are a verb or an adjective.*

**Recommended: 虛 → "empty" (adjective), "to empty" (verb).** *(Never "emptiness," never "the void," never "vacuity," never "nothingness.")* *Chapter 16 is the one line still unsettled; see the close.*

說文解字 (*Shuōwén Jiězì*, c. 100 CE): **大丘也。崐崘丘謂之崐崘虛。古者九夫爲井，四井爲邑，四邑爲丘。丘謂之虛。从丘虍聲。**

*"A great mound. The Kunlun mound is called the Kunlun 虛. In antiquity nine men's allotments made a 井 (jǐng — a well-field), four well-fields made a 邑 (yì — a settlement), four settlements made a 丘 (qiū — a mound). A 丘 is called 虛. From 丘 (qiū — mound), with 虍 (hū — tiger) for sound."*

**虛 is a unit of surveyed land.** The dictionary does not reach for a void; it reaches for the well-field system and counts up from nine households. What makes a settlement-mound *虛* is that the people have gone — the sense later given its own graph, 墟 (*xū* — a ruin, an abandoned site).

So the picture is not boundless space. It is **a bounded place that has been vacated**: walls still standing, nobody home. Everything else in this entry follows from that.

### The book uses it exactly that way, five times

Every occurrence is a container with its contents gone, and every container is a thing you could point at.

**A heart.** 虛其心，實其腹 — *"empty their hearts, fill their bellies"* (ch 3). 虛 is **transitive** here; it takes an object. 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*, d. 249 CE) makes the anatomy explicit: 心懷智而腹懷食，虛有智而實無知也 — *"the heart harbors 智 (zhì — clever knowing) and the belly harbors food; empty what has 智, fill what has no 知 (zhī — knowing)."* 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*, Han) gives the method: 除嗜欲去亂煩 — *"remove craving and desire, cast off disorder and vexation."*

**A bellows.** 天地之間，其猶橐籥乎？虛而不屈，動而愈出 — *"between sky and earth, is it not like a bellows? Empty and never bent shut; the more it moves, the more comes out"* (ch 5). 王弼: 橐排橐也，籥樂籥也。橐籥之中空洞無情無為，故虛而不得窮屈 — *"橐 (tuó) is the blacksmith's bellows-bag, 籥 (yuè) is the musical pipe. Inside the bellows and the pipe it is 空洞 (kōng dòng — hollow and cavernous), without feeling, without doing; therefore it is empty and cannot be used up and bent shut."* **He defines 虛 by what is inside a made object.**

**Words.** 豈虛言哉 — *"were those empty words?"* (ch 22). A saying with nothing in it.

**A granary.** 倉甚虛 — *"the granaries are empty"* (ch 53). The most carefully measured container an agrarian state owns, and the line is an indictment: the grain is gone because it was taken.

**And its opposite is a full vessel.** 盈 (*yíng*), 虛's antonym at chapters 4 and 45, is 說文 滿器也 — *"a full vessel. From 皿 (mǐn — a vessel)."* Vessel-language on both sides of the pair.

### Why the noun is a Buddhist import

**English *emptiness* is the standard rendering of śūnyatā**, the central term of Mahāyāna Buddhist metaphysics — the doctrine that phenomena lack inherent existence. In Chinese that term is **空 (*kōng* — empty)**, and 虛空 (*xū kōng*) renders ākāśa, unbounded space.

**空 does not occur in the Tao Te Ching. Not once, in eighty-one chapters.**

Buddhism reaches China in roughly the first century CE; this text is Warring States, some four centuries earlier. So an English reader meeting *emptiness* here is handed a technical term from a tradition that had not yet arrived — and handed it in the one grammatical form, the abstract noun, that turns a description into a doctrine. It is the same failure as 一 (*yī* — one) rendered *the One*, which imports Neoplatonism, and 道 (*dào*) rendered *the Way*, which imports the missionaries.

**It also imports the wrong physics.** Śūnyatā is a claim that things have no self-standing essence. 虛 is a claim about a container: it has room in it. The bellows is not insubstantial. It is a made object with a hollow inside, and the hollow is what makes it work.

### What is set aside

**emptiness** — the abstract noun, and śūnyatā's English. The adjective and the verb carry everything this book needs.

**the void, vacuity** — *the void* is already refused for 無 (*wú* — absence) in `wu-you-無有.md`, and it is worse here: 虛 is a hollow with walls, and a void has none. *Vacuity* additionally carries a slur in modern English that the Chinese does not.

**nothingness** — 虛 is never nothing. It is a something with room in it, which is the whole point of the bellows.

**hollow** — belongs to 窪 (*wā* — a low, sunken place) at chapter 22: 窪則盈, *"be hollowed out, and be filled."* **Chapter 22 contains both 窪 and 虛**, so this is precisely the distinction a `forbidden:` list cannot express — the checker gates on whether a character is present, and both are. It has to be held by the reader.

### Working register

| Form | Chapters | English |
|---|---|---|
| 虛 with an object | 3 | to empty |
| 虛 predicative or attributive | 5, 22, 53 | empty |
| 虛 as the object of a verb | 16 | *(unsettled — see below)* |

### Left open

**Chapter 16 is the only place in the book where 虛 has to be a noun**, and it is therefore the only place the Buddhist reading can get in. 致 (*zhì* — to send all the way there) 虛 (*xū*) 極 (*jí* — the far end) puts 虛 in the object slot, and English wants *emptiness* there.

The way out is to decline the noun and let 虛 be what it is in four lines out of five — **a verb**. Chapter 3's 虛其心 licenses the transitive directly, and 河上公 glosses chapter 16 the same way: 捐 (*juān* — shed) 情 (*qíng* — feeling) 去 (*qù* — cast off) 欲 (*yù* — desire)，五內 (*wǔ nèi* — the five viscera) 清 (*qīng* — clear) 淨 (*jìng* — still). What the object should be, and whether it may be supplied at all where the Chinese elides it, is undecided.

**沖 (*chōng*) is an emptiness word only by borrowing.** 說文 gives it as 涌搖也 — *"surging and shaking,"* water that moves. Its empty sense at chapters 4 and 45 is 盅 (*zhōng* — an empty vessel), which shares its sound part 中 (*zhōng*): Xu Shen quotes chapter 4 as 道盅而用之 under 盅：器虛也 (*"a vessel's emptiness"*), defining it by this very character, and Fu Yi writes 盅 at both chapters. So both lines print *empty*, which is 虛's English, though 虛 itself stands in neither chapter. The argument is in `glossary/chong-沖.md`.

**寥 (*liáo* — vast, unpeopled)** at chapter 25 is a third word in the same field, and 說文 has no entry for it under any graph the importer can verify.

## 玄 (Xuán) & 妙 (Miào) — The Dark and the Subtle

*Say "shwen," rising, and "meow," falling. Two words that meet in the last line of Chapter 1 — and that nearly every translation melts into a single word: "mystery."*

Chapter 1 ends: 玄之又玄，眾**妙**之門. Render both characters as "mystery" and you get the sentence English readers know — *"the mystery of mysteries, the gate of all mysteries"* — which sounds profound and says nothing. It is a tautology in a chapter that is building an *architecture*. The two words are not synonyms, not even close relatives. **玄 is a depth. 妙 is a fineness.** One is how far down a thing goes; the other is how small a thing is before it disappears. Chapter 1's closing line puts them in a precise relation — and that relation is the whole cosmology of the opening chapter, lost the moment both become "mystery."

### The graph: 玄 (xuán — dark), the dyed silk, the night sky

玄 is a **color word**. The oldest graph draws a small twisted skein of silk thread, and the *Shuowen* defines it exactly as a dyer would: 黑而有赤色者為玄 — "black with red in it is called 玄." Not flat black: the deep blackish-red of silk that has been dipped in the vat again and again, each immersion carrying the color further down. From that dye-lot the word rose into the sky: the classics call heaven's own color 玄, the dark of the night vault you look into and never reach the end of. Depth, distance, obscurity — 幽遠, "hidden and far."

Hold the dye vat when you read 玄之又玄. The line is literally *"dark it, and dark it again"* — the exact motion of a dyer re-dipping the silk. Laozi's most metaphysical phrase is built on the humblest of crafts: not a mystery *declared*, but a darkness *deepened*, one immersion at a time.

### The graph: 妙 (miào — subtle), the vanishing fineness

妙 is built from 女 (woman) and 少 (small, few — also the sound). Its core is **minuteness**: the fine, the delicate, the exquisitely small. An older variant writes it 玅, with 玄 standing where 女 stands — a small graphic accident that says plainly how close these two live, and how firmly the tradition still kept them apart. Where 玄 is *too deep to see into*, 妙 is *too fine to quite see* — subtlety at the very threshold of perception, and, because such fineness astonishes, "marvelous, exquisite, wonderful" as its second breath.

The distinction is not our invention; Laozi uses both in a single four-character phrase. **Chapter 15**: 微**妙**玄通 — the ancient masters were *subtle-fine* (微妙) and *dark-penetrating* (玄通), 深不可識, "so deep they cannot be known." Two qualities, deliberately paired *because they differ*. No one writes "mysterious and mysterious." That line alone settles the matter.

### What each one does across the book

**玄** is almost always a **naming of depth**, and it attaches to the greatest things: 玄牝, the *dark female* whose gate is the root of heaven and earth (6); 玄覽, the *dark mirror* to be wiped clean (10); 玄德, *profound integrity* — the book's highest praise, the bearing-without-possessing refrain (10, 51, 65: 玄德深矣，遠矣, "profound integrity is deep, is far"); 玄同, *profound sameness*, being the same as the dust (56). Every appearance is vertical: down, in, far.

**妙** is rarer and always **perceptual** — a quality noticed by a refined attention: 觀其妙 and 眾妙 in Chapter 1, 微妙 in 15, and 要妙 in 27, "the essential subtlety." It is what the finest seeing catches, and only the finest.

### How they meet in Chapter 1

Now the architecture. Chapter 1 sets its two modes of attention side by side: 常無欲，以觀其**妙**；常有欲，以觀其**徼** — *ever desireless, you can observe its subtlety; ever desiring, you can observe its direction.* The still, wanting-nothing gaze perceives the fine grain where things begin (妙); the wanting gaze reads which way they are heading (徼). Neither is ranked: in the next line both emerge together. Then both modes, both names, are gathered: 同謂之**玄** — *together they are called dark.* And the last line: 玄之又玄，眾**妙**之門 — *dark, and dark again — the gate of all subtlety.*

Read with the words kept apart, the line is not a tautology but a *structure*: **the unfathomable dark is the gate; the countless fine wonders are what come through it.** One darkness, ten-thousand delicacies. Note the grammar proving it — 妙 takes 眾, "the many": subtleties are **plural and countable**. 玄 never pluralizes; it only deepens, by repetition (玄之又玄). Fineness spreads out; darkness goes down. And note the practical stake: 妙 is the object of 觀, *to observe.* It is something you can actually **see** — barely, and only when desire quiets. Call it "mystery" and you have told the reader that what Laozi just instructed them to look at cannot be looked at. The instruction dissolves into fog.

### What is set aside

**"Mystery" for either word, and above all for both.** It is the single most common flattening in the English tradition, and it costs the chapter its shape. We also set aside "the occult" and "the arcane" for 玄 — imports from Western esotericism, secret societies and hidden doctrines, where Laozi has only a dye vat and a night sky. And we set aside the fused phrase **"profound mystery,"** which welds the two words into one blur (this is why 玄同 in Chapter 56 is *profound sameness*, not "the profound mystery" — 同 is the sameness, and 玄 only says how deep it goes).

### Working register

**玄** flexes by position, and we let it, within one image — *darkness that is depth*:

- bound in a compound → **profound** (玄德 *profound integrity*; 玄同 *profound sameness*; 玄通 *dark-penetrating*)
- standing alone and being *named*, as in Chapter 1 → **dark** (同謂之玄, "together they are called dark"; 玄之又玄, "dark, and dark again"), because here the color-image is doing the work and "profound" abstracts it away
- as an attribute of the feminine → **dark female** for 玄牝 (6), keeping the womb-dark literal (*mysterious* is refused, below and in the frontmatter)

**妙** holds one root — **subtle / subtlety** — with *wonder, marvel* available where the astonishment, not the fineness, is the point. In Chapter 1 we keep the **echo** word for word: "observe its subtlety" … "the gate of all subtlety." The two 妙 stand in different slots, owned by 其 (*qí* — its) in line 5 and counted by 眾 (*zhòng* — the many) in line 9, and one English has to survive both; *subtlety* does, with *all* carrying 眾. The plural *subtleties* was the earlier rendering and was let go on 2026-11-14 (Shalom's call): in English it leans toward *nuances*, fine points of an argument, and it broke the echo. What the singular softens is Wang Bi's distributive reading, 眾妙皆從同而出 (*"the many subtle things all come out from the same"*); *all* keeps the many in it. "The gate of all wonders" is the more beautiful English, and we give it up on purpose — 妙 sounds twice in twenty-odd characters, and the second use must be recognizably the first: *what you glimpsed in your stillness is what the gate is the gate of.*

### Left open

Are they two things, or one thing seen from two sides? Laozi will not say. He calls the pair 同出而異名 — "issuing together, differently named" — and then names *that* 玄, as if darkness were the last name available before the naming stops. The subtleties come through the dark gate, so they are not separate; but he never builds the system that would tell us how. We keep both words, distinct and unreconciled, and let the reader stand where the chapter leaves them: at a gate they cannot see into, through which everything fine and astonishing is quietly arriving.

And one honesty to end on. 玄 never stops being a *color.* Whatever metaphysics gathers around it, the word keeps its silk and its dye, its night sky — the concrete never burned off. That is the whole habit of this book: the deepest thing it can say about the source of the world is what a dyer says about cloth that has been in the vat one time too many to name the shade.

## 言 (Yán) — Words, and Speaking

*Say "yen," rising. Twenty-one appearances in nineteen lines across eighteen chapters. A book that distrusts speech, written in it, and it knows.*

**Recommended: 言 → "words" for what is said · "speech" for the saying of it · "speak" as a verb.** *(Not "discourse," "rhetoric" or "eloquence," which are 語 (yǔ — debate)'s ground and the Shuowen's opposite of 言. Not "the Word," whose capital is John's Logos.)* **Two flexions:** *saying* where a chapter quotes a proverb (41, 69), and *say* where 言 opens an explanation (31).

### The graph: a mouth, speaking straight out

> 言，直言曰言，論難曰語。从口，䇂聲。
> *"言: speaking straight out is 言; debating is 語 (yǔ — argument). From 口 (kǒu — a mouth), with 䇂 for the sound."* — Shuowen (說文, *Shuōwén* — Xu Shen's dictionary, c. 100 CE)

**The Shuowen defines 言 by what it is not.** 言 is plain speech, said straight; 語 is speech turned against someone, the give and take of argument. Laozi never uses 語. Every speech word in the book is the plain one, and the book's quarrel is not with argument but with the plain act of talking: 知者不言 (*zhī zhě bù yán* — "those who know do not speak").

### Nineteen lines: what is said, and the saying of it

**As a noun, 言 is words, the things said.**

> *Trustworthy words are not pretty.*
> *Pretty words are not trustworthy.*
>
> 信言不美，
> 美言不信。
>
> — chapter 81

Also 22's *empty words*, 62's *fine words can buy honor*, 70's *my words* and *words have an ancestor*, 78's *words on the mark seem like their opposite*.

**As a verb, 言 is to speak.**

> *Those who know do not speak.*
> *Those who speak do not know.*
>
> 知者不言，
> 言者不知。
>
> — chapter 56

Also 73's *it does not speak, yet is masterful at answering*, and 66's *you must speak from below them*.

**As the act, a verbal noun, 言 is speech**: 8's *in speech, masterful at trust*, 23's *brevity in speech*, 27's *masterful speaking*, 5's 多言 (*duō yán* — much speech).

**The book's speech is never praised for being beautiful or clever.** It is praised for being trustworthy (8, 81), on the mark (78), few (23), or absent (2, 43, 56, 73). The sky is the model: Heshang Gong on chapter 73, 天不言，萬物自動應以時, *"the sky does not speak, and the countless things move of themselves, answering in their season."*

### The teaching without words, twice, and it must read the same

> *and carries out the teaching without words.*
>
> 行不言之教。
>
> — chapter 2

> *The wordless teaching, the benefit of non-doing —*
>
> 不言之教，無為之益，
>
> — chapter 43

**不言之教 (*bù yán zhī jiào*) is a formula, verbatim in both chapters, and it reads two ways.** A formula repeated in the Chinese is repeated in the English. *The teaching without words* keeps 不言 what it is everywhere else in the book, *not speaking* (56, 73). The recommendation is chapter 43 → *"The teaching without words, the benefit of non-doing —"*. Wang Bi on chapter 17 names the pair together, 居無為之事，行不言之教, *"dwelling in the affairs of non-doing, carrying out the teaching without words,"* which is chapter 2's line, and chapter 43 sets them side by side again.

### Chapter 17: they prize their words, and their words are answered

> *Hesitant, they prize their words.*
>
> 悠兮其貴言。
>
> — chapter 17

**The line has 貴 (*guì* — to prize) and 言, and until 2026-11-19 our English rendered neither**: *"The greatest leaders speak sparingly."* Wang Bi says what the prizing is: 無物可以易其言，言必有應，故曰悠兮其貴言也, *"nothing can take the place of their words, and their words always meet an answer; so it says, they prize their words."* The greatest leaders speak little because each word counts, and each is answered. *Speak sparingly* kept the result and lost the reason, and 貴's price word with it (`glossary/gui-jian-貴賤.md`).

**The first word is a fork, and the English follows the witnesses.** Our base alone prints 悠 (*yōu*), by its own editors' note; Heshang Gong, the silks and every other edition print 猶 (*yóu* — hesitant), chapter 15's *"Hesitant, like someone wary of the neighbors."* The base's 悠 points the same way: the Shuowen gives it 憂也, *anxious care*. Heshang Gong: 太上之君舉事猶貴重於言, *"the highest ruler, in undertaking affairs, still prizes words and weighs them."* (Shalom's call, 2026-11-19; `sources/variants.yaml` fork 126.)

### What the commentators did with it

**Heshang Gong reads speech as a cost.** On chapter 56: 知者貴行不貴言也, *"the knower prizes action and does not prize words,"* and 駟不及舌，多言多患, *"a team of four horses cannot catch the tongue; many words, many troubles."* On chapter 81: 滋美之言者，孳孳華詞，不信者，飾偽多空虛也, *"pretty words are phrase upon ornate phrase; untrustworthy, they are dressed falsehood, mostly empty."*

**And he lets the book's own words off.** On chapter 70: 吾所言省而易知，約而易行, *"what I say is spare and easy to know, brief and easy to carry out."* A book against talking is allowed to talk if it talks like this.

### What is set aside

**"Utterance."** A linguist's word, and Latinate. It makes speech a specimen.

**"Discourse."** The academy's word for speech in general, and the Shuowen's 語, extended argument, which Laozi never uses.

**"Rhetoric," "eloquence," "eloquent."** The art of speaking well, which is exactly what chapter 81 distrusts in 美言 (*měi yán* — pretty words). Ch 81's 辯 (*biàn* — to argue) already reads *argue*; giving 言 an eloquence word would hand it the very quality the book refuses.

**"The Word."** John 1:1, *"In the beginning was the Word,"* the Logos. The Chinese Union Bible rendered Logos as 道, not 言, but the English capital is still the creed's, and *the Word* in a chapter about not speaking would read as theology. Forbidden with its capital, so the plain *word* stays free.

**"Silent," for 不言.** Silence is a state; 不言 is the act of not speaking, done by someone who could. Chapter 56's knower *does not speak*; chapter 73's sky *does not speak, yet answers*. It cannot be forbidden, because 希 (*xī* — sparse) and other characters share these chapters, and it is held by the entry.

**"Talk."** Casual where the book is not, and *talk* has no plain noun for the things said.

### Working register

| line | grammar | English |
|---|---|---|
| 豈虛言哉 (22) · 美言 (62) · 吾言 · 言有宗 (70) · 正言 (78) · 信言 · 美言 (81) · 貴言 (17) | a noun, what is said | *words* |
| 知者不言，言者不知 (56) · 不言而善應 (73) · 以言下之 (66) | a verb | *speak* |
| 多言 (5) · 言善信 (8) · 希言 (23) · 善言 (27) | the act | *speech* · *speaking* |
| 不言之教 (2, 43) | a formula | *the teaching without words* (43 recommended) |
| 建言有之 (41) · 用兵有言 (69) | a quoted saying | *saying* — flexion |
| 言以喪禮處之 (31) | opening an explanation | *which is to say* — flexion |

### What no rule can enforce

***Words* in chapter 22's last line renders no 言.** 誠全而歸之 (*chéng quán ér guī zhī* — "truly whole, return to it") reads *"These words hold. Return to them. Stay whole."* 誠 (*chéng* — truly) has 言 in its graph, words that are made good, and the English leans on that; but the line prints no 言, and `concordance.py --english "word"` is the only check that sees it.

***Silent* and *wordless* are held by argument.** *Wordless* can only be ruled once chapter 43 changes, since it prints it now.

### Left open

**One line would change, and it is Shalom's call.** Chapter 43's *the wordless teaching* → *the teaching without words*, to match chapter 2. (Chapter 17 became *"Hesitant, they prize their words"* on 2026-11-19.)

**Chapter 5's 多言數窮 loses 多 (*duō* — much).** *"Speaking of this is a dead end"* renders 言 and drops the *much*, which is the line's point: not speech but too much of it, against 守中 (*shǒu zhōng* — "hold to the center"). And 數 is contested: Wang Bi's sound note reads it as reckoning, a later note as *often*. The line wants its own reading.

**The book distrusts speech and is made of it.** Chapter 70 claims its own words are *very easy to know, very easy to follow*, and that no one knows or follows them. The English should not soften either half.

entries.body:
## 一 (Yī) — one

*Say "ee," level and flat. The simplest character in the language, and the one this edition has had to defend against two different mysticisms eighteen centuries apart.*

**Locked: 一 → "the one," lowercase — and at Chapter 22, "one thing."** *(Never "the One," never "Oneness," never "the Absolute.")*

### The graph: there is nothing to read

一 is a single horizontal stroke. It is not a pictograph. Nothing is depicted, no radical is combined, no sound is borrowed. It is the mark you make when you have counted to one.

That matters more than any etymology could, because **every mystical reading of 一 has to be imported from outside the graph.** There is no hidden picture to appeal to. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (~100 CE) does import one, and grandly:

> 惟初太始，道立於一，造分天地，化成萬物
> *"At the very beginning, the Tao was established in the one; it divided and made sky and earth, transformed and completed the countless things."*

Worth knowing that reading existed by the Han. Worth knowing it is **Han cosmology written backward onto a tally mark.**

### 王弼 refuses the mystical reading outright

The decisive gloss is on Chapter 22, and it is five characters:

> **一，少之極也** — *"the one is the extreme of 少 (*shǎo* — few, little)."*

Not a unity. Not a hypostasis. **The floor of "few."** And it is anchored in the line above it: 少則得，多則惑 — *little, then gain; much, then confusion.* If less is better, the least you can hold is one. 是以 (*shì yǐ* — **therefore**) does the welding, and Wang Bi is telling us the *therefore* is load-bearing.

河上公 keeps it just as functional: 抱，守也…聖人**守一**乃知萬事，故能為天下法式也 — *"抱 means hold fast to… the sage holds fast to one and thereby knows the countless affairs, and so can be the world's standard."* One grip that gives you the rest.

### The text's own refutation of "the One"

Chapter 42 ends the argument before it starts:

> **道生一** — *"the Tao gives birth to the one."*

生 (*shēng*) is our locked **give birth to**. Whatever 一 is, it is **borne**. Neoplatonism's One has nothing above it — that is the entire content of the doctrine. This one has a mother. Any rendering that makes 一 ultimate contradicts a line of the book.

### Why we took the mysticism out, deliberately

**一 has collected two overlays, and they arrived eighteen centuries apart.**

The old one is **Neoplatonism** — the One as the ineffable source above being, imported through the same missionary-scholar channel that gave us "the Way" for 道 and "Heaven" for 天. It capitalizes the word and turns a count into a godhead.

The new one is worse, and it is why the line could not stand as it was. **"The One" is now a chosen-one trope in English** — prophecy, destiny, the singular anointed figure. A modern reader meets *"the sage embraces the one"* and hears something being revealed to them. The Chinese is doing arithmetic.

Both overlays make 一 a **status** or an **entity**. It is neither. And the cost is not only accuracy — it is *usability*. **"Embrace one thing" is something a reader can go and do. "Embrace the One" is an invitation to feel reverent**, which is precisely the substitution this edition exists to undo. The hymn test fails on sight; the pointing test decides it. Laozi could point at one thing. Nobody can point at the One.

*This is a deliberate de-mystification, recorded as such so that no future sweep mistakes it for carelessness.*

### The two registers, held apart honestly

一 is not doing one job in this book, and flattening it would be its own error.

**The arithmetic register — 一 against 多 (*duō* — much).**
- **Ch 22**: 少則得，多則惑…聖人抱一 — the few/much/one sequence, welded by *therefore*. **This is where "one thing" is licensed.**
- **Ch 10**: 載營魄抱一 — the twin phrase, 抱一 again. Rendered *"embracing the one."*
- **Ch 11**: 三十輻共**一**轂 — *thirty spokes share one hub.* A plain numeral, and a useful reminder of what the character is when nobody is doing metaphysics with it.
- **Ch 67**: 一曰慈 — *"the first is compassion."* Numeral again.

**The cosmological register — 一 as something attained or arrived at.**
- **Ch 39**: 昔之得**一**者 — *"those of old who attained the one,"* then the litany: sky attained it and became clear, earth attained it and became settled.
- **Ch 14**: 混而為**一** — *"they mix into one,"* of the invisible, inaudible, and intangible.
- **Ch 42**: 道生**一** — *"the Tao gives birth to the one,"* the first step of a cosmogony.

**"One thing" would be wrong in all three of the second group.** Ch 22's rendering is therefore a **licensed per-chapter exception, not a lock** — recorded here so the next sweep reads it as a decision. What licenses it is that ch 22 is the only chapter where 一 sits inside an explicit few/much sequence with a *therefore* pointing at it.

### What the two registers share

Even at ch 39, 一 is what a thing holds to in order to be *itself* — 天得一以清 (sky attains the one and is clear), 地得一以寧 (earth attains the one and is settled). That is not far from 河上公's 守一乃知萬事. **Both registers land on staying gathered rather than scattered**, which is why the deflationary reading and the contemplative one are not really rivals. 守一 (*shǒu yī* — guarding the one) later became a formal Daoist meditation, and concentration is exactly what "holding to one thing" describes. The mysticism was never in the idea. It was in the definite article.

### The thread across the book: 一 is the answer to 多

河上公 glosses ch 22's 多則惑 as **學多者惑於所聞** — *"those with much learning are confused by what they have heard."* That is Chapter 81's 博者不知 (*"those who have heard it all do not know"*), stated fifty-nine chapters earlier by the same commentator — and his prescription is the same word in both places: **守一** here, **守一元** there.

**抱一 is the cure for 博.** The two ends of the book are one argument, and 一 is the hinge.

### Working register

- default → **the one**, lowercase (抱一 → "embraces the one"; 得一 → "attained the one")
- ch 22 only → **one thing** (抱一 → "embraces one thing"), licensed by the 少/多/一 sequence
- as a plain count → **one / the first** (三十輻共一轂; 一曰慈)
- 守一 → **hold fast to the one**, using 守's locked verb

**Never** "the One," "Oneness," "the Absolute," or any capitalization. 道 is the only word in this translation that keeps a capital.

### One risk in our own move, named

**"Embraces one thing" can be misread as monomania** — the sage as a person with a single fixation. 河上公 is the guard against it: 守一乃**知萬事**, *"holds fast to one and thereby knows the countless affairs."* Holding one thing is what makes the many legible; it is not a narrowing of attention but the condition for attending at all. If a reader takes the line as narrowness, the rendering has failed and should be revisited.

flexions.why: 抱一 takes 一 as the object embraced, not as the name of the Tao

## 尤 (Yóu) — Blame

*Say "yo," rising. One line in the whole book.*

**Locked: 尤 → "blame."** *(Not "fault," which is 咎's. Not "blameless," which turns an absence into a verdict.)*

### The graph: what stands out

> 尢，**異**也。从乙又聲。
> *"Out of the ordinary. From 乙 (yǐ — a shoot coming up bent), with 又 (yòu) for sound."* — 說文解字 (*Shuōwén Jiězì*, the Han dictionary), which files the character under its Han graph 尢

The everyday sense *especially*, as in 尤其 (*yóu qí*), is the same idea: the one that stands out from the rest. What stands out is also what gets singled out, and classical Chinese uses 尤 for both the slip and the singling-out. The Analects has each. 言寡尤 (*yán guǎ yóu* — "few slips in speech," 2.18) is the noun, the error that is yours. 不怨天，不尤人 (*bù yuàn tiān, bù yóu rén* — "does not resent heaven, does not blame others," 14.37) is the verb, with other people as its object.

The oldest graph is contested. The oracle-bone form long read as 尤 has been reread as 拇 (*mǔ* — thumb), which leaves no secure 尤 before the Western Zhou (季旭昇 *Jì Xùshēng*, 2009). Nothing here rests on it.

### One line, and it points outward

> *Only because it does not contend*
> *is there no blame.*
>
> 夫唯不爭，
> 故無尤。
>
> — chapter 8

Word for word, the second half is 故無尤 (*gù wú yóu* — "therefore no 尤").

**The only commentary on the line makes 尤 something done to water.** 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*): 水性如是，故天下无有怨尤水者也 — *"water's nature is like this, so in all the world there is no one who resents or blames water."* 怨尤 (*yuàn yóu* — to resent, to blame) is the Analects' pair, and water is its object. 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) says nothing about the word.

**The frame agrees.** Wherever the book says what not contending earns, the answer is how other people respond. Ch 22 and 66: 天下莫能與之爭 (*tiān xià mò néng yǔ zhī zhēng* — "no one in the world can contend with them"). Ch 72, in the same 夫唯 (*fú wéi* — only because) frame: 夫唯不厭，是以不厭 — *"only because you do not oppress them do they not tire of you."* Water does not contend, so nobody has anything to hold against it.

### 尤 and 咎: blame and fault

The book has two characters for something gone wrong, and they face opposite ways.

| | 尤 (*yóu*) — **blame** | 咎 (*jiù*) — **fault** |
|---|---|---|
| 說文 | 異也 — out of the ordinary | 災也 — disaster; a person at odds |
| where it comes from | other people, who hold it against you | yourself: 自遺其咎 (*zì yí qí jiù* — you leave it to yourself), ch 9 |
| 河上公 | 怨尤水者 — *those who resent and blame water* | 必被禍患 — *will surely suffer disaster and trouble* |
| chapters | 8 | 9, 46 |

Ch 8 and ch 9 sit side by side. With one English word across both, a reader would meet water that has *no fault* and, on the next page, the arrogant who *leave themselves the fault*, and take it as a deliberate pairing. The Chinese uses two characters and pairs nothing.

### What is set aside

**"fault"** is a real sense of 尤, as 言寡尤 shows, and it is 咎's word in this book (`jiu-咎.md`). It also moves the claim inside water: *there is no fault* reads as *nothing is wrong with it*, where the line, as its one commentator reads it, says *nobody holds anything against it*.

**"blameless"** turns an absence into a virtue. *No one blames water* is a report; *water is blameless* is a verdict on its purity, and it would sit comfortably in a sermon.

### This lock stays in this book

**In the I Ching, 尤 cannot be *blame*.** That book gives *blame* to 咎, its verdict word, and 尤 stands beside it in six lines of the 小象傳 (*Xiǎo Xiàng Zhuàn* — the commentary on the lines): 終无尤也 (*zhōng wú yóu yě* — "in the end, no 尤"), five times, and 中无尤也 (*zhōng wú yóu yě* — "at the center, no 尤") once. Inside one book two graphs cannot share a word. *(Shalom's call, 2026-10-20: the books diverge on purpose.)* So this entry carries `binds: [taoteching]`, and the I Ching, which vendors this glossary's locks as its own, decides 尤 for itself.

### Left open

**The I Ching's echo.** *No blame* is the familiar English of 无咎 (*wú jiù* — "no 咎"), the I Ching's most repeated formula, so a reader who knows that book hears 咎 in this line, the very character this edition renders *fault*. The echo comes from outside the book and is accepted: inside it, nothing collides.

**Who blames is never said.** 無尤 (*wú yóu* — no blame) names no one; 河上公 supplies *all the world*. The English keeps the line agentless, as the Chinese does, and *blame* still implies someone who would have done the blaming. That is the word's cost, and the Chinese carries it too.

entries.body:
## 愚 (Yú) — Foolish

*Say "yü," rising. Three lines in three chapters. The ordinary word of its day for a fool, and the book takes it up as its own.*

**Locked: 愚 → "a fool" / "foolishness" / "foolish."** *(Shalom's call, 2026-11-16. Not "guileless," which turns a word of contempt into a compliment and cannot stand at chapter 38. Not "simple," which sweetens it the same way, more quietly. Not "ignorant" or "stupid," which are a lack and an insult with no reversal left in them.)*

Chapters 20 and 38 have long said *fool* and *foolishness*. Until 2026-11-16 chapter 65 alone sweetened the word, as *guileless*, at the one line where it is done to the people, which is where the discomfort is. **愚 is an insult, and the book takes the insult for itself.** The English has to keep the insult, or the taking means nothing.

### The graph: a heart, and a monkey

> 愚，戇也。从心从禺。禺，猴屬，獸之愚者。
> *"愚 is dull-wittedness. From 心 (xīn — heart) and 禺 (yú). 禺 is a kind of monkey, the most foolish of beasts."*

Xu Shen's 禺, in its own entry: 母猴屬。頭似鬼。从甶从禸 — *"a kind of macaque; its head looks like a ghost's. From 甶 (fú — a ghost's head) and 禸 (róu — an animal's track)."* So to Xu Shen 愚 is a heart like a monkey's: the dullest animal Xu Shen could name, under the organ of thought.

**Where the picture stops.** 禺 is almost certainly in the graph for its sound. It reads \*ŋo in reconstructed Old Chinese, and it gives the same sound to 隅 (yú — corner), 遇 (yù — to meet) and 偶 (ǒu — an image), none of which has anything to do with monkeys. The monkey is Xu Shen's reading of the part, not the word's origin. The sources this entry consulted record no oracle-bone form. **What holds is the heart.** 愚 is a condition of the 心 (xīn — heart), and chapter 20 puts it exactly there: 愚人之心 (yú rén zhī xīn — "the heart of a fool").

The silks bear this out. At chapter 20 silk A writes only 禺 where silk B and our base write 愚, and at chapter 41 silk B writes 禺 for 隅 (yú — corner): 大方無禺 (dà fāng wú yú — "the great square has no corners"). The silks borrow 禺 for its sound, so silk A's 禺 is the same word spelled by ear, not a monkey.

### Three lines, and the word changes sides

> *The crowd all have more than enough.*
> *I alone seem to have missed out.*
> *I have the heart of a fool!*
> *How fluid!*
>
> 眾人皆有餘，
> 而我獨若遺。
> 我愚人之心也哉！
> 沌沌兮！
>
> — chapter 20

> *Knowing in advance is the blossom of the Tao, and the beginning of foolishness.*
>
> 前識者，道之華，而愚之始。
>
> — chapter 38

> *The ancients who were masterful at the Tao*
> *did not use it to make the people see clearly,*
> *but to make them fools.*
>
> 古之善為道者，
> 非以明民，
> 將以愚之。
>
> — chapter 65

**At chapter 38, 愚 is where a bad road ends. At chapter 20 it is the speaker's boast. At chapter 65 it is where the masters bring the people.** One word, carrying both valences, as 強 (qiáng — strong) does. Whatever English the word takes must stand in all three lines. *Guileless* cannot stand at chapter 38: knowing in advance is not the beginning of guilelessness. *Fool* stands in all three, and two of them already print it.

### In its own language, 愚 is an insult

The book did not choose a gentle word. In the writing of its time 愚 is the plain opposite of knowing, and a term of contempt:

- Xunzi: 是是非非謂之知，非是是非謂之愚 — *"calling right right and wrong wrong is knowing; calling right wrong and wrong right is foolishness."*
- The Analects (17.3): 唯上知與下愚不移 — *"only the highest knowers and the lowest fools do not change."*
- Zhuangzi uses it as an insult too: 愚者自以為覺 — *"the fool takes themselves to be awake."*

**So when the book says 愚, it picks up a word everyone uses to look down on someone.** It does the same with the low place, the soft and the empty. Others of its time did it too, and kept the insult in the word when they did:

- Confucius, of the minister Ning Wuzi (Analects 5.21): 邦有道則知，邦無道則愚。其知可及也，其愚不可及也 — *"when the state had the Tao, Ning Wuzi was knowing; when it lost the Tao, a fool. That knowing can be matched; that foolishness cannot."*
- Zhuangzi: 衆人役役，聖人愚芚 — *"the crowd toil and bustle; the sage is foolish and dull."*

The praise lands only because the word is still an insult. Turn 愚 into a virtue word in English and there is nothing left to reverse.

### Chapter 20 says what the fool's heart is

**The two lines in chapter 20 are a turn, and the second answers the first.** 我愚人之心也哉！沌沌兮！ — *"I have the heart of a fool! How fluid!"* The first is the insult, what the bright and sharp world calls this heart. The second says what the heart is. 沌沌 (dùn dùn) is not a word of contempt: it is the book's word for the whole before it divides, which Guodian writes for the ancients' bearing in chapter 15, and which Heshang Gong, as 混沌 (hùn dùn), uses for the Tao at chapter 25. Wang Bi glosses it 無所別析 (*"it divides and parses nothing"*), Heshang Gong 无所分別 (*"it makes no distinctions"*).

**So the fool of this book is not the one who is confused. It is the one who has not cut the world into pieces.** The worldly are 察察 (chá chá — sharp, scrutinizing), the edge that sorts; the fool's heart is fluid, and water cannot be cut. This is what 愚 means wherever the book claims it, and it is what the masters of chapter 65 bring the people to. *(The meaning opened when Shalom pressed on 沌沌, 2026-11-16: seeking to understand that one word, rather than letting* muddled *stand beside* fool*, unlocked the deeper meaning of the fool. `chapters/020.md` → Notes.)*

### Chapter 65 ends where Zhuangzi puts the fool

Chapter 65 opens with the masters making the people 愚, and closes on 玄德 (xuán dé — profound integrity) and 大順 (dà shùn — the great current). A chapter of the Zhuangzi joins the same three words in the same order:

> 其合緡緡，若愚若昏，是謂玄德，同乎大順。
> *"Its joining is seamless, as if foolish, as if dim: this is called profound integrity, at one with the great current."*

The Zhuangzi is not the Laozi, and it is not a commentary on it. A parallel like this locates a reading. It does not prove one (`process/principles/distribution-locates.md`). But it shows how a near-contemporary heard these words together: **the foolishness is the profound integrity.** Read that way, chapter 65 closes where it opened. The masters bring the people to foolishness, and the chapter ends in profound integrity running with the great current.

### What the commentators did with it

**At chapter 65 both turn the word into praise.** Wang Bi: 愚謂無知守真，順自然也 — *"愚 means unknowing, keeping to what is genuine, following what is so of itself."* Heshang Gong: 將以道德教民使朴質不詐偽 — *"they would teach the people by the Tao and integrity, making them plain and uncarved, without deceit or falsity."* *Guileless* is Heshang Gong's 不詐偽 (bù zhà wěi — "without deceit or falsity") put into the line. That is a gloss doing a rendering's job (`process/principles/commentary-is-not-a-rendering.md`). The commentators explain why the masters wanted it. The line says what they wanted.

**At chapter 20 they say what the fool's heart does not do.** Wang Bi: 絕愚之人，心無所別析，意無所好欲，猶然其情不可覩，我頹然若此也 — *"the utterly foolish person: the heart divides and parses nothing, the mind likes and wants nothing, and their state cannot be made out. I am slumped like that."* Heshang Gong: 不與俗人相隨，守一不移，如愚人之心也 — *"not following the worldly, keeping to the one without moving: like the heart of a fool."* Neither softens the word. Wang Bi's fool sorts nothing, and that is the point.

**At chapter 38 Han Fei tells a story that holds both sides of the word.** The diviner Zhan He sits with disciples, and an ox lows outside the gate. A disciple says it is a black ox with a white forehead. Zhan He says it is black, but the white is on its horns. They send someone to look: a black ox, with cloth wrapped round its horns. Then Han Fei: 嘗試釋詹子之察，而使五尺之愚童子視之，亦知其黑牛而以布裹其角也。故以詹子之察，苦心傷神，而後與五尺之愚童子同功，是以曰：「愚之首也。」 — *"Set Zhan He's discernment aside and have a foolish child of five feet look: the child too sees a black ox with cloth round its horns. So Zhan He's discernment, with a troubled heart and a wearied spirit, achieves only what a foolish child achieves. That is why it says 'the head of folly.'"* The forecaster's art is the folly. The foolish child just looks, and sees.

Heshang Gong on the same line: 言前識之人愚闇之倡始 — *"those who know in advance are the first to lead into folly and darkness."*

### The silks and Han Fei read "the head of folly"

At chapter 38 both silks and Han Fei's lemma read 愚之首 (yú zhī shǒu — "the head of folly") where our base reads 愚之始 (yú zhī shǐ — "the beginning of folly"). That makes the two lines a pair: 亂之首 (luàn zhī shǒu — "the head of disorder") and 愚之首, the head of disorder and the head of folly. Our base keeps 始, and the chapter keeps *head* and *beginning* apart, as its notes argue. The fork is recorded in `sources/variants.yaml`.

### What is set aside

**Guileless.** It turns contempt into a compliment, which is a verdict the Chinese does not carry (`process/principles/no-verdict-the-chinese-lacks.md`). It comes from a commentator's gloss, not the line. It cannot stand at chapter 38. And it hides the one link that answers the reader who calls chapter 65 authoritarian. With *fool* in both chapters, a reader who meets the masters making the people fools can find the speaker of chapter 20 saying *"I have the heart of a fool!"* The masters bring the people to where the sage stands. *Guileless* cut that thread.

**Simple.** The same sweetening, done more quietly. It slides between *pure* and *simple-minded* and lets the reader pick the kinder one, so it hides the insult rather than translating it. The uncarved, 樸 (pǔ), already holds the sense of plainness in this book.

**Ignorant, ignorance.** These name a lack, knowledge withheld. That is the authoritarian reading in one word, *"kept them ignorant."* The fool of chapter 20 lacks nothing they want. *Unknowing*, Wang Bi's 無知 (wú zhī), is already that phrase's English at chapters 3 and 10.

**Stupid.** A modern insult, and harder than the Chinese. It has none of the long tradition of the fool, and *"I have a stupid heart"* carries no boast.

**Dull.** Already spoken for. It renders 悶悶 (mèn mèn — dull) in chapter 20 itself, *"I alone am dull,"* and again in chapter 58.

**Make fools of them.** The English idiom means to dupe or humiliate someone, the opposite of what the masters do. Chapter 65 reads *make them fools*, never *make fools of them*.

**Foolish, at chapter 65.** Accurate, but it names only a lapse of judgment, and it settles toward blame what the Chinese leaves open. *Fools* keeps both sides of the word, the one looked down on and the long tradition of the court fool and the wise fool, and it repeats chapter 20's noun exactly. The bare 愚 can name people: the Analects' 下愚 (xià yú — "the lowest fools"). *(Shalom's intuition, 2026-11-16.)*

**The fool.** It would point at the archetype outright, and the Chinese marks no figure: there are no articles, and 愚 here is a plain verb about the people. *Make them the fool* also sets a plural against a singular, and it lands on the idiom *make someone the fool*, to make them the dupe. *Fools* lets the reader reach the archetype through chapter 20's echo, the way the book does.

**Great wisdom seems foolish.** The proverb 大智若愚 (dà zhì ruò yú) is not in this book. It comes from the Song dynasty, from Su Shi, whose words were 大智如愚 (dà zhì rú yú — "great wisdom is like foolishness"). It sweetens 愚 into wisdom in disguise. The book never says the fool is secretly wise. It says the sage is the fool.

### Working register

| Ch | Chinese | Our English | Form |
|---|---|---|---|
| 20 | 我**愚**人之心也哉 (*wǒ yú rén zhī xīn yě zāi*) | *I have the heart of a fool!* | 愚人 (yú rén — a foolish person), a noun |
| 38 | 而**愚**之始 (*ér yú zhī shǐ*) | *the beginning of foolishness* | a noun |
| 65 | 將以**愚**之 (*jiāng yǐ yú zhī*) | *but to make them fools* | a causative verb, set as *make them* + the noun |

**The chapter 65 block:**

> *The ancients who were masterful at the Tao*
> *did not use it to make the people see clearly,*
> *but to make them fools.*

The two halves are parallel causatives in the Chinese, 以明民 (yǐ míng mín — "using it to make the people see clearly") and 以愚之 (yǐ yú zhī — "using it to make them fools"), and the English keeps them parallel. 將 (jiāng) marks what was meant, and in the frame 非 X，將 Y (fēi X, jiāng Y — "not X, but rather Y") it works as *but*. The supplied *return* goes: nothing in the Chinese turns back (`WORKLIST.md` T1-27).

### What no rule can enforce

**Dull** belongs to 悶悶 (mèn mèn — dull), which shares chapter 20, so only this entry rules it out for 愚.

**Simple** is left off the list, because other characters may need it in these chapters. Only this entry holds it.

### Left open

**Chapter 65 reads sharply.** *"Did not use it to make the people see clearly, but to make them fools"* is the sentence quoted to call Laozi an authoritarian, now in plain English. The edition prints it. The answer is in the book itself: the speaker of chapter 20 claims the same word, and chapter 65 closes in profound integrity. `notes/reading.md` → *Ch 65* sets out the charge and the answer, and keeps its honest caveat: Laozi really is suspicious of sophistication as such.

**Chapter 38's fork stays open.** Our base reads *the beginning of foolishness*, and the silks and Han Fei read *the head of folly*, which pairs the line with the one before it (`sources/variants.yaml`).

**Whether the fool of chapter 65 is the fool of chapter 20 is the reader's to decide.** The English now lets a reader ask the question. It does not answer it.

entries.body:
## 欲 (Yù) — Desire, and Wanting

*Say "yoo," falling. Twenty-six appearances in twenty-five lines across fifteen chapters. 無欲 (wú yù — desireless) alone stands in five of them.*

**Recommended: 欲 → "desire" as a state, with nothing after it · "want" when a verb follows · "would" in the phrase 將欲 (jiāng yù — "if you are about to want to").** *(Not "craving," which carries a verdict the character does not and is the standard English for the Buddhist root of suffering. Not "wish," which is idle. Not "urge," a drive in the psychologist's sense. Not "lust," "covet" or "the passions," the hymn test's vocabulary of sin.)* **Settled within it, by Shalom's calls:** *ever desireless* and *ever desiring* at chapter 1 (2026-11-14); *wants the not-wanting* at chapter 64. *The desirable* at chapter 3 belongs to 可 (kě — can be), as its flexion.

### The graph: an open mouth, and a valley

> 欲，貪欲也。从欠，谷聲。
> *"欲: greedy wanting. From 欠 (qiàn — a person with the mouth open), with 谷 (gǔ — a valley) for the sound."* — Shuowen (說文, *Shuōwén* — Xu Shen's dictionary, c. 100 CE)

**欠 is a person with the mouth open.** It is the yawn, the gasp, the gape: breath going out, and a gap that wants filling. Most of the characters built on it are things a mouth does, breathing, singing, drinking, sighing. 欲 is the gape turned toward something.

**谷 is the book's valley.** The Shuowen: 泉出通川爲谷, *"a spring coming out to reach a river is a valley"* (`glossary/gu-谷.md`).

*A calibration.* The Shuowen counts 谷 as sound only, and so does this entry. But the two halves are both openings, a mouth and a valley, and the book sets them side by side more than once. Chapter 15 likens the ancients to a valley and then says they 不欲盈 (*bù yù yíng* — "do not want to be full"); chapter 39 fills the valley and, in Heshang Gong's reading, warns it not to want to stay full. The empty place and the wish to fill it are one graph. We do not claim the scribes meant it. The book's own pairings do the arguing.

### Twenty-five lines, and three grammars

The lines sort cleanly by what follows the character.

**With nothing after it, 欲 is a state, and the English is *desire*.** 無欲 (*wú yù* — without desire), 有欲 (*yǒu yù* — with desire), 寡欲 (*guǎ yù* — little desire), and 不欲 standing alone:

> *Ever desireless, you can observe its subtlety;*
> *Ever desiring, you can observe its direction.*
>
> 故常無欲，以觀其妙；
> 常有欲，以觀其徼。
>
> — chapter 1

> *I am desireless, and the people become plain of themselves.*
>
> 我無欲，而民自樸。
>
> — chapter 57

Also chapter 3's 常使民無知無欲 (*"so the people are ever unknowing, ever desireless"*), chapter 19's 少私寡欲 (*"diminish the self, diminish desire"*), chapter 34's 常無欲 (*"ever desireless, it can be named small"*), and the second and third 欲 of chapter 37.

**With a verb after it, 欲 is wanting to do something, and the English is *want*.**

> *Do not want to be gleaming like jade,*
>
> 不欲琭琭如玉，
>
> — chapter 39

> *The large state wants nothing more than to gather and rear people.*
> *The small state wants nothing more than to enter and serve people.*
> *Both get what they want.*
>
> 大國不過欲兼畜人，
> 小國不過欲入事人。
> 夫兩者各得所欲，
>
> — chapter 61

Also 15 (不欲盈), 37 (欲作), 46 (欲得), 66 (欲上民, 欲先民) and 77 (不欲見賢), each of which takes a verb.

**After 將 (*jiāng* — about to), 欲 is the conditional, and the English is *would*.**

> *If you would draw it in, you must first stretch it out.*
>
> 將欲歙之，必固張之；
>
> — chapter 36

Four times in chapter 36 and once in chapter 29 (*"Those who would take the world and handle it"*). English *would* holds both halves of 將欲 at once, the intention and the nearness, which is why the phrase takes one word and not *wants to be about to*.

**In none of these lines is 欲 evil in itself.** Chapter 1 gives *ever desiring* its own capacity, to observe the Tao's direction. Chapter 61 lets both states get what they want, and approves. Chapter 66 tells anyone who wants to rise above the people how to do it. What the book condemns is particular: 欲得 (*yù dé* — wanting to get) is the greatest fault at chapter 46, and displaying 可欲 (*kě yù* — the desirable) disturbs the people at chapter 3. The character describes. The verdicts come from the lines around it.

### Chapter 37 is the hardest line: three 欲, one chain

> *Transforming, if they want to act, I will stabilize them with the nameless uncarved wood.*
> *With the nameless uncarved wood, they too will be desireless.*
> *Not desiring, and so still, the world will right itself.*
>
> 化而欲作，吾將鎮之以無名之樸。
> 無名之樸，夫亦將無欲。
> 不欲以靜，天下將自正。
>
> — chapter 37

The chapter runs a chain, and 欲 is its thread: the things **want** to act (欲作, *yù zuò*); they too will be **desireless** (無欲, *wú yù*); **not desiring** (不欲, *bù yù*), and so still, the world will right itself. Three grammars of one character in three lines, each handing the word to the next.

**The grammar sorts all three, and the chapter now reads so** (Shalom's call, 2026-11-19). 欲作 takes a verb, so *want*. 無欲 and 不欲 take nothing, so *desire*: *desireless*, and *not desiring*. One root runs through all three. *Urge*, the old English, rendered no character the line prints, and *relinquishing* supplied a giving-up the Chinese does not have: 不欲 is not wanting, not letting go of a want once held. The same rebuilding restored 化's chain (T3-8) and the subject Heshang Gong gives the second line, the people, not the wood.

**Wang Bi reads the chain as the end of contending.** On 化而欲作: 作欲成也, *"the acting wants to complete itself."* On the uncarved wood's 無欲: 無欲競也, *"desireless: not wanting to compete."* The wanting he means is the wanting to win, which is 爭 (*zhēng* — contend)'s ground (`glossary/zheng-爭.md`).

**The silks read the chapter otherwise.** In the collated silk text the close is 夫將不辱。不辱以靜 (*fū jiāng bù rù. bù rù yǐ jìng* — "they will not be disgraced; not disgraced, and so still"), with 辱 (*rù* — disgrace) where our base has 欲 twice. The chain's thread there is disgrace, not desire. Our base and both commentaries print 欲.

### What the commentators did with it

**Wang Bi gives desire a use.** On chapter 1: 故常無欲空虚，可以觀其始物之妙, *"so the ever desireless, empty, can observe the subtlety by which things begin,"* and 故常有欲，可以觀其終物之徼也, *"so the ever desiring can observe the heading where things end."* Desirelessness sees beginnings; desire sees where things go. Neither is a fault. Heshang Gong keeps only the first: 人常能無欲，則可以觀道之要, *"a person who can be ever desireless can observe the essential of the Tao,"* and his ever-desiring person observes 世俗之所歸趣, *"where the worldly are heading."*

**Wang Bi's chapter 57 is the silks' chapter 57.** Our base reads 我無欲 (*wǒ wú yù* — "I am desireless"). Wang Bi glosses it 上之所欲，民從之速也。我之所欲唯無欲，而民亦無欲而自樸也, *"what those above want, the people follow quickly. What I want is only desirelessness, and the people too are desireless, and plain of themselves."* The collated silk text prints exactly that wanting: **我欲不欲而民自樸** (*wǒ yù bù yù ér mín zì pǔ* — "I want the not-wanting, and the people become plain of themselves"), the formula of chapter 64. **The sage's desirelessness is itself a want**, and the oldest witness and the oldest commentary on our base both say so.

**At chapter 64 the commentators split on the formula.** Wang Bi reads it as the book's reflexive, X-ing the not-X, the shape of chapter 63's 為無為 (*wéi wú wéi* — "do the not-doing"), and adds 好欲雖㣲，争尚為之興, *"a fondness for wanting, however slight, gives rise to contention and esteem."* Heshang Gong reads a comparison: 聖人欲人所不欲。人欲彰顯，聖人欲伏光, *"the sage wants what people do not want. People want to stand out; the sage wants to hide their light."* The verse keeps the reflexive, Shalom's call, on the shape chapters 63 and 64 share.

**Heshang Gong ties little desire to enough.** On chapter 19's 寡欲: 寡欲者，當知足也, *"to want little is to know you have enough"* (`glossary/zhizu-知足.md`). Chapter 46 makes the same join in the Chinese itself, setting 不知足 (*bù zhī zú* — not knowing enough) and 欲得 (*yù dé* — wanting to get) in one couplet.

### What is set aside

**"Craving."** The verdict word. *Craving* is a want gone wrong, and it is the usual English for the Buddhist *taṇhā*, the thirst that is the root of suffering in the second noble truth. Put it on 欲 and the book becomes a sermon against wanting, which chapters 1, 61 and 66 refuse. At chapter 46 the fault is named by 咎 (*jiù* — fault); 欲得 is only *wanting to get*, and English needs nothing harsher (`process/principles/no-verdict-the-chinese-lacks.md`).

**"Lust," "covet," "the passions," "concupiscence."** The vocabulary of sin. *Covet* is the tenth commandment; *the passions* and *concupiscence* are Augustine's. Each fails the hymn test on sight, and each makes the people of chapter 3 sinners to be cured.

**"Wish," "no wish."** Too light. A wish can sit idle; 欲 leans toward its object, as the open mouth does. And *no wish* turns a verb into a noun the line does not print: 不欲盈 is *do not want to be full*, not *have no wish to be*.

**"Urge," "drive."** The psychologist's words, Freud's *Trieb* in English. At chapter 37 *urge* also stands where 欲 should and renders nothing the line prints.

**"Relinquish," "renounce," "give up."** They supply a want first held and then surrendered. 不欲 and 無欲 say only that the wanting is not there.

**"Passionless," "dispassionate."** The Stoic sage's *apatheia*, an ideal of calm achieved by reason against feeling. The desireless one in this book is plain like uncarved wood, not composed against an inner storm.

**"Appetite."** Heshang Gong's 嗜欲 (*shì yù* — appetites) is the body's version of the word, and *appetite* is right in a note. In the verse it narrows 欲 to food and sex, and 欲 at chapter 61 is a state's wish for people.

**"Will," "intend," "aim."** *Will* belongs to 志 (*zhì* — ambition, will) at chapter 33. *Intend* and *aim* are plans, and 欲 is the leaning before a plan.

### Working register

| line | grammar | English |
|---|---|---|
| 常無欲 · 常有欲 (1) · 無欲 (3, 34, 37, 57) | a state, no verb after | *ever desireless · ever desiring · desireless* |
| 寡欲 (19) | a state | *diminish desire* |
| 不欲以靜 (37) | a state, no verb after | *not desiring* |
| 可欲 (3) | 可 + 欲, a fixed noun | *the desirable* — 可's flexion |
| 不欲盈 (15) · 不欲琭琭 (39) · 不欲見賢 (77) | 欲 + verb, negated | *do not want to…* (77 recommended; 15 Shalom's call, 2026-11-19) |
| 欲作 (37) · 欲得 (46) · 欲兼畜人 · 欲入事人 (61) · 欲上民 · 欲先民 (66) | 欲 + verb | *want to…* (46, 66 recommended) |
| 所欲 (61) | 所 + 欲, what is wanted | *what they want* |
| 欲不欲 (64) | the reflexive formula | *wants the not-wanting* — one verb on both sides, as at chapter 63 |
| 將欲 (29, 36 ×4) | the conditional | *would* |

**The formula outranks the split.** In 欲不欲 the second 欲 stands with nothing after it, which by the rule above would read *desire*. But X-the-not-X takes one English on both sides wherever the book uses it (63's *do the not-doing*, *serve the not-serving*), and the formula is a signature of the book. So chapter 64 reads *want* twice.

### What no rule can enforce

***Craving*, *wish*, *urge* and *relinquish* are ruled out, and cannot go on the list yet.** Each still stands in a chapter where 欲 does (46, 15 and 77, and 37), and a forbidden word in such a chapter is an error the build reports at once. They join the list as their lines change.

***Want* also renders 求 (*qiú* — to seek) at chapter 75**, in *"those over them want their own lives so rich"* (以其上求生之厚, *yǐ qí shàng qiú shēng zhī hòu*). 欲 is not in chapter 75, so no rule sees the collision; only `concordance.py --english "want"`, run by hand, does. 求 is seeking, a search with hands, and it has its own English to find.

***Desire* is free.** No other character in the book wears it, and nothing needs to be forbidden to keep it so.

### Left open

**Three lines need new English, and each is Shalom's call.** Chapter 46's *craving to acquire* (with 得's *wanting to get*), 77's *have no wish to appear exceptional*, and 66's two, where *to rise above* and *to walk ahead* drop 欲 altogether and lose the frame chapter 66 shares with chapter 36: 欲X，必Y (*yù X, bì Y* — "if you want to X, you must Y"). (Chapters 15 and 37 were settled on 2026-11-19.)

**The silks have two readings our base does not, and neither is yet recorded per silk.** Chapter 57's 我欲不欲 and chapter 37's 不辱 were read in Wikisource's collated silk text, which does not say which silk prints which. Both want rows in `sources/variants.yaml` once checked against each silk. The base and both commentaries print 我無欲 and 無欲 / 不欲, and we keep them.

**Whether the sage wants is the real tension, and the book leaves it standing.** Chapter 3 makes the people desireless; chapter 57 makes the sage so. Yet chapter 66 hands the sage a want, to be above the people, and Wang Bi's chapter 57 and the silks make desirelessness itself the thing wanted. The English should let the sage want where the Chinese says so, at 64 and 66, and not tidy the sage into someone beyond wanting. That is the overlay the Stoic and Buddhist words would bring, from the other direction.
