If it weren’t laughed at, the Tao wouldn’t be what it is.
41.5: Therefore, as the established sayings have it:
41.6: 明道若昧，進道若退，夷道若纇。
Míng dào ruò mèi, jìn dào ruò tuì, yí dào ruò lèi.
The clear Tao seems murky. The advancing Tao seems to retreat. The level Tao seems rough.
41.7: Shàng dé ruò gǔ, dà bái ruò rǔ,
The highest integrity seems a valley. The whitest white seems soiled.
41.8: 廣德若不足，建德若偷，質真若渝。
Guǎng dé ruò bù zú, jiàn dé ruò tōu, zhì zhēn ruò yú.
Broad integrity seems not enough. Sturdy integrity seems slack. Substantial truth seems to waver.
41.9: Dà fāng wú yú, dà qì wǎn chéng,
The great square has no corners. The great vessel is never completed.
42.1: 道生一，一生二，二生三，三生萬物。
Dào shēng yī, yī shēng èr, èr shēng sān, sān shēng wàn wù.
The Tao births the one, the one births the two, the two births the three, the three births the countless things.
42.2: 萬物負陰而抱陽，沖氣以為和。
Wàn wù fù yīn ér bào yáng, chōng qì yǐ wéi hé.
The countless things carry yin on their backs and embrace yang with their arms, and the breath within makes harmony.
42.3: Rén zhī suǒ wù, wéi gū, guǎ, bù gǔ,
What most people hate is to be called orphaned, meager, or unworthy,
42.4: ér wáng gōng yǐ wéi chēng.
Yet rulers and lords take these very descriptions for themselves.
42.5: 故物或損之而益，或益之而損。
Gù wù huò sǔn zhī ér yì, huò yì zhī ér sǔn.
For so it is: what is decreased is thereby increased, and what is increased is thereby decreased.
42.6: Rén zhī suǒ jiào, wǒ yì jiào zhī.
What others teach, I also teach:
42.7: Qiáng liáng zhě bù dé qí sǐ,
The strong and rigid do not die a natural death.
42.8: Wú jiāng yǐ wéi jiào fù.
I take this as the father of learning.
43.1: 天下之至柔，馳騁天下之至堅。
Tiān xià zhī zhì róu, chí chěng tiān xià zhī zhì jiān.
The softest thing in the world gallops over the hardest thing in the world.
43.3: Wú shì yǐ zhī wú wéi zhī yǒu yì.
This is how I know the benefit of non-doing.
43.4: Bù yán zhī jiào, wú wéi zhī yì,
The wordless teaching, the benefit of non-doing —
44.1: Your name or your body — which is dearer?
44.2: Your body or goods — which is worth more?
44.3: Gain or loss — which does more harm?
44.4: Shì gù shèn ài bì dà fèi,
Therefore, extreme attachment inevitably brings great cost
44.5: And hoarding inevitably brings heavy loss.
44.6: Know when you have enough, and you are never disgraced.
44.7: Know when to stop, and you come to no danger.
44.8: And so you can last long.
45.1: Dà chéng ruò quē, qí yòng bù bì.
Great completeness seems deficient, yet when used, it never wears out.
45.2: Dà yíng ruò chōng, qí yòng bù qióng.
Great fullness seems empty, yet when used, it never runs dry.
45.6: Zào shèng hán, jìng shèng rè.
Restlessness overcomes cold; stillness overcomes heat.
45.7: Qīng jìng wéi tiān xià zhèng.
Clear stillness brings order to the world.
46.1: Tiān xià yǒu dào, què zǒu mǎ yǐ fèn.
When the world embraces the Tao, swift horses are retired to work the fields.
46.2: Tiān xià wú dào, róng mǎ shēng yú jiāo.
When the world lacks the Tao, war horses are bred in the borderlands.
46.3: Huò mò dà yú bù zhī zú;
There is no greater disaster than discontent,
46.4: Jiù mò dà yú yù dé.
No greater fault than craving to acquire.
46.5: Gù zhī zú zhī zú, cháng zú yǐ.
And so the contentment of knowing you have enough is ever-present contentment.
47.1: Bù chū hù, zhī tiān xià;
Without leaving home, you know the whole world.
47.2: Bù kuī yǒu, jiàn tiān dào.
Without looking out the window, you see the way of nature.
47.3: Qí chū mí yuǎn, qí zhī mí shǎo.
The further out you venture, the less you know.
47.4: Shì yǐ shèng rén bù xíng ér zhī,
Therefore, the sage knows without venturing,
47.5: Bù jiàn ér míng, bù wéi ér chéng.
names without seeing, and accomplishes without acting.
48.1: Wéi xué rì yì, wéi dào rì sǔn.
In pursuit of learning, you increase daily; in pursuit of the Tao, you decrease daily.
48.2: Sǔn zhī yòu sǔn, yǐ zhì yú wú wéi.
Decreasing and decreasing, until you reach non-doing.
48.3: Wú wéi ér wú bù wéi.
Non-doing, yet nothing is left undone.
48.4: Qǔ tiān xià cháng yǐ wú shì,
The world always comes to you by not meddling with it.
48.5: 及其有事，不足以取天下。
Jí qí yǒu shì, bù zú yǐ qǔ tiān xià.
The moment you meddle, it stops coming.
49.1: 聖人無常心，以百姓心為心。
Shèng rén wú cháng xīn, yǐ bǎi xìng xīn wéi xīn.
The sage has no fixed heart; they take everyone's heart as their own.
49.2: The masterful, I count as masterful;
49.3: Bù shàn zhě, wú yì shàn zhī;
the unmasterful, I count as masterful too.
49.6: Bù xìn zhě, wú yì xìn zhī;
the untrustworthy, I trust as well.
49.8: 聖人在天下，歙歙焉，為天下渾其心，
Shèng rén zài tiān xià, xī xī yān, wéi tiān xià hún qí xīn,
In the world, the sage breathes gently; for the sake of the world, they let their heart go muddy.
49.9: 百姓皆注其耳目，聖人皆孩之。
Bǎi xìng jiē zhù qí ěr mù, shèng rén jiē hái zhī.
Everyone pours out their attention, all eyes and ears; the sage sees them pure as infants.
5.1: 天地不仁，以萬物為芻狗；
Tiān dì bù rén, yǐ wàn wù wéi chú gǒu;
Sky and earth are not concerned with humaneness: they treat the countless things as straw dogs.
5.2: 聖人不仁，以百姓為芻狗。
shèng rén bù rén, yǐ bǎi xìng wéi chú gǒu.
The sage is not concerned with humaneness: they treat everyone as straw dogs.
5.3: Tiān dì zhī jiān, qí yóu tuó yuè hū?
Isn't the space between sky and earth like a bellows?
5.4: Xū ér bù qū, dòng ér yù chū.
Empty but never depleted, the more it moves, the more it yields.
5.5: Duō yán shù qióng, bù rú shǒu zhōng.
Speaking of this is a dead end. Instead, hold to the center.
50.1: Emerge into life, enter into death.
50.10: Hǔ wú suǒ yòng qí zhǎo,
the tiger’s claws have nowhere to tear into,
50.11: Bīng wú suǒ róng qí rèn.
the weapon blades have nothing to cut.
50.12: Fú hé gù? Yǐ qí wú sǐ dì.
Why? Because they give death no foothold.
50.2: Shēng zhī tú, shí yǒu sān;
Three in ten people are followers of life.
50.3: Sǐ zhī tú, shí yǒu sān;
Three in ten are followers of death.
50.4: 人之生，動之於死地，亦十有三。
Rén zhī shēng, dòng zhī yú sǐ dì, yì shí yǒu sān.
Three in ten, though alive, move toward deadly ground.
50.5: Fú hé gù? Yǐ qí shēng shēng zhī hòu.
Why? Because they cling too tightly to life.
50.6: Gài wén shàn shè shēng zhě,
It’s been said that one who truly tends life
50.7: Lù xíng bù yù sì hǔ,
can travel the land without meeting rhinos or tigers,
50.8: Rù jūn bù pèi jiǎ bīng;
and can enter into battle untouched by armor or weapons.
50.9: Sì wú suǒ tóu qí jiǎo,
The rhino’s horn has nowhere to thrust,
51.1: Dào shēng zhī, dé xù zhī,
The Tao gives birth to the countless things, integrity rears them,
51.2: Wù xíng zhī, shì chéng zhī.
matter forms them, circumstance completes them.
51.3: 是以萬物莫不尊道而貴德。
Shì yǐ wàn wù mò bù zūn dào ér guì dé.
Therefore the countless things, without exception, revere the Tao and value integrity.
51.4: Dào zhī zūn, dé zhī guì,
This reverence for the Tao, this valuing of integrity — no one commands it.
51.5: Fú mò zhī mìng ér cháng zì rán.
This reverence for the Tao, this valuing of integrity — no one commands it. It is always so, of itself.
51.6: Gù dào shēng zhī, dé xù zhī;
Thus, the Tao births the countless things and integrity rears them,
51.7: 長之育之；亭之毒之；養之覆之。
Zhǎng zhī yù zhī; tíng zhī dú zhī; yǎng zhī fù zhī.
grows and raises them, settles and matures them, nourishes and protects them.
51.8: 生而不有，為而不恃，長而不宰。
Shēng ér bù yǒu, wéi ér bù shì, zhǎng ér bù zǎi.
Giving birth without possessing, acting yet relying on nothing, growing them without ruling them —
52.1: Tiān xià yǒu shǐ, yǐ wéi tiān xià mǔ.
The world has a beginning, which serves as the mother of the world.
52.2: Jì dé qí mǔ, yǐ zhī qí zǐ;
Find our mother, and you know her children.
52.3: 既知其子，復守其母，没身不殆。
Jì zhī qí zǐ, fù shǒu qí mǔ, mò shēn bù dài.
Know her children, return and hold fast to our mother, and to the end of your days, no danger will find you.
52.4: 塞其兌，閉其門，終身不勤。
Sè qí duì, bì qí mén, zhōng shēn bù qín.
Block the openings, close the doors, and to the end of your days you will not strain.
52.5: 開其兌，濟其事，終身不救。
Kāi qí duì, jì qí shì, zhōng shēn bù jiù.
Open the openings, multiply your affairs, and to the end of your days you are beyond saving.
52.6: Jiàn xiǎo yuē míng, shǒu róu yuē qiáng.
Seeing the small is called clarity. Holding to the soft is called strong.
52.7: 用其光，復歸其明，無遺身殃；
Yòng qí guāng, fù guī qí míng, wú yí shēn yāng;
Use the outer light, return to your inner clarity, and leave no calamity for the body.
52.8: This is called the ever-present worn covered.
53.1: 使我介然有知，行於大道，唯施是畏。
Shǐ wǒ jiè rán yǒu zhī, xíng yú dà dào, wéi shī shì wèi.
If I had just a scrap of knowledge, walking the path of the great Tao, my only fear would be to stray from it.
53.2: Dà dào shèn yí, ér rén hào jìng.
The great Tao is very level, yet people love to take shortcuts.
53.3: Cháo shèn chú, tián shèn wú, cāng shèn xū;
The courts are immaculate, the fields are choked with weeds, the granaries are empty;
53.4: 服文綵，帶利劍，厭飲食，財貨有餘；
Fú wén cǎi, dài lì jiàn, yàn yǐn shí, cái huò yǒu yú;
Wearing ornate, colorful clothes, carrying sharp swords, gorged on food and drink, possessing excess wealth and goods —
53.5: Shì wèi dào kuā. Fēi dào yě zāi\!
This exposes the ringleader of thieves. It is not the Tao\!
54.1: 善建者不拔，善抱者不脫，子孫以祭祀不輟。
Shàn jiàn zhě bù bá, shàn bào zhě bù tuō, zǐ sūn yǐ jì sì bù chuò.
What is masterfully planted cannot be uprooted. What is masterfully embraced cannot slip away. Descendants will never cease offering sacrifices honoring this.
54.2: Xiū zhī yú shēn, qí dé nǎi zhēn;
Cultivate this in your body, and its integrity becomes authentic.
54.3: Xiū zhī yú jiā, qí dé nǎi yú;
Cultivate this in your family, and its integrity becomes abundant.
54.4: Xiū zhī yú xiāng, qí dé nǎi cháng;
Cultivate this in your community, and its integrity becomes long-lasting.
54.5: Xiū zhī yú bāng, qí dé nǎi fēng;
Cultivate this in your state, and its integrity becomes bountiful.
54.6: Xiū zhī yú tiān xià, qí dé nǎi pǔ.
Cultivate this in the world, and its integrity becomes universal.
54.7: Gù yǐ shēn guān shēn, yǐ jiā guān jiā,
Therefore, observe the body through your own body. Observe the family through your family.
54.8: 以鄉觀鄉，以邦觀邦，以天下觀天下。
Yǐ xiāng guān xiāng, yǐ bāng guān bāng, yǐ tiān xià guān tiān xià.
Observe the community through your community. Observe the state through your state. Observe the world through the world.
54.9: 吾何以知天下然哉？以此。
Wú hé yǐ zhī tiān xià rán zāi? Yǐ cǐ.
How do I know the world is so? By this.
55.1: Hán dé zhī hòu, bǐ yú chì zǐ.
A person with abundant integrity is like a newborn.
55.2: 毒蟲不螫，猛獸不據，攫鳥不搏。
Dú chóng bù shì, měng shòu bù jù, jué niǎo bù bó.
Venomous creatures do not sting them, fierce beasts do not seize them, birds of prey do not attack them.
55.3: Gǔ ruò jīn róu ér wò gù.
Their bones are yielding and their muscles soft, yet their grip is firm.
55.4: 未知牝牡之合而朘作，精之至也。
Wèi zhī pìn mǔ zhī hé ér zuī zuò, jīng zhī zhì yě.
They do not yet know the union of female and male, yet their whole being quickens with life — this is vital essence at its utmost.
55.5: 終日號而不嗄，和之至也。
Zhōng rì háo ér bù shà, hé zhī zhì yě.
It cries all day and never goes hoarse — this is harmony at its utmost.
55.6: Zhī hé yuē cháng, zhī cháng yuē míng.
Harmony is called the ever-present. Knowing harmony is called clear-seeing.
55.7: Yì shēng yuē xiáng. Xīn shǐ qì yuē qiáng.
To force life to increase is an ill omen. When the heart drives the breath, that is called strong.
55.8: 物壯則老，謂之不道，不道早已。
Wù zhuàng zé lǎo, wèi zhī bù dào, bù dào zǎo yǐ.
When things reach their prime, they decay. This is called not-Tao. Not-Tao comes to an early end.
56.1: Zhī zhě bù yán, yán zhě bù zhī.
Those who know do not speak. Those who speak do not know.
56.2: Sè qí duì, bì qí mén,
Block the openings, close the doors.
56.3: Cuò qí ruì, jiě qí fēn,
Blunt the sharpness, untangle the knots.
56.4: Hé qí guāng, tóng qí chén,
Harmonize your light, be the same as the dust.
56.6: 故不可得而親，不可得而疏；
Gù bù kě dé ér qīn, bù kě dé ér shū;
You cannot draw them near nor hold them off,
56.7: 不可得而利，不可得而害；
Bù kě dé ér lì, bù kě dé ér hài;
56.8: 不可得而貴，不可得而賤。
Bù kě dé ér guì, bù kě dé ér jiàn.
56.9: And so, they become the most honored in the world.
57.10: Wǒ wú wéi, ér mín zì huà;
I do not do, and the people transform themselves.
57.11: Wǒ hào jìng, ér mín zì zhèng;
I love stillness, and the people right themselves.
57.12: Wǒ wú shì, ér mín zì fù;
I do not meddle, and the people enrich themselves.
57.13: Wǒ wú yù, ér mín zì pǔ.
I am desireless, and the people become plain of themselves.
57.3: yǐ wú shì qǔ tiān xià.
and win the world by not meddling.
57.4: Wú hé yǐ zhī qí rán zāi? Yǐ cǐ:
How do I know it is so? By this:
57.5: Tiān xià duō jì huì, ér mín mí pín;
The more taboos in the world, the poorer the people become.
57.6: Rén duō lì qì, guó jiā zī hūn;
The more sharp weapons the people have, the more clouded the state becomes.
57.7: Rén duō jì qiǎo, qí wù zī qǐ;
The more cunning people become, the more strange contrivances appear.
57.8: Fǎ lìng zī zhāng, dào zéi duō yǒu.
The more laws are proclaimed, the more thieves there are.
58.1: Qí zhèng mèn mèn, qí mín chún chún;
When the government is dull and undiscerning, the people are pure and honest.
58.2: Qí zhèng chá chá, qí mín quē quē.
When the government is sharp and prying, the people turn cunning.
58.3: Huò xī fú zhī suǒ yǐ,
Disaster is what fortune leans on;
58.4: Fú xī huò zhī suǒ fú.
58.5: Shú zhī qí jí? Qí wú zhèng.
Who knows where it ends? It has no fixed norm —
58.6: Zhèng fù wéi qí, shàn fù wéi yāo.
The straight turns crooked, the good turns monstrous.
58.7: Rén zhī mí, qí rì gù jiǔ.
People have been lost in this for a very long time.
58.8: Shì yǐ shèng rén fāng ér bù gē,
Therefore the sage is square but does not cut,
59.1: Zhì rén shì tiān, mò ruò sè.
When governing people and serving nature, nothing compares to conserving.
59.2: Fú wéi sè, shì wèi zǎo fú;
Only conserving is called accepting early,
59.3: Zǎo fú wèi zhī zhòng jī dé;
accepting early is called a heavy accumulation of integrity,
59.4: Zhòng jī dé zé wú bù kè;
a heavy accumulation of integrity is when nothing cannot be overcome,
59.5: Wú bù kè zé mò zhī qí jí;
when nothing cannot be overcome, no one knows its limit,
59.6: Mò zhī qí jí, kě yǐ yǒu guó;
when no one knows its limit, you can have the state.
59.7: Yǒu guó zhī mǔ, kě yǐ cháng jiǔ.
Have the mother of the state, and you can last long.
59.8: 是謂深根固柢，長生久視之道。
Shì wèi shēn gēn gù dǐ, cháng shēng jiǔ shì zhī dào.
This is called the Tao of deep roots, firm base, long life, and enduring vision.
6.1: The spirit of the valley is deathless.
6.2: This is called the dark female.
6.4: this is called the root of sky and earth.
6.6: use it, and there is no strain.
60.1: Zhì dà guó, ruò pēng xiǎo xiān.
Governing a large state is like cooking a small fish.
60.2: Yǐ dào lì tiān xià, qí guǐ bù shén;
Oversee the world with the Tao, and the ghosts lose their potency,
60.3: 非其鬼不神，其神不傷人；
Fēi qí guǐ bù shén, qí shén bù shāng rén;
not only do ghosts lose their potency, their potency causes no harm to people,
60.4: 非其神不傷人，聖人亦不傷人。
Fēi qí shén bù shāng rén, shèng rén yì bù shāng rén.
not only does their potency do no harm, the sage, too, does no harm to people.
60.5: 夫兩不相傷，故德交歸焉。
Fú liǎng bù xiāng shāng, gù dé jiāo guī yān.
And since the two do no harm to each other, their integrity converges and returns.
61.1: The large state is the downstream flow,
61.2: tiān xià zhī jiāo, tiān xià zhī pìn.
the confluence of the world, the female of the world.
61.3: 牝常以靜勝牡，以靜為下。
Pìn cháng yǐ jìng shèng mǔ, yǐ jìng wéi xià.
The female always overcomes the male by stillness. By stillness she is underneath.
61.4: 故大國以下小國，則取小國；
Gù dà guó yǐ xià xiǎo guó, zé qǔ xiǎo guó;
So the large state, by going below the small state, takes the small state.
61.5: 小國以下大國，則取大國。
Xiǎo guó yǐ xià dà guó, zé qǔ dà guó.
The small state, by going below the large state, takes the large state.
61.6: Gù huò xià yǐ qǔ, huò xià ér qǔ.
The large state takes by going low, the small state by staying low.
61.7: Dà guó bù guò yù jiān xù rén,
The large state wants nothing more than to gather and rear people.
61.8: Xiǎo guó bù guò yù rù shì rén.
The small state wants nothing more than to enter and serve people.
61.9: 夫兩者各得所欲，大者宜為下。
Fú liǎng zhě gè dé suǒ yù, dà zhě yí wéi xià.
Both get what they want. The large one ought to be underneath.
62.1: Dào zhě wàn wù zhī ào.
The Tao is the sanctuary of the countless things,
62.10: And so it is the most honored in the world.
62.2: 善人之寶，不善人之所保。
Shàn rén zhī bǎo, bù shàn rén zhī suǒ bǎo.
the treasure of those who are masterful, and what keeps safe those who are not.
62.3: 美言可以市尊，美行可以加人。
Měi yán kě yǐ shì zūn, měi xíng kě yǐ jiā rén.
Fine words can buy honor. Fine conduct can raise a person above others.
62.4: Rén zhī bù shàn, hé qì zhī yǒu?
So when a person is unmasterful, why abandon them?
62.5: Gù lì tiān zǐ, zhì sān gōng,
When they raise up a child of the sky and install the three ministers,
62.6: Suī yǒu gǒng bì yǐ xiān sì mǎ,
though jade discs go before teams of four horses,
62.7: Bù rú zuò jìn cǐ dào.
better to sit where you are and offer this Tao.
62.8: Gǔ zhī suǒ yǐ guì cǐ dào zhě hé?
What made the ancients honor this Tao?
62.9: 不曰：求以得，有罪以免邪？
Bù yuē: qiú yǐ dé, yǒu zuì yǐ miǎn xié?
Did they not say: seek, and you find; commit a crime, and you are spared?
63.1: Wéi wú wéi, shì wú shì, wèi wú wèi.
Do the not-doing, serve the not-serving, taste the flavorless.
63.2: Dà xiǎo duō shǎo, bào yuàn yǐ dé.
Great or small, many or few, repay resentment with integrity.
63.3: 圖難於其易，為大於其細。
Tú nán yú qí yì, wéi dà yú qí xì.
Map out the difficult while it is easy. Do the great while it is slight.
63.4: Tiān xià nán shì, bì zuò yú yì;
The world's difficult affairs always begin easy.
63.5: Tiān xià dà shì, bì zuò yú xì.
The world's great affairs always begin slight.
63.6: 是以聖人終不為大，故能成其大。
Shì yǐ shèng rén zhōng bù wéi dà, gù néng chéng qí dà.
So the sage never does the great, and so completes their greatness.
63.7: 夫輕諾必寡信，多易必多難。
Fú qīng nuò bì guǎ xìn, duō yì bì duō nán.
Promise lightly and you will be little trusted. Take much to be easy and much will be difficult.
63.8: 是以聖人猶難之，故終無難矣。
Shì yǐ shèng rén yóu nán zhī, gù zhōng wú nán yǐ.
So the sage still finds it difficult, and in the end has no difficulty.
64.1: Qí ān yì chí, qí wèi zhào yì móu.
What is at rest is easy to hold. What shows no sign is easy to plan for.
64.10: Shèn zhōng rú shǐ, zé wú bài shì.
Be as careful at the end as at the beginning, and nothing will be ruined.
64.11: 是以聖人欲不欲，不貴難得之貨；
Shì yǐ shèng rén yù bù yù, bù guì nán dé zhī huò;
Therefore, the sage wants the not-wanting and does not prize rare goods,
64.12: Xué bù xué, fù zhòng rén zhī suǒ guò.
learns to unlearn, brings the crowd back from where they have gone too far,
64.13: 以輔萬物之自然，而不敢為。
Yǐ fǔ wàn wù zhī zì rán, ér bù gǎn wéi.
and supports the countless things in being so of themselves, and never pushes them.
64.2: Qí cuì yì pàn, qí wēi yì sàn.
What is fragile is easy to shatter. What is faint is easy to scatter.
64.3: 為之於未有，治之於未亂。
Wéi zhī yú wèi yǒu, zhì zhī yú wèi luàn.
Handle it before it exists. Order it before it falls into disorder.
64.4: Hé bào zhī mù, shēng yú háo mò;
The tree the width of both arms is born from a hair's tip.
64.5: Jiǔ céng zhī tái, qǐ yú lěi tǔ;
The nine-tiered terrace rises from a heap of dirt.
64.6: Qiān lǐ zhī xíng, shǐ yú zú xià.
The thousand-mile journey begins beneath your feet.
64.7: Wéi zhě bài zhī, zhí zhě shī zhī.
Those who handle it ruin it. Those who grasp it lose it.
64.8: 是以聖人無為故無敗，無執故無失。
Shì yǐ shèng rén wú wéi gù wú bài, wú zhí gù wú shī.
Therefore, the sage does not do, and so ruins nothing, does not grasp, and so loses nothing.
64.9: 民之從事，常於幾成而敗之。
Mín zhī cóng shì, cháng yú jī chéng ér bài zhī.
People always ruin their affairs just short of completing them.
65.1: 古之善為道者，非以明民，將以愚之。
Gǔ zhī shàn wéi dào zhě, fēi yǐ míng mín, jiāng yǐ yú zhī.
The ancients who were masterful at the Tao did not use it to make the people see clearly, but to make them fools.
65.2: Mín zhī nán zhì, yǐ qí zhì duō.
The people are hard to govern because they have too much cleverness.
65.3: Gù yǐ zhì zhì guó, guó zhī zéi;
So to govern a state with cleverness robs the state.
65.4: Bù yǐ zhì zhì guó, guó zhī fú.
Not to govern it with cleverness is the state's good fortune.
65.5: Zhī cǐ liǎng zhě yì jī shì.
Knowing these two is itself the pattern.
65.6: Cháng zhī jī shì, shì wèi xuán dé.
Always knowing the pattern is called profound integrity.
65.7: 玄德深矣，遠矣，與物反矣，然後乃至大順。
Xuán dé shēn yǐ, yuǎn yǐ, yǔ wù fǎn yǐ, rán hòu nǎi zhì dà shùn.
Profound integrity is deep, and far, and turns back together with things, and only then runs with the great current.
66.1: 江海所以能為百谷王者，
Jiāng hǎi suǒ yǐ néng wéi bǎi gǔ wáng zhě,
Rivers and seas can rule the hundred valleys
66.2: 以其善下之，故能為百谷王。
Yǐ qí shàn xià zhī, gù néng wéi bǎi gǔ wáng.
because they are masterful at staying below them. That is how they come to rule the hundred valleys.
66.3: 是以欲上民，必以言下之；
Shì yǐ yù shàng mín, bì yǐ yán xià zhī;
So to rise above the people, you must speak from below them.
66.4: Yù xiān mín, bì yǐ shēn hòu zhī.
To walk ahead of the people, you must put your body behind them.
66.5: 是以聖人處上而民不重，
Shì yǐ shèng rén chǔ shàng ér mín bù zhòng,
The sage stands above, and the people are not weighed down,
66.6: Chǔ qián ér mín bù hài.
stands in front, and the people are not harmed.
66.7: Shì yǐ tiān xià lè tuī ér bù yàn.
So the world gladly pushes them forward and never tires of them.
66.8: 以其不爭，故天下莫能與之爭。
Yǐ qí bù zhēng, gù tiān xià mò néng yǔ zhī zhēng.
Because they do not contend, no one in the world can contend with them.
67.1: 天下皆謂我道大，似不肖。
Tiān xià jiē wèi wǒ dào dà, sì bù xiào.
The world says my Tao is great, and looks like nothing.
67.10: 夫慈，以戰則勝，以守則固。
Fú cí, yǐ zhàn zé shèng, yǐ shǒu zé gù.
Tenderness. Fight with it and you win, guard with it and you stand firm.
67.11: Tiān jiāng jiù zhī, yǐ cí wèi zhī.
When nature would rescue someone, it shields them with tenderness.
67.2: Fú wéi dà, gù sì bù xiào.
Only because it is great does it look like nothing.
67.3: Ruò xiào, jiǔ yǐ qí xì yě fú\!
If it looked like anything, it would long since have been slight.
67.4: Wǒ yǒu sān bǎo, chí ér bǎo zhī:
I have three treasures. I hold them and keep them safe.
67.5: 一曰慈，二曰儉，三曰不敢為天下先。
Yī yuē cí, èr yuē jiǎn, sān yuē bù gǎn wéi tiān xià xiān.
The first is tenderness. The second is frugality. The third is never pushing to be first in the world.
67.6: Tenderness, and so you can be brave.
67.7: Frugality, and so you can be broad.
67.8: 不敢為天下先，故能成器長。
Bù gǎn wéi tiān xià xiān, gù néng chéng qì zhǎng.
Never pushing to be first in the world, and so you can become chief of the vessels.
67.9: 今捨慈且勇，捨儉且廣，捨後且先，死矣！
Jīn shě cí qiě yǒng, shě jiǎn qiě guǎng, shě hòu qiě xiān, sǐ yǐ\!
Now: to abandon tenderness and grab at courage, to abandon frugality and grab at breadth, to abandon the rear and grab at the front. That is death.
68.1: Shàn wéi shì zhě, bù wǔ;
Those masterful in service are not martial.
68.2: The master fighter does not rage.
68.3: Shàn shèng dí zhě, bù yǔ;
The master of overcoming enemies does not engage them.
68.4: Shàn yòng rén zhě, wéi zhī xià.
The master of using people puts themselves below them.
68.5: Shì wèi bù zhēng zhī dé,
This is called the integrity of not contending.
68.6: Shì wèi yòng rén zhī lì,
This is called using people's force.
68.7: Shì wèi pèi tiān, gǔ zhī jí.
This is called partnered with the sky, the pinnacle of the ancients.
69.10: Gù kàng bīng xiāng ruò, āi zhě shèng yǐ.
Therefore, when the armies are evenly matched, the side that grieves wins.
69.2: Wú bù gǎn wéi zhǔ, ér wéi kè;
I do not push to move first. I move second.
69.3: Bù gǎn jìn cùn, ér tuì chǐ.
I do not push an inch into another's ground. I give up a foot of my own.
69.4: This is called marching where there are no ranks,
69.5: baring an arm where there is no arm,
69.6: hauling where there is no enemy,
69.7: grasping where there is no weapon.
69.8: Huò mò dà yú qīng dí,
There is no disaster greater than making light of the enemy.
69.9: Qīng dí jī sàng wú bǎo.
Making light of the enemy nearly costs me my treasures.
7.1: The sky is lasting, the earth enduring.
7.2: Tiān dì suǒ yǐ néng cháng qiě jiǔ zhě,
Sky and earth can last and endure
7.3: because they do not live for themselves,
7.5: 是以聖人後其身而身先，
Shì yǐ shèng rén hòu qí shēn ér shēn xiān,
So the sage puts their body last, and their body comes first;
7.6: wài qí shēn ér shēn cún.
puts their body outside, and their body survives.
7.7: Fēi yǐ qí wú sī xié?
Is it not because they have no private self?
7.8: And so their private self is fulfilled.
70.1: Wú yán shèn yì zhī, shèn yì xíng.
My words are very easy to know, very easy to follow.
70.2: Tiān xià mò néng zhī, mò néng xíng.
In all the world, no one can know them. No one can follow them.
70.3: Yán yǒu zōng, shì yǒu jūn.
Words have an ancestor. Affairs have a ruler.
70.4: Fú wéi wú zhī, shì yǐ bù wǒ zhī.
Only because there is no knowing it do they not know me.
70.5: Zhī wǒ zhě xī, zé wǒ zhě guì.
Those who know me are few. Those who pattern themselves on me are precious.
70.6: Shì yǐ shèng rén pī hè ér huái yù.
Therefore, the sage wears coarse cloth, but carries jade against their chest.
71.1: To know you do not know is highest.
71.2: To not know yet claim to know is sickness.
71.3: Fú wéi bìng bìng, shì yǐ bù bìng.
Only because you are sick of the sickness are you not sick.
71.4: 聖人不病，以其病病，是以不病。
Shèng rén bù bìng, yǐ qí bìng bìng, shì yǐ bù bìng.
The sage is not sick because they are sick of the sickness.
72.1: Mín bù wèi wēi, zé dà wēi zhì.
When the people no longer fear authority, the great collapse comes.
72.2: 無狎其所居，無厭其所生。
Wú xiá qí suǒ jū, wú yàn qí suǒ shēng.
Do not crowd people in their homes. Do not oppress their livelihoods.
72.3: Fú wéi bù yàn, shì yǐ bù yàn.
Only because you do not oppress them do they not tire of you.
72.4: Shì yǐ shèng rén zì zhī, bù zì jiàn;
And so the sage knows themselves and does not display themselves,
72.5: loves themselves and does not hold themselves precious.
72.6: They let go of what is out there and take what is here.
73.1: Bravery in pushing gets you killed.
73.10: Tiān wǎng huī huī, shū ér bù shī.
Nature's net is vast. Its mesh is wide, and nothing slips through.
73.2: Yǒng yú bù gǎn zé huó.
Bravery in not pushing keeps you alive.
73.3: Cǐ liǎng zhě, huò lì huò hài.
Of these two, one benefits and one harms.
73.4: Tiān zhī suǒ wù, shú zhī qí gù?
What nature turns against, who knows why?
73.5: Shì yǐ shèng rén yóu nán zhī.
So the sage still finds it difficult.
73.6: Tiān zhī dào, bù zhēng ér shàn shèng,
The way of nature: it does not contend, yet is masterful at overcoming.
73.7: It does not speak, yet is masterful at answering.
73.8: It does not summon, yet things come of themselves.
73.9: It is unhurried, yet masterful at planning.
74.1: 民不畏死，奈何以死懼之？
Mín bù wèi sǐ, nài hé yǐ sǐ jù zhī?
When the people do not fear death, why try to frighten them with death?
74.2: 若使民常畏死，而為奇者，吾得執而殺之，孰敢？
Ruò shǐ mín cháng wèi sǐ, ér wéi qí zhě, wú dé zhí ér shā zhī, shú gǎn?
Suppose the people always feared death, and I could seize whoever steps out of line and kill them. Who would still push?
74.3: Cháng yǒu sī shā zhě shā.
There is always one who does the killing.
74.4: 夫代司殺者殺，是謂代大匠斫。
Fú dài sī shā zhě shā, shì wèi dài dà jiàng zhuó.
To take their place is to take the place of the master carpenter.
74.5: 夫代大匠斫，希有不傷其手矣。
Fú dài dà jiàng zhuó, xī yǒu bù shāng qí shǒu yǐ.
Of those who carve in place of the master carpenter, few fail to cut their own hand.
75.1: 民之飢，以其上食稅之多，是以飢。
Mín zhī jī, yǐ qí shàng shí shuì zhī duō, shì yǐ jī.
The people go hungry because those over them eat up so much in taxes.
75.2: 民之難治，以其上之有為，是以難治。
Mín zhī nán zhì, yǐ qí shàng zhī yǒu wéi, shì yǐ nán zhì.
The people are hard to govern because those over them will not stop doing.
75.3: 民之輕死，以其上求生之厚，是以輕死。
Mín zhī qīng sǐ, yǐ qí shàng qiú shēng zhī hòu, shì yǐ qīng sǐ.
The people make light of death because those over them want their own lives so rich.
75.4: 夫唯無以生為者，是賢於貴生。
Fú wéi wú yǐ shēng wéi zhě, shì xián yú guì shēng.
Only those who don't use living for doing are worthier than those who hold life precious.
76.1: 人之生也柔弱，其死也堅強。
Rén zhī shēng yě róu ruò, qí sǐ yě jiān qiáng.
In life a person is soft and yielding. In death, hard and strong.
76.2: 萬物草木之生也柔脆，其死也枯槁。
Wàn wù cǎo mù zhī shēng yě róu cuì, qí sǐ yě kū gǎo.
In life the countless things, the grasses and trees, are soft and fragile. In death, withered and dry.
76.3: Gù jiān qiáng zhě sǐ zhī tú,
So the hard and strong are followers of death.
76.4: Róu ruò zhě shēng zhī tú.
The soft and yielding are followers of life.
76.5: 是以兵強則不勝，木強則折。
Shì yǐ bīng qiáng zé bù shèng, mù qiáng zé zhé.
This is why a strong army does not win, and a strong tree snaps.
76.6: Qiáng dà chǔ xià, róu ruò chǔ shàng.
The strong and the big dwell below. The soft and the yielding dwell above.
77.1: Tiān zhī dào, qí yóu zhāng gōng yǔ?
The way of nature: is it not like stringing a bow?
77.2: Gāo zhě yì zhī, xià zhě jǔ zhī;
The high is pressed down, the low is lifted.
77.3: 有餘者損之，不足者補之。
Yǒu yú zhě sǔn zhī, bù zú zhě bǔ zhī.
What is too much is drawn off. What is too little is filled in.
77.4: 天之道，損有餘而補不足。
Tiān zhī dào, sǔn yǒu yú ér bǔ bù zú.
The way of nature takes from where there is too much and mends where there is too little.
77.5: 人之道，則不然，損不足以奉有餘。
Rén zhī dào, zé bù rán, sǔn bù zú yǐ fèng yǒu yú.
The way of people is not like this. It takes from those who have too little and offers it up to those who have too much.
77.6: 孰能有餘以奉天下？唯有道者。
Shú néng yǒu yú yǐ fèng tiān xià? Wéi yǒu dào zhě.
Who has more than enough, and offers it up to the world? Only those who are with the Tao.
77.7: 是以聖人為而不恃，功成而不處，其不欲見賢。
Shì yǐ shèng rén wéi ér bù shì, gōng chéng ér bù chù, qí bù yù jiàn xián.
Therefore the sage acts yet relies on nothing. The work is done, and they do not stay in it. They have no wish to appear exceptional.
78.1: Tiān xià mò róu ruò yú shuǐ,
In all the world nothing is softer and more yielding than water,
78.2: 而攻堅強者莫之能勝，以其無以易之。
Ér gōng jiān qiáng zhě mò zhī néng shèng, yǐ qí wú yǐ yì zhī.
yet at attacking the hard and the strong nothing overcomes it, for nothing can take its place.
78.3: 弱之勝強，柔之勝剛，天下莫不知，莫能行。
Ruò zhī shèng qiáng, róu zhī shèng gāng, tiān xià mò bù zhī, mò néng xíng.
The yielding overcomes the strong. The soft overcomes the unbending. No one in the world fails to know this, yet no one can follow it.
78.4: 是以聖人云：受國之垢，是謂社稷主；受國之不祥，是謂天下王。
Shì yǐ shèng rén yún: shòu guó zhī gòu, shì wèi shè jì zhǔ; shòu guó zhī bù xiáng, shì wèi tiān xià wáng.
So the sage says: whoever takes on the shame of the state is the keeper of the soil and the grain. Whoever takes on the ill omen of the state is the ruler of the world.
78.5: Words on the mark seem like their opposite.
79.1: 和大怨，必有餘怨；安可以為善？
Hé dà yuàn, bì yǒu yú yuàn; ān kě yǐ wéi shàn?
Settle a great grudge and some grudge always remains. How could that count as masterful?
79.2: 是以聖人執左契，而不責於人。
Shì yǐ shèng rén zhí zuǒ qì, ér bù zé yú rén.
So the sage grasps the left half of the tally and never asks for the other.
79.3: Yǒu dé sī qì, wú dé sī chè.
Those with integrity keep the tally. Those without integrity keep score.
79.4: Tiān dào wú qīn, cháng yǔ shàn rén.
The way of nature plays no favorites. It stays with those who are masterful.
8.1: The most masterful are like water.
8.10: In affairs, masterful at what can be done.
8.12: Only because it does not contend
8.2: Shuǐ shàn lì wàn wù ér bù zhēng,
Water is masterful at benefiting the countless things and does not contend.
8.3: chǔ zhòng rén zhī suǒ è,
It dwells in what the crowd loathes,
8.4: and so is nearly the Tao.
8.5: In settling, masterful at choosing ground.
8.6: In the heart, masterful at staying deep.
80.1: 小國寡民。使有什伯之器而不用；
Xiǎo guó guǎ mín. Shǐ yǒu shí bǎi zhī qì ér bù yòng;
A small state, few people. Let the people have tools that do the work of ten, of a hundred, yet no need to use them.
80.2: Shǐ mín zhòng sǐ ér bù yuǎn xǐ.
Let the people find death heavy, and not move far away.
80.3: 雖有舟輿，無所乘之；雖有甲兵，無所陳之。
Suī yǒu zhōu yú, wú suǒ chéng zhī; suī yǒu jiǎ bīng, wú suǒ chén zhī.
Though there are boats and carts, there is no call to travel in them. Though there are armor and weapons, there is no call to march them out.
80.4: Shǐ mín fù jié shéng ér yòng zhī.
Let the people go back to keeping their records in knotted cord.
80.5: 甘其食，美其服，安其居，樂其俗。
Gān qí shí, měi qí fú, ān qí jū, lè qí sú.
They find their food sweet, their clothes fine, their houses restful, their ways a pleasure.
80.6: 隣國相望，雞犬之聲相聞，民至老死，不相往來。
Lín guó xiāng wàng, jī quǎn zhī shēng xiāng wén, mín zhì lǎo sǐ, bù xiāng wǎng lái.
Neighboring states lie within sight of each other. They hear each other's chickens and dogs. The people grow old and die and never once go next door.
81.1: Xìn yán bù měi, měi yán bù xìn.
Trustworthy words are not pretty. Pretty words are not trustworthy.
81.2: Shàn zhě bù biàn, biàn zhě bù shàn.
Those who are masterful do not argue. Those who argue are not masterful.
81.3: Zhī zhě bù bó, bó zhě bù zhī.
Those who know have not heard it all. Those who have heard it all do not know.
81.4: 聖人不積。既以為人己愈有，既以與人己愈多。
Shèng rén bù jī. Jì yǐ wéi rén jǐ yù yǒu, jì yǐ yǔ rén jǐ yù duō.
The sage does not hoard. Having done for others, they have more. Having given to others, they have more still.
81.5: 天之道，利而不害；聖人之道，為而不爭。
Tiān zhī dào, lì ér bù hài; shèng rén zhī dào, wéi ér bù zhēng.
The way of nature benefits and does not harm. The way of the sage acts and does not contend.
9.1: Rather than keep filling what you hold, stop.
9.10: The work done, the body withdraws. This is the way of nature.
9.2: Rather than keep filling what you hold, stop.
9.3: Hammer a point ever sharper, and it will not keep for long.
9.4: Hammer a point ever sharper, and it will not keep for long.
9.5: Gold and jade fill the hall, and no one can guard them.
9.6: Gold and jade fill the hall, and no one can guard them.

notes.1:
**道可道 → *The Tao that can be made a way*.** **The book opens on a paradox, and the paradox is in the grammar.** 道可道，非常道 (*dào kě dào, fēi cháng dào* — "the Tao that can be *dào*-ed is not the ever-present Tao") prints one graph three times in six characters: the name, the same word acting as a verb, and the name again. The line turns its own central word back on itself, so the ever-present Tao is denied in its own word. To keep the paradox, the English has to hold three things together:
- **the name**, *Tao*, which the line also teaches means *way*;
- **the turn**, the middle 道 being the same word, made to act;
- **the voice**, the Tao being what the verb is done to.

**How the second 道 is a verb.** Classical Chinese does not inflect; a word's job is its position. 可 (*kě* — can, may) always takes a verb and makes it passive — 可食 (*kě shí*) is *can be eaten*, edible — so whatever stands after 可 is an action. 道 (noun: the Tao) · 可 (can be) · 道 (verb: *dào*-ed). The next line is the same shape, and English can follow that one: 名可名, *the name that can be named*. The move was ordinary in Laozi's century — the 論語 (*Lúnyǔ* — the *Analects*) has 君君，臣臣 (*jūn jūn, chén chén* — "let the lord be a lord, the minister a minister") — so it is not a joke on two meanings but **one word turned on itself.** 說文 (*Shuōwén*) gives the noun as 所行道也 (*suǒ xíng dào yě* — "the road that is walked"), and the verb grows from it: to tread a way, to lead along it (later split off as 導, *dǎo* — to guide), to tell it in words.

**Why the voice is the point.** 可 + verb puts the subject on the receiving end (`glossary/ke-可.md`). The Tao is not doing the *dào*-ing; it is what would be *dào*-ed. So someone other than the Tao does it: a person who lays it out as a route, a course, a program to follow. The Tao's own manner is 自然 (*zì rán* — so of itself), and ch 25 ends on it: 道法自然, *"the Tao models itself on being what it is."* Being made a way is not something the Tao does of itself. It is done to the Tao, by human hands, and the line says that what comes of it is not the ever-present Tao. An English in another voice loses this. *The Tao that can become a way* makes the change the Tao's own, a claim about what the Tao does, where the Chinese speaks of what is done to it.

**How the English makes it a verb.** *Tao* is locked as a name (`glossary/dao-道.md`), and *"the Tao that can be Tao'd"* is not English. So the middle 道 is rendered by **what the name means**, and *made* turns it into a verb: *made a way*. *Made* is supplied scaffolding (`process/principles/supplied-verb-is-scaffolding.md`); *way* is 道's own word. The line reads *Tao · way · Tao*, carrying the word all three times the Chinese prints it, and a reader learns what the name means before learning anything else. *Made a way* is the ordinary English passive of *make it a way*, as in *she was made a judge*, and nothing in it is spare. **The precedent is already in the book**: where 道 is an ordinary way and not the name, this manuscript renders it *way* — 天之道 and 天道 (*tiān zhī dào*, *tiān dào* — the way of heaven) are *"the way of nature"* at ch 9, 47, 73, 77, 79 and 81; 人之道 (*rén zhī dào*) is *"the way of people"* at ch 77; 聖人之道 (*shèng rén zhī dào*) is *"the way of the sage"* at ch 81. The lock forbids *the Way* as a stand-in for the Tao; a lowercase *a way* is the common noun doing its own job.

**Where other translations let it go.** English versions keep one or two of the three and give up the rest. What goes most often is the turn.
- **The middle 道 becomes speech.** Waley (1934), *the Way that can be told of*; Lau (1963), *the way that can be spoken of*; Feng and English (1972), *the Tao that can be told*. The word appears twice, not three times, and the paradox becomes a claim about language: the Tao cannot be put into words. That is the next line's subject (名可名, *the name that can be named*), so the opening line is folded into its partner.
- **A different word takes the middle.** Legge (1891), *the Tao that can be trodden*, keeps the road and the passive, but the reader hears two words where the Chinese has one.
- **The turn is kept by translating the name.** Carus (1898), *the Reason that can be reasoned*, turns the word on itself exactly as the Chinese does, but only by making the Tao *Reason*: the Logos of John 1:1, which the Chinese Union Bible renders with 道 (`process/overlay-audit.md`).
- **The walker is kept, and the name is lost.** Le Guin (1997), *the way you can go*, names the person the line implies, but the Tao is gone from the sentence and *go* is a different word from *way*.

None of these keeps all three. *The Tao that can be made a way* does: the name, the same word in the middle, and the passive.

**What the line says, and who says it with us.** *Made a way* — laid out as a route, a course, a program to follow:
- 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) glosses the second 道 with the noun itself: 謂經術政教之道也 — *"it means the **way** of classical learning and political instruction."* A Tao that can be laid out and taught.
- 韓非 (*Hán Fēi*, the oldest reader we carry): the ever-present has 無定理 (*wú dìng lǐ* — "no fixed pattern"), 是以不可道也…然而可論 — *"therefore it cannot be **dào**-ed… and yet it can be discussed."* On a reading of *spoken* that sentence contradicts itself; on *made a way* it is exact. A fixed course is the thing it cannot be.
- 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) is half with us: 可道之道，可名之名，指事造形，非其常也 — *"the Tao that can be dào-ed and the name that can be named point at affairs and **make forms**; they are not its constant."* 造形 (*zào xíng* — to make a form) is the making; 指事 (*zhǐ shì* — to point at affairs) is the designation, and that half we lose.

**And the two lines do two things, as the Chinese does.** Line 1 asks whether the Tao can be made a way; line 2, 名可名, whether it can be named. A speech reading folds the first into the second.

**What it costs, named rather than hidden.** **The speech sense goes.** It is real: the 詩經 (*Shījīng* — the Book of Songs) has 中冓之言，不可道也 (*"the words of the inner chamber cannot be told"*), and 河上公 closes his own gloss on this line with 不可稱道 (*bù kě chēng dào* — "it cannot be spoken of"). **This is a line where the commentators diverge and the English picks a side** — the route reading of 河上公's lemma gloss and 韓非, over 王弼's pointing — which `divergence-stays-open` would refuse. It is taken here on Shalom's call, because the route reading is the one that lets the English keep the paradox. *Made a way* is also longer than 道可道's three syllables, and a little longer than its partner line, *the name that can be named*. And it brushes the English idiom *make a way*, to clear a path; in this sentence the Tao is what is made, so the idiom does not take hold.

**What was refused, and why.**
- ***spoken*** — *speak* is 言 (*yán* — speech)'s English at ch 5, 17, 27, 56, 66 and 73, and it makes ch 1 rhyme in English with ch 56's 知者不言 (*"Those who know do not speak"*), where the Chinese uses a different character. It also makes 韓非 contradict himself.
- ***told*** — the strongest alternative: it carries speech *and* directions (*tell someone the way*). It loses the word *way*, which is the point of the line.
- ***followed*** — the book says the Tao *is* followed, and praises it: 惟道是從 (*wéi dào shì cóng* — ch 21, *"follows only the Tao"*), 從事於道 (*cóng shì yú dào* — ch 23). *Follow* is also 從 (*cóng*)'s, 隨 (*suí*)'s and 徒 (*tú*)'s word already.
- ***conceived as Tao*** — keeps three *Tao*s, but moves the act inside the head, where no commentator puts it; turns line 1 into line 2's naming; and is seminar register.
- ***mapped*** is 圖 (*tú* — to plan)'s word at ch 63; ***traced*** chimes with 跡 (*jì* — footprints) at ch 27, *"leaves no tracks."*
- ***become a way*** — lighter, and wrong in voice. It has the Tao turn into a way of itself, where the Chinese has the Tao made one. It breaks the parallel with 名可名, which English keeps passive. And *become* is the English of a verb the line does not print, 為 (*wéi* — to do, to serve as, to become).
- ***made into a way*** — the same passive with a spare word. *Made* already does the work *into* was added to do.

*The Literal column for this line was changed with it — it read "can be spoken", which was one reading set down as the gloss.*

**同謂之玄。玄之又玄 → *"Together, they are called dark. / Dark, and dark again"*: the chain, kept.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-11-14.)* *(was: "Together, they are called profound darkness." and a stanza break before "Dark, and dark again".)* **The Chinese passes 玄 (*xuán* — dark) from one line into the next, and the English now does too.** 同謂之玄 (*tóng wèi zhī xuán* — "together they are called dark") ends on 玄, and 玄之又玄 (*xuán zhī yòu xuán* — "dark, and dark again") opens on it: a chain, 頂真 (*dǐng zhēn* — "capping"), as at ch 6. *Profound darkness* spent two abstract words on one character, so the link was nearly kept and not quite, and a blank line then cut it (`WORKLIST.md` T3-15; `process/form-audit.md` → *The page*, rule 3). **The glossary's own register already said *dark* for this line**: 玄 standing alone and named takes the colour word, because the image is doing the work and *profound* abstracts it (`glossary/xuan-miao-玄妙.md` → *Working register*).

**This is where the chapter's mystery lives, and why it needs no word *mystery*.** Wang Bi on this line: 玄者冥也，默然無有也 — *"玄 is the dim dark: silent, nothing there."* It is called 玄 only 取於不可得而謂之然也 — *"because it cannot be grasped, and so it is called that."* And if it were fixed as one 玄, 則是名則失之遠矣，故曰玄之又玄也 — *"that would make it a name, and miss by far; so it says 'dark, and dark again.'"* The doubling exists so the word cannot harden into a name. Said with one plain *dark*, then *dark* twice more, the English deepens the way a dyer re-dips silk, which is what English readers have heard as *mystery*. *Mystery* itself stays refused: it says the thing cannot be known, where line 5 has just said to observe it (`glossary/xuan-miao-玄妙.md`).

**The cost.** *Dark* alone is starker than *profound darkness*, and a reader may hear only absence of light. The next line's doubling, and 玄's uses elsewhere (玄牝 *the dark female*, 玄德 *profound integrity*), give it its depth. 同 (*tóng* — together, the same) keeps *Together*; see the note on line 7, below.

**眾妙之門 → *"the gate of all subtlety"*: one English for 妙 in both its slots.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-11-14.)* *(was: "the gate of all subtleties.")* 妙 (*miào* — subtle) appears twice. In line 5, 以觀其妙 (*yǐ guān qí miào* — "to observe its subtle"), it is owned by 其 (*qí* — its): one quality, the subtlety of what the still gaze looks at. In line 9 it is counted by 眾 (*zhòng* — the many). **When a character takes two slots in one chapter, the English has to survive both** (`notes/translation.md` → *同 finished*, the ch 56 rule). *Subtlety* does: *its subtlety*, then *all subtlety*, with *all* carrying 眾. The echo is now word for word, as `glossary/xuan-miao-玄妙.md` asks: what you glimpse in stillness is what the gate opens onto.

**Why not the plural.** *Subtleties* leans in English toward *nuances*, the fine points of an argument, which no commentator reads here. Wang Bi has 妙者微之極也 — *"妙 is the faint at its limit."* Heshang Gong has 妙，要也 — *"妙 means the essential."* *The gate of subtlety* and *the gate of the subtle* were weighed the same day; both drop 眾. **The gate stays *of*, not *to*:** 之 (*zhī* — 's) is possessive and carries no direction, and the commentators split on which way the gate faces. Wang Bi has the subtle things coming out: 眾妙皆從同而出 — *"the many subtle things all come out from the same."* Heshang Gong has a person going in: 是謂知道要之門戶也 — *"this is called the door to knowing the Tao's essential."* *Of* holds both. **And *gate*, not *gateway*:** 門 (*mén* — gate) is *gate* at ch 6 and ch 10, a gate that opens and closes (天門開闔 — "the gate of the sky opens and closes").

**The cost.** Wang Bi's reading is distributive, 皆 (*jiē* — each, all): each subtle thing comes out on its own. The singular softens that plurality. *All* keeps the many in it, but not as countable things.

**常無欲，以觀其妙 → *"Ever desireless, you can observe its subtlety"*: a capacity, not a command.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-11-14.)* *(was: "Ever desireless, observe its subtlety; / Ever desiring, observe its boundaries.")* 以 (*yǐ* — thereby, by this means) says what the state makes possible. **Both commentators read it as a capacity:** Wang Bi: 故常無欲空虛，可以觀其始物之妙 — *"so, ever desireless and empty, one **can** observe the subtlety where things begin"*. Heshang Gong: 人常能無欲，則可以觀道之要 — *"if a person can always be desireless, then they **can** observe the Tao's essential."* The back-translation audit's blind readers of the old line came away with an order (`process/back-translation-audit.md` → *Minor*, ch 1).

- ***You*** is scaffolding the commentators supply: Heshang Gong's 人 (*rén* — person), Wang Bi's 空虛 (*kōng xū* — empty), a state of the seer. *"In the absence of desire, its subtleties can be observed"* was weighed the same day and declined: the passive makes the subtlety a property of the thing and leaves no one to be desireless, and *in the absence of* turns 常 (*cháng* — ever) into a moment. The general *you* is the book's voice elsewhere: ch 47, *"Without leaving home, you know the whole world."*
- ***Ever* opens both lines**, as 常 opens both in the Chinese, so the word is heard where it repeats. 故 (*gù* — so) is left without English for that reason; the *Yongle Dadian* prints no 故 on this line (`sources/variants.yaml`). **Settled for this chapter**: whatever the book-wide 故 decision (`WORKLIST.md` T3-12) makes *So*, line 5 stays bare, as ch 23's 故飄風 (*gù piāo fēng* — "so a squall") does. *"So, ever desireless"* was proposed and withdrawn: it buried *ever* behind a connective.
- ***Present* is not carried into these lines.** *"Ever present and desireless"* would bring in the mindfulness register of *being present*, which the line does not hold, and would break the match with chs 32, 34 and 37 (below).

**The cost.** *You* is not printed. 徼 (*jiào*) is the next note.

**常有欲，以觀其徼 → *"Ever desiring, you can observe its direction."*** *(Shalom's call, 2026-11-14.)* *(was: "observe its boundaries.")* **徼 is a heading, not an edge.** The graph has the road radical, 彳 (*chì* — a step), and our *Shuowen* defines it 循也 — *"to go along, to go round."* *Border* is a later sense, 邊徼 (*biān jiào* — the patrolled frontier), and no commentator we carry reads it here. Both read a destination:

- **Heshang Gong:** 徼，歸也。常有欲之人，可以觀世俗之所歸趣也 — *"徼 means returning. A person ever desiring can observe where the worldly are **heading**."* *Direction* is this reading exactly.
- **Wang Bi:** 徼，歸終也 — *"徼 is where things return to their end"* — and 故常有欲，可以觀其終物之徼也 — *"so, ever desiring, one can observe the 徼 where things end."* He pairs it with line 5's 始物之妙 (*"the subtlety where things begin"*), so that 妙 and 徼 are beginning and end: 萬物始於微而後成 — *"the countless things begin in the faint, and then are completed."*

**Why *direction*.** It keeps the Chinese parallel, 其 (*qí* — its) + a noun in both lines, so the frame 以觀其▢ (*yǐ guān qí ▢* — "thereby observe its ▢") is whole: *its subtlety / its direction*. And it is a quality the eye follows while it happens, as *subtlety* is, not a product read off afterwards. **It does not rank the two ways of seeing.** Desire reads which way things are going, which is real knowledge, and the next line has both gazes *emerge together*.

**What was weighed and why it lost.**
- ***boundaries*** and ***limits*** rest on the later frontier sense, and both make what desire sees the surface of things, a ranking the Chinese does not make; *limits* adds *limitation*.
- ***manifestations*** reads 徼 as 皦 (*jiǎo* — bright, *Shuowen*: 玉石之白也, *"the white of jade"*), the same sound element and ch 14's *bright*. Five Latinate syllables, and the two-realm metaphysics this edition refused at ch 21 (*the manifest realm*). The Mawangdui reading here is said to be 所噭 (*suǒ jiào*), variously taken as 皦, 竅 (*qiào* — an opening) or 徼; **unverified, and not in `sources/variants.yaml`**, so nothing rests on it.
- ***ends***, ***outcomes***, ***results***, ***consequences*** — Wang Bi's end, but each is a product, not something watched, and *observe its ends* is awkward English; *consequences* brings a moral warning; *its ends* can be heard as *its purposes*, a Tao with aims.
- ***where it leads***, ***where it ends***, ***where it goes*** — natural, but each breaks the noun parallel; *leads to* is 乃 (*nǎi* — then)'s supplied English in ch 16's chain, and *where it ends* is 極 (*jí* — the utmost)'s exact phrase at ch 58.

**The cost.** The line sides with Heshang Gong over Wang Bi's explicit end, 終 (*zhōng* — end): a direction is a heading, not an arrival, and Wang Bi's beginning-and-end pairing of 妙 and 徼 is implied rather than said. Both commentators gloss with 歸 (*guī* — returning), so this is a lean, not a split. *Direction* can also mean guidance (*under the direction of*); in a line about seeing, it reads as heading. **The Literal column for lines 5–9 was changed with these notes**; it had glossed 妙 as *mysteries* and 玄 as *profound*, the pre-lock English this chapter was revised to refuse.

**此兩者，同出而異名，同謂之玄 → *"These two emerge together, but differ in name. / Together, they are called dark."*** *(Shalom's call, 2026-11-14.)* *(was: "These two have the same origin, but differ in name.")* **同 (*tóng*) stands twice in two lines, and both times before a verb:** 同**出** (*tóng chū* — "together emerge") and 同**謂** (*tóng wèi* — "together are called"). In that slot it is an adverb, and **one English has to survive both** (`notes/translation.md` → *同 finished*, the ch 56 rule). The old lines had *the same* in one and *Together* in the other. *The same* cannot be an adverb here: *emerge the same* means *turn out identical*, which is the flattening the line refuses, so every attempt to keep it had to turn 同 into a noun. ***Together* survives both slots**, and it keeps the two as two: it needs two, and never says they are one. Ch 23's *the same* (`WORKLIST-CLOSED.md` T2-25) was settled for 同於X (*tóng yú* — "the same as X"), a different slot, and stands.

- **出 (*chū* — to come out) is *emerge*,** as at ch 50's 出生入死 (*chū shēng rù sǐ*), *"Emerge into life, enter into death,"* and among its senses in the atlas. ***Origin* is retired.** It turned a plain verb into a noun nobody printed, and it blurred 出 with 始 (*shǐ* — beginning): line 3's *beginning*, and ch 52's only other *origin*, which renders 始. On Wang Bi's reading that collapses the chapter, since his two are 始與母 (*shǐ yǔ mǔ* — "the beginning and the mother"), and *same origin* has the beginning come out of a beginning.
- **The commentators.** Heshang Gong reads 同 as an adverb, *alike*: 同出人心 — *"come out alike from the human heart"*; 同受氣於天 — *"alike receive breath from the sky."* Wang Bi reads it as a noun, the shared source: 同出者，同出於玄也 — *"'come out the same' means coming out the same from the dark"*, and on line 9, 眾妙皆從同而出 — *"the many subtle things all come out from the same."* **This line follows Heshang Gong's grammar.** Wang Bi's source is implied, not said: what both call dark is what the two come out of (Wang Bi: 始母之所出也 — *"that from which the beginning and the mother come out"*; Heshang Gong: 玄，天也 — *"the dark is the sky"*).
- **Weighed the same day and declined:** *Their sameness is called dark* — it says the two are the same, where the line says they share a source and differ, as twins share a womb. *What is the same is called dark* and *These two emerge from the same* — Wang Bi's noun, exact, but elliptical, and a supplied *from*. *They both arise together* — *arise together* is ch 16's 並作 (*bìng zuò* — arise side by side), and *They both* breaks 此兩者 (*cǐ liǎng zhě* — these two), *these two* at chs 65 and 73. *Their togetherness* — the register of greeting cards, and it calls their bond dark where both commentators call the source dark.

**The cost.** *Together* against *differ* is a weaker opposition than *same* against *different*, the antonym pair the Chinese prints; *but* carries the contrast. *Together* can suggest the two emerge at one moment; both commentators' co-emergence allows it. Closes `WORKLIST.md` T2-27: its worry, that *together* reads as *jointly they form one thing*, is answered by line 7, where the two emerge together *and differ in name*.

**For the reader: 常, the one word four times.** 常 (*cháng* — ever) stands four times in this chapter: *the ever-present Tao*, *the ever-present name*, *ever desireless*, *ever desiring*. The oldest copy, the Mawangdui silk, writes all four with a still older word, 恒 (*héng* — ever), drawn in the earliest script as **a crescent moon between two lines**: the constancy of the moon, which changes shape every night and never once fails to come back. Not a thing outside time. Change that keeps its appointment.

The oldest reader, Han Fei (d. 233 BCE), says what the word is doing in line 1. What rises and falls, what flourishes first and fades after, cannot be called 常. Then the turn: 常者無攸易，無定理 — *"the ever-present has nothing it changes into, and **no fixed pattern**,"* 非在於常所 — *"it is in no fixed place,"* 是以不可道也 — *"and that is why it cannot be made a way."* **What is constant here is what is not fixed.** A way that has been made — a teaching, a method, a program to follow — has a fixed shape, and so it rises and falls like everything else. The Tao that is there every time has no fixed shape, and so it does not fade. That is the paradox of the first line.

And the chapter does not leave the word with the Tao. Lines 5 and 6 give it to the one who looks: *ever* desireless, *ever* desiring. Elsewhere the book uses these same words for the Tao's own condition: *"The Tao is ever nameless"* (ch 32), *"The Tao is ever non-doing"* (ch 37), and in ch 34, word for word, 常無欲 — *"Ever desireless, it can be named small."* So the instruction underneath the chapter is this: **to see what is ever-present, you become ever something yourself**, and what you become is what the Tao already is.
notes.10:
**Five of this chapter's Englishes were attached to characters that are not in it.** *(2026-09-01, Pass D, `WORKLIST.md` T1-1.)* 全 (*quán* — whole), 萬物 (*wàn wù* — the countless things), 鑑 (*jiàn* — a mirror) — **all zero occurrences here** — plus 無為 and 無知, each wearing the other's English. **Every one is invisible to `check_locks`**: its evidence gate keys off the character being *present*, so a locked English on a chapter that lacks the character cannot fire. `--english` is the only thing that finds this class.

**The book's two great negations had swapped lines.** 愛民治國，**能無知乎** read *"can you lead without doing?"* and 明白四達，**能無為乎** read *"can you be unknowing?"* — four lines apart, each carrying the other's word. *Unknowing* has not left the chapter; **it has moved up two lines onto 無知**, where ch 3 settled it. 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) reads this 無知 as **無以智**, *"without cleverness,"* and links it outright to ch 19's 絕聖棄智: 玄覽無疵猶絕聖也，治國無以智猶棄智也 — *"'the dark mirror without blemish' is like 'cut off sagacity'; 'governing the state without cleverness' is like 'discard cleverness.'"* 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) reads it differently — 治國者布施惠德，**無令下知**也, *"one governing the state spreads kindness and lets none below know of it"* — but that requires supplying a second party the grammar does not have. **無為 keeps the lock's word**, used predicatively as ch 37 already does (*"The Tao is ever non-doing"*).

**疵 was not mistranslated; it was deleted.** 能無疵乎 asks *"can you be without blemish?"* — 說文解字: **病也**, under 疒, the sickness radical. Ours asked *"can you see what truly is?"*, which renders nothing at all. **國 (*guó* — the state) was dropped too**, from 愛民治**國**, in a chapter whose whole second couplet is about governing.

***"The dark mirror" was challenged and survives, and my objection to it was wrong.*** *(Caught by Shalom.)* I had argued that *mirror* renders 鑑 / 監 (*jiàn*), which our text does not print — the ch 52 襲/習 fault. **說文 defeats that: 覽，觀也。从見、監，監亦聲** — *"覽 means to look at; from 見 (to see) **and 監**, and 監 is also the phonetic."* **監 is a constituent of the very character we print**, and 監 is a person bending over a water basin at their own reflection, the ancestor of 鑑. The mirror is the character's own base, not an imported variant. **And the draft *"the dark seeing"* failed on the verb**: 滌除 (*dí chú* — wash and clear) needs a washable surface, and 河上公 says exactly what gets washed — 當**洗其心**使潔淨也, *"wash the heart and make it clean."* **疵 confirms it**: a blemish sits on a surface, and 王弼's gloss is more surface-like still — 能不以物**介**其明，**疵之**其神乎, *"can you keep things from **coming between** you and your clarity, or **blemishing** your spirit?"* **The cost, recorded:** both commentators gloss 覽 with *activity* verbs (觀 · 覽知萬事 · 極覽), so **the mirror is a reading of the graph, not of the lemma.**

**專 → "gathering," on the graph against a commentator.** 說文 makes 專 a **spindle whorl** — 一曰專，紡專 — thread wound onto a core. 河上公 agrees: 專守精氣使不亂 (*"concentrate and guard the essential breath so it is not disordered"*). **王弼 goes the other way** — 專，**任**也, *"專 means to entrust oneself to"* — nearly the opposite. **The character decides**, per the tie-breaking order, and the divergence is recorded rather than averaged.

**氣 → "breath," not "life energy."** 河上公's reading here is bodily and concrete: 呼吸精氣 (*"breathing the essential 氣"*), and 治身者愛氣則身全 (*"one who governs the body loves the 氣 and the body is whole"*). *Energy* is the register ch 28 has just been cleared of. **Locked book-wide, 2026-11-01, Shalom's call** (`glossary/qi-氣.md`): *breath* in all three lines, 10, 42 and 55.

**能為雌乎 → "can you be the hen?"** — the rider ch 28 left. 為 is *serve as / be*, not *embody*, and *"the flow of the feminine"* invented **flow** and abstracted the bird away. **王弼 ties the hen straight to this chapter's last question:** 雌**應而不倡，因而不為** — *"the hen responds and does not lead off; she goes along and does not act."* 河上公 pairs her with the other female graph — 治身當如**雌牝**安靜柔弱 — and gives the political half: 治國應變和而不唱, *"governing the state, respond to change harmoniously and do not lead off."* **The line's own graph is contested**; see `notes/manuscript.md`.

**嬰兒 → "an infant," closing T2-22.** It read *"a newborn"* here and *"an infant"* at ch 20 and ch 28, while 赤子 (*chì zǐ* — a red child) reads *"a newborn"* at ch 55. One character, one English, each way. 王弼: 能若嬰兒之**無所欲**乎 — *"can you be like an infant that has no wants?"*

**能如嬰兒乎 → "can you be an infant?", following every witness, closing T2-76.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-11-01.)* *(was: "can you be like an infant?")* Both Mawangdui silks, the Siku Wang Bi lemma and Heshang Gong's lemma all read 能嬰兒乎 (*néng yīng ér hū* — "can you be an infant?"), without 如 (*rú* — like). Our base stands alone, and both commentators supply the likeness in their glosses, which may be where it came from. The chapter's other questions ask for the thing itself, as *"can you be the hen?"* does. **The base text and the Source table keep 如; only the verse follows the witnesses**, the practice at chapters 21, 41, 42, 47 and 53. `notes/manuscript.md`.

***"Things," not "the countless things."*** 生之畜之 has **no antecedent anywhere in this chapter** — 萬物 does not occur — and both commentators supply one: 河上公 道生**萬物**而畜養之, 王弼 則**物**自生. So the English must supply one too, and **物 (*wù* — things)** is what the glossary carries as the secondary character, where 萬物 is a locked compound this chapter does not contain.

**長 → "growing," which also repairs ch 51.** 長而不宰 read *"leading without mastering,"* but 長 (*zhǎng*) here is the causative *make grow* — and **ch 51 already renders it *"grows"* four lines earlier** (長之育之 → *"grows and raises them"*), so that chapter was running two Englishes for one character in one stanza. 河上公: 道**長**養萬物，不**宰割**以為器用 — *"the Tao grows and nourishes them and does not **butcher** them into **vessels** for use"* — 宰 with 割 and 器, both of them ch 28's words. 說文 on 宰: **辠人在屋下執事者。从宀从辛** — *"a criminal under a roof doing service,"* from a roof and 辛, the tattooing knife. **Ch 51 takes the same change**, since T2-15 closed these two as a matched pair and they must stay matched.

**魄 → "aliveness": *"Housing your aliveness."*** *(Shalom's word, 2026-10-15. Full argument: `glossary/po-魄.md`.)* *(was: "housing your soul," from 2026-09-01.)* **"Housing" did the watchlist's work with a verb, and the noun was still the watchlist's word.** Every early source puts 魄 on the body's side: 杜預 (*Dù Yù*) 魄，**形**也, *"魄 is the form"*; 孔穎達 (*Kǒng Yǐngdá*) **附形之靈**為魄, *"the life clinging to the form,"* and then a newborn's senses, moving limbs and cry, 初生之時，耳目心識，手足運動，啼呼為聲，此則魄之靈也; 鄭玄 (*Zhèng Xuán*) **耳目之聰明**為魄, *"the sharpness of ear and eye."* **Aliveness** carries all three, comes in degrees as the 魄 does (左傳 魂魄**強**), and carries no theology, no breath and no energy. **The couplet now names the two halves the 禮記 pairs**: 氣也者神之盛也，魄也者鬼之盛也, *"breath is the fullness of spirit, the 魄 the fullness of ghost,"* aliveness in line 1 and the breath in line 2, and the infant line 2 asks for is 孔穎達's own picture of the 魄. ***Life force*, *vitality* and *vigor* were refused**: the first is the popular English for 氣; *vital* is 精's and 氣's (21, 42, 55); *vigor* leans toward virility, which is 精's at ch 55.

**Two claims below are corrected, and stay where they were made.** The pair 魂魄 is **not a Han invention**: the 左傳 has it (人生始化曰魄，既生魄，陽曰魂) and so does 韓非子 解老 on ch 60 (魂魄去而精神亂). What is Han in 河上公's gloss is the **organ map**, 魂在肝，魄在肺. And **"housing" does not follow 王弼**: his 營魄 is the house and the person dwells in it (言人能處常居之宅, *"a person who can dwell in the house where they always live"*). The direction *housing* takes, a person holding the 魄, is 王逸 (*Wáng Yì*)'s on 楚辭 遠遊's 載營魄而登霞兮 (抱我魂靈而上升也, *"embracing my soul I rise"*) and 河上公's 當愛養之, *"you must cherish and nourish it."* The verb stands on 營's graph and on those readings.

**載營魄 → "housing your soul," and the decisive fact is a character that is not in this book.** *(Shalom's line, 2026-09-01.)* *(was: "Being embodied"; then a draft, "carrying the body's soul.")* **魂 (*hún* — the cloud-soul) occurs zero times in all 81 chapters.** 魄 and 營 each occur once, both here. So 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*)'s reading — 營魄，**魂魄**也…魂在肝，魄在肺, *"營魄 is the 魂 and the 魄… the 魂 is in the liver, the 魄 in the lungs"* — is a **Han two-soul system imported onto a text that never uses the other half of the pair.** That is why a draft rendering *"the body's soul"* read as jargon: it answered a question neither English nor this book asks.

**王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) needs nothing imported, and the graphs back him.** 載猶**處**也。營魄，人之**常居處**也。一，人之**真**也 — *"載 is like 'to dwell.' 營魄 is a person's constant dwelling place. 一 is a person's genuine self."* **A person's constant dwelling place is the body.** 說文解字: **營，市居也。从宮** — a walled residence; **魄，陰神也。从鬼白聲** — the yin spirit, with a ghost for its radical, the one billeted in the flesh, not the one that leaves; **載，乘也。从車** — to ride, with a cart in the graph. **So 營魄 is not two souls. It is one thing: the quarters your animating part is camped in.**

**The rendering does the watchlist's work with a verb rather than a label.** CLAUDE.md flags 精/魄 → *soul*, and the corrective for 魄 is that it is the **corporeal** one. *"The body's soul"* said so with a possessive and read as jargon; **housing** says so with an action, and it renders 營's own graph. ***These*** carries 能無離乎 onto the two things the line has just named, which is how both commentators read it: 王弼 抱一清神，**能常無離乎**; 河上公 抱一使**不離於身**.

**Four candidate Englishes were blocked, and it is worth recording which.** *Spirit* is 神 (*shén*)'s at ch 6, 39, 60. *Flesh* is free and Pauline — *the flesh* against *the spirit*, Romans 8 — the hymn test. *Quarters* is taken four lines below by this chapter's own 四達. And ***body* is 身 (*shēn*)'s** at ch 13, 54 and 76; 身 does not occur in ch 10, so nothing clashed inside the chapter, but the noun was avoided rather than borrowed. ***Embodying* was refused too**: it is this manuscript's junk-drawer verb, wearing 為 at ch 28 until this pass removed it and still wearing 執 at ch 35 (`WORKLIST` T1-12).

**This also gives the chapter its floor.** Question 1 is the bodily ground, question 2 the breath, then the mirror, then governing, then response, then non-doing — **it moves outward from the flesh**, and the old *"Being embodied"* left it starting nowhere.

**天門 keeps *the gate of the sky*, and its strain case gains a second reading.** 河上公 gives both: 天門謂**北極紫微宮** (*"the Purple Tenuity Palace at the north pole"*) and, for the body, 天門謂**鼻孔**，開謂喘息，闔謂呼吸也 — *"天門 means the **nostrils**: 開 is breathing out, 闔 breathing in."* 王弼 takes neither: 天門謂天下之所由從也 — *"that by which the world proceeds."* Logged at `notes/translation.md` → 天 family, strain cases.

**The en-dash stays.** `WORKLIST` T4-3 is deferred, and this line's fault was its words, not its punctuation. *(T4-3 closed 2026-10-25: the dash stays, its subject named on both sides, and is now the em-dash, Shalom's call.)*
notes.11:
**Rewritten 2026-09-05** (Pass D, `WORKLIST.md` D11 · T3-3). Full reasoning in `notes/translation.md`; the 埏/挻 fork in `notes/manuscript.md`.

- **The repetition is the argument.** 當其無 and 有X之用 repeat letter for letter three times; only 車 / 器 / 室 change. Our English changed everything else instead, so the click never happened. Eleven lines for eleven, the middle line of every stanza identical.
- 無 → **in what is not there** (its locked wording), not *emptiness* — 虛 is not in this chapter. 有 → **presence**, not *filled space*. This is the chapter `glossary/wu-you-無有.md` names as its own test case.
- 當 → **right where**, not *through*. 說文 田相值也, fields matching: it locates, it is not instrumental.
- 利 → **advantage**, the covered lock in `wu-you-無有.md`, **applied here for the first time anywhere** — the word had zero occurrences in the book. 利 wants its own entry: nine chapters, three jobs.
- **No check could find the central fault**: both tools indexed segments into a *set* of chapter numbers, so three occurrences in one chapter collapsed to one and were dropped as "not shared". **This chapter is where that was found and repaired** — `DISCOVERIES.md` §6 · `PLAN.md` → *What Chapter 11 taught the tools*.
notes.12:
**故去彼取此 → "They let go of what is out there and take what is here."** *(2026-08-30, Pass C, `WORKLIST.md` T2-13.)* *(was: "Rejects the hungry gaze, chooses gut wisdom.")* 故去彼取此 (*gù qù bǐ qǔ cǐ* — "therefore let go of that and take this") is a **stock closing tag** — five characters, the last line of ch 12, ch 38 and ch 72, and **彼 (*bǐ* — that, yonder) occurs nowhere else in the book.** All three now carry the same English, ch 72's, where the axis was first argued.

**The old line translated the referents and deleted the deixis.** 彼 and 此 (*cǐ* — this) are **spatial** words — *yonder* and *here* — and the chapter's own pair is 目 (*mù* — eye) against 腹 (*fù* — belly): the organ that reaches outward and can never be filled, against the organ that is already here and can be satisfied. 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) states it exactly: 為腹者，以物養己；為目者，以物役己 — *"one who acts for the belly uses things to nourish themselves; one who acts for the eye uses things to enslave themselves."* 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*): 去彼目之妄視，取此腹之養性 — *"let go of that, the eye's reckless looking; take this, the belly's nourishing of one's own nature."*

***"Gut wisdom" was forbidden by this chapter's own locked entry.*** `glossary/xin-心.md` carries a paragraph headed *"Why 'belly' and not 'gut'"* which names *trust your gut* as the import that must not happen — and **cites ch 12 as its evidence.** The chapter used the word anyway, one line below its own correctly rendered *belly*. Two things were wrong with it: it invents 智 (*zhì* — knowing, wisdom), a character not in this chapter, and it swaps the chapter's actual contrast — **inner need against outer craving** — for a modern one, *intuition against analysis*. It is the same failure as *"here, now"* at ch 21: see [`imported-register`](https://github.com/opencosmos-ai/taoteching/blob/main/process/principles/imported-register.md).

**The checker could not see it, and now can.** 腹 sits inside 心 (*xīn* — heart) as a `covers:` character, and **`covers:` records a `render:` but never a `forbidden:` list** — so *gut* was unforbidden book-wide. `"gut"` is now on 心's `forbidden:` list, which fires here because 心 is present in this chapter.

***What "the hungry gaze" was worth, and why it still goes.*** It was the most vivid phrase in the chapter. But 目 is already *"the eye"* in the line directly above, so the image is not lost — only not repeated — and *hungry* was borrowed from 河上公's gloss 妄視, a commentator's word rather than the text's.

**難得之貨 → "rare goods."** *(2026-08-30, Pass C, `WORKLIST.md` T2-14.)* *(was: "Rare treasures make actions corrupt.")* **"Treasures" is 寶 (*bǎo*)'s word** — ch 62, 67 and 69 — and 寶 never appears in this chapter. 說文 reads the two apart: 寶 is 珍也, a *precious thing*, its graph 宀 (*mián* — a roof) over 王 (jade) and 貝 (*bèi* — a cowrie shell), **a hoard that does not move**; 貨 (*huò*) is 財也, *property*, 貝 under 化 (*huà* — a body turning over), **a shell that changes hands**. Locked to *goods* book-wide: `glossary/huo-貨.md`.

**This chapter is why "scarce" was refused for 難得.** *Scarce* means a need going unmet — and the chapter's whole hinge is 為腹不為目 (*wèi fù bù wèi mù*), 腹 (*fù* — the belly), the organ that **can** be satisfied, against 目 (*mù* — the eye), the one that cannot. **Scarcity is a fact about bellies. This chapter is about eyes.**

**令人行妨 → "Rare goods hinder people's conduct."** *(2026-10-20, Shalom's call, `WORKLIST-CLOSED.md` T1-26.)* *(was: "Rare goods make actions corrupt.")* 令人行妨 (*lìng rén xíng fáng* — "makes a person's conduct hindered"). Three words moved, and the stanza with them.

**人 (*rén* — a person) is restored in all five lines.** The stanza says 令人 (*lìng rén* — "makes a person's") five times, and the English had dropped 人 every time: *"makes the eyes blind."* That is a claim about eyes. The Chinese is about what happens to a person, and it chose to say so when 五色盲目 (*"colors blind the eyes"*) would have been grammatical. Both commentators read the organs as a person's own faculties, spoiled by that person's own use. 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*): 夫耳目口心皆順其性也…反以傷自然 — *"ears, eyes, mouth and heart are all meant to follow their nature… instead they are turned to wounding what is so of itself."* The silks press harder, binding three of the organs to the person with 之 (*zhī* — 's): 使人之行, 使人之口, 使人之耳. And five lines of 人 set up the turn to 聖人 (*shèng rén* — the sage, literally "sage person"). Rendered *people's*, which `glossary/min-民.md` licenses for 人 while keeping *the people* for 民. **Caught by Shalom.**

**行 (*xíng*) → conduct, as at ch 62** (美行, *"fine conduct"*). 行 starts as walking, 說文 人之步趨也 — *"a person's walking and hurrying"* — and extends to how a person goes. Both commentators take the extension here. 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) marks the sound 行下孟反, which gives *xìng*, the conduct reading, and glosses 行傷身辱 — *"conduct is harmed and the person disgraced."* 王弼's 塞人正路 — *"blocks a person's straight road"* — is Mencius's road, 義，人之正路也, *"duty is a person's straight road"* (孟子 (*Mèngzǐ*) · 離婁上, not vendored): a road of conduct, not of feet. **Not *actions*:** *act* and *action* belong to 為 (*wéi* — to do) and 作 (*zuò* — to arise) across seventeen other lines, including this chapter's next one, *"the sage acts for the belly."* *Steps* was proposed and refused; it kept the root and lost the extension. `glossary/xing-行.md`.

**妨 (*fáng*) → hinder.** 說文 妨，害也。从女方聲 — *"to harm; 女 for its meaning, 方 for its sound."* The commentators split: 王弼 reads *block* (塞), 河上公 reads *harm* (妨，傷也), and 說文 sides with harm. **We follow 王弼**, which is also the word's ordinary sense, and record that the English does not carry 河上公's harm. *Corrupt* fit neither of them. Blocked and harmed are done to conduct from outside; *corrupt* is a verdict on the person. Even the Mencian road does not license it: being kept off the straight road happens to you, and corruption is something you become.

**The graph has a seam in it.** 女 (*nǚ* — woman) carries the meaning: a word for harm filed under woman, as 說文 also files 妄 (*wàng* — reckless; 亂也, "disorder"), the 妄 of ch 16. In a book whose highest image is the female, that is the incidental male default inside a single character. **Named here, not rendered.** It is also the pull the old line was half obeying: the English 女 reaches for is *tempt, lure, seduce*, and *corrupt* was on the way there. The sound component may carry sense too: 方 (*fāng*) also stands in 防 (*fáng* — 說文 隄也, "a dike"), a bank thrown across water. No source found says 妨 and 防 are one word, so that is a suggestion, not evidence.

**The fifth *makes* is carried by the verb.** Four lines say what an organ becomes: 盲 (*máng* — blind), 聾 (*lóng* — deaf), 爽 (*shuǎng* — spoiled), 發狂 (*fā kuáng* — breaking out wild). 妨 is the one thing *done to* a faculty. *"Make people's conduct hindered"* is not English, and a transitive verb is how English says *cause to be hindered*, so 令 (*lìng* — makes) is rendered by *hinder* in this line alone. The English shifts where the Chinese does. *(Hobbled* was proposed to keep *make*, and refused as too esoteric.*)*

**Hinder came back from ch 66.** It was 害 (*hài* — harm)'s English in one line there, borrowed through the compound 妨害 (*fáng hài* — to obstruct); 害 reads *harm* in its other four chapters (35, 56, 73, 81). Ch 66 now reads *"the people are not harmed,"* and *hinder* belongs to 妨. `notes/translation.md` → *Ch 66 · 處前而民不害*.

**The silks** read 使 (*shǐ* — to cause) for 令, put the five lines in another order, write 妨 by its sound (方 in silk A, 仿 in silk B), and close 是以聖人之治也 — *"therefore the sage's governing"* — which is ch 3's frame. Recorded in `sources/variants.yaml`; the one that bears on meaning is argued in `notes/manuscript.md` → *Ch 12*.
notes.13:
**Rewritten 2026-09-05** (Pass D, `WORKLIST.md` D13 · T1-10 · T3-7). Full reasoning in `notes/translation.md`; two forks in `notes/manuscript.md`.

- **One word per character, and the argument appears.** 身 ×6 had four Englishes, 患 ×4 had two, 貴 ×3 had two. Now **身 → body ×6 · 患 → trouble ×4 · 驚 → shock ×5 · 貴 → prize ×3 · 下 → below ×1.**
- 無身 → **if I had no body** (T1-10). *The separate self dissolves* was Advaita, and it broke **有/無 on the one line in the book where the pair is applied to a person**. 王弼: 歸之自然也.
- **The closing couplet — Shalom's call, Reading B.** 以身為天下 → *the body as a way to serve the world*, supported by ch 26's 以身輕天下 (same 以身 + verb + 天下 shape) and by 河上公: 能愛其身，**非為己也**，乃欲為萬民之父母. **The cost is 王弼's whole chapter**, which reads it as immunity rather than devotion: 不以寵辱榮患損易其身，然後乃可以天下付之也. Reading A was drafted and withdrawn because **in English it lands as egotism** — a construal can be defensible in the Chinese and still arrive as a different claim.
- 寄/託 → **trusted with**, both (T3-7). Near-synonyms; **王弼 swaps them in his own commentary**, and 說文 defines each by the other. Two English verbs in a parallel frame read as an escalation the text does not make. 貴/愛 stay varied, because 王弼 *does* distinguish those: 無以**易**其身 (will not sell it) against 無物可以**損**其身 (will not let it be harmed).
- 若驚 → **a shock**, not *cause alarm*: 若 is *like*, not *cause*. 是謂 → **this is what is meant**, not *this is why* — 謂 is *to call*, and eight other chapters read *"This is called."*
- **Open:** T2-1 — 身 is settled inside this chapter only; it still reads three ways at ch 7, 9, 44 and 54.
notes.14:
**搏之不得 keeps *touch*.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-11-19.)* `glossary/de-shi-得失.md` proposed *cannot get it*, for one English across 得, and withdrew it: the triad is sight, hearing and touch, and *invisible · inaudible · intangible* depends on it. *Grasp* stays out, as below: it is 執's, and this chapter needs *grasp* for 執古之道, the holding it asks for, against the reaching that comes away with nothing.

**能知古始，是謂道紀 → "If you can know the ancient beginning, / this is called the thread of the Tao."** *(Shalom's call, 2026-09-24. `WORKLIST.md` T1-11.)* *(was: "Know the primordial source, / The thread of the Tao.")* **古始 (*gǔ shǐ* — the ancient beginning) had become *the primordial source*.** *Source* is on 母 (*mǔ* — mother)'s forbidden list and is the register the naturalistic razor strips; 古 is plainly *ancient* and 始 is *beginning*, the word ch 1 gives it. **Two characters had also gone missing.** 能 (*néng* — can) is the plain modal in 31 of its 32 lines. 是謂 (*shì wèi* — "this is called") is the formula this chapter already renders twice above (*"This is called the elusive"*). 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) reads the line as possibility, not command: 故雖在今可以知古始也, *"so although it is now, one can know the ancient beginning."* 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) prints 以知古始 (*yǐ zhī gǔ shǐ* — "by this, know the ancient beginning"). That drops 能 and makes the knowing follow from the line before. The English follows our base's 能. 紀 (*jì*) keeps *thread*: 說文 **絲別也**, *"the separate end of a silk thread,"* the end you pick up to unwind the rest.

**其上不皦，其下不昧 — 昧 → *murky*.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-09-20. `WORKLIST.md` T2-54.)* Rode in with ch 41's 明道若昧, since one character takes one English. The line had read *"a dark bottom"*, and *dark* belongs to 玄 (*xuán*), which is absent from this chapter. 皦 (*jiǎo*) keeps *bright* and still has no entry.

**執古之道 → "Grasp the ancient Tao," and 搏 gives back the word it had taken.** *(2026-09-08, Pass E, `WORKLIST.md` T2-19 — the holding family.)* 執 (*zhí*) is 說文 **捕罪人也**, *"to seize a criminal"* — a reaching hand and a set of manacles — and it is locked to *grasp* (`glossary/zhi-執.md`).
