- **The close is *neither* jade *nor* stone**, not *"not jade but stone."* One 不欲 governs both clauses, and both commentators say so outright. *Instead* was supplied.
- **Two strains, named:** 琭琭/珞珞 have no 說文 entries; 靈 → *numinous* fails the pointing test. 神 and 靈 want an entry together · T2-37.
notes.4:
*Rewritten 2026-08-31 — the first Pass D chapter. `WORKLIST.md` T1-2, and it closes T2-14c's deferred question. Four things were wrong and one whole line was missing.*

**道沖 was inverted, and given 器's word.** 沖 (*chōng*) is **empty**; 不盈 (*bù yíng*) is **never fills**. The line read *"The Tao is a vessel that never runs empty"* — **both halves flipped**, and *vessel* is locked to 器 (*qì*). 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) states the mechanism: 沖而用之，用乃不能窮…滿以造實，實來則溢 — *"empty, and using it, the use cannot be exhausted… fill it to make it solid, and when solidity comes it overflows."* **Emptiness is the capacity; the old line made the Tao a reservoir that never drains, which is the opposite metaphysics.** 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) reads 或 as 常 (*cháng* — always): 道常謙虛不盈滿.

**Why 沖 can mean *empty* at all** *(2026-11-15)*: read as itself it is 涌搖也, *"surging and shaking."* The empty sense is 盅 (*zhōng* — an empty vessel), which shares its sound part 中. Xu Shen's copy of this very line wrote 道盅而用之 (the *Shuowen*, under 盅：器虛也, *"a vessel's emptiness"*), and Fu Yi writes 盅. Heshang Gong reads the word as 中 (*zhōng* — middle) instead, 其用在中 (*"its use lies in the middle"*); the English keeps Wang Bi's reading. `glossary/chong-沖.md`, `notes/manuscript.md` → Ch 4.

**淵 was dropped, and with it a frame.** 淵兮，似X and 湛兮，似X are **two matched frames** around the quatrain; the English rendered only the second, so the symmetry was invisible and the 湛 line arrived as a new topic with nothing to rhyme against. 說文解字 on 淵: 回水也…左右，岸也，中象水皃 — *"eddying water; the left and right are the banks, the middle depicts the water."* A pool of turning water between two banks. 河上公: 道淵深**不可知**也 — *"deep as an abyss and cannot be known"*, which is what **fathomless** means.

**湛 is not "still" — it is submerged.** 說文: **沒也**, *"to sink under"* (水 with 甚 for sound). That matters, because it makes the line **answer the quatrain** rather than start a new thought: the Tao has just blunted its own edge, harmonized its light and become the same as the dust, and now it is **under**.

**兮 (*xī*) never hedges, and that decided where the doubt goes.** Across its twelve occurrences the pattern is **[asserted quality] 兮，[hedged predicate]** — ch 15 runs seven in a row (豫兮**若**冬涉川, 猶兮**若**畏四鄰, 儼兮**其若**客). So 湛 is **stated**; 似 hedges 存 alone. An earlier draft read *"Submerged. It seems to be."*, which let English's ellipsis reach backward and take *submerged* as the missing complement — putting the doubt on the submersion, which the Chinese asserts. *(Caught by Shalom.)* Both frames now take a comma, matching how the manuscript already handles 兮 at ch 15.

**存 is not "exist" and not "remain."** It is **being-still-there**, against 亡 (*wáng* — to perish): ch 41 pairs them, 若存若亡, and 河上公 glosses this line 長存**不亡**. *Remain* imports a **depletion frame the first line explicitly denies** — leftovers are what survive consumption, and 用之或不盈 says the Tao is not consumed. *Exist* is unavailable: it already serves 有 (*yǒu*) at ch 32, 39 and 64, and 有 is half a locked pairing. **"It seems to be here"** reads in English as *presence*, not location, which is exactly 存. *(Shalom's line.)*

**吾不知誰之子 was not translated at all** — *"I do not know whose child it is."* The book's one flat admission of ignorance about the Tao's parentage, and it was missing. **It is also the only unhedged line in the chapter**, which is why the closing line can follow it as a hedge without going slack.

**帝 was erased, and that erasure deleted the chapter's argument.** See `glossary/di-帝.md`, now locked. The short version: **帝 (*dì*) is not a god this text is importing — it is a god the text is demoting**, and English translation has only ever inflated it (*God*, *the Lord*, *the Creator*) or deleted it, as we had. 帝 reaches Laozi as **the Shang high power that the Zhou deposed and replaced with 天** (*tiān*) when they invented 天命 (*tiān mìng* — the Mandate of Heaven) to justify the conquest; and by 288 BCE living kings were grabbing the title (東帝 / 西帝), with 秦始皇帝 fixing it to the throne in 221. **Read with 誰之子 above it, the line takes the floor out of legitimation:** authority in this culture descends — the Zhou king rules as 天子, *the child of 天* — and a thing with **no parent** standing **before any god** leaves the chain of descent with nothing at the bottom.

***"Any god," not "the high god."*** The definite article asserts a **singular supreme deity at the top of a hierarchy**, which the scholarship on Shang religion has not settled — and it smuggles that in where no reader weighs it, since articles are not words people notice. **The definite article confers status exactly as a capital does.** *Any* also makes the stronger claim the argument needs: precede only *the* high god and a claimant can answer *"my line descends from a different power."* *(Caught by Shalom.)*

**象 is the comparison, not the noun — and this was argued the other way first.** 象 (*xiàng*) is the book's word for **image** at 無物之象 (14), 其中有象 (21), 執大象 (35) and 大象無形 (41), and 似 is the dedicated hedge, already used twice here — so a draft read the last line *"An image, older than any god."* **The grammar defeats it: in all four noun uses 象 is marked as one, by 之, by 有, or by 大, and here it stands bare before a noun phrase, which is verb-plus-object.** Both commentaries read it as a comparison. Ch 4 is also 象's first appearance, so an English *image* would land where no reader can hear the thread.

**One sentence, not two, because English cannot strand a subject.** The four phrases are one sentence in the Chinese — 挫其銳，解其紛，和其光，同其塵 — with the subject elided, as classical Chinese elides freely. A draft broke them into two sentences and left the second without one: *"Dims its own light, merges with the dust."* That is the fault standing rule 3 names in its reasoning about em-dashes, reached with a full stop instead of a dash. The couplet now runs on a comma with a **lowercase continuation line**, which is this manuscript's convention at ch 2, 7, 16, 19, 25, 31, 34, 43, 47, 48 and 49. *(Caught by Shalom.)* **Ch 56 needs no such repair**, because its version is imperative and each line stands as a complete sentence — the nouns match, the grammar differs because the subject does.

**同 → *the same as*, not *merges with*.** *(2026-09-03, `WORKLIST.md` T2-26, the rider ch 23 left.)* 同 (*tóng* — the same) is the antonym of 異 (*yì* — different), printed against it in ch 1's own clause 同出而異名, and ch 23's six occurrences were repaired first. **河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) glosses this very line 不當自别殊也** — *"one should not set oneself apart as separate and distinct"* — where 别 (*bié* — to separate) and 殊 (*shū* — distinct) are 同's opposites. **王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) makes the couplet a matched pair**: 和其光 is 無所**特顯** (*"nothing specially displayed"*), 同其塵 is 無所**特賤** (*"nothing specially despised"*) — do not stand out above, do not hold yourself apart from below. ***Merges with* read as self-dissolution**, losing yourself into dust; the Chinese says do not consider yourself too good for the common muck. **The cost:** *is the same as the dust* is the one stative in a run of actions (*blunts, untangles, harmonizes*), which is the price of one English for one character across ch 4, 23 and 56.

**和其光 → *"harmonizes its light,"* not *"dims its own light."*** *(Shalom's call, 2026-11-18, `WORKLIST-CLOSED.md` T2-84.)* *Dim* was Heshang Gong's word, the result of his 當和之使闇昧 (*dāng hé zhī shǐ àn mèi* — "one should harmonize it, making it dark and dim") with his verb dropped, and it was an instruction he wrote for a person. This chapter's subject is the Tao, which is Wang Bi's reading, and Wang Bi dims nothing: 和光而不汙其體 (*hé guāng ér bù wū qí tǐ* — "it harmonizes with the light and does not soil its substance"). Decided against so that a commentator's word does not stand in for the character. `glossary/he-和.md`; `notes/translation.md` → *Ch 4, 56 · 和其光*.

**誰之子 → "whose child," never "whose descendant."** 說文解字 on 孫 (*sūn* — grandchild): **子之子曰孫。从子从系。系，續也** — *"the 子 of a 子 is called 孫; from 子 and 系 (to connect), and 系 means to continue."* **Chinese separates the generations, and has a word for descendants — 子孫 — which this book uses at ch 54** (子孫以祭祀不輟). Ch 4 declines it and writes bare 子, whose 說文 entry is simply 象形, a **pictograph of an infant**. The distinction is load-bearing: **天子 (ch 62) is the *child* of 天, one generation, direct** — and ch 52 pairs 母/子, mother and child. *Descendant* would soften the claim into *"its ancestry is long and untraceable"*, when the claim is that **there is no parent at all.**

**The quatrain keeps the Tao as its subject**, closing the question deferred from Pass C. With 道沖 restored the subject chain runs unbroken — Tao → 淵兮 → the four lines → 湛兮 → 吾不知 → 象帝之先 — which is 王弼's reading: 銳挫而無損…同塵而不渝其真, *"the sharp is blunted and nothing is lost… it shares the dust and does not alter its truth."* Ch 56 keeps its imperative; the nouns match, the verb forms differ, and the divergence is now argued rather than inherited.

**Not attested at Guodian** (~300 BCE) — this chapter rests on the silks and later. The 或/若 fork at 湛兮似或存 is recorded in `sources/variants.yaml`: 河上公 reads 似若存, and the Siku 王弼 carries 〔案或一作若〕. Both are hedges of the same force, so nothing turns on it.
notes.41:
**昧 (*mèi*) → *murky*, not *dark*.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-09-20. `WORKLIST.md` T2-54.)* 說文 gives the character both senses — 昧爽，旦明也 for the compound (*daybreak*), 一曰**闇**也 for the graph alone (*shut-in dark*) — so *dark* was defensible about 昧 and **unavailable** all the same: it is 玄 (*xuán*)'s English across six lines, including ch 1's 玄之又玄, *"dark, and dark again."* There is no 玄 in this chapter, so the old line made a reader hear the book's deepest word where the text has only the plain antonym of 明. *Dim* is 和 (*hé*, ch 4 and 56) and 冥 (*míng*, ch 21); *faint* is 微 (*wēi*); *dull* is 爽 and 悶. **The chime with 濁 (*zhuó* — *muddy*, ch 15 and 49) was weighed and accepted as resonance rather than an invented link** — the two are distinct enough to stand apart. 雲 (*yún* — cloud) occurs nowhere in the book, so *clouded* was free too and was declined for this.

**And the English must not settle the commentators, who diverge here.** 王弼: 光而不耀, *"bright but not dazzling"* — the light is present and merely unshowy, and he is quoting ch 58 at it. 河上公: 明道之人若**闇昧**，無所見, *"one of the clear Tao seems dark and obscure, as if seeing nothing"* — genuine obscurity. *Murky* holds both: a murky light is still light, and you cannot see through it.

**大器晚成 — our base prints 晚成, and the English follows the witnesses.** 王弼's text reads 晚成 (*wǎn chéng* — "completed late"); Mawangdui A reads 免成 and Guodian 曼成, both **"never completed."** We follow the witnesses, because *never* completes the parallel the other three lines make — 無隅 (no corners), 希聲 (barely heard), 無形 (no form) — each *"the great X lacks its defining mark."* Recorded in `sources/variants.yaml`; reasoning in `notes/manuscript.md`.

**The 建言 catalogue rebuilt, one saying per line.** *(2026-09-06.)* 故建言有之 (*gù jiàn yán yǒu zhī*) introduces a **quotation** — 河上公: 建設也，設言以有道, *"建 is to set up; sayings set up so as to have the Tao"*; 王弼: 建猶立也. What follows is twelve proverbs, and our English had packed them onto five lines while changing shape as it went: *"Bright Tao seems dark"* with no article against *"The highest integrity seems **like** a valley"* with one and an inserted *like*. **`--formulas 41` shows the chapter is almost nothing but frames** — ▢士聞道 ×3, ▢道若▢ ×3, ▢德若▢ ×2, 大▢無▢ ×2, and 大▢若▢ five times across **this chapter and ch 45 together**. A catalogue rendered as prose stops being a catalogue.

**大白若辱 → "The great white seems disgraced."** *(Was: "true purity seems soiled.")* Three faults in four characters. **大 had been replaced by *true***, which is a breach of the lock at `glossary/da-大.md` that **no check can catch** — every rule keys off a forbidden word, and this one is an absence. **白 (*bái*) is *white*, not *purity*** — an abstraction where the Chinese has a colour, and *purity* is separately forbidden for 樸 (*pǔ*). And **王弼 reads the line straight into ch 28**: 知其白守其黑，大白然後乃得 — *"know the white, hold to the black; only then is the great white attained"* — quoting 知其白，守其黑 verbatim. Ch 28 renders those *"Know the white, hold to the black,"* so *"true purity"* had severed a link the commentator states outright. 辱 (*rǔ*) → **soiled** here, against *disgrace* at ch 13 and ch 28 — a licensed split, argued below.

### 大白若辱 → "The whitest white seems soiled" — an English overlay removed

*(2026-09-07, Shalom's call.)* An intermediate rendering read **"The great white seems disgraced."** It was right about the Chinese and wrong about the English.

**The Chinese carries no racial content, and the question is worth answering with evidence.** 白 and 黑 meet in only one place in the book, ch 28's 知其白，守其黑, and 河上公 glosses the pair outright: 白以喻**昭昭**，黑以喻**默默** — *"白 figures **being conspicuous**; 黑 figures **being unnoticed**."* **It is a figure for visibility, and the instruction is 守其黑 — hold to the black.** 說文 agrees on both graphs: 白 is 西方色也。**陰**用事 (the **yin** colour, of autumn and the west), and 黑 is 火所熏之色也, *"the colour of what fire has smoked"* — **soot**. **There is also no 大黑, and could not be:** the 大▢若▢ frame never pairs opposites, it pairs a thing with the look of its own deficiency — 大方無**隅**, 大成若**缺**, 大白若**辱**. 黑 is not a positive in the frame; it is the hiding place.

**But *"the great white"* is a fixed phrase in English** — *great white hope*, coined for a white challenger to Jack Johnson, and *great white hunter* — and it imports to the reader a reading the Chinese does not contain. This edition exists to strip overlays the English adds; the hymn test and the pointing test both missed this one because both are aimed at theology.

**"The whitest white"** removes the phrase, reads naturally, and doubles 白 the way English intensifies a colour. **The cost, which is real and is the reason this note exists: 大 reads as an intensifier here and as *great* in the four lines of block 3** — 大方, 大器, 大音, 大象 — eleven lines below, inside the same catalogue. A reader cannot see that all five share a character. **That is a deliberate exception to the lock at `glossary/da-大.md`, taken because the alternative ships a line that says something the text never said.** It also touches the question that entry leaves open — whether the whole 大▢若▢ frame wants a superlative — which must still be settled across ch 41 and ch 45 together, not from this line.

**辱 → "soiled" here** rather than *disgrace*, on 河上公's warrant in this very line: 大潔白之人若**汙辱**，不自彰顯 — *"a person of great cleanness-and-whiteness is as though **soiled**, not displaying themselves."* At ch 28 辱 pairs with 榮 (*róng* — glory) and is social standing; here it is a mark on a surface. *(Corrected 2026-10-25: ch 28 now follows the silks' 白 (*bái* — white), so 辱 is* soiled *there too. The split is by partner: soiled beside white (28, 41), disgrace beside favor or as a consequence (13, 44).)* 說文 gives 恥也, shame, from a graph about **missing the ploughing season** and being punished at the field's boundary.

**夷 (*yí*) → "level," not "smooth."** 王弼: 大夷之道因物之性，**不執平以割物**，其平不見，乃更反若纇㘨也 — *"the great level Tao follows the nature of things and does not grasp levelness to cut them; its levelness is not visible, so it looks instead like unevenness."* 割 (*gē* — to sever) ties this to ch 28's 大制不割. **夷 is polysemous across the book** and this is not ch 14's 夷, which is the unseeable one of the three (名曰夷).

### 建 flexes, and this is the argument — do not relitigate it

**建 (*jiàn*) occurs twice in this chapter and takes two Englishes on purpose:** 故**建**言有之 → *"the **established** sayings"*, and **建**德若偷 → *"**Sturdy** integrity."* *(Settled 2026-09-07, Shalom's call.)*

**The character is one thing.** 說文: **立朝律也**。从**聿**从廴 — *"to establish the laws of the court,"* from 聿 (*yù* — a writing brush) and 廴 (*yǐn* — to stride). 王弼 glosses it plainly: 建猶立也, *"建 is 立 — to set up."* 河上公 reads 建言 compositionally too: 建設也，設言以有道, *"建 is to set up; sayings set up so as to have the Tao."*

**They were unified to *established* first, and the unification had to be undone**, because it made the second line unreadable. *"Established integrity"* collapses in English into **long-standing** — a reputation, which is the opposite of what the line says. The saying needs *fully built* against *looks idle*; **建言** needs *received body of maxims*. One English cannot be both, and the consistency was bought at the price of the sense.

**The grammar differs, which is what licenses the flexion.** 建言 is a **fixed compound** — maxims, a received corpus — where 建德 is 建 **modifying a noun**. This is the same licensed-flexion pattern as 事 (*shì* — affairs / to attend to) and 弱 (*ruò* — yielding / *yield*): the register holds, the word bends with the grammar.

**The cost, recorded rather than hidden:** a reader cannot see from the English that these two lines share a character. The chapter notes are where that lives; the verse cannot carry it.

**廣 → "broad."** *(2026-11-15, Shalom's call, setting aside the call below. Was: "Boundless integrity seems not enough.")* One English for 廣 in both its chapters, the hall's own width: a hall too broad to fill looks empty, which is Wang Bi's 不可滿 (*bù kě mǎn* — "cannot be filled"). *Boundless* removed the hall's walls to explain the paradox, and it could not stand at ch 67. `glossary/guang-廣.md`.

**Superseded: 廣 → "boundless," not "broad."** *(2026-09-07, Shalom's call.)* *Broad* states a width without implying abundance, so *broad → not enough* read as no paradox at all. **Boundless says why it seems insufficient: there is no edge to arrive at** — which is 王弼's argument exactly, 廓然無形，**不可滿也**. *(Runner-up: **ample**, which literally means more-than-enough, so *"ample… not enough"* is a flat contradiction — sharper as wordplay, but it only states the paradox where *boundless* explains it.)*

**建德 → "sturdy," and the reason is in the section below.** *Sturdy* sets a solidly-built thing against *slack* and the tension reads at once. **Its cost:** 建 is the **act** of erecting and *sturdy* is the resulting property, so the building is implied rather than named.

**廣德若不足 and 建德若偷 are a matched pair, and the pairing is architectural.** 說文 on 廣: **殿之大屋也**。从**广**黃聲 — *"a great hall of a palace,"* on 广 (*yǎn* — a roof). **Both characters build.** One is the span of the hall, the other the setting-up of the code, and each saying pairs the thing with the look of its own deficiency. **廣 — the hall so wide it can never be filled looks empty:** 王弼, 廣德**不盈**，廓然無形，**不可滿也**, *"broad integrity does not fill; open and formless, it cannot be filled"* (不盈 is ch 15's word, and 盈 is 滿器, a filled vessel); 河上公, 德行廣大之人**若愚須不足**也. **建 — the code so well established that nobody enforces it looks unenforced:** 王弼, 建德者因物自然，**不立不施**, *"sets nothing up and dispenses nothing"*; 河上公, 建設道德之人**若可偷引使空虛**也, *"as though one could rob them and empty them out."* **Extent produces the appearance of deficiency; structure produces the appearance of sloth.** With 上德若谷 above them the 德 sayings are three, not two.

**⚠ `--formulas` missed the third one.** ▢德若▢ reported ×2 (上/谷, 建/偷) and did not catch 廣德若不足, because 不足 is two characters and the finder matches whole comma-segments. That is `WORKLIST.md` T5-13, confirmed here on a live line.

**不足 → "not enough,"** carrying ch 35's settled rendering rather than *insufficient*.

**質真 → "substantial truth."** *(Was "the most solid truth" — the superlative was invented.)* 王弼: 質真者**不矜其真**，故渝 — *"the substantially true does not boast its truth, and so seems to change."*

### Open, and not settled here

**明 (*míng*) reads "clear," which the lock does not license in so many words.** `glossary/ming-明.md` locks 明 to *clear-seeing / clarity* and lists ch 41 among its chapters — and the entry's own body glosses this very line as *"the clear path seems dim."* *Bright* was worse: it is 皦 (*jiǎo*)'s word at ch 14 (*"a bright top"*), so the old line had two characters wearing one English. **The entry needs an adjectival flexion stated in its frontmatter, or this line needs a different word.** *(That entry also glosses 道 as **path** here, which `glossary/dao-道.md` rejects — the glossary-self-check hole, `WORKLIST.md` T5.)*

**夷 and 希 both run back to ch 14, which is where the book names them.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-09-10 — `WORKLIST.md` T2-52.)* 視之不見，名曰夷 and 聽之不聞，名曰希 give the two as *"the invisible"* and *"the inaudible"* — the meanings rather than the words, chosen for that chapter's legibility, with 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) supplying both readings (無**色**曰夷 · 無**聲**曰希). **This chapter is the strongest argument against that choice, and it was made anyway:** 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) defines 希 here by quoting ch 14 outright, 聽之不聞名曰希, so 大音希聲 and 名曰希 are one word by his own hand. The connection is carried in the notes instead of in ch 14's verse.

**希 (*xī*) is left as "barely heard."** 王弼 defines it by quoting ch 14 outright — 聽之不聞名曰希 — so 大音希聲 and ch 14's 名曰希 are **the same word**, and ours reads *the inaudible* there. 希 runs six chapters with four Englishes and is TRIAGE 14b; the graph is 爻 (crossed threads) over 巾 (cloth), **loosely woven fabric you can see through**. Not settled inside a chapter review.

**Settled 2026-11-15:** 廣 (*guǎng*) once read "boundless" here and "reach far" at ch 67. It is now *broad* in both (`glossary/guang-廣.md`, `WORKLIST-CLOSED.md` T2-45, T2-81).

**王弼 explains 大音 and 大象 with the same mechanism he uses for 大 at ch 25.** 有聲則有分，有分則不宫而商矣 — *"if it has sound it has divisions, and divided it is either the note 宫 or the note 商"*; 有形則有分 — *"if it has form it has divisions."* At ch 25 he argued 大有繫則必有分，有分則失其極矣, *"大, once tied, must have divisions; having divisions, it loses its utmost."* **One argument, three places:** whatever is fully itself cannot be a particular instance of itself.

### 士 → "in service", settled across 15, 41 and 68

*(2026-09-07, Shalom's call. Was "student" here, "warrior" at 68, "masters" at 15 — three Englishes for one character, two of them on the **identical phrase** 善為士者.)*

**"Student" fails on the evidence.** 說文: **士，事也** — *"a 士 is one who handles **affairs**."* Service, not study. 河上公 reads them as governors: the middle 士 治身以長存，**治國以太平** — *"governs the body for long life, governs the state for great peace"* — and the lowest as 貪狼多欲, *"greedy as wolves and full of desire."* Nobody in this chapter is at school. Historically a 士 was the **lowest rank of Zhou nobility**, a person with a sword and a post, between the 大夫 (*dà fū* — grandee) and the commoner.

**Why "in service" and not "officer."** *Officer* was the stronger English — concrete, it takes 上/中/下 naturally, and it repairs ch 68, where *"The master warrior is not martial"* cancels itself. It was declined because **it reads as bureaucratic and carries a negative valence for many readers**, where 士 covers the swordsman and the gentleman-in-waiting as well as the official. *(It also collided with 官 at ch 28, *"chief of the officers."*)* **"In service" is wider and costs only compactness** — five English words for two characters, and a weaker noun.

**Note the seam, per standing rule 1:** 士 named a **male** class, and *in service* is deliberately neutral. The male-default is not erased silently; it is recorded here.

**⚠ Ch 68 now has a seam of its own.** 善為士者 is verbatim at ch 15 and ch 68, so all three must read alike — but ch 68's other three lines run the frame 善▢者 as *"The master fighter,"* *"The master of overcoming enemies,"* *"The master of using people."* Its first line now breaks that shape. `WORKLIST.md` T2-47.

### The closing line

**夫唯道，善貸且成 → "Only the Tao is masterful at lending, and at completing."** *(Was: "Yet the Tao alone masterfully provides for the countless things and brings them to completion.")*

**萬物 is not in the line.** *"The countless things"* was supplied by the English.

**貸 (*dài*) is to lend.** The graph is 貝 (*bèi* — a cowrie shell, money) with 代 phonetic; 說文 glosses it 施也 (*to bestow*), but 王弼 rules out exactly the reading our English had: **貸之非唯供其乏而已**，一貸之則足以永終其德，故曰善貸也 — *"as for its lending, **it is not merely supplying what they lack**; one lending suffices to complete their integrity forever, hence 'masterful at lending.'"* *Provides for* **is** 供其乏. **Things hold what they have on loan** — one that never runs out and is never called in. 善 governs both verbs, since 王弼 glosses 善貸 and 善成 separately.

**道隱無名 keeps "hidden," and the character is ch 15's.** 說文 defines 隱 as **蔽也** — the graph we settled at ch 15 as *stay covered*. The Tao does at the end of this chapter what the ancients do in that one.

**⚠ 大笑之 renders 大 adverbially as "aloud,"** which `glossary/da-大.md` does not license among its flexions. The entry needs it added. `WORKLIST.md` T2-48.

**勤而行之 → "labor to practice it."** *(Shalom's call, 2026-10-24. `glossary/qin-勤.md`.)* *(was: "practice it with diligence.")* *Diligence* is a virtue, and English hears praise in it. 勤 (*qín*) describes strength spent: 說文 (*Shuōwén*) 勞也, *"labor,"* and 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) 自勤苦竭力而行之, *"of themselves strain and suffer, using up their strength, to practice it."* 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) hears 有志也, *"they have resolve."* **This is the one line where 勤 is not *strain*, its lock.** In chs 6 and 52 the character is negated, and *strain* is the thing avoided. Here it is affirmed, and *strain* would fault the best students for forcing it, a verdict the Chinese does not pass. *Labor* is 說文's own word for 勤, and it keeps a little difficulty, so the silks' 堇 (*jǐn*), which some scholars read as 僅 (*jǐn* — barely), is not shut out (unverified here, `WORKLIST.md` T2-66). The cost: ch 41 and chs 6, 52 now say near-echoes, *labor* and *strain*, not one word.
notes.42:
**沖氣以為和 → "and the breath within makes harmony."** *(Shalom's call, 2026-11-15.)* *(was: "blending the breath into harmony.")* We follow silk A's 中 (*zhōng* — middle), read as a word: *within*, the English 中 takes in chapter 21. Silk A writes 沖 in full at chapter 45 but the bare 中 here, Beida writes 中 too, and Heshang Gong reads the received 沖 as 中: 萬物中皆有元氣 (*"within all the countless things is the original breath"*). No witness or commentator supports *blending*. *Within* stands bare so it holds both readings: the breath between yin and yang, which makes the third of 二生三 (*èr shēng sān* — "the two births the three"), and Heshang Gong's breath inside each thing. The 2026-11-01 call on 氣 (*qì* — breath) stands; what changes is that 氣 is no longer the object of a verb here but the thing that makes the harmony. **The cost:** the Source table still prints 沖 beside *within*; the motion of Fu Yi's 衝 (*chōng* — to rush) is let go; and 中 beside 和 (*hé* — harmony) is the Zhongyong's pair, which *within* keeps clear of where *center* would not. `glossary/chong-沖.md`, `notes/manuscript.md` → Ch 42.

**學父 → "the father of learning."** *(2026-10-26, Shalom's call.)* *(was: "the root of learning.")* 父 (*fù* — father) stands in every witness: the received 教父 (*jiào fù* — "father of teaching") and the silk's 學父 (*xué fù* — "father of learning"). The fork is only the first character. *Root* came from Heshang Gong's 父，始也 (*fù, shǐ yě* — "父 means beginning"), a commentator's gloss on the sense, not a doubt about the word. 父 is *father* as 母 (*mǔ* — mother) is *mother*: the edition does not cool the mother into *the Source*, and it does not cool the father into *a root*. English *the father of* already names the one who began a thing, so Heshang Gong's sense stays in the word. *Root* is 根's (*gēn*). `notes/manuscript.md` → Ch 42.
notes.43: **希 (*xī*) — the thread from ch 14.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-09-10 — `WORKLIST.md` T2-52.)* *"Few ever reach this"* renders **希**. **Chapter 14 is where the book names this character**: 聽之不聞，名曰希, given there as *"its name is the inaudible."* The graph is 爻 (*yáo* — crossed threads) over 巾 (*jīn* — cloth), **loose-woven fabric you can see through** — so *scarce among people* and *barely audible* are the same property in Chinese, read across a crowd or across a sound. Ch 14 renders the meaning rather than the word for that chapter's legibility, so the link is carried here. Also ch 23, 41, 70, 74.
notes.44:
**貨 → "goods," swept.** *(2026-08-30, Pass C, `WORKLIST.md` T2-14.)* 身與貨孰多 (*shēn yǔ huò shú duō*) read *"Your self or **wealth** — which is worth more?"* **Wealth belongs to 富 (*fù*)** — *wealth · wealthy · enrich* at ch 9, 33 and 57 — and 富 does not appear in this chapter, so nothing licensed the word here. 貨 (*huò* — goods) is now locked: `glossary/huo-貨.md`. The line's three pairs are 名 (*míng* — name), 身 (*shēn* — the self), 貨 (goods), and *goods* is the plainest thing the third can be.

**知止不殆 → "Know when to stop, and you come to no danger."** *(2026-08-31, Pass C, `WORKLIST.md` T2-11.)* *(was: "you avoid depletion.")* The same clause stands at ch 32 and the two now read alike. 殆 (*dài*) is **peril** — 說文解字 危也, built on 歺 (*è*), the bare-bone radical that carries 死 (*sǐ* — to die) and 殃 (*yāng* — calamity). *Depletion* is an energy metaphor and renders no character.

**河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) on this line:** 知可止則財利不累身，聲色不亂於耳目，則身**不危殆**也 — *"knowing when one can stop, wealth and profit do not burden the body, sounds and colours do not disorder the ears and eyes; then the body is not in peril."* Note that it is **the body** that is spared, which ties the line back to this chapter's opening question, 身與貨孰多 (*"the self or goods, which is worth more?"*).

**名 → *name*, not *reputation*.** *(2026-11-15, with `glossary/ming-名.md`. Was: "Reputation or your body — which is dearer?")* **This is the same word as chapter 1's, and English *name* carries both of its senses**, a word for a thing and a person's standing, as in *a good name* or *make a name for yourself*. *Reputation* spent a second English on one character and cut this chapter off from the two that argue with names. **Chapter 32 makes the link outright:** 名亦既有，夫亦將知止，知止可以不殆, *"Since names already exist, one must know when to stop. / Knowing when to stop, you come to no danger,"* and this chapter closes on the same 知止不殆, *"Know when to stop, and you come to no danger."* Both chapters put names beside knowing when to stop, and with one English a reader can hear it. The commentators keep the word too: 王弼, 尚名好高其身必疏, *"whoever exalts a name and loves height, their body must grow distant"*; 河上公, 名遂則身退也, *"when the name is achieved, the body withdraws,"* the phrase the longer reading of chapter 9 prints (`sources/variants.yaml`). *Your name* answers *your body* in the line, as 名 answers 身 (*shēn* — the body).
notes.45:
**躁 (*zào*) → *restless*, one word in all three of its lines.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-11-19.)* *(was: "Movement overcomes cold.")* *Movement* was neutral where both commentators condemn: Wang Bi, 躁則犯物之性 (*"restlessness violates the nature of things"*); Heshang Gong, 言人不當剛躁也 (*"a person should not be hard and restless"*). It also cut the tie to ch 26, where the same character loses the ruler. A body that cannot keep still does keep warm, so the line's plain sense survives. Closes `process/accuracy-audit.md` finding 14, which had proposed *agitation*. *Agitation* fails in both its English senses. As stirring, it is something done to a thing, and 躁 is never moved by anything outside it; as upset, it is a mood, and the early texts' 躁 is not one. Analects 16.6: 言未及之而言，謂之躁 (*"speaking before your turn has come is called 躁"*); the Xici: 躁人之辭多 (*"the 躁 person's words are many"*); the Monthly Ordinances: 毋躁 (*"do not rush about"*). 躁 is impatience moving of its own accord, the want of rest, and *restless* is the plain antonym of *still*. The argument: `glossary/jing-靜.md` → 躁.

**大辯若訥 → "Great argument seems halting."** *(2026-08-31, Pass C, `WORKLIST.md` T2-9. Closes Pass C.)* *(was: "Great eloquence seems awkward.")* 辯 (*biàn*) read *eloquence* here and *argue* at ch 81, and ch 81's Notes had licensed the split on the grounds that **辯 is praised here**. It is not.

**The 大X若Y frame does not endorse its X — it says the greatest form of X is unrecognizable as X.** The proof is one line up. **大巧若拙** puts 巧 (*qiǎo*) in the frame, and 巧 is condemned twice elsewhere: ch 19's 絕巧棄利 (*jué qiǎo qì lì* — "cut off cunning, abandon profit") and ch 57's 人多伎巧 ("the more cunning people become, the more strange contrivances appear"). Nobody read that line as praise either.

**The commentators put 大辯 and ch 81's 不辯 almost on top of each other.** 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*): 大辯**因物而言**，己**無所造**，故若訥也 — *"great 辯 speaks according to things; the self **invents nothing**, and so it seems halting."* 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*): 大辯者智無疑，如訥者口尤辭 — *"one of great 辯 knows without doubt, and like a halting person has few words."* Against ch 81's 善者以道修身，**不綵文**也 — *"the masterful do not **ornament** their words."* **The paradox is that the greatest arguing looks like inarticulacy because it is not arguing.**

***Eloquence* is also not what 辯 means.** 說文解字: 治也。从言在辡之閒 — *"to put in order; from 言 (*yán* — words) placed between 辡."* 辡 is two 辛 (*xīn* — tattooing knives, the convict's mark) facing each other: **words between two disputants.** Fine speech is 美言 (*měi yán* — "pretty words"), ch 81's opening.

**訥 → "halting," not "awkward."** 說文: **言難也**, *"difficulty in speech"* — specifically speech, where *awkward* is generic and overlaps 拙 (*zhuō* — clumsy) in the line above.

**大盈若沖 → "Great fullness seems empty" stands, and rests on 盅** *(2026-11-15)*. Read as itself, 沖 (*chōng*) is 涌搖也, *"surging and shaking"*; the empty sense is 盅 (*zhōng* — an empty vessel), which Fu Yi writes here outright (大滿若盅), and which shares 沖's sound part 中. The frame needs the opposite of 盈 (*yíng* — full), as 缺 (*quē* — lacking) answers 成 (*chéng* — complete). 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) reads it so: 大盈充足……故若沖也 (*"great fullness is ample… so it seems 沖"*). `glossary/chong-沖.md`, `notes/manuscript.md` → Ch 45.

**Still owed here: 巧 reads *skill* in this chapter and *cunning* at ch 19 and ch 57** — the same fault as 辯, one line up. `WORKLIST` T2-20.
notes.47:
**不見而名 → "names without seeing."** *(Shalom's call, 2026-09-24. `WORKLIST.md` T1-24.)* *(was: "understands clearly without seeing," over 不見而明.)* **We restore the received text's 名 (*míng* — to name) and stop following the Mawangdui A silk's 明 (*míng* — clear-seeing).** The two are homophones, and this is the one line in the book where they fork.

**Why the fork was reopened.** 明's locked English puts *see* in its predicate form (*see clearly*), and 見 (*jiàn* — to see) is *see* in this chapter's own second line (*"you see the way of nature"*). So a line rendering both characters had to use *see* twice for two characters. The old *understands* dodged that by borrowing 知 (*zhī* — to know)'s English from three characters away. Every alternative was worse: *has clarity* broke the verb triad, and *is clear* is 清 (*qīng* — clear, as water is)'s predicate English at ch 15 and 39. **Then the evidence settled it: both of our commentaries print 名.** 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) reads it plainly: 識物之宗，故雖不見而是非之理可得而名也, *"knowing the ancestor of things, though not seeing, the principles of right and wrong can still be named."* The triad holds with 名 as well as with 明, since each verb is done without its usual means: *knows* without going, *names* without seeing, *accomplishes* without doing. Naming is what you do once you can tell things apart.

**The Chinese in this file and `source/chinese.md` now print 名.** They had printed the silk's 明 since the Google Doc, while `sources/variants.yaml` recorded 名 as the base. The apparatus was right and the text was not.
notes.49: **百姓 → "everyone," twice.** *(2026-10-14, Shalom's call, `glossary/baixing-百姓.md`. Was: "the people.")* 以百姓心為心 → *"they take everyone's heart as their own"*; 百姓皆注其耳目 → *"everyone pours out their attention."* The sage takes the heart of the whole population, not of the governed.
notes.5:
**以百姓為芻狗 → "they treat everyone as straw dogs."** *(2026-10-14, Shalom's call, `glossary/baixing-百姓.md`. Was: "the people.")* *The people* is 民 (*mín*)'s, and 百姓 (*bǎi xìng*) is the whole population. *Everyone* answers the line above it: sky and earth treat the countless things as straw dogs, and the sage treats everyone the same way.

*不仁 revised 2026-08-28 under the 仁 lock (`glossary/ren-仁.md`). The verse had read "lack benevolence," which was wrong twice: the word, and **lack** — 不仁 is a refusal, not a deficit.*

**The line is not about cruelty, and both commentators say so.** 王弼 names what 仁 would require: 仁者必造立施化，**有恩有為** — *"the 仁 one must construct and impose transformation; there is 恩 (ēn — favour with a debt attached) and there is 為 (wéi — doing)."* So 不仁 is the absence of **management that keeps accounts**, not the absence of care.

河上公 is blunter still: 聖人**愛養**萬民，不以仁恩，法天地行自然 — *"the sage **loves and rears** the people, not by humane favour, but modelling sky and earth in acting so of themselves."* The sage of this chapter is not indifferent.

**A 芻狗 (*chú gǒu*) is a dog plaited from straw for a sacrifice** — dressed and honored through the rite, thrown away after. 河上公 gives the point in five characters: 不貴望其報也, *"expecting no repayment."* The straw dog is not contempt. It is what you are to something that plays no favorites and keeps no ledger.

*English "humane" now means chiefly "not cruel," so "are not humane" would deliver the one reading the commentaries forbid. Hence the longer phrase.*

**守中 → "hold to the center," and *in silence* rendered nothing.** *(2026-09-08, Pass E, `WORKLIST.md` T2-19 — the holding family.)* 守 (*shǒu*) is locked to *hold to* (`glossary/shou-守.md`): 說文 守官也，从宀从寸…寸，法度也 — a roof over a regulation, **the only member of the holding family with no hand in its graph**. What you 守 is a post you are answerable for, which is why the English takes a preposition. The line's *"in silence"* rendered no character and is gone; 多言 (*duō yán* — much speech) two lines above already carries the contrast.
notes.50: **入軍不被甲兵 → "untouched by armor or weapons."** *(2026-10-14, Shalom's call. Was: "unharmed by weapons.")* 甲 (*jiǎ* — armor) had been dropped. Ch 80 keeps 甲兵 as *armor and weapons*. 河上公's lemma reads 不避甲兵, *"does not avoid armor and weapons"*; either way the line names both.
notes.51: **長而不宰 → "growing them without ruling them."** *(2026-09-01, with ch 10.)* *(was: "leading without mastering.")* **長 (*zhǎng*) was reading two ways four lines apart in this chapter** — *grows* at 長之育之 and *leading* here. It is the causative *make grow* in both. 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*): 道**長**養萬物，不**宰割**以為器用 — *"the Tao grows and nourishes them and does not butcher them into vessels for use."* 說文解字 on 宰: **辠人在屋下執事者。从宀从辛** — *"a criminal under a roof doing service,"* from a roof and 辛, the tattooing knife; *mastering* lost the knife. Ch 10 carries the identical formula and takes the same wording (`WORKLIST` T2-15).
notes.52:
**天下有始 → "The world has a beginning."** *(Shalom's call, 2026-11-19.)* *(was: "The world has an origin.")* 始 (*shǐ*) reads *beginning* in every other line of the book (1, 14, 38, 64 ×2) and *begin* as a verb (2, 32, 64). *Origin* was the cooling `glossary/mu-母.md` refuses for the mother, *the Origin* without its capital, standing in the very line where the beginning becomes her. And it hid the echo: this line sets down the same two characters as ch 1's 無名，天地之始；有名，萬物之母 (*"the nameless is the beginning of sky and earth; the named is the mother of the countless things"*), and now a reader hears ch 1 again. Wang Bi reads ch 1 as two times in one life, the beginning before form and the mother who grows and rears; 以為 (*yǐ wéi* — "serves as") is the moment taken up into a body, which is why the next lines can say *return*. The argument is in `glossary/mu-母.md` → 始.

**見小曰明 → "Seeing the small is called clarity."** *(Shalom's call, 2026-10-15. Was: "To recognize things in their smallest form is clear-seeing.")* The old line rendered 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*)'s gloss, 萌芽未動，禍亂未見為小, *"before the sprouts stir and before disaster shows, that is 'the small'"*, which supplied *things*, *smallest* and *form*. The line has none of them. Bare *the small* keeps the reading open: 小 (*xiǎo*) is also the Tao's own name at ch 34 (可名於小, *"it can be called small"*) and the uncarved wood at ch 32 (樸雖小, *"though small"*). *Recognize* had dropped 見 (*jiàn* — to see), and with it the eye that 明 (*míng* — clear-seeing) completes.

**The two halves are one couplet, and both old readers say so.** 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) answers them in one matched sentence: 見大不明，見小乃明；守強不強，守柔乃強也, *"seeing the great is not clear-seeing; seeing the small is truly clear-seeing. Holding to the strong is not strong; holding to the soft is truly strong."* 韓非子 (*Hán Fēizǐ*, 喻老) gives each half a story, one after the other. For 見小曰明, 箕子 (*Jīzǐ*) saw the tyrant 紂 (*Zhòu*)'s new ivory chopsticks and foresaw the jade cups, the silk and the wine pools that would end the dynasty: 箕子見象箸以知天下之禍, *"箕子 saw the ivory chopsticks and knew the disaster of the world."* For 守柔曰強, 勾踐 (*Gōujiàn*) served the king of 吳 (*Wú*) as his groom and later destroyed him. The English now matches the halves: *Seeing the small* / *Holding to the soft*.

**Why *clarity* and not *clear-seeing*.** 明's lock allows both (*clear-seeing / clarity*), and *seeing* already stands in the line on 見, so the noun loses nothing and avoids saying *seeing* twice, which ch 47's reversal had ruled against (2026-09-24). It also lets the chapter's two 明 match: 復歸其明, four lines down, is already *"return to your inner clarity."* **The cost:** the frame ▢▢曰明 now reads two ways. Ch 16 and 55 say *"Knowing the ever-present is called clear-seeing."* The frame is not verbatim (知常 there, 見小 here), so the rule to repeat what the Chinese repeats does not bind it, but a reader will hear the difference.

**没身不殆 → "and to the end of your days, no danger will find you."** *(2026-08-31, Pass C, `WORKLIST.md` T2-11.)* *(was: "no harm will come to you.")* The reading was right; the word was another character's. ***Harm* belongs to 害 (*hài*)** — ch 35, 56, 66, 73, 81 — and 殆 (*dài*) is **peril**: 說文解字 危也, the graph built on 歺 (*è*), the bare-bone radical of 死 (*sǐ* — to die) and 殃 (*yāng* — calamity). 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) glosses this line in three characters: **不危殆也**.

**This chapter's version was the sound one, and ch 16 has been brought to it.** 没身不殆 is verbatim in both; 没身 (*mò shēn* — "to the end of one's body") is an idiom for **all one's life**, which this chapter already had right while ch 16 read it as *death itself*.

**是謂襲常 → "This is called holding the ever-present covered" — and a manuscript fork that had been driving the English unrecorded.** *(2026-08-31, Pass C, `WORKLIST.md` T2-10.)* *(was: "This is the practice of the ever-present.")* The old line was not a loose rendering of 襲. It was a **faithful rendering of a different character**: 習 (*xí* — to repeat, to drill), which our base text does not print here.

**Both commentaries do print 習.** 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*): 人能行此，是謂**習修**常道 — *"if a person can do this, it is called **practising and cultivating** the constant Tao."* The Siku edition of 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) sets 習 in the lemma with the compilers' note 〔案**習各本作襲**〕 — *"for 習, all editions read 襲."* **We keep the base text and read 襲**, because 是謂襲明 at ch 27 is the identical frame and 明 (*míng* — clear-seeing) / 常 (*cháng* — the ever-present) are bonded by 知常曰明 at ch 16 and ch 55: one gesture, both halves. Reading 習 here dissolves the pair. Recorded in `sources/variants.yaml`; reasoning in `notes/manuscript.md`.

**襲 is 說文's 左衽袍, a robe closed to the left — grave-clothes**, a garment put on over another. Hence *covered*, which is the motion this movement has just described: 用其光，復歸其明 — *"use the outer light, return to your inner clarity."* The shine is put away, not put on display.

**守 read two ways twelve lines apart, and a third "holding" belonged to 襲.** *(2026-09-08, Pass E, `WORKLIST.md` T2-19 — the holding family.)* 守柔曰強 had read *"To **stay with** the soft is called strong"* against 復守其母's *"hold fast to."* Both are now 守's locked *hold to* (`glossary/shou-守.md`), and the chapter's paradox survives it — 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) on this very line: **守強不強，守柔乃強也**, *"holding to the strong is not strong; holding to the soft is truly strong."* Same verb in both halves of his sentence; only the object changes. **是謂襲常 → "This is called the ever-present worn covered,"** matching ch 27's 是謂襲明 exactly and taking *holding* off 襲 (*xí* — one garment worn over another) in a chapter where 守 stands twice.

**終身不勤 → "you will not strain."** *(Shalom's call, 2026-10-24. `glossary/qin-勤.md`.)* *(was: "you will not toil.")* 勤 (*qín*) is locked to *strain* across its three lines, beside ch 6's; ch 41, where the character is affirmed, reads *labor*, its one flexion. 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*): 無事永逸，故終身不勤也, *"no affairs, forever at ease, so to the end of your days you do not strain."*
notes.53: **夷 (*yí*) — the thread from ch 14.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-09-10 — `WORKLIST.md` T2-52.)* 大道甚夷 renders **夷** as *level*. **Chapter 14 is where the book names this character**: 視之不見，名曰夷, given there as *"its name is the invisible."* 說文解字 has 夷 as **平也**, *"level"* — the graph is 大 (*dà* — a person) with 弓 (*gōng* — a bow). 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) glosses ch 14's line 無**色**曰夷, *"colourless is called 夷"*: what is perfectly level has no feature to catch the eye, which is how one character reaches both readings. Ch 14 renders the meaning rather than the word for that chapter's legibility, so the link is carried here. Also ch 41 (夷道若纇).
notes.54:
**邦 → "state," twice.** *(2026-10-14, Shalom's call. Was: "nation.")* 邦 (*bāng*) and 國 (*guó*) are one word split by the Han taboo on 劉邦's name (`notes/manuscript.md`), and 國 is *state* throughout. *Nation* is also a modern word, the people as a political body, which neither character is.

**以此 → "By this."** *(2026-08-30, Pass C, `WORKLIST.md` T2-12.)* The line closed *"By precisely this."* 以此 (*yǐ cǐ*) is 以 (*yǐ* — by means of) + 此 (*cǐ* — this), and **there is no intensifier in the Chinese**. 吾何以知…**然**哉？以此 (*wú hé yǐ zhī… rán zāi? yǐ cǐ* — "how do I know… it is so? by this") closes ch 21, ch 54 and ch 57 verbatim but for the object, and it had three different Englishes; all three now read **"By this."** The full argument is in ch 21's Notes and `notes/translation.md`; the claim it protects is `DISCOVERIES.md` §2.

**What 此 points at here is the ten preceding lines, and 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) names the count.** 以此**五事**觀而知之也 — *"by observing **these five matters**, he knows it"*: the cultivation and the observing run through body, family, community, state and world. The referent is unusually concrete in this chapter, which is precisely why the English must not specify it — ch 21's 此 is not five of anything, and the formula has to sound the same in both.
notes.55:
**知和曰常，知常曰明 → "Harmony is called the ever-present. / Knowing harmony is called clear-seeing.", following Guodian and silk A, closing T2-77.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-11-01.)* *(was: "Knowing harmony is called the ever-present. / Knowing the ever-present is called clear-seeing.")* The two oldest witnesses, a century apart, read 和曰常，知和曰明 (*hé yuē cháng, zhī hé yuē míng*). Our base and silk B run the chain 和 → 常 → 明 (*harmony → the ever-present → clear-seeing*) that chapter 16 ends on, likely a copyist bringing this chapter into line with that one. In the oldest reading, clear-seeing is knowing harmony itself, the harmony of the infant who cries all day and never goes hoarse, one line before. **The base text and the Source table keep 知和曰常，知常曰明; only the verse follows the witnesses.** `notes/manuscript.md`.

**心使氣曰強 → "When the heart drives the breath, that is called strong."** *(Shalom's call, 2026-11-01, locking `glossary/qi-氣.md`.)* *(was: "When the heart drives the vital energy, that is called strong.")* 氣 (*qì* — breath) reads *breath* in all three of its lines. *Vital* is 精 (*jīng* — vital essence)'s word, and chapter 55 holds both, a reserve against a current; *energy* fails the pointing test.

**握固 → "their grip is firm."** *(2026-09-08, Pass E, `WORKLIST.md` T2-19 — the holding family.)* *(was: "their grasp is firm.")* 握 (*wò*) is 說文 **搤持也**, *"to squeeze and grip"* — the tightening word the dictionary defines 持 (*chí* — to hold) by, and defines back in the same breath (持，握也). *Grasp* is now 執's alone book-wide (`glossary/zhi-執.md`), and *grip* is the plainer and better English for an infant's fist besides.
notes.56:
**同 occurs twice in this chapter, two lines apart, and the English had used two unrelated words.** *(2026-09-03, `WORKLIST.md` T2-26, the rider ch 23 left.)* 和其光，**同**其塵。是謂玄**同** — *"be the same as the dust; this is called profound sameness."* It had read *"merge with the dust"* and *"the profound union,"* hiding the chapter's own move: **the practice and the name for it are one word.**

**同 (*tóng* — the same) is 異 (*yì* — different)'s antonym**, printed against it in ch 1's 同出而異名, and settled at ch 23 on 2026-09-03. **河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) glosses 同其塵 with 同's opposites**: 不當自**别殊**也 — *"one should not set oneself apart as **separate** and **distinct**."* **王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) makes the couplet a matched pair**: 和其光 is 無所**特顯** (*"nothing specially displayed"*), 同其塵 is 無所**特賤** (*"nothing specially despised"*) — do not stand out above the light, do not hold yourself apart from the dust. ***Merge* read as self-dissolution**; the Chinese says do not consider yourself too good for the common muck.

***Union* was another character's English.** The reverse check returns two lines and the other is ch 55's 牝牡之**合** (*pìn mǔ zhī hé* — "the union of female and male"), where 合 (*hé* — to join) genuinely means union. 同 is not 合.

***Profound sameness* because 是謂玄同 is the same formula as 是謂玄德**, which reads *"This is called profound integrity"* at ch 10, 51 and 65. Same 是謂玄X frame, same English shape. **河上公 reads 玄 here as 天**: 玄，天也。人能行此上事，是謂與天**同道**也 — *"玄 means sky; a person who can do the above is said to be of the **same way** as sky"* — which is 同 again, in his gloss of the compound.

***"Share the dust"* was the first candidate and failed on the link** — short, idiomatic, free in the reverse check, but it gives no noun for 玄同, so the two 同 come apart again. **One test decided it: whatever renders 同 at line 5 must still render it at line 6.**

**和其光 → *"Harmonize your light,"* not *"Dim your own light."*** *(Shalom's call, 2026-11-18, `WORKLIST-CLOSED.md` T2-84.)* *Dim* had been left standing with this note, which named it as the commentator's word: 說文解字 makes 和 **相譍也**, *"to answer one another"* — the same 應 (*yìng* — to answer) as 河上公's 同聲相應 at ch 23 — and *dim* comes from his 當和之使闇昧 (*"blend it, make it dim"*). `glossary/ming-明.md` already glosses ch 4 and ch 56 together this way, so it is settled rather than sloppy; but **和 and 同 are a pair and only one of them has been repaired.** Now both are. *Dim* was Heshang Gong's result clause with his verb dropped, and Wang Bi dims nothing; it was decided against so that a commentator's word does not stand in for the character (`glossary/he-和.md`).

**挫其銳，解其紛，和其光，同其塵 — ch 4 now matches this chapter, not the reverse.** *(2026-08-31, Pass C, `WORKLIST.md` T2-14.)* These four lines are verbatim at ch 4, which had rendered them *"It blunts sharpness, / Untangles the tangled, / Softens brilliance, / Is one with every grain of dust."* **This chapter's wording and its couplet lineation were kept**, on two grounds. **This chapter is attested complete at Guodian** (~300 BCE, bundle A, unit 4), the oldest witness there is, while **ch 4 is not attested at all**. And `glossary/ming-明.md` had already prescribed this chapter's word for 和其光: *brilliance* is on 明 (*míng* — clear-seeing)'s `forbidden:` list, and 光 (*guāng*) is 明's counter-term — *"the light a thing **emits**… what the sage is told to soften in Chapters 4 and 56 (和其光 — **dim your light**)."* *(That gloss changed with 和其光, 2026-11-18.)*

**What was not unified, deliberately: the subject.** 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) reads the four lines **here** as a person's practice — 含守質也 (*"holding to and keeping one's substance"*), 除爭原也 (*"removing the source of contention"*), and on 和其光 無所特顯則物無所偏爭也 (*"nothing stands out, so things have nothing to contend over"*) — but reads them at **ch 4** with the **Tao** as subject. Both chapters' contexts back him: here the lines follow 塞其兌，閉其門 (*"block the openings, close the doors"*), which is addressed to a person; at ch 4 they sit between two lines about the Tao. 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) reads both chapters as instruction to a person. **The divergence is left standing** — ch 4's subject travels with its Pass D rewrite (`WORKLIST` T1-2). The nouns match in both chapters now; only the verb forms differ.
notes.57:
**國家滋昏 → *the more clouded the state becomes*.** *(2026-09-20, `WORKLIST.md` T2-54.)* Was *"the darker the state becomes."* 昏 (*hūn*, 說文 日冥也 — the sun below the line) took 玄's English in a chapter with no 玄; it now matches ch 20 and ch 18.

**以此 → "By this:" — the colon stays, the formula is now uniform.** *(2026-08-30, Pass C, `WORKLIST.md` T2-12.)* 吾何以知…**然**哉？以此 (*wú hé yǐ zhī… rán zāi? yǐ cǐ* — "how do I know… it is so? by this") closes ch 21, ch 54 and ch 57, and it had three Englishes; all three now read **"By this."** The colon is **punctuation, not a word** — lineation and pointing are ours by standing principle — and it does real work here, because **this is the only one of the three that points forward.** Ch 21 and ch 54 are chapter-final and 此 points back; here it opens the four 天下多… lines (*"the more taboos… the more sharp weapons…"*) that follow. Same two words, same formula, and the colon lets the reader hear where the evidence is.

**其 → "it," not "this."** The line read *"How do I know **this** is so? By **this**:"*, putting 其 (*qí* — it, its) and 此 (*cǐ* — this) in the same English word one clause apart. The Source table's own gloss already had it right. Now **"How do I know it is so?"**, and *this* belongs to 此 alone.

**河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) glosses this 以此 with the identical five characters he uses at ch 21** — 此，今也 (*cǐ, jīn yě* — "'this' means now"), continuing 以今日所見知 (*"by what is seen today, he knows it"*). That repetition is the tradition's own evidence that this is **one fixed formula**, which is the claim `DISCOVERIES.md` §2 turns on. It is not, however, a candidate rendering — see ch 21's Notes.
notes.59:
**夫唯嗇 → "Only conserving is called accepting early."** *(2026-10-19, Shalom's call, `glossary/wei-唯.md`. Was: "Conserving is called accepting early.")* 唯 (*wéi* — only) had no English. Both commentators keep it exclusive. 河上公 puts 獨 (*dú* — alone) in its place: 夫獨愛民財、愛精氣，則能先得天道也, *"only by cherishing the people's wealth and the vital essence can one obtain the Tao of nature first."* 王弼 opens 唯重積德, *"only by heavily accumulating integrity."* The chain below keeps its *is called*, which is 是謂 (*shì wèi*)'s and 謂之 (*wèi zhī*)'s.

**早服 → "accepting early," twice.** *(2026-10-14, Shalom's call. Was: "returning early"; "early accord" was tried the same day and dropped as jargon.)* 服 (*fú*) has no sense of return, and no witness recorded here reads 復 (*fù* — return). All three commentators read it as accord or taking in. 王弼: 早服常也 (*"early 服 is constancy"*). 河上公: 服得也 (*"服 is to obtain"*). 韓非 (*Hán Fēi*): 夫能令故德不去，新和氣日至者，蚤服者也 (*"one who keeps their old integrity from leaving while new harmonious breath arrives each day is one who 蚤服"*). *Submit* was the literal column's word and reads as defeat. *Accepting* is how you 服 a command or a medicine: you take it in and go along. Set aside: *harmony* (和's word in five lines, and 韓非's 和氣 would turn his explanation into the rendering), *alignment* (self-help register), *receptivity* (names a quality where 服 is an act), *yielding* (弱's locked word).

**有國之母 → "Have the mother of the state," and 有 stops reading two ways in adjacent lines.** *(2026-09-08, Pass E, `WORKLIST.md` T2-19 — the holding family.)* The lines had read 可以**有**國 → *"one can **maintain** the state"* and 有國之母 → *"**Holding** the mother of the state"* — the same character, two Englishes, one line apart, and neither of them 有's. 有 (*yǒu*) is locked in `glossary/wu-you-無有.md`, and *hold* belongs to 持 (`glossary/chi-持.md`). Both now read **have**, so the repetition the Chinese builds the couplet on is audible. **有's transitive uses stay open** beyond the settled 有道者 → *those who are with the Tao* (24, 31, 77).
notes.6:
**谷神 → "the spirit of the valley": 谷 (*gǔ* — valley) is a noun, as Wang Bi reads it, not Heshang Gong's 谷，養也 (*gǔ, yǎng yě* — "gǔ means to nourish").** *(2026-10-25, Shalom's call.)* The other nine lines where it stands are all a valley, and both Mawangdui silks spell this one with the 浴 (*yù*) they use for the valley in lines that can only mean land. We keep Wang Bi's grammar without his emptiness: the valley is land, and water passes through it. The cost is Heshang Gong's breathing body. `glossary/gu-谷.md`.

**玄牝之門，是謂天地根 → "The gate of the dark female, / this is called the root of sky and earth."** *(Shalom's call, 2026-10-24.)* *(was: "This dark gateway birthed the sky and the earth.")* **The gate is hers, and the Chinese names her twice to say so.** 玄牝 (*xuán pìn* — "the dark female"), then 玄牝之門 (*xuán pìn zhī mén* — "the gate of the dark female"). *This dark gateway* named her once and cut the gate loose from her, the quiet version of the cooling `glossary/mu-母.md` refuses. Both commentators keep the gate hers. 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*): 門，玄牝之所由也 — *"the gate is where the dark female comes from."* 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) reads it as the gate of nose and mouth, 通天地之元氣所從往來 — *"through which the original breath of sky and earth comes and goes."* 門 (*mén* — gate) is *gate*, as in ch 1's 眾妙之門 (*"the gate of all subtlety"*). *(Reshaped 2026-10-25, next note.)*

**是謂玄牝。玄牝之門 → "This is called the dark female. / The dark female's gate —": the anadiplosis, kept on purpose.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-10-25.)* *(was: "The gate of the dark female,")* **The Chinese hands its last words to the next line, and the English now does too, by design.** *Anadiplosis* (Greek, "doubling back") is the device: a line ends on words the next line opens with. 是謂玄牝 (*shì wèi xuán pìn* — "this is called the dark female") ends on 玄牝, and 玄牝之門 (*xuán pìn zhī mén* — "the dark female's gate") opens on it: a chain, 頂真 (*dǐng zhēn* — "capping"), anadiplosis in English. *The gate of the dark female* kept every word and moved them to the end of the line, so the link was gone. *The dark female's gate* keeps the Chinese order, 玄 (*xuán* — dark) · 牝 (*pìn* — female) · 之 (*zhī* — 's) · 門 (*mén* — gate), and still names her twice, as the 2026-10-24 call asked. **The dash holds the gate up before it is named**, as 是 (*shì* — this) points back at its topic. *This* names the subject, so nothing is stranded, and chs 10 and 51 use the same mark in the same formula. It is the rule the dashes have answered to since that day (`CLAUDE.md` standing rule 3). **Two stanzas, 4 / 2:** the naming, 是謂 twice, with the chain inside one stanza; then the use. **Cost:** 之門 (*zhī mén* — "'s gate") now reads two ways, *the gate of all subtlety* at ch 1 and *the dark female's gate* here. Ch 1 has no chain to keep. `process/form-audit.md` → *Chapter 6*.

**根 (*gēn* — root) is a root, not a birth.** 說文 (*Shuōwén*): 木株也, *"the stump,"* what stays in the ground. It reads *root* at ch 16 (×2) and ch 26, and *birthed* was its only other English. *Birthed* made the gate something that happened once. 根 says it holds now. Neither commentator reads an event: 河上公 glosses 根，元也 (*gēn, yuán yě* — "root means origin"), and 王弼 says the gate is 與極同體 (*yǔ jí tóng tǐ* — "one body with the ultimate"), so it is called the root. **The cost, named:** *birthed* was the warmest verb in the chapter. The birth is still there in the gate of a female, a womb, but no longer in the past tense.

**是謂 (*shì wèi* — "this is called") ×2, now rendered both times.** Line 2 had read *"This is the dark female,"* and the fourth line had dissolved the formula altogether. The book reads it *this is called* at chs 10, 14, 16, 51, 56 and 68, and ch 14's *"If you can know the ancient beginning, / this is called the thread of the Tao"* is this line's shape. **天地 (*tiān dì* — sky and earth)** loses the articles it carried here alone, per its lock. The stanza is now six lines, one for each line of the Chinese, so the chapter pairs by count and needs no `## Alignment`.

**用之不勤 → "use it, and there is no strain."** *(Shalom's call, 2026-10-24. `glossary/qin-勤.md`.)* *(was: "it can never be exhausted.")* **用之 (*yòng zhī* — "use it") had gone missing, and 勤 (*qín*) is spending strength, not running out.** 說文 (*Shuōwén*): 勞也, *"labor."* 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*): 用而不勞也, *"it is used, and does not labor."* 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) reads the breath: 用氣常寬舒，不當急疾懃勞也, *"use the breath always loose and easy, never hurried or toiling,"* and *strain* is the opposite of loose and easy. **The two commentators disagree about whose strain it is**: for 王弼 the thing's, for 河上公 the breather's. *There is no strain* names no one, so it carries both. The line has its own line now, as in the Chinese.
notes.61: **以靜為下 → "By stillness she is underneath," kept against both silks.** *(2026-10-26, Shalom's call.)* Both Mawangdui silks read 為其靜也，故宜為下 (*wèi qí jìng yě, gù yí wéi xià* — "because she is still, therefore it is fitting that she be underneath"). **We keep the base, because no English for the silks' line survives being lifted out of this chapter.** 宜 (*yí*) is the Shuowen's 所安也 (*"where one is at rest"*), her ease, but *"it is fitting that she be underneath"* reads in English as a verdict on where the female belongs, and so do *"she belongs underneath"* and *"underneath suits her."* **This translation allows no rendering that could be used as a rationale for the domination of the female**, least of all in the chapter where she overcomes. In the base she is the subject of both lines, she overcomes and she is underneath, and nobody rules on her place. The Chinese says 以靜 (*yǐ jìng* — "by stillness") twice, and the English says it twice. **The silks' reason is still in the line.** Wang Bi reads our base causally, 以其靜故能為下也 (*"because she is still, she is able to be underneath"*), and English *by* holds the cause as well as the means. **Cost:** one transmitted reading kept against both excavated witnesses, and the silks' clasp, 宜為下 (*yí wéi xià* — "fitting to be underneath") said once of her and once of the large state, given up. The base's 為下 (*wéi xià* — "be underneath") twice still binds them, and the last line's *ought* falls only on the large state, as counsel to a power. `notes/manuscript.md` · `sources/variants.yaml`.
notes.62:
**求以得 keeps *seek, and you find*.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-11-19.)* The words are Matthew 7:7's, and *seek, and you get* was proposed (`glossary/de-shi-得失.md`), following Wang Bi's 以求則得求 (*"seek, and you get what you seek"*). The line keeps *find*, and the echo is a known cost, recorded so no later pass removes it as an oversight.

**不善人之所保 → "and what keeps safe those who are not."** *(2026-09-08, Pass E, `WORKLIST.md` T2-19 — the holding family.)* *(was: "the safekeeping of those who are not.")* Both commentators make the Tao **the agent** here, not a receptacle. 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) gives the outcome in four characters — **保以全也**, *"保, because it keeps them whole"* — where 全 (*quán*) is locked to *whole* in `glossary/quan-全.md`. 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) is warmer: 道者，不善人之**保倚**也，遭患逢急，猶自知悔卑下 — *"the Tao is what the unmasterful lean on for safety; meeting trouble and sudden danger, they still know to repent and humble themselves."* **The reciprocity now sounds across chapters:** at ch 15 a person keeps the Tao safe, here the Tao keeps a person safe, and it is one word. **寶 / 保 keep their split** — 王弼 寶以為用也 / 保以全也 — and English still cannot chime them.
notes.64:
**常於幾成而敗之 → "People always ruin their affairs just short of completing them."** *(Shalom's call, 2026-10-14. Was "often.")* 常 (*cháng* — the ever-present) before a verb is **always** under its lock (`glossary/chang-常.md`), and *often* had been the one exception, reducing a rule to a frequency. **Every excavated copy has the stronger word.** Mawangdui A reads 民之從事也，**恒**於其成事而敗之, and Guodian bundle C reads 人之敗也，**恆**於其且成也敗之 — *"when people fail, it is always just as they are about to succeed."* 恒 (*héng*) is the manner-word *ever*. **The stanza around it is categorical**: 為者敗之，執者失之, *"those who handle it ruin it, those who grasp it lose it."* *Often* was the one hedge in a run of rules. ***Always* is not fatalism, because the next line is the way out**: 慎終如始，則無敗事, *"be as careful at the end as at the beginning, and nothing will be ruined."* 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) glosses the failure in three characters, 不慎終也, *"they are not careful at the end."* The pattern holds unless you break it. **Set aside:** *forever* (the habitual idiom, *"people are forever ruining"*, is exact, but it brings *eternal* back into 常's family and sounds exasperated where the line only reports); *invariably* and *as a rule* (labels, in prose register).

**治之於未亂 → *Order it before it falls into disorder*.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-09-21.)* Was *"before it is chaotic."* **This is the clause 說文 describes** — 亂，治也 — and it is the one line in the book that prints both characters together, so the English has to keep them visibly related. *Chaos* has no antonym inside it; *disorder* does. 王弼 reads the counsel as a matter of scale rather than kind: 治之於未亂 → 謂㣲脆也, *"this refers to what is faint and fragile."* Catch the tangle while it is still a thread or two.

**難得之貨 → "rare goods."** *(2026-08-30, Pass C, `WORKLIST.md` T2-14.)* *(was: "and does not prize precious goods.")* 不貴難得之貨 is verbatim ch 3's second line, and the two had been rendered differently. **"Precious" is 貴 (*guì*)'s word** — ch 70, 72, 75 — and 貴 is the verb standing directly over 貨 here, so *"does not prize precious goods"* argued in a circle: if the goods are already precious, the counsel dissolves. 貨 (*huò* — goods) is locked to *goods*; the full argument, and the reading of 貨 against 寶 (*bǎo* — treasure) and 貴, is in `glossary/huo-貨.md`.

**河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) supplies this chapter's image for the whole thread:** 聖人不眩為服，不賤石而貴玉 — *"the sage is not dazzled into adorning themselves; does not despise stone and prize jade."* **賤 (*jiàn* — to hold cheap) and 貴 (to prize) are both things a person does.** Stone and jade differ in what someone does about them, which is the claim the English had been erasing.

**微 (*wēi*) — the thread from ch 14.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-09-10 — `WORKLIST.md` T2-52.)* 其微易散 renders **微** as *faint*. **Chapter 14 is where the book names this character**: 搏之不得，名曰微, given there as *"its name is the intangible."* 說文解字 has 微 as 隱行也, *"to move concealed,"* on 彳 (*chì* — the step radical). The two readings are one thing seen twice: what is too faint to catch is also what has not yet declared itself, which is this chapter's whole argument about acting early. Ch 14 renders the meaning rather than the word for that chapter's legibility, so the link is carried here. Also ch 15 and ch 36.
notes.65:
**非以明民 → "did not use it to make the people see clearly": 明 holds its lock.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-11-16: "We shouldn't gloss over this actual usage of 明 for the sake of an easier translation, or because this usage may create some discomfort.")* *(was: "did not use it to make the people clever," a declared exception from 2026-09-24, in the superseded note below.)* Every witness that has the line reads 明 (*míng* — clear-seeing): Wang Bi's text, Heshang Gong's, and silk A; silk B has 明 and loses what follows. Nothing in the line qualifies it. 非以明民，將以愚之 (*fēi yǐ míng mín, jiāng yǐ yú zhī* — "not using it to make the people see clearly, but meaning to make them 愚") is two causatives in parallel with one object. *Clever* was Wang Bi's gloss put into the line, and it set two characters under one word, since 智 (*zhì* — cleverness) follows four lines later. *See clearly* is the lock's own form in a predicate. The case, and what it costs: `glossary/ming-明.md` → *Left open*.

*(⚠ Superseded 2026-11-16 by the note above.)* **非以明民 → "did not use it to make the people clever," a declared exception to 明's lock.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-09-24. `WORKLIST.md` T1-17.)* 明 (*míng*) is locked to *clear-seeing / clarity* everywhere else, where seeing clearly is what the book asks for (16, 33, 52, 55). Here the ancient masters do **not** use the Tao to make the people 明. Rendered by the lock, the line would say the sages kept people from seeing clearly. 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) says what 明 means here: 明謂多見巧詐蔽其樸也, *"明 here means seeing too much, craft and deceit, which covers over their simplicity."* So this is a different sense of the word, and it gets a different English, recorded as a `flexions:` entry in `glossary/ming-明.md` so the tools report it rather than miss it. The argument, and what the choice costs, are in that entry.

**將以愚之 → *"but to make them fools,"* and *return* is gone.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-11-16, locking 愚 (*yú* — a fool): `glossary/yu-愚.md`.)* *(was: "They used it to return them to being guileless.")* 愚 is the ordinary word of its time for a fool, and the book claims it for the sage at ch 20, *"I have the heart of a fool!"* *Guileless* turned the insult into a compliment, came from Heshang Gong's 不詐偽 (*bù zhà wěi* — "without deceit or falsity"), and could not stand at ch 38. ***Fools*, not *foolish*:** the bare 愚 can name people (the Analects' 下愚, *xià yú* — "the lowest fools"), the noun repeats ch 20's, and it keeps both sides of the word, the one looked down on and the wise fool. Not *the fool*: the Chinese marks no figure, and *make them the fool* means to dupe them. 將 (*jiāng*) works as *but* in the frame 非 X，將 Y (*fēi X, jiāng Y* — "not X, but rather Y"), and nothing in the line turns back, so *return* goes. The chapter's reading, the authoritarian charge and the fool: `notes/reading.md` → *Ch 65*.

**將 (*jiāng*) does not mean *return*, and the chapter's return is 反 (*fǎn*), in its last lines.** *(2026-11-17. Shalom asked whether dropping* return *had lost something, since its removal had been folded into the 愚 lock rather than decided on its own.)* 將 stands in 22 lines of the book, and every one marks what is about to happen or what someone means to do: *about to melt* (15), *would take* (29), *will* (32, 37), *likely to* (39), *would rescue* (67); at 31 it is 將 (*jiàng* — a general). The Shuowen gives 帥也 (*shuài yě* — "to lead"), and none of its classical senses is *return*. 將以愚之 has the shape of ch 42's 吾將以為教父 (*wú jiāng yǐ wéi jiào fù* — "I take this as the father of learning"): *would use it to make them fools*. Silk A reads 將以愚之也 (*jiāng yǐ yú zhī yě*), and Heshang Gong keeps 將 as *would*. **So line 1 states an intention, and the English keeps it so: *"but to make them fools."*** *"But meant to make them fools"* was weighed and declined, since *to* already carries the purpose (Shalom's call, 2026-11-17).

**The return the old line supplied belongs to 反, in 與物反矣 (*yǔ wù fǎn yǐ* — "and turns back together with things").** It follows ch 25's arc: 深矣，遠矣，與物反矣 (*shēn yǐ, yuǎn yǐ, yǔ wù fǎn yǐ* — "deep, far, turning back") against 遠曰反 (*yuǎn yuē fǎn* — "going far means returning"). **Wang Bi joins the two ends of the chapter.** His gloss on 愚 in line 1 is 守真 (*shǒu zhēn* — "keeping to what is genuine"); on 反, 反其真也 (*fǎn qí zhēn yě* — "they return to what is genuine in them"). In his reading, making the people fools and the final return are one movement, begun in the first line and completed in the last. The draft's *"to return them to being guileless"* was that whole-chapter reading moved into a line that does not say it. **Do not re-supply *return* in line 1:** the return is in the chapter, where the Chinese puts it. Heshang Gong reads the same 反 as *contrary*, and *turns back* holds both (`notes/translation.md` → *Ch 65 · 與物反矣*).

**以其智多 · 以智治國 ×2 → *"too much cleverness"* · *"with cleverness"*.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-11-16, locking 智 (*zhì* — cleverness): `glossary/zhi-智.md`.)* *(was: "too much guile," "with guile.")* The Chinese says 智 three times and the book says it in five other chapters, so the English says *cleverness* each time. *Guile* had been chosen to mirror 愚 (*yú*) as *guileless*, and that pairing rested on a mistranslation of Wang Bi's gloss on 愚, 無知 (*wú zhī* — unknowing), as "without cunning." Both commentators make artifice what cleverness produces, not what it is: Heshang Gong, 以其智多，故為巧偽 — *"because their cleverness is great, they therefore practise artifice."* *Guile* also made the chapter a platitude, since nobody defends governing with guile; the Chinese says governing with cleverness, a recognised virtue, robs the state. **Owed then:** 愚's English, with the supplied *return*; settled the same day, in the note below.

**常知稽式 → *"Always knowing the pattern"*.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-11-16. was: "Always to know the pattern," then briefly "To always know the pattern.")* 常 (*cháng*) keeps its English, *always*, as the lock rules before a verb. *Knowing* is the form line 5 already uses for the same 知 (*zhī* — to know), *"Knowing these two is itself the pattern,"* and the form of ch 16's 知常曰明, *"Knowing the ever-present is called clear-seeing,"* whose two characters this line reverses: 知常 (*zhī cháng*) there, 常知 (*cháng zhī*) here. The chain holds too: *pattern* ends line 5 and opens line 6, as 稽式 (*jī shì*) does.
notes.67:
**天下皆謂 → "The world says."** *(2026-10-14, Shalom's call. Was: "Everyone says.")* 天下 (*tiān xià*) is *the world*, as in ch 2's 天下皆知 (*"when the world knows"*). *Everyone* is now 百姓 (*bǎi xìng*)'s (`glossary/baixing-百姓.md`), and ch 17's 百姓皆謂 is this line's frame with the people in the subject slot. *The world* says the Tao is great; *everyone* says we did it ourselves. The note below keeps the 2026-09-06 call on 道 (*dào*), which stands.

**天下皆謂我道大 → "Everyone says my Tao is great."** *(2026-09-06, Shalom's call. Was: "Everyone says I am vast, and look like nothing.")* **道 (*dào*) had been dropped and the whole passage handed to the speaker.** The Chinese says 我**道**大 — *my Tao is great* — and the three lines that follow are about the Tao, not about the person speaking. With 道 restored the subject runs *it* throughout, and 王弼's argument lands: 肖則失其所以為大矣 — *"to resemble [things] is to lose what makes it great."* The Tao looks like nothing because anything it resembled would have shrunk it to that thing's size.

**大 → "great"**, completing the sweep begun at ch 25 — 大 is *great* in 41 lines and was *vast* only here and at ch 25.

**細 (*xì*) → "slight," matching ch 63.** *(Was "petty.")* 細 occurs in two chapters and had two Englishes; ch 63's 為大於其細 and 天下大事，必作於細 already read **slight** twice. *Petty* also imported a moral verdict the character does not carry — 細 is the **silk radical** 糸, thread-fine, a matter of size.

**夫唯 (*fú wéi*) reads "Only because" here, and now reads it everywhere.** *(2026-10-19, Shalom's call. This note had left the line untouched, a formula across 11 chapters and 12 lines that carried five Englishes.)* The frame 夫唯…故 / 是以 (*gù / shì yǐ* — therefore) reads *"Only because X, Y,"* with the clause after it inverted, in all nine of its lines. 唯 (*wéi*) is *only*, and 河上公's gloss here doubles it: 唯**獨**名德大者為身害, *"only for one whose name for integrity is great does it become a harm to the body."* `glossary/wei-唯.md` · `WORKLIST.md` T2-43.

**Three of the four holding characters meet on this page, and two of them were sharing an English.** *(2026-09-08, Pass E, `WORKLIST.md` T2-19 — the holding family.)* 我有三**寶**，**持**而**保**之 puts 持 (*chí* — to hold), 保 (*bǎo* — to keep safe) and 寶 (*bǎo* — treasure) in one line; 以**守**則固 adds 守 (*shǒu*); 以慈**衛**之 adds 衛 (*wèi* — to escort, to guard). **守 had read *defend* and 衛 had read *guards*.** Now 守 takes its locked flexion — 以戰則勝，以守則固 → *"Fight with it and you win, **guard** with it and you stand firm"* — which is 說文's own second sense for 守 (寺府之事者, the business of a court, sentry included) and which 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) expands to 以**守衛**則堅固. 衛 moves to *shields*, and 固 (*gù* — 說文 四塞也, *"blocked on all four sides"*) gives up *hold firm* for *stand firm*. See `glossary/shou-守.md`, `glossary/bao-保.md`, `glossary/chi-持.md`.

**廣 (*guǎng*) → "broad," and "breadth" as a noun.** *(2026-11-15, Shalom's call. Was: "Frugality, and so you can reach far" and "to abandon frugality and grab at reach.")* 廣 is a hall's width (說文 (*Shuōwén* — the Han dictionary): 殿之大屋也 (*diàn zhī dà wū yě* — "the great hall of a palace")), and *far* is 遠's (*yuǎn* — far) at 25, 65 and 80. All three commentators put the breadth on others: Han Fei's 民衆則國廣 (*mín zhòng zé guó guǎng* — "when the people are many, the state is broad"), Wang Bi's 天下不匱 (*tiān xià bù kuì* — "the world does not run short"), Heshang Gong's 民日用廣 (*mín rì yòng guǎng* — "the people's daily means are broad"). The new line keeps the parallel with the one before it: *brave*, *broad*. Ch 41 reads *broad* too. `glossary/guang-廣.md` · `glossary/jian-儉.md`.
notes.69: **執無兵 → "grasping where there is no weapon."** *(2026-09-08, Pass E, `WORKLIST.md` T2-19 — the holding family.)* *(was: "gripping.")* 執 (*zhí*) is locked to *grasp* (`glossary/zhi-執.md`), and the four-beat 無 (*wú* — without) run — 行無行 · 攘無臂 · 扔無敵 · 執無兵 — now keeps one English per character across all four. 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) reads the line with the compound: 雖欲**執持**之，若無兵刃可持用也 — *"though you would grasp and hold it, there is no blade to hold and use."*
notes.7: **是以聖人後其身而身先 keeps *last / first*.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-11-19.)* *"Puts their body behind, and their body ends up ahead"* was proposed (`glossary/xian-hou-先後.md`), to give the move one pair of words with ch 66 and 67 and to drop the cadence of Matthew 20:16, *"the last shall be first."* The line keeps its snap, and the echo is a known cost, recorded so no later pass removes it as an oversight.
notes.70:
**是以不我知 → "do they not know me."** *(2026-10-19, Shalom's call, `glossary/wei-唯.md`. Was: "they do not know me.")* The 2026-08-24 note in `notes/translation.md` recorded this line with an inversion the verse never carried. After a fronted *only because*, English turns the next clause round, and without the turn the line drifts toward *merely because*. 夫唯 (*fú wéi* — "now, only") now reads *Only because…* in all nine lines of its frame.

**希 (*xī*) — the thread from ch 14.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-09-10 — `WORKLIST.md` T2-52.)* 知我者希 renders **希** as *few*. **Chapter 14 is where the book names this character**: 聽之不聞，名曰希, given there as *"its name is the inaudible."* The graph is 爻 (*yáo* — crossed threads) over 巾 (*jīn* — cloth), **loose-woven fabric you can see through** — one property, read across a crowd here and across a sound at ch 41's 大音希聲. **河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) ties this chapter's couplet to it directly**: 希，少也…故為貴也, *"希 means few… and that is why it is prized"* — scarcity is where the 貴 (*guì* — precious) of the next clause comes from. Ch 14 renders the meaning rather than the word for that chapter's legibility, so the link is carried here. Also ch 23, 43, 74.
notes.71:
**夫唯病病 → "Only because you are sick of the sickness are you not sick."** *(2026-10-19, Shalom's call, `glossary/wei-唯.md`.
